data.authors: Nicola Marchi1,3., Jeffrey J. Bazarian7., Vikram Puvenna1,2, Mattia Janigro4, Chaitali Ghosh1,2, Jianhui Zhong7, Tong Zhu7, Eric Blackman7, Desiree Stewart1, Jasmina Ellis1,5, Robert Butler6, Damir Janigro1,2,3,4*
data.core_methodology: ELISA for S100B measurement (Diasorin kit, 98 wells, anti-human S100B); reverse immunoassays for anti-S100B autoantibodies (Maxisorp ELISA 96-well plates coated with human S100B protein, 1 µg/well, calibration with monoclonal anti-S100B antibody, polynomial standard curve: y = 0.24420.92X +0.89 X2); Head Hit Index (HHI) questionnaire (score 0–6 derived from number of head collisions × overall severity); blinded game film review (4 cameras, two operators); computerized cognitive testing with ImPACT (concussion symptom inventory and six modules generating five composite scores); diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) on Siemens 3T Tim Trio (TR/TE = 10 s/89 ms, 2x2x2 mm voxel, 60 diffusion directions with b = 1200 s/mm², one average, b = 0 images with 10 averages); home-built software based on FSL for eddy-current and susceptibility corrections and tensor calculations; bootstrap sampling (250 samples) for empirical distributions of FA/MD; pair-wise permutation t-test (2500 permutations) using Randomise in FSL; cluster-based threshold (cluster size 10) for multiple-comparison correction; immunohistochemistry on porcine brain sections using human serum as primary antibody (dilutions 1:500, 1:1000, 1:5000); gel-filtration chromatography (Superdex 200 column, 40 mM EPPS pH 7.6, 3 mM DTT, 10% glycerol, 150 mM NaCl, 0.5 ml/min); Western blot (15% SDS-PAGE, PVDF membrane, player serum 1:5000, anti-human IgG 1:5000, ECL detection); mass spectrometry (LC-MS Finnigan LTQ-Orbitrap Elite, acetonitrile/0.1% formic acid gradient, 0.25 ml/min, data-dependent acquisition, NCBI database with human taxonomy filter); statistical analysis with OriginPro 8.5, JMP Pro 9.0, SAS; co-linearity tests; repeated measures backward elimination regression; one-way ANOVA; within-subjects factor ANOVA with Dunnett's correction; linear regression t-tests; significance threshold p < 0.05.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: S100B BBBD threshold: 0.12 ng/ml (shaded area in Figure 2); average S100Bpost-game – pre-game = 0.045 ± 0.05 ng/ml; average S100Bpost-game – baseline = 0.051 ± 0.05 ng/ml; P = 0.61 for comparison; specificity 0.875 for BBBD measured by albumin coefficient; sensitivity >0.90 for enhancement on MRI; HHI range 0–6; correlation S100Bpost-game – baseline vs HHI: R² = 0.51, p < 0.05; correlation total S100B increases vs anti-S100BAb: R² = 0.54, P < 0.01; impulse control vs auto-antibodies: p = 0.07, r = 0.58; DTI parameters: TR/TE = 10 s/89 ms, 2x2x2 mm voxel, 60 directions, b = 1200 s/mm², 1 average, b = 0 with 10 averages; bootstrap samples = 250; permutations = 2500; cluster size = 10; ELISA coating concentrations: 1 or 5 µg/well; standard curve polynomial: y = 0.24420.92X +0.89 X2 (y in mg/ml, x absorbance); significance threshold p < 0.05.

data.paper_title: Segmentation of Football Video Broadcast
data.authors: Sławomir Ma´ckowiak
data.core_methodology: Dominant color based segmentation technique for football playfield detection; 3D playfield modeling algorithm based on Hough transform; dedicated algorithm for player tracking; player detection system based on combination of Histogram of Oriented Gradients (HOG) descriptors with Principal Component Analysis (PCA) and linear Support Vector Machine (SVM) classification; shot classification using SVM, artificial neural network, and Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA); MPEG-7 dominant color descriptor (DCD); Euclidean distance to trained dominant color in IHS color space; Gaussian mixture model for hue value classification; Hough transform modifications: probabilistic Hough transform, Block Hough transform; random searching methods for line detection; edge detection approaches (Canny edge detector); LBG vector quantization algorithm for temporal consistency of quantized colors; derivative of Gaussian masks for gradient images (0°, 45°, 90°, 135°); centerline response computation; adaptive thresholding for centerline response; morphological closing, labeling, morphological thinning; linear regression for line parameter extraction; Hough transform voting with adaptive thresholding of accumulator; line tracking with lifetime and timeout counters; playfield model fitting using 4-point to 4-point correspondence and homography matrix; HOG descriptor parameters: window size 16×32 pixels, 8×8 blocks of 2×2 cells, block overlap 4 pixels, L2Hys normalization, 9-bin gradient histogram using maximum gradient of RGB channels, 756 numbers per descriptor; PCA-HOG descriptor with dimensionality reduction to 150, 175, 225 features for profile, frontal, vertical poses; three SVM classifiers for vertical frontal, vertical profile, and joint vertical poses; box aggregation using cost function incorporating overlap area and size; motion vector prediction for tracking; shot classification features: grass pixel ratio (GRn), edge pixel ratio (EDn), skin color pixel ratio; grid sizes from 3×3 to 10×10 blocks; semantic color ratio features; multi-layer perceptron neural network with one hidden layer, error back propagation; LDA with k-nearest neighbor classifier
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Precision = TP/(TP+FP); Recall = TP/(TP+FN); Overlap degree s0(a,b) = |a∩b|/|a∪b|; Threshold T from 0.4 to 0.9; δ = Σ_{n=4}^{9} [α·P(n/10) + β·(1-M(n/10))]; Three scenarios: (I) α=β=1/2, (II) α=1, β=0, (III) α=0, β=1; Classification error = number of false detected shots / all defined shots in the sequence; Grid sizes: 3×3 to 10×10 blocks; HOG descriptor: window 16×32, blocks 8×8, cells 2×2, overlap 4 pixels, L2Hys, 9 bins, 756 numbers; PCA-HOG features: 150 (profile), 175 (frontal), 225 (vertical); Logo detection: n=10, Canny weak/strong thresholds 0.1 and 0.3; Line detection gradient directions: 0°, 45°, 90°, 135°; Playfield model fitting: 4-point correspondence; Shot classification features: GRn = Σ B(w,h)/(Hn Wn), EDn = Σ E(w,h)/(Hn Wn); SVM optimal grid size >4×4; Average classification error >15%; Neural network: N inputs, M=4 outputs, one hidden layer; LDA projection to 3D space

data.paper_title: A Computer Vision Based Web Application for Tracking Soccer Players
data.authors: Jo˜ao Rodrigues1,2, Pedro J.S. Cardoso2, Tiago Vilas2, Bruno Silva3, Pedro Rodrigues2, Antonio Belguinha2, and Carlos Gomes2
data.core_methodology: Soccer pitch detection using HSV segmentation (H ∈[0%, 50%], S ∈[12%, 100%], V ∈[27%, 100%]), Canny edge detection, Hough transform; players and ball detection using morphological filters (dilation, erosion, 9×9 median filter), vertical mask, shape analysis (circular/oval vs vertical-rectangular), white color threshold (V ∈[75%, 100%]), blob size threshold (M × N/k, k = 100000); assignment of players to teams using average Hue values and middle threshold; perspective transformation (homography) for player positions with calibration using known pitch markings (center circle, penalty area, goal areas); tracking of players and ball using distance matching (in meters), Hue matching, trajectory prediction from previous 5 frames, circular search areas with increasing diameters, collision handling (junction of blobs, reassignment by Hue); game analysis: heat maps (incremental matrix HM normalized by maximum element), passes maps (ball distance threshold 3 meters, vectorial velocity and direction over 5 frames, probabilistic pass detection via significant change in velocity/direction), ball loss maps (passes log, distance threshold 2× player radius to distinguish dribbling vs passing loss).
data.key_metrics_and_variables: HSV thresholds: H ∈[0%, 50%], S ∈[12%, 100%], V ∈[27%, 100%] for pitch; V ∈[75%, 100%] for white detection; blob size threshold k = 100000 (M × N/k); player radius default = 3 meters for pass detection; ball loss distance threshold = 2 × player radius; heat map normalization: each entry divided by matrix maximum element; tracking uses previous 5 frames for trajectory; lost player search after 2 seconds (long frame set); cross-multiplication for mapping positions to heat map matrix.

data.paper_title: Real Time Quantification of Dangerousity in Football Using Spatiotemporal Tracking Data
data.authors: Daniel Link*, Steffen Lang, Philipp Seidenschwarz
data.core_methodology: Dangerousity (DA) is computed as the product of Zone (ZO) and a linear combination of Control (CO), Pressure (PR), and Density (DE) (Eq 1): DA(t) = ZO(t) * (1 - (CO(t) + PR(t) + DE(t))/k1). Zone is quantified on a 2x2 m grid starting 34 m from the goal line. Control is estimated via average relative speed (vrel) of ball and player over last 0.5 s using a quadratic function (Eq 2): CO(vrel) = 1 - k2 * vrel^2, with CO=0 for vrel > 25 ms^-1. Pressure is determined by defenders within a Pressure Zone (PZ) with four sub-areas (Head on, Lateral, Hind, High Pressure) based on angle α; individual defender pressure (Eq 3): PRDi(dDi, α) = 1 - dDi / rZO(α); total Pressure (Eq 4): PR(x) = 1 - e^{-k3 x} where x = sum of PRDi for defenders inside PZ. Density combines Shot Density (SD) and Pass Density (PD) weighted by Centrality C (Eq 5): DE(c) = C * SD + (1-C) * PD. Shot Density for a defender in Blocking Zone (Eq 6): SDDi(dD, dgoal) = 1 dD / (dD/dgoal) (as printed). Pass Density depends on Majority M (defenders minus attackers in Interception Zone) via arctan function (Eq 7): PD(M) = 0.5 + arctan(k5 M)/π. Derived metrics: Action Value (AV) (Eq 8): AV(IBAn) = DA(Start IBAn+1) - DA(Start IBAn). Performance (PE) over period ts via 5 s intervals (Eq 9): MP(ts) = sum_{i in ts} DAi. Dominance (DO) (Eq 10): DO(T1) = PE(T1) - PE(T2). Calibration optimizes model constants k1, k2, k3, k4, k5 manually using expert analysis of >100 match situations. Evaluation: reliability via ANOVA (F=170.31, p<.01) and Fleiss' kappa (κ=.32) on 100 scenarios rated by three experts; performance relevance via correlation with win probability from betting odds (13 bookmakers) for 64 Bundesliga 2014/15 matches.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Correlation coefficients (r) between performance indicators and win probability (WP): Goal difference (G) r=.55, Shots on Goal (SG) r=.58, Passing Accuracy (PA) r=.56, Tackling Rate (TR) r=.24, Ball Possession (BP) r=.71, Match Dominance (MD) r=.82. Inter-correlations: SG vs MD r=.83, BP vs MD r=.76, PA vs BP r=.93 (Table 1) / r=.92 (text). Reliability: ANOVA F=170.31, p<.01; Fleiss' kappa κ=.32. Thresholds: Zone grid starts 34 m from goal line; Control uses vrel over last 0.5 s, CO=0 for vrel>25 ms^-1; Performance intervals 5 s; Current Performance uses last 5 min. data.authors: Rahul Anand Sharma, Bharath Bhat, Vineet Gandhi, C.V.Jawahar
data.core_methodology: Semi-supervised dictionary generation: manually annotate 75 images with four point correspondences to compute homography H1, then simulate pan, tilt, zoom to generate a dictionary D = {Ij, Hj} of N ≈ 100K synthetic edge maps and homography pairs. Nearest neighbour search over dictionary using three approaches: (1) Chamfer matching with distance transform T(.) and chamfer distance j* = argmin_j T(x)·Ij / ||Ij||_1; (2) HOG features with Euclidean distance j* = argmin_j ||φh(x) - φh(Ij)||_2; (3) CNN features (AlexNet and SketchNet) with Euclidean distance j* = argmin_j ||φc(x) - φc(Ij)||_2. Camera stabilization via convex optimization over projected plane parameters Pt = {cxt, cyt, θt, φt, r1t, r2t} minimizing Ec = Σ_t (P*_t - Pt)^2 + λ1 Σ_t ||P*_{t+1} - P*_t||_1 + λ2 Σ_t ||P*_{t+2} - 2P*_{t+1} + P*_t||_1 + λ3 Σ_t ||P*_{t+3} - 3P*_{t+2} + 3P*_{t+1} - P*_t||_1, solved with CVX. data.authors: David Card, Gordon Dahl
data.core_methodology: Poisson regression framework with municipality fixed effects, time-varying controls (year, week, holiday dummies, weather variables, Nielsen television ratings), and a function of the Las Vegas point spread and game outcome. The model uses National Incident Based Reporting System (NIBRS) data on police-reported intimate partner violence and NFL game data. Games are classified by pre-game point spread into predicted win (spread < -3), predicted close (-3 ≤ spread ≤ 3), and predicted loss (spread > 3). Upset loss (loss when predicted win) and upset win (win when predicted loss) are key variables. A simple behavioral model with gain-loss utility and a rational reference point (Koszegi and Rabin, 2006) is specified, where the probability of losing control h = h0 - μ(y-p) with μ(y-p) = α(y-p) for y-p<0 and β(y-p) for y-p>0, and loss aversion implies α > β. Robustness checks include Negative Binomial model, alternative missing data treatments, date fixed effects, and subsamples by agency size and offender age.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Baseline upset loss coefficient (Loss * Predicted Win): 0.080 (8% increase in at-home male-on-female IPV) (Table 4, col. 3). Close loss coefficient: 0.036. Timing effects: 1 PM games upset loss 0.142 in 3-6 PM window; 4 PM games upset loss 0.347 in 6-9 PM window (Table 5). Salient games: playoff contention upset loss 0.102; rivalry upset loss 0.138; frustrating games (sacks≥4, turnovers≥4, penalties>80 yds) upset loss 0.152; highly salient (playoff contention and rivalry or frustrating) upset loss 0.154 (Table 6). Alcohol involved upset loss 0.127; minor assault 0.096; serious assault 0.063 (Table 7). Away from home upset loss -0.114; total male-on-female 0.049; female-on-male 0.0162; spouse 0.126; girlfriend 0.075 (Table 8). Robustness: treat missings as zeros 0.078; subsample no missings 0.067; smaller agencies (pop<50K) 0.096; larger agencies (pop≥50K) 0.070; negative binomial 0.084; date fixed effects 0.074; younger offenders (age<30) 0.097; older offenders (age≥30) 0.075; non-IP family violence 0.002; non-IP friend violence 0.077 (Appendix Table). Nielsen ratings: average 24.2% of households watch, max 47.9%; audience size falls by 0.38 percentage points per one-point increase in spread. Holiday effects: Christmas +17%, Thanksgiving +22%, Memorial Day +30%, New Year's Day +19%, New Year's Eve +32%, Fourth of July +28%. Hot day effect: 8-10% increase when max temperature >80°F. Behavioral model equations: (1) h = h0 - μ(y-p), μ(y-p) = α(y-p) for y-p<0, = β(y-p) for y-p>0; (2) hL = h0 + αp, hW = h0 - β(1-p); (3) G(p;q) = p uW + (1-p) uL - u0 - (α-β)p(1-p)qv; (4) q*(p) = [p uW + (1-p) uL - u0] / [(α-β)p(1-p)v]; (5) Δ(risk|p) = [β + (α-β)p] ∫_0^{q*(p)} q dF(q).

data.paper_title: Sports Field Recognition Using Deep Multi-task Learning
data.authors: Shuhei Tarashima
data.core_methodology: SFLNet (single shot regressor) trained in an end-to-end multi-task learning framework combining (A) Semantic Segmentation Module based on 50-layer ResNet pretrained on ImageNet with Context Encoding module [12] and Joint Pyramid Upsampling module [25], (B) Parameter Regression Module as a tiny CNN with architecture C36-C48-C60-F8 (Ck: Convolution-BatchNorm-Relu-Maxpool block with k filters, Fk: fc layer with k neurons) regressing an 8-dimensional parameter vector p = [p1, p2, p3, p4, p5, p6, p7, p8]^T related to homography H ∈ R3×3 via H = [[p1+1, p2, p3], [p4, p5+1, p6], [p7, p8, 1]] (Equation 1), (C) Label Adjacency Prediction (LAP) Module implemented as a fully connected layer with sigmoid activation taking encoded feature from Context Encoding layer, predicting adjacencies of label pairs (output dimension Nlabel(Nlabel+1)/2). Training uses semi-automatically built dataset from human annotated point-to-point correspondences via Direct Linear Transform (DLT) algorithm [13] and person segmentation [30]. Loss function LD(Θ) = Σ τ(pi, p*i) + wφ Σ φ(Bi, B*i) + wψ Σ ψ(ai, a*i) (Equation 2) with τ as L1 loss, φ as per-pixel cross-entropy, ψ as binary cross-entropy, wφ=1.0, wψ=0.2. Two-step optimization: first train segmentation and LAP modules, then whole model. Implemented in PyTorch with SGD optimizer (momentum 0.9), input frames scaled to 448×448, mini-batch size 16, 50 epochs per step.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Jp (IoU between predicted court and metric model), JB (IoU for semantic segmentation), Ja (IoU for label adjacency prediction), JB→a (IoU between segmentation-derived adjacency and ground truth). data.paper_title: Multi-Object Tracking in Aerial and Satellite Imagery
data.authors: Maximilian Kraus
data.core_methodology: AerialMPTNet, a regression-based deep neural network fusing appearance features by a Siamese Neural Network (SNN) with movement prediction of a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) and adjacent graphical features of a Graph Convolutional Neural Network (GraphCNN). The network encodes motion model and adjacent neighbor modeling in an end-to-end fashion. It uses Squeeze-and-Excitation (SE) layers and Online Hard Example Mining (OHEM). The SNN consists of five 2D convolutions, two local response normalization, and three max-pooling layers. The LSTM module consists of two bidirectional LSTM layers with hidden size 64 and dropout p=0.5. The GraphCNN module consists of three 1D convolution layers with 1x1 kernels and output channels 32, 64, 128. The adjacency graph uses eight closest neighbors within 7.5 m. Training uses SGD optimizer with initial learning rate 10^-6, L1 loss, mini-batch size 150, context factor 4 for pedestrians and 3 for vehicles.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: MOTA = 1 − ∑t(FNt + FPt + IDt) / ∑t GTt; MOTP = ∑t,i dt,i / ∑t ct; MOTAL = 1 − ∑t(FNt + FPt + log10(IDt + 1)) / ∑t GTt; FAR = ∑FPt / f; Rcll = ∑TPt / ∑(TPt + FNt); Prcn = ∑TPt / ∑(TPt + FPt). Key results: On KIT AIS pedestrian dataset, AerialMPTNet achieves MOTA -16.2 and MOTP 69.6; on AerialMPT dataset, MOTA -23.4 and MOTP 69.7; on KIT AIS vehicle dataset, MOTA 42.0 and MOTP 76.3. Compared to SMSOT-CNN baseline, MOTA improves by 18.8 points to -16.2 and by 13.8 points to -23.4 on KIT AIS pedestrian and AerialMPT respectively. Other metrics: IDF1, IDP, IDR, GT, MT%, PT%, ML%, FP, FN, ID, FM. Hyperparameters: learning rate 10^-6, batch size 150, context factor 4 (pedestrian) and 3 (vehicle), neighbor distance 7.5 m, eight neighbors, LSTM hidden size 64, dropout 0.5, GraphCNN channels 32, 64, 128.

data.paper_title: Homography Estimation for Camera Calibration in Complex Topological Scenes
data.authors: Giacomo D’Amicantonio, Egor Bondarau, Peter H.N. De With

4,500 homographies for the World Cup 2014 dataset; 200k homographies for intersections; 3,000, 500 and 1,000 images for the training set, test set and dictionary; 3000, 500 and 1000 samples; dictionary contains only 0.5% of the total homographies; α, β=0.3; N=16; Table III warmup schedule and parameters setting for end-to-end training of the complete model: UNet ≤20 η=1 τ=0 γ=0, Siamese 20-40 η=0 τ=1 γ=0, End-to-end ≥40 η=0.05 τ=0.05 γ=0.9; warm up the UNet and the Siamese network for 20 epochs each; data.paper_title: Automatic event detection in football using tracking data
data.authors: Ferran Vidal‑Codina, Nicolas Evans, Bahaeddine El Fakir, Johsan Billingham
data.core_methodology: Deterministic decision tree-based algorithm using 2D player and ball tracking data, with two steps: (1) a possession step evaluating which player was in possession of the ball at each frame using possession zone (PZ), a circular area of radius Rpz around every player, and duel zone (DZ), a circular area of radius Rdz ≥ Rpz around the ball; control frames; possession losses and gains via hyperparameters εs, εθ, εv; Savitzky-Golay filter [55] using a second-order polynomial and a window of seven frames around each datapoint; set piece triggers; (2) an event detection step combining changes in ball possession with the Laws of the Game [54] to determine in-game events and set pieces, including shot-save decision trees; no learning involved.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Tracking data sampled at 25 Hz; a football match at 25 Hz contains roughly 3 million tracking data points, compared to 3K events; tagging differences 10–15%; PZ radii: 50 cm for provider A and 1 m for both provider B and provider C; Rdz = 1m for all providers; Savitzky-Golay window of seven frames corresponds to neighboring 0.25 s; possession loss condition Δsf above εs; possession gain conditions d0_f0 · d1_fn < εθ and {||v0_fi − v1_fi|| > εv}i=0n on at least one frame; penalty kick trigger uses εp2/4 in front to 3εp2/4 behind the active penalty mark and 9.15 m from the penalty mark with tolerance εp3; set piece tolerances εk1, εk2, εp1, εc, εt; shot on/off target distinction with a 0.25 m tolerance beyond the goalposts; +90% detection rate in most event categories; pass precision and recall supra 90%; shot precision 78 vs recall 53; 70% of the 254 misclassifications; 15% of shots (compared to less than 6% of passes) either not detected or attributed to another player; 569 cross misclassifications; over 30K open play passing instances; six goalscorer mistakes and two last-minute goal events; six goalscoring mistakes broken down as ball goes missing after the assist was made (3) and data reflects an inaccurate situation (3); 1 CPUs and 4 GB of RAM; mean computational wall time three minutes for a 90 minute match; annotated event times more than 10 s before/after they occurred.

data.paper_title: Reducing video verification burden: machine learning classification of head acceleration events in youth football
data.authors: A. Giovanny A. Romero, Josh Cherian, N. Stewart Pritchard, Joel D. Stitzel, Lyndia C. Wu, Jillian E. Urban, Ryan S. McGinnis
data.core_methodology: Machine learning pipeline for binary classification of sensor-triggered head acceleration events (HAEs) using 267 distinct features from linear acceleration (g) and rotational velocity (rad/s) signals, including all three axes and resultant vectors. Features included time-domain, frequency-domain, time-frequency, nonlinear, and biomechanical risk metrics. Biomechanical risk metrics: linear risk (LR), rotational risk (RR), combined probability of concussion (CP), youth combined probability of concussion (CPyouth), and Diffuse Axonal, Multi-Axis, General Evaluation (DAMAGE) via a second-order system approach. Frequency-domain: amplitude spectral density (ASD) in decibels from resultant linear acceleration and angular velocity using a fast Fourier transform (FFT), sampled every 50 Hz up to Nyquist 1600 Hz. Time-frequency: continuous wavelet transform (CWT) for resultant linear acceleration and rotational velocity, frequency range segmented into 200 Hz bands up to Nyquist. Time-domain: peak-based features, zero crossings and zero-crossing rate, maximum absolute first difference, area under the curve, sample entropy, 5th/50th/95th percentiles, time to first peak, average absolute slope, slopes in short windows around the main peak, segment-specific areas under the curve in ten equal segments, Higuchi fractal dimension up to 10 scale levels, and second derivative inflection points. Algorithms explored: K-Dimensional (KD) tree, logistic regression, random forest, Support Vector Machine (SVM), decision tree, K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), binary Kernel classification, and eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost). Model evaluation used 5-fold stratified group cross-validation with participant-level folds, random shuffling within each fold, feature standardization fit on training data only, and class-weighting factor computed from training labels. XGBoost used tree-based gradient boosting for binary classification with maximum tree depth 10, learning rate 0.2, 80% row and feature subsampling per tree, maximum delta step 1, log-loss evaluation metric, positive class weighted by ratio of negative to positive training samples, and early stopping after 100 rounds without improvement. Model complexity chosen through 5-fold internal cross-validation. Permutation testing randomly shuffled training labels while keeping feature matrix, test labels, model hyperparameters, and class-imbalance weighting fixed; model retrained on permuted training data and performance recomputed on held-out test set. Feature evaluation added features sequentially by XGBoost importance, using 70% training and 30% testing with a stratified group split. Post-hoc threshold-based analysis selected impacts with resultant linear acceleration greater than specified thresholds defined by percentiles from 5th to 95th in 5-percentile increments. Time-savings analysis assumed average 30 s of video review per impact and applied a symmetric window around the conventional classification threshold of 0.5. Simulation-based sensitivity analysis randomly removed the corresponding proportion of true impacts for prespecified false negative rates across 1,000 simulation repetitions and recalculated total DAMAGE and CP; bias defined as (reduced-data value − full-data benchmark)/full-data benchmark × 100. Implemented in Python 3.12.7 using scikit-learn 1.5.1 and XGBoost 2.1.1.

Features: 267 distinct features; ASD sampled every 50 Hz up to Nyquist 1600 Hz; CWT segmented into 200 Hz bands; Higuchi fractal dimension up to 10 scale levels; quantiles 5th, 50th, 95th; ten equal segments. XGBoost cross-validation: F1-score 0.765 ± 0.005, recall 0.713 ± 0.006, precision 0.825 ± 0.005, AUC 0.931 ± 0.004. Abstract: F1-score = 0.765, recall = 0.713, precision = 0.825, AUC = 0.931. Time-savings: average 30 s video review per impact; reviewing only model-flagged events reduced estimated video review time from approximately 90 h to under 8 h; thresholds in 10–15 g range reduced review time by more than half while missed impacts approximately 2.5–3% of all impacts. data.core_methodology: R package nflscrapR; multinomial logistic regression for expected points; generalized additive model (GAM) for win probability; nﬂWAR framework using multilevel models (varying-intercepts, random-effects, or mixed-effects models) fit using penalized likelihood via the lme4 package; Normal distributions for group intercepts and play values; leave-one-season-out cross-validation (LOSO CV) with calibration testing; drive resampling approach with 1000 simulated seasons; linear regression approach for conversion from points to wins; play values δ f,i as expected points added (EPA) or win probability added (WPA).
data.key_metrics_and_variables: 304,896 non-PAT plays; seven scoring events: touchdown (7 points), field goal (3 points), safety (2 points), no score (0 points), opponent safety (-2 points), opponent field goal (-3 points), opponent touchdown (-7 points); two-point success rate 47.35% from 2009-2016, EP = 2 · 0.4735 = 0.9470; 16,906 extra point and field goal attempts from 2009-2016; field goal miss adjustments eight yards and 5.07 seconds; EP model LOSO CV calibration e ≈0.013; ordinal logistic regression e ≈0.022; average length of time for incomplete passing plays 5.7 seconds; Philly special V i ≈2.78, EPA ≈7 −2.78 = 4.22, WPA ≈0.1266; replacement level counts for 2017: rushing 52 of the 148 RBs, 278 of the 310 of the WR/TEs, receiving 52 of the 148 RBs, 73 of the 201 WRs, 45 of the 109 TEs; QB replacement: 25 replacement level QBs with ten percent cutoff, 39 replacement level QBs out of the 71 in total with one QB for each team; 1000 simulated seasons; Kamara leads Hunt in nearly 71% of simulated seasons; autocorrelation QB WAR 0.598, Passer Rating 0.478, ANY/A 0.295; autocorrelation RB WAR 0.431, Success Rate 0.314, Yards per Attempt 0.337; NFL level counts: rushing RBs = 32·3 = 96 RBs, rushing WR/TEs = 32·1 = 32 WR/TEs, receiving RBs = 32·3 = 96 RBs, receiving WRs = 32·4 = 128 WRs, receiving TEs = 32·2 = 64 TEs; EP = E[Y|X] = ∑ y y·P(Y = y|X); δ f,i = V f −V i; Winst = β0 +βSSt +εt, where εt ∼N(0,σ2) (iid).

data.paper_title: Forecasting extremes of football players’ performance in matches
data.authors: Michał Nowak, Bartosz Bok, Artur Wilczek, Łukasz Oleksy, Mariusz Kamola
data.core_methodology: Simple linear or piecewise linear predictive models; linear multivariate model yhat = a0 + a^T x with a ≥0, x ≥0; piecewise linear model where two linear regression tasks are solved simultaneously to fit two line segments so that mean square error of the predicted value is minimized; APX-Ind, APX-Grp, APX-Ind2, APX-Grp2; pre-match metrics aggregation transformations T and M with xd = T(s : d −H ≤ t < d), yd = M(s : t = d); weighted aggregation procedure T with value decay αk: xid = (Σ_{k=1...4} αk qn)/(Σ_{k=1...4} αk); Mutual Information method for selection of non-redundant model inputs with correlation threshold 0.99; standard scaling procedure: x′ij = (xij − xbar_j)/σ_j, y′ij = (yij − ybar_j)/ς_j; GPS-Cnt base GPS model using S(tmin, vmin, d, H) = {Si} where Si = {(t, v) : d −H ≤ t < d, v ≥ vmin} and max_{Si} t − min_{Si} t ≥ tmin, xd = ||S(tmin, vmin, d, H)||; GPS-Time (value of tmin corresponding to p-th percentile of samples for a given vmin); GPS-Vel (value of vmin corresponding to p-th percentile of samples for a given tmin); GPS-X cross-checking (tmin, vmin) against (t′min, v′min) with yd = ||S(t′min, v′min, d + 1, 1)||; complementary cumulative distribution function (ccdf); Apex Pro Series metrics and raw GPS traces aggregation.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Data: January to June 2023; average 9000 records per month; 29 professional players reserve teams (5 goalkeepers, 8 defenders, 14 midfielders, 2 forwards); mean age 18.3 ± 3.3 years; mean height 185 ± 5.4 cm; mean weight 78.2 ± 2.7 kg; standard workweek 5 training units, 1 match (MD), 1 day off; GPS sampling 10 Hz position and 100 Hz instantaneous acceleration; τ = 0.1 s; cutout value 6 m/s2; 94 isolated measurements; 536 elements derived from 94 general metrics; correlation threshold 0.99; 4-week macrocycle; α values 0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9; H = 14, 21, 28 days; p ∈ {.5, .75, .9, .95, .98, .99, .999}; 3 min sliding window; 3-week training period before match day on 2023-05-06. Equations: s = (t, t + τ, A, q); yhat = a0 + a^T x; xd = T(s : d −H ≤ t < d); yd = M(s : t = d); xid = (Σ_{k=1...4} αk qn)/(Σ_{k=1...4} αk); x′ij = (xij − xbar_j)/σ_j; y′ij = (yij − ybar_j)/ς_j; s = (t, v); S(tmin, vmin, d, H) = {Si} where Si = {(t, v) : d −H ≤ t < d, v ≥ vmin} and max_{Si} t − min_{Si} t ≥ tmin; xd = ||S(tmin, vmin, d, H)||; yd = ||S(t′min, v′min, d + 1, 1)||. Named metrics/variables: Total Loading; Total Acceleration/Deceleration; Metabolic Time; HML Distance; HML Time; Distance Zone; Metabolic Time Zone 5 and 6 Per Distance; Decelarations Total Distance in Zone 5 and 6 Per Distance; Speed Intensity Zone 6 (Relative) Per Distance; Accelerations Total Time Per Distance in Zone 6 (s/m); Distance in Zone 6 (m); HML Efforts Max Speed; High Metabolic Load Distance (HMLD). Results: base APX-Ind player A1 α=0.5 MAPE 2.3%, R2 0.52; piecewise linear MAPE 1.9%; APX-Ind2 extra input Speed Intensity Zone 6 (Relative) Per Distance, MAPE reduced by 0.1 pp to 2.2%, R2 improved by 0.051 to 0.571; APX-Grp2 MAPE reduced marginally to 2.2% for player A1; other linear models reach MAPE as small as 0.8%; Total Acceleration Loading Per Distance and Total Loading Per Distance output models have error 2.3% due to almost flat regression line; player A2 previous-match model α=0.1 R2 0.84 with input Accelerations Total Time Per Distance in Zone 6 (s/m) and output Distance in Zone 6 (m); Table 1 MAPE values: APX-Ind A1 α=0.1 2.7, α=0.3 2.3, α=0.5 2.3, α=0.7 2.3, α=0.9 2.1; APX-Grp A1 2.6,2.3,2.3,2.2,2.1; A2 17.5,17.5,17.5,17.4,17.3; A3 2.1,2.3,2.6,2.8,3.1; A4 12.2,12.3,12.1,11.8,11.5; APX-Ind2 A1 2.2,2.2,2.2,2.2,2.2; APX-Grp2 A1 2.3,2.1,2.2,2.4,2.7; Table 2 GPS models: GPS-Cnt R2 H=14 0.77, H=21 0.36, H=28 0.30; MAPE H=14 0.10, H=21 0.07, H=28 0.14; GPS-Time R2 0.56,0.32,0.22; MAPE 0.16,0.11,0.11; GPS-Vel R2 0.53,0.45,0.37; MAPE 0.14,0.09,0.12; GPS-X R2 0.45,0.35,0.31; MAPE 0.15,0.15,0.15; GPS-Cnt best H=14 R2=0.77 for vmin=5.75 m/s and tmin=10 s; MAPE calculated for last 20% of available samples; best prediction quality for intervals of much smaller vmax ≈4m/s; GPS-Time highest R2 for maximal interval time at speed of 6 m/s; GPS-Vel best R2 and MAPE parameters within tmax from 12 to 17 s and percentile of vmax from 0.75 to 0.95; GPS-X shift: extreme training intervals correlate with match intervals less intense by 0.7 m/s and by 3 s; results setting: players age 17 to 21, spring 2023, 10 to 16 matches per player, 75% training and rest verification, training data correlation measured with R2 score, predictive quality scored with mean absolute prediction error (MAPE).

data.paper_title: The outcome prediction method of football matches by the quantum neural network based on deep learning
data.authors: Yang Sun, Hongyang Chu
data.core_methodology: Deep learning (DL)-based quantum neural network (QNN) model; multilayer perceptron model consisting of an input layer, multiple hidden layers, and an output layer; quantum bits (qubits); superposition and entanglement; Quantum State Input Module; quantum neuron units (QNEs); quantum weights; quantum activation function f Q; gradient descent; mean square error; cross-entropy loss function; quantum algorithms integrated to continuously adjust network weights; Pennylane library; algorithm design for optimizing a two-layer neural network using qubits; feedforward mechanism; quantum gate operations; quantum measurement operations and post-processing; reverse quantum encoding and data scaling operations; Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) for data augmentation; adaptive dynamic adjustment module based on an attention mechanism; quantum error correction techniques; comparison models: Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), Long-Short Term Memory (LSTM), Back Propagation Neural Network (BPNN), Transformer, Convolutional Recurrent Neural Network (CRNN), and Connectionist Temporal Classification (CTC).
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Equations: y = f Q(∑_{i=1}^{n} xi ⊗ wi) (1); E = 1/2 ∑j(yj − tj)^2 (2); wi = wi − α ∂E/∂wi (3); y = f Q(∑_{i=1}^{7} xi ⊗ wi) (4); E = −∑_{k∈{win,draw,lose}} tk log(yk) (5). Variables: input vector x = (x1, x2, ..., xn); quantum weight vector w = (w1, w2, ..., wn); quantum activation function f Q; learning rate α; predicted and real output yj and tj; one-hot encoding tk; predicted probability yk; x1 Team A’s recent goals; x2 Team A’s recent goals conceded; x3 Team B’s recent goals; x4 Team B’s recent goals conceded; x5 number of wins of Team A in historical meetings between the two teams; x6 number of draws for Team A in historical meetings between the two teams; x7 number of losses for Team A in all-time meetings between the two teams; quantum weight vector w = (w1, w2, ..., w7). Performance: accuracy improvement over 22.3%; precision improvement over 20.5%, up to about 38%; recall improvement over 23.2%, maximum approximately 40%; F1 score increase over 21.8%, maximum approximately 36%. European Championship championship probabilities: Spain 31.72%, France 27.61%, England 22.58%, Netherlands 18.09%. Table 1 values (mean probability of winning championship %, average goals scored per game, average standard deviation of goals scored per game, lower limit of 95% confidence interval for average goals scored per game, upper limit of 95% confidence interval for average goals scored per game, average goals conceded per game, average standard deviation of goals conceded per game, lower limit of 95% confidence interval for average goals conceded per game, upper limit of 95% confidence interval for average goals conceded per game): Spain 31.72, 2.1, 0.3, 1.5, 2.7, 0.8, 0.2, 0.4, 1.2; France 27.61, 2.3, 0.4, 1.5, 3.1, 1.0, 0.3, 0.4, 1.6; England 22.58, 1.8, 0.2, 1.4, 2.2, 0.6, 0.1, 0.4, 0.8; Netherlands 18.09, 1.9, 0.3, 1.3, 2.5, 0.7, 0.2, 0.3, 1.1. Datasets: International Football Match Outcome (1872–2020) dataset covers 41,586 international football match outcomes; Football Match dataset encompasses 9,074 matches from the top five European leagues across the 2011/2012 to 2016/2017 seasons, totaling 941,009 events; detailed match records from 2008 to 2022 of major European football leagues from the Kaggle public dataset 'European Football Database'.

data.paper_title: Soccer line mark segmentation and classiﬁcation with stochastic watershed transform

data.paper_title: CHASING THE 'BIG-TIME' Football Apprenticeship in the 1990s
data.authors: Andrew Parker
data.core_methodology: qualitative study of Youth Training (YT); case-study analysis of one professional English Football League club; methods of sociological enquiry traditionally associated with ethnography (i.e. participant observation, unstructured interviews, and documentary analysis); tape-recorded interviews; detailed fieldwork diary
data.key_metrics_and_variables: youth team squad of twenty players; professional playing staff of approximately thirty-five; eight were first year Youth Trainees; eleven were second year Youth Trainees; one individual, although officially recognised as a full-time professional player, was eligible for youth team selection on account of his birth-date; All first year trainees were between the ages of sixteen and seventeen; were all between the ages of seventeen and nineteen; research period which lasted the full duration of the 1993/4 season - from early July 1993 until May 1994; attended the club for three days each week as a participant observer, spending two days training, working and socializing with trainees, and one day at a local college of Further Education as a fellow student; After the initial three months of participant observation I began to conduct interviews; collective requests of seven second year boys; first years received £31.50 per week with no charge for food or lodgings at the club's residential hostel; Trainees aged seventeen received £160 per week with £225 per month being deducted to cover accommodation fees; Those aged eighteen and over received £200 per week with corresponding monthly deductions; paid in three equal instalments during the course of the trainee period; ranged from £1,600 to £4,000 per trainee; First year trainees reported to the ground for 9.00am, whilst second years arrived at 9.30am; breakfast was available at the club hostel between 8.00am and 9.30am; lived within forty-five minutes drive/bus-ride of the club; 5 minute walk, (or, more often than not, a two minute run); All full-time professionals ('pro's') were required to arrive at the club between 9.45am and 10.30am; Morning training sessions for trainees usually took place between 10.30am and 12.00 noon; afternoon training sessions between 2.00pm and 4.00pm were only the norm during the month of pre-season training; second years were free to leave the club from 1.30pm onwards; first year boys were usually free to leave the club by around 4.00pm; Dinner was served at the trainee hostel at 4.45pm; All trainees had to return to club residence by 10.30pm (10.00pm the night before match-days) and had to be in their own rooms with lights out by 11.00pm; provided at around 8.00pm; weighed prior to training every Friday morning; vocational progress of trainees was chartered every four weeks; during the introductory season of the football apprenticeship scheme (1960/61) English league clubs registered only 220 apprentices against 3022 professionals (or 1 apprentice for every 14 senior players); by 1966/67 apprentice registrations had risen to 592 whilst the number of professionals had fallen by around one-fifth to 2395 (a ratio of 1 in 4); three-fold rise in young player recruitment from approximately 200 to over 600 individuals per year; one-in-ten; for every ten young players recruited at the age of sixteen it is generally assumed that only one will remain in football until the age of twenty-one; prior to the introduction of the Youth Training Scheme within football 50% of players failed to secure professional contracts at the end of their apprenticeships, and that of those that were successful, a further 50% found themselves discarded from the professional game within six years; 60% of trainees do receive professional contracts at the end of their YT experience, of these offers approximately half are for a further one year only; 75% of the professional players sampled during the course of his research said that managerial criticism 'drove them to action'; a further 91% expressed a preference for managers exhibiting 'dominating personality' traits; 89% also admitted that they played better when praised by those in positions of authority; ninety-nine percent of footballers; 15 young players as opposed to the 12 allowed previously; boys to join clubs at the age of 15; boys as young as 13 to attend clubs; under the age of 17 as practising professionals; from the age of 17; data.paper_title: Predicting player skills and optimizing tactical decisions in football data analysis using machine learning methods
data.authors: Akmaral Kassymova1, Tolegen Aibatullin1, Shynar Yelezhanova2, Assem Konyrkhanova3, Ainur Mukhanbetkaliyeva3, Assemgul Tynykulova4, Ulzhan Makhazhanova5, Gulmira Azieva5
data.core_methodology: Deep neural networks; convolutional neural networks (CNNs); long short-term memory (LSTM) networks; recurrent neural network (RNN); gradient boosting machines (GBM); eXtreme gradient boosting (XGBoost); random forest (RF); K-means clustering; logistic regression; valuing actions by estimating probabilities (VAEP); two separate XGBoost classifiers for ∆Pgoal and ∆Pagainst; tactical decision optimization framework with player ranking, substitution rule, and formation shift rule; simulated match scenarios using substitution and formation-shift rules; stratified sampling method; 5-fold cross-validation; Z-score normalization; One-Hot Encoding; Adam optimizer; dropout; L2-regularization; early stopping; grid search; ANOVA; McNemar’s tests; binary classification models; unsupervised clustering with supervised classification; modular decision-support pipeline; lightweight tactical recommendation engine; softmax output; rectified linear unit (ReLU) activation; max-pooling; convolutional layers; dense layers.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Dataset: over 150,000 professional match actions; approximately 1,200 matches; 3,800 unique players; six full seasons (2017/18–2022/23); aged 18 to 37; 28% defenders, 42% midfielders, and 30% forwards; on average 1,800 events per match across more than 600 competitions. Split: 70% training and 30% testing; 5-fold cross-validation. CNN: three convolutional layers (64, 128, and 256 filters, kernel size 3×3); max-pooling (2×2); two dense layers with 128 and 64 units; Dropout (rate=0.5); L2-regularization (λ=0.01); Adam optimizer with a learning rate of 0.001 for 50 epochs and batch size of 64. LSTM: two layers with 128 and 64 memory units; dropout (0.3) and recurrent dropout (0.2); Early stopping with a patience of 10 epochs. XGBoost: 500 trees, maximum depth of 6, learning rate 0.05, and subsample ratio of 0.8; λ=1 and α=0.1. Equations: VAEP(a) = ∆Pgoal(a) − ∆Pagainst(a); z_i,j = Σ_{m=1}^{M} Σ_{n=1}^{N} x_{i+m,j+n} w_{m,n} + b; f_t = σ(W_f∗[h_{t−1}, x_t] + b_f); i_t = σ(W_i∗[h_{t−1}, x_t] + b_i); o_t = σ[h_{t−1}, x_t] + b_0; L = Σ_{i=1}^{n} l(y_i, ŷ_i) + Σ_{k=1}^{K} Ω(f_k); Contribution(i) = VAEP(i) − α·Fatigue(i). Decision rules: if Contribution(i) < θ and Fatigue(i) > β, then substitution of player i is recommended; if opponent pressing intensity exceeds a predefined threshold γ, a tactical adjustment is triggered (e.g., shifting from 4-4-2 to 4-2-3-1). Features: passing accuracy = successful passes/total passes; dribbling efficiency = successful dribbles/attempts; defensive contribution = successful tackles+interceptions per match; fatigue index = ratio of high-intensity sprints to playing time; biometric variables aggregated using mean, maximum, and variability per match. Metrics: CNN precision 0.91, recall 0.88, ROC-AUC 0.94, F1-metric 0.89; GB lowest recall (0.83); XGBoost injury prediction precision 0.89, recall 0.85, F1-score 0.87, ROC-AUC 0.92; logistic regression precision 0.84, recall 0.79, F1-score 0.81, ROC-AUC 0.87; VAEP scores +1.8 to +3.0; Player 3: 40 actions, 33 successful, VAEP +3.0; Player 1: 35 actions, 28 successful, VAEP +2.5; Player 2: 22 actions, 17 successful, VAEP +1.8; optimized substitutions improved predicted win probability by an average of +6.5% compared to the baseline (p<0.05); tactical formation shifts increased possession efficiency by 4.2%; average expert rating 4.3 on a 5-point Likert scale; ANOVA p<0.01; McNemar’s tests p-values<0.05.

data.paper_title: BroadTrack: Broadcast Camera Tracking for Soccer
data.authors: Floriane Magera1,2, Thomas Hoyoux1, Olivier Barnich1, Marc Van Droogenbroeck2
data.core_methodology: Pinhole model with calibration matrix K = [[f,0,px],[0,f,py],[0,0,1]]; broadcast pixels are squares so focal length is the same for both axes and skew ignored; principal point at image center so intrinsic parameters reduce to f. Camera pose modeled by focal point position C = (Cx, Cy, Cz) and rotation matrix R parameterized by pan ϕ, tilt θ, and roll γ in Euler angles convention R = Rz(γ)Rx(θ)Rz(ϕ); projection matrix P = KR[I −C]. Brown-Conrady radial distortion model with L(r) = 1 + k1r2 and x = f L(r)x + p; unknown camera parameters κ : {f, k1, ϕ, θ, γ, Cx, Cy, Cz}; projection function πκ : X → x. Pan-tilt head and tripod model: pan and tilt rotation axes intersect in a point T fixed during the game; point O on the camera optical axis remains at fixed distance δ of T; O = T −δr2; focal point C = T −δr2+λr3; {T, δ} fixed over time while λ varies with camera view. Tracking system: sports field detection with semantic classes S, soccer field template F : S → E, projection πκ(F); keypoint detector of Gutiérrez-Pérez and Agudo; semantic field markings detector of Theiner and Ewerth; mean shift algorithm to fit points. Optical flow with pyramidal version of Lucas-Kanade’s algorithm. Update through non-linear optimization minimizing L = LF + LOF + ωLT, with LF = sum over c∈S* sum i=0 to Nc ρ(min over p∈πκ(F(c)) ||p − xi_c||2), LOF = sum i=0 to No ρ(||πκ(Xi_t−1) − xi_t||2), LT = δ − ||O* − T||2, O* = C + ⟨(T −C), r3⟩r3 / ||r3||2 2, ρ(.) is Cauchy loss, optimized with Levenberg-Marquardt. Online confidence evaluation with Jaccard index s = |B ∩ πκ(F)| / |B ∪ πκ(F)|. Reinitialization algorithm using two point correspondences, estimating focal length, pan, and tilt; focal point set to tripod rotation center and roll set to zero; focal length estimated with equations originally derived by Gedikli and summarized in Appendix 6.1 of [9]; pan and tilt iteratively refined with dϕ = sum_i 1/2 tan−1(xi − πκ(Xi)x, f), dθ = sum_i 1/2 tan−1(yi − πκ(Xi)y, f), ϕk+1 = ϕk + dϕk, θk+1 = θk + dθk, k less or equal to 5; RANSAC if more than two correspondences; optimization without LOF. RTMDet for player detection.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Camera parameters κ : {f, k1, ϕ, θ, γ, Cx, Cy, Cz}; tripod parameters {T, δ}; λ varies with camera view; confidence threshold s < 0.5 for reinitialization; reinitialization evaluation uses s < 0.2; JaC tolerance τ = 5 and 10 pixels; HD 1920×1080; 960×540; 25× zoom; 16 frames per second (fps) for HD (1920×1080 pixel resolution) images on a server equipped with two RTX 4090 GPUs; 30 seconds; 49 sequences of 750 images each, extracted from 3 games of the Swiss Football League; reinitialization had to be used 33 times, and the loss of tracking lasted for 15 frames on average; 20 minutes (60,000 frames); first 5,000 frames; reinitialization step is only performed 60 times, and lasts for 4 frames on average; default focal point localizations Cmain = (0, 55, −12), C16m = (±36, 55, −12), CHBG = (−65, 0, −15), Cdefault = (0, 90, −18), all expressed in meters; sn-calibration test set comprises 3,141 images. JaC metric [44] (previously denoted by AC in the sn-calibration challenges [12,29]) expresses the percentage of soccer field elements that are correctly reprojected in the image, the correctness being tuned by a tolerance parameter τ in pixels. MRE stands for Mean Reprojection Error and is measured in pixels; CR stands for completeness rate in percent. Table 1 sn-gamestate metrics in order JaC5, JaC10, MRE, CR: TVCalib [56] 19.88, 50.42, 12.4, 99.93; NBJW [31] 37.14, 68.24, 10.28, 93.67; PTZ-SLAM [41] 25.87, 45.28, 27.64, 26.67*; Ours (fixed C) 50.97, 74.93, 5.39, 100; BroadTrack 56.88, 79.79, 5.02, 100. Table 2 sn-calibration metrics in order JaC5, JaC10, CR: TVCalib [56] 52.9, 73.4, 66.5; NBJW [31] 73.7, 86.7, 77.5; Ours 75.25, 86.8, 69.8. To enable fairer comparison with TVCalib, filter out their calibrations with JaC5 = 0. data.core_methodology: Supervised binary classification problem estimating the probability of securing at least one point by match end (90 minutes plus stoppage time) using match data; predictors engineered to represent average team age, tactical deployment, and key-player exposure; implemented in R using tidyverse and tidymodels; five classification algorithms benchmarked: Logistic regression via glmnet engine tuning penalty and mixture; Random Forest with ranger engine, number of trees fixed at 700, tuning mtry and min_n; Gradient boosting via XGBoost with xgboost engine, number of trees fixed at 1000, tuning tree_depth, min_n, loss_reduction, sample_size, mtry, and learn_rate; Radial basis function support vector machines via kernlab engine tuning cost, rbf_sigma, and margin; Multilayer perceptron via nnet engine tuning hidden_units, penalty, and epochs; preprocessing pipeline included k-NN imputation for missing values, dummy encoding for nominal predictors, and removal of zero-variance predictors; initial dataset split randomly into training subset (75% of observations) and test subset (25%) with stratification; training dataset split into five folds using stratification for cross-validation; hyperparameters optimized via random grid-based search with grid size 200 for logistic regression, random forest, support vector machine and multi-layer perceptron models, and 600 for extreme gradient boosting models; best combination of hyperparameters chosen based on highest ROC AUC averaged along cross-validation training folds; best selected model of each algorithm assessed on test dataset; predictors importance assessed with vip package; bivariate relationships examined with classical statistical tests, ggstatsplot, non-parametric Spearman test, Mann–Whitney U, and chi-square tests.

data.paper_title: Hypergraph-State Collaborative Reasoning for Multi-Object Tracking
data.authors: Zikai Song1, 2, Junqing Yu1*, Yi-Ping Phoebe Chen3, Wei Yang1, Xinchao Wang2*
data.core_methodology: HyperSSM: unified architecture integrating Hypergraph computation and State Space Model (SSM) for spatial collaborative reasoning and temporal motion estimation. Hypergraph construction: G = {V, E}; each object is a vertex with motion feature x ∈ R^d; distance threshold θ constructs an e-ball around each motion feature as a hyperedge; E = {ball(v, e) | v ∈ V}; ball(v, e) = {u | ||xu − xv||d < θ, u ∈ V}; incidence matrix H. Motion feature: historical trajectory pL ∈ R^{L×4}; pt = (x, y, w, h); velocity vt = pt − pt−1, t = 2, . . . , L; exponential moving average (EMA) weighting: ˆv = Σ_{t=1}^{L} α(1 − α)^{L−t} vt; trajectory embedding module. Hypergraph convolution gathering/scattering: Y ← W D−1_e H^T X; Xh ← σ(D−1_v H Y Θ). Hyper Convolution (HConv): xe = 1/|Nv(e)| Σ_{v∈Nv(e)} xvΘ; x′v = xv + 1/|Ne(v)| Σ_{e∈Ne(v)} xe; HConv(X) = σ(D−1_v H W D−1_e H^T Xv Θ). S4 model: ht = Aht−1 + Bxt; yt = Cht + Dxt. HConv-embedded SSM: ht = Aht−1 + B · HConv(Xt); Yt = Xt + Cht + HConv(Xt). data.paper_title: KaliCalib: A Framework for Basketball Court Registration
data.authors: Adrien Maglo, Astrid Orcesi, Quoc-Cuong Pham
data.core_methodology: KaliCalib estimates the position in the frame space of keypoints sampled on the field template with an encoder-decoder convolutional neural network [21]. At inference time, this model generates heatmaps for each keypoint and the background. Keypoint positions are retrieved at the center of mass of the heatmaps. Since some of the positions may be inaccurate, a RANSAC algorithm [13] with DLT [15] estimates a robust homography between the court space and the image space by excluding outliers. KaliCalib is built upon the approach of Nie et al. [21] without the homography refinement. The model has an encoder-decoder architecture similar to U-Net [23]. The encoder is based on a ResNet-18 network [17]. Dilated convolutions [4] with a factor two and non-local blocks [27] are used in the last two ResNet blocks. The decoder is composed of four deconvolution layers followed by a Relu activation. Skip connections are added between the encoder and the decoder. KaliCalib’s model generates heatmaps for each of the keypoints at a resolution of 1/4 of the input resolution. K different keypoints are sampled from the court template but the network also outputs a heatmap for the background. The network generates a softmax score for each pixel of the heatmaps and is trained with a cross-entropy loss. Ground-truth heatmaps use a disk with a radius of 10 pixels. The model also generates two additional heatmaps for the baskets (basket localization). Perspective aware keypoint sampling models w_i as an arithmetic progression. Data augmentation includes random image flips and heavy brightness, contrast and color jittering. Degenerated homographies are detected by re-projecting frame points [240, 270] and [720, 270] in the court space and checking distance below 1800 cm. Camera calibration parameters are computed with the estimated homography thanks to the OpenCV function calibrateCamera [2, 31].

data.authors: Jiacheng Sun1, Hsiang-Wei Huang1, Cheng-Yen Yang1, Zhongyu Jiang1, and Jenq-Neng Hwang1
data.core_methodology: Global Tracklet Association (GTA), an appearance-based global tracklet association algorithm and plug-and-play post-processing method with two modules: Tracklet Splitter and Tracklet Connector. Tracklet Splitter addresses mix-up errors by splitting a tracklet T = {t0, ..., tn} into fragments ti using DBSCAN clustering (Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise) on box-grained appearance embedding features generated by an OSNet ReID model; the adapted DBSCAN assigns outliers to the nearest clusters at the end, uses cosine similarity as the distance metric, and has hyperparameters Minimum Samples (s), Maximum Neighbor Distance (ϵ), and Maximum Clusters (k). Tracklet Connector addresses cut-off errors by constructing a symmetric cosine distance matrix, enforcing temporal and spatial constraints, and applying hierarchical clustering following [14] with a distance threshold α; spatial constraints use θ_hor = β Δ_max,hor and θ_ver = β Δ_max,ver, and D_i,j = 1 if Δ_i,j,hor > θ_hor or Δ_i,j,ver > θ_ver.

data.paper_title: The Importance of the Penalty Kick in the Modern Game of Football
data.authors: Kristine Dalton, OD, MSc, PhD1,2,3, Michel Guillon, PhD, CCTI2,3, Shehzad A. Naroo, MSc, PhD3 *
data.core_methodology: Retrospective study; all data collected from results published on the FIFA (www.fifa.com) and UEFA (www.uefa.com) websites; analysis divided into two sections: penalties taken during open match play and penalties taken in penalty shootouts; match play penalties collected from the 2002, 2006 and 2010 World Cup and the 2004 and 2008 European Championship (EURO) tournaments; the 2000 EURO was not included in this analysis because some of the data (i.e. time of missed penalties) was not available; penalty shootout data taken from the 2002, 2006 and 2010 World Cup and the 2000, 2004 and 2008 EURO tournaments; match play penalties were those awarded during regulation time (90 minutes plus extra time awarded at the end of each half for stoppages of play) and added extra time (AET) of elimination rounds; matches divided into four quarters based on the number of minutes played (i.e. 1st quarter: 0 – 23min, 2nd quarter: 24 – 45min, 3rd quarter: 46 – 68min, 4th quarter: 69 – 90min); if extra time/injury time was added to either half, it was considered to be part of the last quarter of that half (i.e. 2nd or 4th quarters); AET in elimination rounds was considered to be its own category that included all penalties awarded during AET; penalty shots from match play and penalty shootouts were classified as either a goal or a miss/save as some of the databases did not differentiate between misses and saves in their results; AET penalty shots (3.2%) were not included in the statistical analyses to avoid the risk of sample size bias; statistical and graphical analyses were completed using SPSS 16.0 (www.spss.com) and Graph Pad Prism 5 software (www.graphpad.com); binomial, chi-square and Kruskal-Wallis tests were used for statistical comparisons between groups; the significance value for all analyses was α = 0.05 unless otherwise stated; in the match play analysis, a significance value of α = 0.10 was also considered as this has been used as the threshold of practical significance in previous penalty shot publications [6, 7]; in addition to their success rate, the valence of 5th shooters’ penalty shots was determined using Jordet and Hartman’s definition [7].

data.core_methodology: Augmentation of the Neovision2 Tower ground-truth meta-data with unique object IDs (sequential integers starting with 1, incremented as new objects appear, not recycled, former ID re-assigned on re-entry); use of the standard Multi Object Tracking (MOT) framework; use of the CLEAR MOT metrics (MOTP and MOTA) and the CLEAR MOT metrics implementation provided by MOT Challenge; use of the Munkres algorithm to find an optimum mapping (in terms of total spatial overlap) between system tracks and unique ground truth objects; use of Neovision2 detection metrics; spatial overlap dt between each ground truth bounding box region Ri,t and each candidate bounding box region Rj,t; MATLAB based tool for missing bounding boxes and dedicated MATLAB script to visualise IDs.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Classes: Car, Bus, Truck, Person, Cyclist; 24 videos of 871 image frames each; 50 training and 50 test image sequences; each video consists of 898 frames; ground-truth annotations for the first 871 of 898 frames; recorded at 29.97 frames/s; resolution 1920 x 1088; 8-bit PNG frames; 201690 object annotations; 463 unique objects; 20904 annotated image frames; limited to first 24 of 50 videos; Neovision2 Tower contains five target class labels (bus, truck, car, cyclist, person); Neovision2 Heli contains ten target class labels (car, truck, tractor-trailer, bus, container, boat, airplane, helicopter, person, cyclist) annotated in every fourth video frame; MOT16 meta-data contains 12 ground truth class labels; UA-DETRAC ground truth meta-data contains four vehicle class labels: car, bus, van, others; dt = (Ri,t ∩Rj,t)/ (Rj,t ∪Rj,t); Td threshold can range between 0 and 1; MOTP = dt,k t,k∑ / ct t∑; ct is the number of matches; dk,t is the spatial overlap of the kth matched system track in frame t; MOTA = 1− (FNt + FPt + IDSWt) t∑ / GTt t∑; GTt is the number of unique ground truth objects; FNt is the number of false negatives; FPt is the number of false positives; IDSWt is the number of ID switches; scale is calculated as the square root of the bounding box area, in units of pixels; maximum occlusion ratio is the largest fraction of its bounding box being occluded by one of its neighbouring objects; average speed in units of pixels/frame; Confidence ranges from 0 to 1.0, where 1.0 shows complete certainty of the classification.

data.authors: Felipe J. A. Maia, José E. B. Maia
data.core_methodology: Gaussian Process (GP) Regression; mean function m(x) and covariance function (or kernel) k(x, x′); joint Gaussian distribution; Gaussian distribution with zero mean N(0, σ2_n) for observation noise; Matérn kernel selected with ν = 1.5; four independent Gaussian Process (GP) regression models, one for each of the subject’s positional variables (x, y, h, w); subsampling every k-th frame to simulate sparse annotation; sensitivity analysis over RBF, Matérn, and Rational Quadratic kernels.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: GP: f(x) ∼ GP(m(x), k(x, x′)); m(x) = E[f(x)]; k(x, x′) = E[(f(x) − m(x))(f(x′) − m(x′))]. Training: D = {(xi, yi)}^n_i=1; yi = f(xi) + ϵi; ϵi ∼ N(0, σ2_n). Joint distribution: [y; f∗] ∼ N([0; 0], [[Ky, K(X, x∗)], [K(x∗, X), K(x∗, x∗)]]), with Ky = K(X, X) + σ2_n I. Predictive: f∗|X, y, x∗ ∼ N(µ∗, σ2_∗); µ∗ = K(x∗, X)K−1_y y; σ2_∗ = K(x∗, x∗) − K(x∗, X)K−1_y K(X, x∗). Matérn kernel: k(xi, xj) = 1/(Γ(ν) 2ν−1) (√(2ν)/ℓ d(xi, xj))^ν Kν(√(2ν)/ℓ d(xi, xj)). Log marginal likelihood: log p(y | X) = log N(y | 0, Ky) = −1/2 y⊤K−1_y y − 1/2 log |Ky| − N/2 log(2π). data.paper_title: Frame by frame completion probability of an NFL pass
data.authors: Gustavo Pompeu da Silva1*, Rafael de Andrade Moral1,2
data.core_methodology: Two-stage procedure: first calculate empirical probabilities of each offensive player being the pass target using distance measures d(1), d(2), d(3), d(4), weights W(1), W(2), W(3), W(4), and logistic-model weight W(2,3); then conditional on the target predict completion probability using a Random Forest model; general completion probability via the law of total probability. Models tested: Random Forest, Binomial Regression with Logit, Probit and complementary-log-log links, Linear and Quadratic Discriminant Analysis. Validation: Leave Group Out Cross-Validation (LGOCV) with 5 or 10 folds using plays as grouping factor; performance metric area under the Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve computed with the trapezoidal rule (AUC). Random Forest mtry=15, subsets containing between 5 to 20 variables at every split. R packages: tidyverse, caret, randomForest, gganimate, raster.

data.paper_title: Video Pose Distillation for Few-Shot, Fine-Grained Sports Action Recognition
data.authors: James Hong1, Matthew Fisher2, Micha¨el Gharbi2, Kayvon Fatahalian1
data.core_methodology: Video Pose Distillation (VPD), a weakly-supervised technique in which a student network learns to extract robust pose features from RGB video frames in a new video domain; teacher variants: 2D-VPD uses an off-the-shelf pose estimator [54] to estimate 2D joint positions from xt, normalize by rescaling and centering as in [53], and collect joint coordinates into pt ∈ Rd; VI-VPD uses VIPE⋆ to generate a view-invariant pose descriptor pt; student feature extractor F consumes color video frame xt ∈ R3hw cropped around the athlete and optical flow ϕt ∈ R2hw from the previous frame, produces descriptor F(xt, ϕt) ∈ Rd, implemented as a standard ResNet-34 with 5 input channels and input crops resized to 128×128; auxiliary decoder D is a fully-connected network predicting current pose pt and temporal derivative ∆pt := pt − pt−1; training objective Equation (1): minimize over Student and PoseDecoder of sum from Time=1 to NumFrames of || D(F(Frame{Time}, Flow{Time})) - [WeakPose{Time}; PoseMotion{Time}] ||_2^2; data selection excludes frames with low mean estimated joint score (default threshold 0.5, 0.7 for tennis) and withholds 20% frames uniformly at random as validation; data augmentation includes random resizing and cropping, horizontal flipping, color and noise jitter, and flipping teacher output pt; optical flow ϕt is computed using RAFT; pose uses HRNet; tracking uses Mask R-CNN, SORT, and OpenCV CSRT; downstream action recognition uses a bidirectional Gated Recurrent Unit network (BiGRU) trained atop fixed features, and nearest-neighbor search (NNS) uses dynamic time warping (DTW) with pairwise L2 distance and symmetricP2 step pattern; action retrieval ranks by L2 distance between pose features and dynamic time warping alignment score; few-shot action detection uses a BiGRU that outputs per-frame predictions merged to produce predicted action intervals.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Equation (1): minimize_{Student, PoseDecoder} sum_{Time=1}^{NumFrames} || D(F(Frame{Time}, Flow{Time})) - [WeakPose{Time}; PoseMotion{Time}] ||_2^2; variables: pt ∈ Rd, ∆pt := pt − pt−1, F(xt, ϕt) ∈ Rd, xt ∈ R3hw, ϕt ∈ R2hw, h and w are crop spatial dimensions, t frame index; d = 64 for VIPE⋆, d = 26 for normalized 2D joints, and for Diving48 VIPE⋆ has d = 128; ResNet-34 with 5 input channels; input crops resized to 128×128; weak-pose selection threshold default 0.5, 0.7 for tennis; 20% validation frames; 13 of 17 COCO keypoints (ignoring LEye, REye, LEar, and REar); bounding box expanded to square and padded each side by 10% or 25 pixels, whichever is greater; RAFT optical flow: subtract median, clip to ±20 pixels, quantize into 8-bits, target frame rate 25 fps; xt scaled to ±1 and standardized with dataset RGB mean and standard deviation; ϕt centered to ±0.5; Gaussian noise σ = 0.05 when Mask R-CNN score above 0.8; auxiliary decoder D has two hidden layers each dimension 128; student training samples 20,000 frames per epoch, AdamW learning rate 5e−4, batch size 100, 1,000 epochs, approximately 8 hours on a single Titan V GPU; BiGRU: two-layer, hidden dimension h = 128, max-pool across time, FC dimensions 2h, AdamW batch size 50, 500 epochs (200 on Diving48), learning rate initially 1e−3 with cosine schedule, dropout 0.5 on dense layers and 0.2 on input sequence, training times 7 minutes FSJump6, 25 minutes Tennis7, 50 minutes FX35, 100 minutes Diving48; NNS uses DTW with pairwise L2 distance and symmetricP2 step pattern; action detection: frame-level activation threshold 0.2, minimum proposal length 3 frames, expand or trim proposals less than 0.67× or greater than 1.33× mean action length, sequences of 250 frames, batch size 100, 1e4 steps, AdamW learning rate 1e−3, dropout 0.5 dense and 0.2 input, five-fold cross-validation; average jump 1.6 seconds (≈40 frames), swing 200 ms around ball contact (≈5 frames); metrics: Top-1 accuracy, average precision (AP) at temporal intersection over union (tIoU), precision at k, L2 distance, dynamic time warping alignment score; key reported figures: VPD improves fine-grained classification accuracy by 6.8 to 22.8% and by 5.0 to 10.5% over next best method(s) on diving and floor exercises for 8 to 64 training examples per class; VI-VPD increases accuracy by up to 10.5% over VIPE⋆ at k ≤32 and 5% over MS-G3D ensemble at k = 64 on FX35; on Diving48 VI-VPD improves accuracy by 6.8 to 22.8%; VI-VPD trails end-to-end GSM (w/o crop) by 1.6% on Diving48; VI-VPD improves AP up to 7.4 over VIPE⋆ at tIoU = 0.5 for tennis swings; distillation with entire video corpus improvement ≤1.5%, attained on Tennis7 at 16-shot; tracked vs non-tracked difference 48% on FSJump6 for GSM and 40% on FX35 for ST-GCN; dataset figures: figure skating 371 singles short programs, 17 video hours, FSJump6 six jump types, 2018 held out 134 routines and 520 jumps, remaining jumps split 743/183 for training/validation; Tennis seven swing classes, training/validation 4,592/1,142 from five matches, test 2,509 from remaining four matches, 10 professional players; FX35 1,214 routines (34 hours), 35 classes, 7,634 actions; Diving48 16,997 annotated instances of 48 dive sequences; FSJump6 class counts Axel 371, Flip 179, Loop 94, Lutz 244, Salchow 61, Toe-loop 497, Total 1,446; data.paper_title: Jersey number detection using synthetic data in a low-data regime
data.authors: Divya Bhargavi, Sia Gholami, Erika Pelaez Coyotl*
data.core_methodology: Novel synthetic data generation with Simple2D and Complex2D; Simple2D creates two-digit number images from a uniform distribution of 0–9 with jersey-like background colors (Red, Navy Blue, Green, Red, Yellow, White), Freshman font, and Light/Medium/Hard augmentations (Gaussian noise, optical distortion, grid distortion, shuffling RGB channels, random shift-scale-rotation), using U(1,n) for background/font color combinations and U(a,b) for font size scaled factors; Complex2D superimposes Simple2D numbers on random COCO dataset images. Three-step pipeline: Centernet (ResNet50 backbone) person detection and cropping; AlphaPose pose estimation to identify four torso key-points (left and right hips and shoulders), expanding coordinates 60% outward to create a jersey-number bounding box; CNN classifiers with ResNet50 backbone, including a multi-class image classifier for two-digit numbers (101 classes: 0–99 plus unrecognizable class 100) using softmax and a multi-class multi-label classifier for single digits (21 classes: 10 digits for each side—right, left—plus an unrecognizable class) using sigmoid. Sequential pre-training on Simple2D then Complex2D and fine-tuning on the football dataset under curriculum learning; two-model ensemble.

data.core_methodology: iWinRNFL is based on a logistic regression model (a generalized linear model) that calculates Pr(H = 1|x) = exp(wT · x) / (1 + exp(wT · x)); it uses 10 independent variables: Ball Possession Team; Score Differential; Home Timeouts; Away Timeouts; Time Elapsed; Down; Field Position; Yards-to-go; Ball Possession Time; Rating Differential. It includes interaction terms between ball possession team and down count, yards-to-go, and field position, and between time lapsed and team ratings differential and score differential. Team ratings are obtained by solving an optimization problem: minimize ∑_{m=1}^N (μ_m − (h + R_Hm − R_Vm))^2 subject to ∑_{i=1}^{32} R_i = 0; pre-season ratings by minimize ∑_{m=1}^{32} (λ_i − E[W_i])^2 subject to ∑_{i=1}^{32} ρ_i = 0, with E[W_i] = ∑_{j=1}^{16} Pr[i ≻ j] and Pr[i ≻ j] = Φ(p/14) under a normal distribution with mean h + ρ_i − ρ_j and standard deviation of approximately 14 points. Full rating: R̃_i(w) = γ · ρ_i + (1 − γ) · R_i(w), where γ = max(1 − (w − 1)/10, 0). Evaluated alternative models: naive Bayesian classifier, which computes Pr[Ck|x] = Pr[Ck] ∏_{i=1}^n Pr[xi|Ck] assuming conditional independence, and feedforward neural network (FNN) with 2 hidden layers (first hidden layer size 6 nodes, second hidden layer size 3 nodes).

data.paper_title: From Broadcast to Minimap: Achieving State-of-the-Art SoccerNet Game State Reconstruction
data.authors: Vladimir Golovkin*, Nikolay Nemtsev, Vasyl Shandyba, Oleg Udin, Nikita Kasatkin, Pavel Kononov, Anton Afanasiev, Sergey Ulasen, Andrei Boiarov
data.core_methodology: End-to-end single-camera pipeline with three stages: raw tracking, team detection, post-processing. Raw tracking uses a fine-tuned YOLOv5m (abstract) / YOLOv5 detector (methodology); a standard pinhole camera model with zero distortions and principal point fixed to the center of the frame; a custom CNN-Transformer encoder-decoder camera-parameter model with a SegFormer encoder and multiple decoder heads (parameters head with Polarized Self-Attention (PSA) layer, multiple Conv2D layers, average pooling; heatmaps head with PSA layer, Conv2D and Pixel Shuffle layers); loss in Normalized Device Coordinates (NDC); a Field Keypoints Model based on ResNet18 (main text) / ResNet50-based segmentation network (Supplementary B) detecting 74 keypoints; brute-force optimization of predefined camera-parameter corrections with delta values such as [−0.15, −0.10, . . . , 0.15], homography matrices, and L2 distance to the ideal pitch model; Savitzky-Golay filter; DeepSORT-based tracking in real-world pitch coordinates with restrictions based on player orientation (e.g., preventing 180-degree direction changes in one frame) and TeamID Embeddings; Jersey Number Recognition with a modified ResNet architecture for 32×32 input images and two classification heads (leading digit 1–9 or none; second digit 0–9) trained with BinaryFocalLoss and CrossEntropyLoss; ReID Embeddings from a ResNet50-based model; TeamID Embeddings from an OSNet model trained on 111 uniform classes; Player Orientation from a ResNet18 model classifying left/up/right/down; Player Anomaly from a lightweight custom model. Team detection identifies five embedding clusters (left/right team athletes, referees, left/right goalkeepers) using clustering and cosine distance, with a voting mechanism for left vs. right teams and assignment by minimum cosine distance to estimated clusters. Post-processing performs splitting tracklets by jersey numbers and team IDs, merging tracklets by jersey numbers, merging tracklets by ReID similarity using Mean Vector Comparison and Cross-Multiplication Matrix (Pairwise Comparison), and tracklet interpolation via linear interpolation. Datasets use a modified TVCalib framework with labeled keypoints and real-world-space L2 loss, and the Google Research Football Simulator with randomized textures and camera views; training uses Optuna with tree-structured Parzen estimator (TPE) sampler, Kornia augmentations, NVIDIA DeepStream SDK, TensorRT engines with FP16 precision. Evaluation uses GS-HOTA, which extends HOTA by factoring in role, team, and jersey number; Localization Similarity (LocSim) measures Euclidean distance in pitch coordinates smoothed by a Gaussian kernel with a 5-meter tolerance; Identification Similarity (IdSim) requires exact matches for role, team, and jersey number.
