data.paper_title: SportMamba: Adaptive Non-Linear Multi-Object Tracking with State Space Models for Team Sports
data.authors: Dheeraj Khanna, Jerrin Bright, Yuhao Chen, John S. Zelek
data.core_methodology: SportMamba, an adaptive hybrid MOT technique for online tracking under the TBD paradigm; four-stage process: fine-tuned off-the-shelf detector (YOLOX) for sports-specific player detection; mamba-attention motion predictor with Token Embedding, Mamba-Attention Encoder using State-Space Models (SSMs) discretized with Zero-Order Hold (ZOH), Multi-Head Self-Attention (MHSA), FFN, and Prediction Head; high-confidence association (HCA) and low-confidence association (LCA) using a hybrid matching metric combining appearance-based Re-ID features with Height-Adaptive EIoU (HA-EIoU), Extended IoU (EIoU), and HIoU with adaptive buffers b1 and b2; linear assignment solver; tracklet management with update, creation, deletion, and Dynamic EMA; trained with Smooth L1 loss and Complete IoU (CIoU) using AdamW.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: B_d = {x_t, y_t, w_t, h_t}; T_in = {B^{t−l}_d, B^{t−l+1}_d, ..., B^{t−1}_d}; B_p predicted bounding box at time t; st ∈ [0, 1]; l ∈ (2, w); b1 ∈ [0, 1]; b2 < b1; M = 4; w = 10; b1 = 0.4; b2 = 0.3; 60 epochs; batch size 64; AdamW β1 = 0.9, β2 = 0.98; learning rate 10−4; weight decay 10−3; λ^s_l1 = 50; λ_ciou = 1; ≈30 FPS. Equations: (1) h′_k = A h_{k−1} + B x_k; y_k = C h_k. (2) y_ln = LayerNorm(y_k); x_att = LayerNorm(MHSA(y_ln) + y_ln). (3) head_i = Softmax(Q^i (K^i)^T / √d) V^i. (4) x_ff = Linear(GeLU(Linear(x_att)) + x_att). (5) B_p = σ(Linear(x_out)). (6) EIoU = |B′_p ∩ B′_d| / |B′_p ∪ B′_d|. (7) HA-EIoU = HIoU · EIoU. (8) HIoU = |(min(y^2_t, ŷ^2_t) − max(y^1_t, ŷ^1_t)) / (max(y^2_t, ŷ^2_t) − min(y^1_t, ŷ^1_t))|. (9) S_reid(i, j) = (e_i^T · e_j^D) / (||e_i^T|| ||e_j^D||). (10) J_f = λ_reid(1 − S_reid) + λ_ssim(1 − HA-EIoU). (11) e_i^{t−1} = α e_i^{t−2} + (1 − α) f_i^{t−1}. (12) α_d = α + (1 − α)(1 − (s_t − σ)) / (1 − σ). (13) e_i^{t−1} = α e_i^{t−2} + (1 − α_d) f_i^{t−1}. (14) L^s_L1 = 1/2(P_t − G_t)^2 if |P_t − G_t| < 1, |P_t − G_t| − 1/2 otherwise. (15) L = λ^s_l1 L^s_L1 + λ_ciou L_ciou. B′_d = {x_t − 0.5 b w_t, y_t − 0.5 b h_t, w_t + b w_t, h_t + b h_t}; B′_p = {x̂_t − 0.5 b ŵ_t, ŷ_t − 0.5 b ĥ_t, ŵ_t + b ŵ_t, ĥ_t + b ĥ_t}. SportsMOT test SportMamba: HOTA 77.3, IDF1 77.7, AssA 66.8, MOTA 96.9, DetA 89.5. VIP-HTD test SportMamba: HOTA 65.1, IDF1 80.1, AssA 64.6, MOTA 76.2, DetA 65.9. Ablation: best (M = 4, w = 10) HOTA 82.934; b1 = 0.4, b2 = 0.3 HOTA 84.239; HA-EIoU HOTA 84.239, DetA 94.165, AssA 75.379, MOTA 98.692, IDF1 83.931; EIoU HOTA 83.316, DetA 94.108, AssA 73.783, MOTA 98.693, IDF1 82.862; HIoU HOTA 83.421, DetA 94.113, AssA 73.964, MOTA 98.466, IDF1 83.024; IoU HOTA 82.934, DetA 94.073, AssA 73.134, MOTA 98.499, IDF1 82.429. SportsMOT dataset: 240 video sequences, 720p at 25 FPS. VIP-HTD dataset: 8 games, 22 sequences, 720p at 30 FPS. Surpasses DiffMOT by 1.06 HOTA, 1.6 IDF1, and 1.7 AssA. HA-EIoU yields ≈0.9 increase in HOTA and ≈1.1 increase in IDF1 compared to EIoU.

data.paper_title: Action Quality Assessment via Hierarchical Pose-guided Multi-stage Contrastive Regression
data.authors: Mengshi Qi, Hao Ye, Jiaxuan Peng, Huadong Ma
data.core_methodology: Hierarchically pose-guided multi-stage action quality assessment framework; multi-scale visual-skeletal encoder with static visual encoder (ResNetY and multi-branch downsampling module Down_mul), dynamic visual encoder (I3D with mixed convolution layers Convmix and max-pooling), and hierarchical skeletal encoder (GCN with skeletal node adjacency matrices, MLP, point-wise convolution, EdgeConv, HD-GCN base); procedure segmentation network based on Bidirectional Gated Recurrent Unit (Bi-GRU) followed by a fully connected layer and softmax; multi-modal fusion module with pose-guided multi-head self-attention; multi-stage contrastive regression module with stage-wise contrastive loss, Transformer decoder, and MLPs with ReLU activation; splash detection and splash regression module SR; Mean Squared Error (MSE) losses; multi-sample voting strategy.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Problem formulation: Ŝ_q = F(V^q, P^q, V^e, P^e | Θ) + S_e; V ∈ R^{T×H×W×C}, P ∈ R^{T×J×D_c}; F_st = Down_mul(R(V)); F_dy^q = maxpool(Convmix(I(V^q))); H_i^q = ∥_{s∈S} {A_i^s MLP(P^q) ∂_i^s}; F_sk^q = Σ_{i=1}^N [H_i^q ∥ Z_i · (1/T) Σ_{t=1}^T MLP(P^q)]; P(F_dy) = [â_1, â_2, ..., â_T]; L_ce = Σ_{i=1}^K CE(a_i, â_i); α_i = Softmax(K_dy^i·Q_dy^i/√D_dy + ρ K_sk^i·Q_sk^i/√D_pose); Atten_i = Multihead(V_dy^i·α_i); H_dy = Atten_i + LN(F_dy^i); F_fu^i = FFN(LN(H_dy)) + H_dy; δ(F^{q,k}, F^{e,k}) = cos(norm(F^{q,k}), norm(F^{e,k})); ε(F^{q,k}, F^{e,k}) = e^{δ(F^{q,k},F^{e,k})/τ}; ζ(F^{q,k}, F^{e,k}) = Σ_{k=1;k≠l}^K (e^{δ(F^{q,k},F^{e,l})/τ} + e^{δ(F^{q,k},F^{q,l})/τ}); ℓ(F^{q,k}, F^{e,k}) = log(ε/(ε+ζ)); L_cont = 1/(2K) Σ_{i=1}^K [ℓ(F^{q,k},F^{e,k}) + ℓ(F^{e,k},F^{q,k})]; f_fu^k = D(F_fu^{q,k}, F_fu^{e,k}); f_st^k = D(F_st^{q,k}, F_st^{e,k}); Ŝ_q = S_e + CR(F_fu, F_st); CR(F_fu, F_st) = Σ_{k=1}^K λ_k(M_fu(f_fu^k) + M_st(f_st^k)); S_splash = ∫ s(t) dt ≈ Σ_{i=1}^{N-1} (s_i + s_{i+1})/2 · Δt; Ŝ_splash^q = S_splash^e + SR(F_fu, F_st); SR(F_fu, F_st) = Σ_{k=1}^K λ_k(A_fu(f_fu^k) + A_st(f_st^k)); L_aqa = MSE(S_q, Ŝ_q); L_splash = MSE(S_splash^q, Ŝ_splash^q); MSE = 1/N Σ_{i=1}^N (y_i - ŷ_i)^2; L = L_aqa + L_splash + L_ce + L_cont; Ŝ_q = 1/N Σ_{i=1}^N (F(V^q, P^q, V_i^e, P_i^e | Θ) + S_i^e); SRCC ρ = Σ_i(r_i - r̄)(r̂_i - r̂̄) / √(Σ_i(r_i - r̄)^2 Σ_i(r̂_i - r̂̄)^2); RL2 = 1/N Σ_{i=1}^N (|y_i - ŷ_i|/(y_max - y_min)); AIoU@d = 1/N Σ_{i=1}^N J(IoU_i ≥ d); dis_{k+1}^i = √(Σ_{j=1}^2 ((x_j^i - x_j)^2 + (y_j^i - y_j)^2)); P^q = HRNet({V^q_{(x1,y1,x2,y2)_k}}_{k=1}^T); p_k = p_i (k-i)/(j-i) + p_j (j-k)/(j-i). Hyperparameters: τ = 0.5; K = 3; attention heads = 2; Transformer decoder layers = 4; decoder heads = 4; initial learning rate = 5e−4; Adam optimizer with zero weight decay; batch size = 8; 200 epochs; FineDiving: 96 frames per video, 9 clips in I3D; MTL-AQA: 103 frames per video clip, 10 overlapping segments, 16 consecutive frames each; inference: 10 exemplar videos per query. Dataset figures: FineDiving-Pose: 367 videos, 12,722 manually labeled frames, 3,000 videos, 288,000 automatically annotated frames, 96 frames per video, 455×256 pixels, 16 pose keypoints, keypoints 0 to 15; FineDiving: 3000 video samples, 52 dive numbers, 29 sub-action numbers, 23 difficulty degree types, 2,250 training samples, 750 test samples; MTL-AQA: 1,412 samples, 16 events, 1,059 training samples, 353 test samples. Main results: FineDiving w/o DN SRCC 0.9041, RL2 0.411, AIoU 98.17/93.68; w/ DN SRCC 0.9383, RL2 0.269, AIoU 99.07/97.96; MTL-AQA w/o DD SRCC 0.9266, RL2 0.446; w/ DD SRCC 0.9516, RL2 0.278.

data.paper_title: Integrating Unsupervised and Supervised Learning for the Prediction of Defensive Schemes in American football
data.authors: Rouven Michels∗†, Robert Bajons‡, Jan-Ole Fischer§
data.core_methodology: Statistical framework integrating supervised and unsupervised learning using player tracking data; elastic net logistic regression; gradient-boosted decision trees implemented as XGBoost; non-homogeneous hidden Markov model (HMM) with a first-order Markov chain and Gaussian state-dependent distributions (mixture of Gaussian distributions); mixed-effects linear predictors with random effects ur ∼ N(0, σ2_role), vd ∼ N(0, σ2_defense), wp ∼ N(0, σ2_play); inverse multinomial logistic link function; Laplace approximation; forward algorithm; local decoding; Generalized Covariance Measure (GCM) test; covariance measure tests (COMETs); partially linear logistic regression model; cross-fitting strategy with 5-fold cross-validation; leave-one-team-out procedure; AIC for lag selection; softmax initialization with α = 1; Bernoulli log-likelihood for logloss.

Γ(Tm)P(yTm); ˆSt = arg max_{k∈{1,...,5}} Pr(St = k | y1, . . . , yTm); GCM := E[Cov(Y, X | Z)] = E[(Y − E[Y | Z])(X − E[X | Z])]; log(π(X, Z)/(1 − π(X, Z))) = Xβ + g(Z); H(m) = −1/5 Σ_{jm=1}^5 Σ_{k=1}^5 (1/Tm Σ_{t=1}^{Tm} 1(ˆSt,jm = k)) log(1/Tm Σ_{t=1}^{Tm} 1(ˆSt,jm = k)); δij = exp(−α |y(def)_i − y(att)_j|) / Σ_{k=1}^{n_att} exp(−α |y(def)_i − y(att)_k|).

data.paper_title: AI Driven Soccer Analysis Using Computer Vision
data.authors: Adrian Manchado, Tanner Cellio, Jonathan Keane, Yiyang Wang
data.core_methodology: Object detection and tracking system combining an Object Detection model with SAM2 (Segment Anything Model 2); evaluated Faster R-CNN, YOLOv5x, YOLOv8x, and YOLOv11x; used YOLO predictions as initial prompts to SAM2; SAM2 segmentation and tracking with memory attention; custom multi-task convolutional neural network for 12 predefined soccer field keypoints predicting visibility probability and normalized coordinates; preprocessing with thresholding filter, morphological kernel dilation, RGB conversion, resize to 710×400 pixels, normalization to [0, 1]; horizontal flipping augmentation with x-coordinate inversion (1 − x) and left/right label swapping; 80/20 training/testing split; custom loss combining mean absolute error (MAE) only over visible keypoints and binary cross-entropy loss for visibility with weights of 10 for coordinate loss and 1 for visibility loss; Adam Optimizer with exponential decay learning rate schedule; Bayesian Optimization hyperparameter search over dropout rate, layer size, and learning rate; homography via Direct Linear Transformation (DLT) using Singular Value Decomposition; field dimensions from Google Maps API and official NCAA collegiate soccer rules; player mapping and team recognition using average color within a 5 × 5 pixels patch centered at the middle of the bounding box in RGB space and K-Means algorithm with k = 2.

data.paper_title: Training-Free Off-Screen Player Imputation for Broadcast-Based Spatial Football Analytics
data.authors: Seongjin Choi∗
data.core_methodology: Simulated broadcast viewport: virtual main camera pans horizontally following an exponentially smoothed ball position (α = 0.06 per frame at 25 fps), visible region is a width-W window spanning the full pitch height; sensitivity for W ∈{36, 44, 52, 60} m. Benchmark on Metrica Sports open tracking (three matches, first 45 minutes, evaluated at 5 fps; games 1–2 for method/hyperparameter development, game 3 held out). Metrics: hidden-player position error, pitch-control map MAE, team control-share error; pitch control computed on a 3 m grid with an arrival-time model and sigmoid contest function [14], with zero velocities. Training-free causal online imputation ladder using only current-match observations: B0 ignore; B1 last-seen with decay w = e−∆t/τ, τ = 8 s; B2 formation anchor; B5 fixed formation template; B3 = B2 + EMA offsets + velocity extrapolation with blend e−∆t/1.5 s; B3E EMA only; B3V velocity only; B4 role-anchored centroid voting: c_hat(t) = (1/|V_t|) Σ_{i∈V_t}(p_i(t) − off_i(t−)), off_i(t) ← EMA[p_i(t) − c_hat(t)] (i ∈ V_t), EMA weight 0.1 per 5 fps evaluation step, three-voter threshold, fallback to B2 then B1. 95% block-bootstrap confidence intervals over one-minute blocks. End-to-end broadcast-video GSR pipeline: PnLCalib-based camera calibration [6] with a temporal bridge, BoT-SORT tracking [1], colour-based team assignment, and shot-change gating; off-screen players rendered as ghosts with role-anchored positions that fade over a 20 s lifetime; ghosts top the team up to at most eleven players; a ghost is retired when a newly appearing track (within 2 s of its birth) emerges within 3 m of the ghost's prediction. Downstream Space-Creation Index (SCI): SCI = ∆own + ∆opp; verdict classes space creation (SCI ≥+12), weak progression (+4 ≤ SCI < +12), dead possession (SCI < +4).
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Visible players in World Cup broadcast clips: 10–16 of 22; Ochin et al. 9–12; Omidshafiei et al. 12.8±3.7. At W = 44 m viewport shows 14.6–15.0 players on average (games 1–3). B0 ignore: hidden-zone pitch-control MAE 25.1–26.9 percentage points; mean absolute control-share error 11.1–13.4 points. B4: hidden-zone error 12.2–13.8 points; control-share error 28–48% of ignore policy at W = 36–60 m; 4.5–4.7 points at W = 44 m. B4 median position error 9.7–11.6 m vs 12.5–13.6 m for B2. B5 position error 20.7–22.7 m; share error 6.9–10.3 pp. B3E position error 15.2–16.3 m. B3V median position error improvements 13.6→13.2, 12.8→12.2, 12.5→11.9 m. B4 voting path 70–86% of hidden-player estimates (B2 fallback 14–30%, B1 0%) at W = 44 m. Game-3 B4−B2 share-error difference [−0.4, +1.3] pp. Game 1 hidden-zone MAE: B0 [24.5, 29.4] vs B4 [11.2, 15.6]; share error [11.4, 15.7] vs [3.6, 6.1]. Occlusion stratification: ≤2 s B4 median position error 3.3–3.7 m; 2–9.6 s 7.2–8.9 m; >9.6 s 15.6–16.9 m; share of hidden samples ≤9.6 s: 43–50%; >9.6 s: 50–57%. GS-HOTA 35.2 on 11 publicly downloadable sequences; official baseline 22.26. SCI thresholds: space creation SCI ≥+12; weak progression +4 ≤ SCI < +12; dead possession SCI < +4. Window 1 SCI +15.6 → +32.8; Window 2 SCI −10.9 → +4.7; imputation moves SCI by 15.6–17.2 points; 8-point intermediate verdict class. Hyperparameters: α = 0.06 per frame at 25 fps; τ = 8 s; EMA weight 0.1; three-voter threshold; 1.5 s blend constant; 20 s ghost lifetime; 2 s birth window; 3 m retirement distance; 3 m pitch-control grid; 5 fps evaluation; 25 fps tracking; 9.6 s sequence protocol; 105 proprietary EPL tracking matches; 45% jersey-number OCR coverage; window durations 34 s and 57 s; game clock 11:58–12:32 and 72:48–73:45; scorelines 0–0 at min. 12 and 0–1 at min. 73; match 1–1 after extra time, Morocco won 3–2 on penalties.

data.paper_title: A survey of video‑based human action recognition in team sports

data.paper_title: Evaluating deep tracking models for player tracking in broadcast ice hockey video
data.authors: Kanav Vats, Mehrnaz Fani, David A. Clausi, and John S. Zelek
data.core_methodology: Five state-of-the-art tracking algorithms: SORT [3] (Kalman filter with simple IOU based re-id), Deep SORT [26] (Kalman filter with deep CNN based re-id), Tracktor [1] (JDT algorithm with separate detection and re-id networks), FairMOT [28] (JDT algorithm with combined object detection and re-id network), MOT Neural Solver [4] (Tracking using graph message passing with edge classification). SORT [3], deep SORT [26] and MOT Neural Solver [4] are tracking by detection (TBD) algorithms; Tracktor [1] and FairMOT [28] are joint detection and tracking (JDT) algorithms. TBD consists of three steps: (1) detecting objects frame-by-frame in the video (2) calculating affinity between detected objects (3) inference - linking player detections using calculated affinities to produce tracks. Player detection is performed using a Faster-RCNN network [17] with a ResNet50 based Feature Pyramid Network (FPN) backbone [11] pre-trained on the COCO dataset and fine tuned on the hockey tracking dataset. MOT Neural Solver [4] models the tracking problem as an undirected graph G = (V, E), where V = {1, 2, ..., n} is the set of n nodes for n player detections for all video frames; in the edge set E, every pair of detections is connected so that trajectories with missed detections can be recovered; the problem of tracking is posed as splitting the graph into disconnected components where each component is a trajectory Ti; after computing each node embedding and edge embedding using a CNN, the model solves a graph message passing problem; the message passing algorithm classifies whether an edge between two nodes in the graph belongs to the same player trajectory.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Tracking accuracy metrics used: CLEAR MOT metrics [2] and Identification F1 score (IDF1) [18]. Variables: IDF1, MOTA, ID-switches, False positives (FP), False negatives (FN). MOTA = 1 −Σt(FNt + FPt + IDSWt)/ΣtGTt (1). (ti −tj) > δ (2). On average, pan identity switches account for 65% of identity switches at a threshold of δ = 40 frames. Table 3 overall tracking performance: SORT [3] IDF1 53.7, MOTA 92.4, ID-switches 673, FP 2403, FN 5826; Deep SORT [26] IDF1 59.3, MOTA 94.2, ID-switches 528, FP 1881, FN 4334; Tracktor [1] IDF1 56.5, MOTA 94.4, ID-switches 687, FP 1706, FN 4216; FairMOT [28] IDF1 61.5, MOTA 91.9, ID-switches 768, FP 1179, FN 7568; MOT Neural Solver [4] IDF1 62.9, MOTA 94.5, ID-switches 431, FP 1653, FN 4394. MOT Neural Solver obtains the highest MOTA score of 94.5 and IDF1 score of 62.9 on the test videos. MOTA score of all methods is above 90%. Player detection results: AP 70.2, AP50 95.9, AP75 87.5. data.paper_title: ESC: Evolutionary Stitched Camera Calibration in the Wild
data.authors: Grzegorz Rype´s´c, Grzegorz Kurzejamski
data.core_methodology: Evolutionary Stitched Camera calibration (ESC) algorithm (also dubbed ESC (Evolutionary Stitched Camera Calibration)): image segmentation followed by evolutionary optimization of a novel loss function; problem defined as search in N × R6 space, with rn_t ∈ R3 (Rodrigues rotation representation) and ln_t ∈ R3 (translation vector), rn_t+1 = rn_t + rn_t→t+1 and ln_t+1 = ln_t + ln_t→t+1; initial calibration using planar chessboard-like calibration pattern and Zhang [33] method; projection matrix P = Kn(Rn_t | ln_t) (1) from Rodrigues rotation vector rn_t to 3x3 rotation matrix Rn_t; 3D playfield model using four intersecting planes, each plane intersects two playfield corners assumed height z = 0m, two planes intersect points p and p′, third plane intersects p, last plane intersects p′, with p, p′, and playfield size as hyperparameters; semantic segmentation model Ψ maps input camera image In_t to Ψ(In_t) of same size containing only sports field lines; template T obtained by combining several blurred play field template images, each blurred with a Gaussian function of a different radius; adapted U-Net architecture [25] with sigmoid activation after final layer, additional padding of 1 in encoder convolutional layers, LeakyReLU activations, and focal loss [35]; µ + λ elitist evolution strategy with G generations, individual vector length 6N, starting population initialized using extrinsic camera parameters from time t: rn_t, tn_t and randomly mutating them by corrupting with Gaussian noise N(0, sr) to rotation and N(0, st) to translation; recombination interpolates child from two parents: [a ∗ pi + (1 − a) ∗ pj] where a ∈ U(0, 1)6N; offspring mutated by adding random vector N(0, sdecaysr)3N × N(0, sdecayst)3N where sdecay denotes a decay factor of mutation strength; loss L = λLstitch + (1 − λ)/N Σ_{i=1}^N Li_single (4), with Lstitch = | ∩N_{i=1} P i(Ψ(Ii))| / | ∪N_{i=1} P i(Ψ(Ii))| (2) and Li_single = |P i(Ψ(Ii)) ∩ T| / |P i(Ψ(Ii)) ∪ T| (3), where λ ∈ [0; 1] denotes a trade-off between stitch quality and numerical accuracy of projections, and |;| denotes the number of pixels in the image greater than 0.5 (segmented images normalized to range [0; 1]); select µ individuals with lowest loss from parents and offspring pool; after last generation new extrinsic parameters set to best individual; implemented in Python using PyTorch [39], U-Net [25] with four times fewer filters in each convolutional layer, AdamW optimizer with weight decay equal to 0.14, starting learning rate of 0.13 with exponential scheduling and two epochs of a warm-up, data augmentation using random flips, translations, rotation, shears, scaling, and crops; evolution strategy set to G = 100, µ = 64, λ = 128, mutation strengts st = 0.1 and sr = 0.005, mutation decay sdecay = 0.95.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Metrics: Stitch (px) ↓, TrE (cm) ↓, RoE (◦) ↓, IoU (%) ↑; Stitch is distance in pixels on playfield images warped to bird’s eye view, calculated between playfield center registered and warped by first and second camera, with image resolution 1px = 10cm; Translation error (TrE) is L2 distance in real-world centimeters between estimated and ground truth translation vector, mean for a pair of cameras; Rotation error (RoE) is mean angle in degrees between estimated and ground truth rotation vector; Intersection over Union (IoU) is calculated between warped playfield and template, with 100% meaning perfect projection. Dataset: internal football dataset of 35 sports events from 21 playfields, N = 2, 30 images randomly sampled from each recording giving 2100 images of high resolution (3840x2160 pixels), split into train and test sets in proportion 29:6. Experiments repeated three times and report mean and standard deviation. TABLE I CALIBRATION RESULTS: Start: Stitch 14.3 ± 3.5 px, TrE 16.2 ± 1.3 cm, RoE 2.1 ± 0.4°, IoU 96.2 ± 0.9%; Zhang [33]: 10.2 ± 1.1, 5.0 ± 0.5, 1.0 ± 0.1, 98.3 ± 0.5; DHN [40]: 2.2 ± 0.5, 12.6 ± 0.6, 1.7 ± 0.2, 97.1 ± 0.7; OTLE [4]: 8.8 ± 0.9, 6.8 ± 0.5, 1.3 ± 0.1, 97.8 ± 0.6; IHN [37]: 6.8 ± 0.8, 2.5 ± 0.4, 0.7 ± 0.1, 98.7 ± 0.4; SCPR [6]: 4.2 ± 0.6, 0.5 ± 0.1, 0.3 ± 0.0, 99.1 ± 0.4; ESC (ours): 0.3 ± 0.1, 0.2 ± 0.0, 0.1 ± 0.0, 99.4 ± 0.2. Text: ESC achieves stitch quality of 0.3 px, better than second-best method (DHN) by 1.9 px; Zhang’s 10.2 px; ESC achieves 0.2 translation, 0.1 rotation, and 99.4% IoU errors, better than second-best method (SCPR) by 0.3, 0.2, and 0.3, respectively. Real-life scenarios: three different sports fields at four different times of the day: 8:00, 12:00, 16:00, and 20:00. λ analysis: best to set λ to values close to 0.5. TABLE II ABLATION STUDY: ESC: Stitch 0.3 ± 0.1 px, TrE 0.2 ± 0.0 cm, RoE 0.1 ± 0.0°; w/o 3D model: 0.7 ± 0.2, 0.6 ± 0.1, 0.4 ± 0.1; w/o Lstitch: 3.7 ± 0.6, 0.2 ± 0.0, 0.1 ± 0.0. Text: utilizing a 3D model improves stitch quality by 0.4px and decreases stitch and rotation errors by 0.4 and 0.3, respectively; including stitch loss decreases stitch error by 3.4px. TABLE III SEGMENTATION RESULTS: mIoU (%) ↑, F1 (%) ↑; U-Net: 49.6 ± 1.2, 65.8 ± 1.7; with LeakyReLU: 51.9 ± 1.1, 68.0 ± 1.9; with Focal Loss: 55.3 ± 1.3, 71.9 ± 1.8; with both (ours): 57.3 ± 1.2, 73.6 ± 1.8. Text: LeakyReLU improves mIoU and F1 scores by 2.3% and 2.2% points, respectively; Focal Loss boosts metrics by 5.7% and 6.1%, respectively; combining both improves overall results by 7.7% and 7.8%.

data.paper_title: Comparative analysis of automated foul detection in football using deep learning architectures
data.authors: Abdallah Rabee1, Zakaria Anwar2, Ahmed AbdelMoety3, Ahmed Abdelsallam1 & Mahmoud Ali1
data.core_methodology: Comparative evaluation of eight pre-trained Deep Learning (DL) architectures — EfficientNetV2, ResNet50, VGG16, Xception, InceptionV3, MobileNetV2, InceptionResNetV2, and DenseNet121 — for binary foul vs. not foul classification. Convolutional feature extraction layers were frozen to conserve ImageNet representations; a custom classification head was added comprising a Global Average Pooling layer, a fully connected dense layer with 1024 units and Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU) activation, and a last sigmoid output layer. Models were compiled with binary crossentropy loss, Adam optimizer with learning rate 0.0001, and accuracy as the main evaluation parameter. Data were processed with TensorFlow tf.data pipelines, batch_size = 32, input images resized to 224 × 224 pixels, pixel values rescaled to [0, 1], shuffling, batching, and prefetching. Foul images were optionally cropped to annotated bounding boxes from _annotations.csv; Not Foul images used the whole frame. Dataset split used stratified sampling: 70% training (4,900 images), 20% validation (1,400 images), 10% testing (700 images); test set balanced to target 350 Foul and 350 Not Foul subject to class distribution constraints. Training used early stopping with patience 10 epochs, maximum 300 epochs, model check pointing to save the model with lowest validation loss, and a GradCAM++ visualization callback. Evaluation metrics: Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F1 Score, and Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve (AUC-ROC).
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Dataset: 7000 images; 70% training (4,900 images), 20% validation (1,400 images), 10% testing (700 images); test set target 350 Foul and 350 Not Foul; class distribution 64.1% (4487 images) Foul and 35.9% (2513 photos) Not Foul. Hyperparameters: input image size 224 × 224 pixels; batch size 32; image normalization rescaled to [0, 1]; optimizer Adam; learning rate 0.0001; loss function Binary Crossentropy; primary metric Accuracy; secondary metrics Precision, Recall, F1 Score, AUC; maximum epochs 300; early stopping patience 10 epochs; GradCAM++ samples per epoch 5 per training, validation, and test sets; train/validation/test split 70% / 20% / 10%. Equations: Accuracy = (TP + TN)/(TP + TN + FP + FN); Precision = TP/(TP + FP); Recall = TP/(TP + FN); F1-Score = 2 × Precision × Recall/(Precision + Recall); TPR = TP/(TP + FN); FPR = FP/(FP + FN). data.core_methodology: PlayGen-MoG; Mixture-of-Gaussians (MoG) output head with shared mixture weights across all agents; relative spatial attention; non-autoregressive prediction of absolute displacements from the initial formation; Formation Encoder; relative spatial attention blocks; bidirectional temporal attention; cross-attention to formation embeddings; Mixture Density Networks [2]; relative position encoding framework of Shaw et al. data.key_metrics_and_variables: Problem formulation: F ∈ R^{N×2}; N = 11 players; role identifiers r ∈ {0, . . . , 7}^N (QB, RB, FB, WR, TE, C, G, T); X ∈ R^{T×N×2}; T timesteps; forecasting conditions on X_obs ∈ R^{T_obs×N×2} spanning T_obs frames; observed trajectory window of 0.8–2.0 seconds. Eq (1): r_ij = MLP(Δx_ij, Δy_ij, ||p_i - p_j||). Eq (2): Attn(Q, K, V) = softmax(QK^T/√d_k + B_rel)V; B_rel ∈ R^{H×N×N}. Eq (3): π = softmax(MLP((1/N)Σ_{i=1}^N h_i)); π ∈ ∆M−1 shared across all players. Eq (4): L_ik = [[softplus(l_11)+ε, 0], [l_21, softplus(l_22)+ε]]; Σ_ik = L_ik L_ik^T; ε = 0.01. Eq (5): L_NLL = -1/(NT) Σ_t log Σ_{k=1}^M π_k^(t) Π_{i=1}^N N(d_i^(t); μ_ik^(t), Σ_ik^(t)); d_i^(t) = x_i^(t) − f_i. Eq (6): L_ADE = 1/(NT) Σ_{t,i} ||μ_ik*^(t) − d_i^(t)||_2; k* = arg max_k π_k^(t). Eq (7): L_ent = −H(π) = Σ_k π_k log π_k. Eq (8): L_smooth = 1/((T−1)N) Σ_{t,i} ||μ_ik*^{(t+1)} − μ_ik*^{(t)}||_2. Eq (9): L = L_NLL + λ1 L_ADE + λ2 L_ent + λ3 L_smooth; λ1 = 0.1, λ2 = 0.1, λ3 = 0.1. Eq (10): x_i^(t) = f_i + μ_ik^(t) + L_ik^(t) ε; ε ∼ N(0, I) temporally correlated noise. Generation: single mixture component k selected for entire trajectory by sampling from time-averaged weights ¯π = 1/T Σ_t π^(t). data.paper_title: Knock, knock. Who’s there?–Identifying football player jersey numbers with synthetic data
data.authors: Divya Bhargavi, Erika Pelaez Coyotl, Sia Gholami
data.core_methodology: Multi-step pipeline: pretrained person detection model Centernet (ResNet50 backbone) to detect and crop players; pretrained human pose estimation model AlphaPose (ResNet101 backbone) to identify four torso key-points (left and right hips and shoulders); expand torso keypoint coordinates 60% outward to create a bounding box around jersey numbers; crop torso. Synthetic data generators Simple2D and Complex2D. Simple2D: randomly select a number from a uniform distribution of 0 to 9, randomly scale, use color backgrounds (Red, Navy Blue, Green, Red, Yellow, White) and special font Freshman, apply Light, Medium, Hard augmentations, generate 4000 images (100 x 100 px) of each 2-digit number from 00 to 99, total 400,000 images. Complex2D: superimpose Simple2D numbers on random COCO dataset images, 400,000 images (4000 per class). Two light-weight Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) with ResNet50 architecture and deep residual connections as backbone: multi-class image classifier for two-digit number identification with 101 classes (0-99 plus unrecognizable class 100); multi-label classifier with 21 classes to detect single digits (10 digits for each side right, left plus unrecognizable class). Curriculum learning: sequential pretraining with Simple2D then Complex2D and fine-tuning with real-world football dataset. Multi-class loss Lmc = Σ_i L_i = − Σ_i y_i log ŷ_mc(X_i), with ŷ_mc(X_i)=σ(⃗Z) and σ(⃗Z)_k = e^{Z_k}/Σ_{j=0}^{100} e^{Z_j}; multi-label loss Lml = Σ_i L_i = − Σ_i y_i log ŷ_ml(X_i), with ŷ_ml(X_i)=1/(1+e^Z). Two-model ensemble.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Jersey number classes: 101 (0-99 plus 100 for unrecognizable); multi-label classes: 21 (10 digits for each side right, left plus unrecognizable). Torso keypoint area expanded 60% outward. Average torso crop size 20x25 px; jersey numbers smaller than 32x32 px; images on average 20x25px. Videos: 6 practice videos for training and additional 4 for testing; 1280x720 resolution; sampled at 1, 5 and 10 fps; used 5 fps. Generated 9,000 candidate images; 6,000 contained non-players; 3,000 labelled images usable. Simple2D: 4000 images (100 x 100 px) per 2-digit number from 00 to 99; total 400,000 images. Complex2D: 400,000 images (4000 per class). Input image sizes: optimal accuracy at 224x224 px for multi-class and 100x100 px for multi-label. Confidence threshold 0.5. Baseline accuracy 80% for both models. Simple2D + Football dataset: 0.8282 multi-class, 0.82 multi-label. Complex2D + Football dataset: 0.8306 multi-class, 0.88 multi-label. Simple2D + Complex2D + Football dataset: 0.8886 multi-class, 0.86 multi-label. Best (Multi-class + Multi-label): 0.8931 ensemble. Without synthetic data: Football dataset 0.8064 multi-class, 0.8 multi-label; Best (Multi-class + Multi-label) 0.8028. Performance improvement of 2% over baseline (82%) for both models with Simple2D; Complex2D 3% multi-class and 8% multi-label; Simple2D + Complex2D 8.8% multi-class and 6% multi-label. Accuracy increase 9% overall, 18% on low frequency numbers; 18.5% multi-class and 20% multi-label for numbers with less than 50 images; absolute accuracy 81% multi-class vs 78% multi-label. Predictions agree in 84.4% of test cases; additional improvement 0.4% by two-model ensemble. Dataset imbalance: 24% of numbers have less than 100 samples; only 5% reach 400-sample mark; duplicated data points to have 400 images; up sample test-set to maintain 20 images per number. Best multi-label model: positive accuracy improvements on 74 classes, no change in 19 classes, negative change in 8 classes (drop by 10%). Best multi-class model: positive improvements on 63 classes, no change in 21 classes, negative change in 17 classes (drop by 7%). Loss equations: Lmc = Σ_i L_i = − Σ_i y_i log ŷ_mc(X_i); ŷ_mc(X_i)=σ(⃗Z); σ(⃗Z)_k = e^{Z_k}/Σ_{j=0}^{100} e^{Z_j}; Lml = Σ_i L_i = − Σ_i y_i log ŷ_ml(X_i); ŷ_ml(X_i)=1/(1+e^Z).

feed-forward network; residual connection; learnable embeddings for categorical metadata like player positions and a binary indicator of team (offense or defense); static features fused with transformer outputs to produce latent vectors corresponding to each player; final classification head; coverage assignment additional situational features: down, distance, yard line, time left in the game, and overall team coverage scheme; ground truth team coverage scheme label provided directly as input feature during training; at inference time, a separate model [12] predicts the team coverage scheme and this prediction is used as input feature in place of ground truth label; temporal pooling layer to get average representation of each player at play level; feed-forward neural network (FFN) for final predictions; coverage assignment FFN output shape [num_defenders, 20]; target defender FFN output shape [num_defenders + targeted_receiver]; receiver-defender matchups pairwise feature concatenation of all possible receiver-defender matchups fed to FFN output shape [num_defenders, num_receivers + 1] including class for 'no matchup'; NFL NGS data from seasons 2020 through 2024; seasons 2020-2023 training and season 2024 testing; tracking data contains player and ball x,y coordinates within the field at a 10Hz sample rate; events data contains game event markers such as snap, pass forward, and pass arrival; participation data contains player roster information; PFF labels contain coverage responsibility ground truth annotation that includes individual coverage assignment, defender-receiver matchups, and target defender; play data contains metadata such as play direction and field position; extract play sequences from -30 pre-snap frames at 10 Hz to pass forward frame, where frame 0 indicates the snap frame; directional normalization where all plays are normalized to run left-to-right regardless of original play direction; angular transformation on player orientation and movement direction vectors to ensure 0° represents rightward play movement; filtering logic to remove low quality data; initially only include passing plays that contain valid snap and pass forward events; filter out plays that do not contain corresponding PFF annotations for each task; random trajectory truncation during training using 11 fixed truncation strategies combined with random truncation; 60% fixed truncation and 40% random truncation split; cross-entropy loss as fundamental training objective with task-specific adaptations; target defender model performs single-label classification across all defenders on a play; receiver-defender matchup model computes cross-entropy independently for each defender treating each as separate multi-class classification problem over receivers plus a 'no matchup' class; coverage assignment model performs independent multi-class classification for each of the 11 defensive players predicting 20 coverage responsibilities with cross-entropy computed per defender and averaged across defensive unit; target defender post-processing rules: assigning a 'no target defender' label when defense is in preventative alignment or when receptions occur behind line of scrimmage; in other low-confidence cases defaults to receiver-defender matchup model's assignment for targeted receiver classification; data.paper_title: Estimating the Win Probability in a Hockey Game
data.authors: Shudan Yang
data.core_methodology: Three models: Win Probability Algorithm Based on Statistics (WPS); Win Probability Model based on Data Mining Technique using data classification algorithms (Naive Bayes, SVM, VFDT/Hoeffding Tree, Random Tree) in Weka 3.7; Win Probability Model using Stream Mining with incremental data stream mining model (main tree classifier (MT) and auxiliary tree classifier (AT)), Massive Online Analysis (MOA), and formula P_k = (LOSS_k^MTC * ∑_{i=1}^{I} ∑_{j=1}^{J} n_ijk) / (LOSS_k^ATC * W + 1) (6-1). WPS uses leadsize, home/visitor, time, shot, penalty, miss with statistical weights. WPWL uses win/lose class labels and wp = wins_i / i. WPL uses win probability levels A,B,C,D,E,O,V,W,X,Y,Z. Stream mining uses window size 20 and threshold 1 for P_k. Algorithms named: Naive Bayes, SVM, VFDT, Hoeffding Tree, Random Tree, Random decision tree algorithm, Hoeffding bound. Cross-validation is used in data mining models. Equations: P(C_i|X) = P(X|C_i)*P(C_i)/P(X) (5-1); W·X + b = 0 (5-2); W·X + b > 0 (5-3); W·X + b < 0 (5-4); ε = sqrt(R^2 ln(1/δ) / 2n) (5-5).
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Variables: leadsize, home/visitor, time (in seconds), shot, penalty, miss. Equations: LS_i = HS_i - VS_i; S_i = Sh_i - Sv_i; P_i = Ph_i - Pv_i; M_i = Mh_i - Mv_i. WPS: leadsize mapping x: <=-4 1%, -3 10%, -2 20%, -1 40%, 0 50%, 1 60%, 2 80%, 3 90%, >=4 99%; H/V: if home x=x+5%, else x=x-5%; time: <1200 x=x*1, [1200,2400) x=x*1.1, [2400,3000) x=x*1.2, >=3000 x=x*1.5; Shot: <-20 x-10%, [-20,-10) x-4%, [-10,0) x-2%, 0 x+0, (0,10] x+2%, (10,20] x+4%, >20 x+10%; Penalty: <=-5 x+10%, [-4,4] x+0, >=5 x-10%; Miss: <=-3 x+5%, [-2,2] x+0, >=3 x-5%. WPL: time same; Shot: <-20 x-0.4, [-20,-10) x-0.2, [-10,10] x+0, (10,20] x+0.2, >20 x+0.4; Penalty: <=-5 x+0.3, [-4,4] x+0, >=5 x-0.3; Miss: <=-3 x+0.5, [-2,2] x+0, >=3 x-0.5; class type: x <=-4 Z, (-4,-3] Y, (-3,-2] X, (-2,-1] W, (-1,0) V, 0 O, (0,1) E, [1,2) D, [2,3) C, [3,4) B, >=4 A; WP level: Z 1%, Y 10%, X 20%, W 30%, V 40%, O 50%, E 60%, D 70%, C 80%, B 90%, A 99%. WPWL: wp = wins_i / i. Stream mining: P_k formula (6-1), threshold 1, W=20, 5 windows, useful events average 95 to 110. LOSS_k^MTC = T_k^MTC - F_k^MTC; LOSS_k^ATC = T_k^ATC - F_k^ATC. T_k^MTC is the number of correctly classified instances by main tree (MT), and F_k^MTC is the number of incorrectly classified instances by main tree (MT). T_k^ATC is the number of correctly classified instances by auxiliary tree (AT), and F_k^ATC is the number of incorrectly classified instances by auxiliary tree (AT). ∑_{i=1}^{I} ∑_{j=1}^{J} n_ijk is a statistical count of sufficient instances that have been observed and they belong to their respective binary classes I and J (in our model, the binary classes are win and lose). If P_k<1, we update the rule, else we keep the old rule. Data: 8 seasons NHL 2003-2014; 1230 normal games per season; about 470,000 events; average almost 400 events per game; home team won 55% games from 2007 to 2014; at 0 seconds home team's WP taken as 55%; Table 1 average 4054 home wins, 3269 visitor wins, 7324 total games, 55.4% home, 44.6% visitor. Calibration: leadsize 1 period 1 70%, period 2 76%, period 3 85%; leadsize 2 period 1 82%, period 2 88%, period 3 96%; weights 1.1 and 1.2. WPL performances: NaiveBayes 1.57s, 240846, 60.21%; SVM 201.02s, 289510, 72.38%; VFDT 16.72s, 388816, 97.20%; Random Tree 8.51s, 399979, 99.99%. MOA accuracies: Naive Bayes 63%, Random Tree 84%, Hoeffding Tree 90%. Test games: 611, 727, 757; final scores 5-3, 2-4, 4-4. Related work: Poisson scoring distribution average 2.79 goals per 60 minutes = 0.0465 goals per minute.

data.paper_title: Effects of RF Interference on Radar Receivers
data.authors: Frank H. Sanders, Robert L. Sole, Brent L. Bedford, David Franc, Timothy Pawlowitz
data.core_methodology: Interference tests and measurements on radar receivers using hardline coupling: interference and desired targets injected at the radar receiver RF front-end ahead of the first RF filter and LNA; I/N calibration in the radar IF with a spectrum analyzer using average detection and RBW matched to the radar IF, with a 3-dB increase for non-pulsed signals (I=N, I/N=0 dB) and a 20-dB peak increase for pulsed signals; on-tuned rejection (OTR) correction; target injection of fixed-amplitude pulses with ntarget = (θ/360)(Tscan/pri), usually ten targets, target power set to Pd=0.90 without interference; manual target counting by a human operator; Swerling Case 1 fluctuating target distributions for some maritime tests; meteorological radars used actual weather echoes and radar internal noise; named models and processing include the radar equation, Pd(x,n)=1−(1−x)^n, P=kTB, noise factor fn=Nout/kTB=1+ΔN/kTB, noise figure Fn=10log(fn), Smin=kTBFn(S/N)min, square-law/optimum-law/quadratic detector ψ(v)=Av^2=y, logarithmic amplifier detector, zero-crossings detector, coherent detector, MTI/Doppler processing, STC, log-FTC, AGC, CFAR, and interference rejection (IR); interference waveforms included CW, BPSK, QPSK, UWB, OFDM, CDMA, QAM, chirped-pulse, and unmodulated pulsed interference.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Executive summary: communication-type signals degrade radar performance at I/N levels between -9 dB and -2 dB; one radar lost targets at I/N = -10 dB; I/N = -6 dB caused all but one of the radars to lose targets; future weather radar improvements predicted vulnerable at I/N as low as -14 dB; pulsed interference at low duty cycles (less than about 1-3%) tolerated at I/N ratios as high as +30 dB to +63 dB; high duty cycle more than about 1-3%; low duty cycle less than 1-3%. Receiver noise figure increased by 0.5 dB when average interference power is 9.5 dB below nominal receiver noise level, and by 1 dB when average interference power is 6 dB below nominal receiver noise level. Existing I/N limits for CW and noise-like interference between -6 dB to -10 dB. Boltzmann’s constant 1.38⋅10-23 J/(K⋅Hz); at about 290 K and 1 MHz (106 Hz), inherent noise level 4⋅10-15 W, or -144 dBW, or -114 dBm; overall noise figure 10 dB easily achievable, 5 dB or less nominal; with kTB -114 dBm and noise figure 5 dB, overall noise level effectively -109 dBm. For false-alarm probability 10-6, detection probability 0.8, and Swerling case 1, required signal-to-noise ratio about 17 dB (linear factor 50:1); with nominal noise figure 5 dB (linear factor 3.16) in 1-MHz bandwidth, Smin=6.3⋅10-13 W; integrating n pulses with typically n=20 gives Smin about 10-13 W. Logarithmic receiver loss: about 0.5 dB for 10 pulses integrated, about 1.0 dB for 100 pulses integrated, maximum about 1.1 dB for indefinitely large number of pulses. A 1–dB change in threshold-to-noise or threshold-to-clutter ratio can change false alarm rate by 2 orders of magnitude; CFAR tap outputs usually 16 to 20. I/N calibration: 3-dB increase gives [I/(I+N)]=3 dB, I=N, I/N=0 dB; pulsed 20-dB increase gives [I/(I+N)]=20 dB, I/N virtually 20 dB, differing from I/N=20 dB by only 0.04 dB; Figure 12 example 57.55 MHz IF frequency. Equations: (I/N)IF = (I/N)T − OTR; OTR = 0 for BIF ≥ BT; OTR = 10log(BT/BIF) for BIF < BT; N = -114 dBm/MHz + 10log(BIF) + NF; N = -168.6 dBm + 10log(BIF) + 10log(T); Pgen = Pnoise + OTR + PL. data.paper_title: Evaluating NFL Quarterback Decision Making Through Tracking Data
data.authors: Jesse N. Melville
data.core_methodology: Replicates and extends the DeepQB framework; trains deep learning models to estimate expected completion probabilities and expected yards gained for each receiver at the moment of the throw; Model 1 (Classification) predicts pass outcome (complete, incomplete, or interception); Model 2 (Regression) predicts yards gained if the pass is completed; three-layer deep neural network (DNN) following DeepQB, with 230 hidden units per layer, ReLU activation, batch normalization, and dropout at a rate of 0.4; input 276 features per frame scaled using StandardScaler; Model 1 output softmax probabilities over three outcome classes: ˆyclf = softmax(W3 · ReLU(W2 · ReLU(W1 · x))); Model 2 output scalar expected yards: ˆyreg = W3 · ReLU(W2 · ReLU(W1 · x)); cross-entropy loss for Model 1 and mean squared error (MSE) for Model 2; Adam optimizer with learning rate 10−3; dropout (p = 0.4), batch normalization, and early stopping; batch size 64; classification model converged around 30 epochs and regression model required up to 100 epochs; calibration and sharpness analysis; bootstrapping and reported standard errors; public animation tool that overlays model predictions onto play footage; Model 3: Temporal Decision Mode (preliminary experiments only) reused Models 1 and 2 to estimate passing outcomes for each frame and added models to estimate the probability and value of holding the ball and of quarterback runs.

data.paper_title: Proper Scoring Rules
data.authors: Ed Merkle
data.core_methodology: scoring implements the beta, power, and pseudospherical families of proper scoring rules, along with ordered versions of the latter two families. Included among these families are popular rules like the Brier (quadratic) score, logarithmic score, and spherical score. Brier score decompositions, weighted Brier score, Murphy decomposition, and the ordered scoring rule strategy proposed by Jose, Nau, & Winkler (2009).
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Beta family: Log score when parameters are (0,0); Brier score when parameters are (1,1). Power family with baseline parameters all equal (to 1/(number of alternatives)): approaches the log score as gamma goes to 1 (but the family is undefined for gamma=1); Brier score is obtained for gamma=2. Pseudospherical family with baseline parameters all equal: approaches the log score as gamma goes to 1 (but the family is undefined for gamma=1); spherical score is obtained for gamma=2. roundto defaults to .1. WeatherProbs: 8976 observations on 11 variables. WorldEvents: three world events provided by seven MTurkers. Examples use bounds=c(0,1), param=1.001 for bounded log approximation, param=c(2,.5), param=c(1,1), param=c(0,0), param=c(3,.3), param=c(2,.3,.6,.1), r2 <- seq(0, .6, .05), r <- cbind(.4, r2, .6 - r2).

data.authors: Charles Xie, Aneesh Muppidi
data.core_methodology: Five models evaluated with a chronological split: symmetric Markov baseline; Elo-asymmetric Markov model; serve-shrink Markov model; histogram gradient-boosting model (HGBM) implemented with scikit-learn’s HistGradientBoostingClassifier; and Trace, a hybrid model combining predictions from the Elo-asymmetric and serve-shrink Markov models with current score and additional live features passed to a histogram gradient-boosting model (HGBM). Markov score recursion uses point-level serve probabilities and tennis scoring rules; Elo ratings are built from historical ATP and WTA results; serve-shrink uses a simplified form of the Bayesian shrinkage approach described by Colin and Bechler; evaluation uses binary log loss and calibration curves following Guo et al.; XGBoost and LightGBM were also evaluated using the same training and validation procedure.

data.paper_title: A Hybrid Approach for Tracking Individual Players in Broadcast Match Videos
data.authors: Roberto L. Castroa, Diego Andradea, Basilio Fraguelaa
data.core_methodology: Hybrid tracker combining two deep neural networks (DNN), Faster-RCNN and SSD, with the Kernelized Correlation Filter (KCF) algorithm; the three models are executed concurrently with different frequencies of execution, exchanging information to build a hybrid tracker. Faster-RCNN is executed every jump frames; SSD is executed for each of the remaining jump−1 frames; KCF performs fine-grain tracking on each frame in the ROI. KCF is adjusted when it and SSD diverge in more than 3 frames in a row. Datasets for training both networks were generated using a semiautomated tool that uses OpenCV object tracking algorithm.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Average overlap metric: Φ(ΛG, ΛT) = {Φt}N t=1, φ = (RG_t ∩ RT_t)/(RG_t ∪ RT_t); IoU above 0.5 considered successful; OPE curve; AUC is integral of OPE curve, value between 0 and 1. FasterRCNN preliminary: execution time almost constant around 45 ms; 30 fps requires 33 ms; 60 fps requires 16 ms; confidence score between 0 and 1, below 0.6 assigned average overlap 0; threshold 0.5 surpassed by around 50% of video frames; OPE above 50% in 45% of cases; AUC 0.32; subset of 200 frames; successful detection only in around a 20% of the frames. Hybrid tracker: high definition videos (1920x1080 px) at 80 fps; AUC around 0.6; at least 0.5 overlap in between 80% and 90% of frames; 4 players from 2 different soccer teams. Table 2: Player 1 Avg. Overlap 0.620, Avg. Fps 91.75, Avg. AUC 0.610, Lost frames 2; Player 2 0.653, 84.98, 0.651, 0; Player 3 0.650, 86.65, 0.660, 0; Player 4 0.600, 87.36, 0.600, 0. Jump size: jump of three frames reaches highest AUC, concretely 0.64; adjustment when KCF and SSD diverge in more than 3 frames in a row; dataset of 1500 frames labeled with the location of the player for each one of the four players.

data.paper_title: A Survey of Advanced Computer Vision Techniques for Sports
data.authors: Tiago Mendes-Nevesa,b, Lu´ıs Meirelesa,c, Jo˜ao Mendes-Moreiraa,b
data.core_methodology: Survey/review of Computer Vision techniques for sports, covering Image Recognition, Object Detection, 2D Pose Estimation, and 3D Pose Estimation. Use case methodology: collect 145 soccer shots from a single person, 6 meters from the goal, captured using 90 frames per second camera; extract pose data with CenterNet HourGlass104 1024x1024 with keypoints and ROMP; use ROMP SMPL 24-joint data; transform absolute positions to angular speeds; calculate angular speed from the moving average of the absolute position with a window of 5 frames; smooth the angular time series again using the moving average with a window of 5; use TSFresh to transform time series into features and filter to 858 features for 3D and 273 relevant features for 2D; calculate ground truth ball speed under assumptions that the ball hits the center of the left/right side of the goal and the time is between the player’s first contact and right before the ball gets occluded by the goalpost, counting frames until the ball does not register or the ball area is substantially reduced and dividing by the frame rate (90fps), with average speed calculated by dividing the average distance by the calculated time; test Linear Regression, K-Nearest Neighbors, Gradient Boosting, and Random Forest; use K-Fold Cross Validation; do not use Deep Learning due to the low ratio of instances per feature (1 instance per 5 features).
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Metrics: Intersection over Union (IoU); Average Precision (AP); Mean Average Precision (mAP); Percentage of Correct Keypoints (PCK); PCKh@0.5; Mean Per Joint Position Error (MPJPE); Mean Per Joint Angular Error (MPJAE). Equations: Intersection over Union = Area of Intersection / Area of Union (1); AP = Z 1 0 p(r)dr (2); MPJPE = 1 N N X 1 ||kp −kgt|| (3). COCO averages AP for all IoU thresholds between 0.5 and 0.95 with step 0.05; PASCAL VOC uses AP with IoU=0.5. Experimental values: 145 soccer shots; 6 meters from the goal; 90 frames per second camera; average 650 and 43 seconds to produce results for CenterNet HourGlass104 1024x1024 with keypoints and ROMP respectively; goal size 3 meters in width, 2 meters in height; assumption introduces an error of +/- 6%; error follows a uniform distribution; average error is 0%; moving average window of 5 frames; 858 features for each shot (3D); 273 relevant features (2D); 1 instance per 5 features. 3D results: Linear Regression R2=-1.84 corr=0.39; K-Nearest Neighbors R2=-0.03 corr=0.26; Gradient Boosting R2= 0.43 corr=0.65; Random Forest R2= 0.44 corr=0.67. 2D results: Linear Regression R2=-12.14 corr=0.36; K-Nearest Neighbors R2= 0.11 corr=0.4; Gradient Boosting R2= 0.23 corr=0.49; Random Forest R2= 0.28 corr=0.53. Random Forest achieves a correlation of 67% with target variable; r-squared 0.44; 67% correlation in 3D and just 53% in 2D.

data.core_methodology: Five SoccerNet 2026 challenge tasks and evaluation protocols: Ball Action Anticipation using an adaptation of mean Average Precision (mAP) at temporal tolerances δ ∈1, 2, 3, 4, 5, ∞ and mAPavg as the average of the six mAP@δ scores; winning FAANTRA-WS adapts FAANTRA with 448p frames, 64-frame clips, 0.5/0.5 observation-prediction split, RegNetY-GSF backbone, FUTR-style transformer with eight action queries, two-phase warm-start recipe, class-weighted classification and segmentation losses, ℓ1 offset regression, actionness supervision, reduced EOS weight, asymmetric logit ensembling of RegNetY-008 and RegNetY-006 checkpoints, class-wise temporal shifts, and a 10−3 confidence threshold with empty-clip rescue. Player-Centric Ball Action Spotting using macro F1-score in a low-confidence, high-recall regime with τ = 0.15 and ±12 frames, TAAD and DST baselines, and winning PAVE Per-player Attention and Voting Ensemble with ROI-aligned X3D player features, temporal transformer, per-player attention over 26 role slots, weighted event fusion, agreement filtering, and tackle-specific exception. Novel View Synthesis using PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS with PSNR for ranking, 3DGS and Triangle Splatting baselines, and winning DENSER Depth-guided Ensemble with Staged EFA-GS Reconstruction extending EFA-GS alias-free Gaussian splatting with camera-height-based loss weighting, Depth-Anything-V2 scale-and-shift-invariant depth supervision, and a three-model pixel-average ensemble from a shared 90k-iteration checkpoint; dataset created with Blender based on real soccer broadcast footage, player position inferred using inverse kinematics from 3D joint data, COLMAP camera parameters and initial point cloud. Spiideo SoccerNet Synloc using mAP-LocSim and frame accuracy, LocSim defined as eln 0.05 d2 τ2 with τ = 1 m, and winning SSS-1 Boundary-Aware Adaptive Tiling with YOLO26-Large detections, RTMPose-X two-keypoint estimator, SimCC head, Gated Attention Unit, and deterministic ray casting. Visual Question Answering using answer accuracy on a 500-question challenge split and winning task-routed VLM elicitation system with Gemini-3.1-Pro as unified reasoning engine.

data.paper_title: Graph Neural Networks to Predict Sports Outcomes
data.authors: Peter Xenopoulos, Claudio Silva
data.core_methodology: Sport-agnostic graph-based representation of game states: Gt=(Vt,Et), Vt=Xt, eij=1, ∀i,j (or eij set to the distance between player i and player j); fully-connected graph with players as nodes; permutation invariant graph neural networks; graph convolutional networks (GCNs); graph attention networks (GATs); node transformation h′i = σ(Σ_{j∈Ni} eij hj W); attention coefficient eij = exp(LeakyReLU(a^T [hiW∥hjW])) / Σ_{k∈Ni} exp(LeakyReLU(a^T [hiW∥hkW])); multi-head h′i = ∥_{k=1}^{K} σ(Σ_{j∈Ni} e^k_{ij} hj W); global average pool; Spektral library in Python; candidate models: state model, GAT-only model, GCN-only model, GAT+State model, GCN + State model; in GCN model, eij are set to the inverse of the distance between player i and player j; GAT-based models use one attention head; paired t-tests; mean squared error, mean absolute error, log loss, AUC.

data.paper_title: Training-Free Long-Term Multi-Object Tracking for Sports Video Analytics
data.authors: Tomasz Stanczyk1,2, Seongro Yoon1,2, Francois Bremond1,2
data.core_methodology: McByte++ is a training-free tracking-by-detection framework built upon ByteTrack; it uses YOLOX detectors, a Kalman filter for tracklet state propagation, Hungarian matching for bipartite association, and an IoU-based cost matrix constructed as 1 − IoU. It integrates temporally propagated segmentation masks via EdgeTAM as an auxiliary association cue under a regulated gating strategy for ambiguity and isolation, using bounding box coverage mci,j = |mask(trackleti) ∩bboxj| / |mask(trackleti)| and mask fill ratio mf i,j = |mask(trackleti) ∩bboxj| / |bboxj|, with cost update costsi,j = costsi,j IoU −mf i,j when conditions (1)-(3) are satisfied, otherwise costsi,j = costsi,j IoU. It uses conditional camera motion compensation modeled as an affine transformation estimated via ORB-based feature matching, with spatial downscaling factor ds = 4 by default. It uses online re-identification with a pretrained OSNet backbone, ℓ2-normalized appearance features, temporal aggregation favg = 1/N ∑_{i=1}^N ˜fi and ˜favg = favg / ∥favg∥2, cosine similarity sim(˜f (p),˜f (m)) = ˜f (p) · ˜f (m), and a mutual best-match criterion with similarity threshold 0.8. It maintains a long-term identity memory and can use offline GTA-link post-processing.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Metrics: HOTA, IDF1, MOTA, FPS. Mask gating thresholds: mf = 0.05; mc = 0.90. Detection confidence threshold: 0.6. CMC spatial downscaling factors evaluated: ds ∈{2, 4, 6}; default ds = 4. Re-ID similarity thresholds evaluated: {0.6, 0.7, 0.8, 0.9}; default 0.8. Equations: mci,j = |mask(trackleti) ∩bboxj| / |mask(trackleti)|; mf i,j = |mask(trackleti) ∩bboxj| / |bboxj|; costsi,j = costsi,j IoU −mf i,j if cond. (1)-(3) satisfied, otherwise costsi,j = costsi,j IoU; ˜ft = ft / ∥ft∥2; favg = 1/N ∑_{i=1}^N ˜fi; ˜favg = favg / ∥favg∥2; sim(˜f (p),˜f (m)) = ˜f (p) · ˜f (m). Abstract improvements: up to +3.0 HOTA and +6.1 IDF1 over the original McByte in the online setting; up to an order-of-magnitude speed increase. SoccerNet-tracking 2022 test: McByte++ online HOTA 87.5, IDF1 84.5, MOTA 97.1, FPS 8.69; McByte++ with GTA HOTA 88.6, IDF1 87.2, MOTA 97.1, FPS 7.46. SportsMOT test: McByte++ online HOTA 79.9, IDF1 83.6, MOTA 96.9, FPS 14.57; McByte++ with GTA HOTA 81.5, IDF1 86.0, MOTA 96.8, FPS 12.49. SoccerNet-tracking Challenge 2023: McByte++ with re-ID HOTA 64.3, IDF1 78.6, MOTA 81.8, FPS 11.13; McByte++ with GTA HOTA 65.7, IDF1 80.7, MOTA 81.7, FPS 10.06. SportsMOT validation: McByte++ online HOTA 85.5, IDF1 87.6, MOTA 98.7; McByte++ with GTA HOTA 87.2, IDF1 90.4, MOTA 98.6. Ablation: SoccerNet-tracking HOTA 84.1 to 87.5 (+3.4), IDF1 78.9 to 84.5 (+5.6) with re-ID sim th=0.8; SportsMOT HOTA 75.8 to 79.9 (+4.1), IDF1 76.0 to 83.6 (+7.6). Runtime: SoccerNet-tracking 1.04 FPS to 6.49 FPS (ds=2) and 10.51 FPS (ds=4); SportsMOT 3.60 FPS to 18.65 FPS (ds=4).

data.paper_title: Entity-Aware Sequence Transduction for Player-Centric Ball Action Spotting
data.authors: Ruifeng Wang1, Di Yang2∗, Jiangtao Wang2∗
data.core_methodology: Multi-Entity Denoising Sequence Transduction (ME-DST), an extension of Denoising Sequence Transduction (DST) and the FOOTPASS DST framework; preserves the role-slot dimension throughout encoding; factorized temporal–spatial encoding with temporal self-attention applied independently to each player trajectory (Htemp_n = TemporalAttn(H(i−1)_n)) and spatial self-attention among all role slots at every frame (Hspat_t = SpatialAttn(Htemp_t)); two identical factorized attention blocks; learnable role embeddings (h(0)t,n ← h(0)t,n + rn); sinusoidal positional encoding; two-layer multilayer perceptron with GELU activation and LayerNorm (h(0)t,n = MLP(xt,n), h(0)t,n ∈ R512); Pre-LN Transformer encoder layers with eight attention heads and hidden dimension 512; global event representation via learnable query token (Mt = LayerNorm(MHA(q, Hspat_t, Hspat_t) + q)); optional global temporal refinement; six-layer Pre-LN Transformer decoder; autoregressive event decoding over eight action classes augmented with start-of-sequence (SOS) and end-of-sequence (EOS) tokens, no explicit background token; joint action, player-role, and frame prediction heads; joint cross-entropy objective L = Laction + Lrole + Lframe; label smoothing (ϵ = 0.05); class-specific action weights; AdamW with linear learning-rate warmup followed by exponential decay; gradient checkpointing; visual predictions from TAAD branches with pretrained X3D-L and Swin3D-S backbones; one-dimensional Gaussian filter (σ = 1.5) for Swin3D-S; weighted averaging Zfused = 0.6ZX3D + 0.4ZSwin (and z = 0.6zX3D + 0.4zSwin); tracking-derived tactical features: five raw tracking attributes (normalized position (x, y), velocity (vx, vy), binary visibility indicator) and eight engineered tactical descriptors (speed f0 = q v2x + v2y; acceleration magnitude f3 = q (∇vx)2 + (∇vy)2; nearest visible teammate distance f1; nearest visible opponent distance f2; pressure index f7 defined as normalized number of opponents within radius 0.05 in pitch coordinates; Euclidean distance to goal center f4; sine and cosine of goal direction angle f5 and f6); 13-dimensional tracking representation concatenated with fused 9-dimensional visual logits to produce 22-dimensional representation per role slot; 26 predefined team-role slots (13 roles for each team); 750-frame windows; maximum decoding length 25 events; evaluation with micro-averaged precision, recall, and F1 under SoccerNet 2026 Challenge protocol; ±12 frames temporal tolerance; confidence threshold 0.15.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Main results: ME-DST Micro F1 0.778, Precision 0.792, Recall 0.765; TAAD+DST 0.675, 0.682, 0.668; TAAD 0.359, 0.256, 0.599; TAAD+GNN 0.521, 0.445, 0.627; ME-DST improves TAAD+DST by 10.3 percentage points and TAAD+GNN/TAAD by 41.9 and 25.7 percentage points in Micro F1. Evaluation: ±12 frames (±0.48 s at 25 fps), confidence threshold 0.15, 750-frame windows, 26 role slots (13 roles for each team), 22-dimensional representation, 13 tracking-derived features (five raw and eight engineered), 9-dimensional visual logits, R9×26×T, 50-frame clips, 352×640, 25 fps, σ = 1.5, fusion weights 0.6/0.4, pressure radius 0.05, dmodel = 512, eight attention heads, six-layer decoder, maximum decoding length 25 events, label smoothing ϵ = 0.05, FOOTPASS 54 matches (48 training, 3 validation, 3 testing), 102,992 frame-level annotations, eight event categories: Drive, Pass, Cross, Throw-in, Shot, Header, Tackle, and Block. Equations: z = 0.6zX3D + 0.4zSwin; Zfused = 0.6ZX3D + 0.4ZSwin (1); h(0)t,n = MLP(xt,n), h(0)t,n ∈ R512 (2); h(0)t,n ← h(0)t,n + rn (3); Htemp_n = TemporalAttn(H(i−1)_n) (4); Hspat_t = SpatialAttn(Htemp_t) (5); Mt = LayerNorm(MHA(q, Hspat_t, Hspat_t) + q) (6); L = Laction + Lrole + Lframe (7); f0 = q v2x + v2y; f3 = q (∇vx)2 + (∇vy)2; ek = (tk, ℓk, jk, ck, sk), ℓk ∈ {0, 1}. Ablations: visual fusion without tactical features 0.667 to 0.710; with 3-dim tactical features 0.670 to 0.715; +0.3 percentage points for X3D-L and +0.5 percentage points for fused representation; highest 0.715. Temporal preprocessing: Conv1D 0.710, Transformer 0.708, GRU 0.703; differences within 0.7 percentage points; best 0.714. Feature dimensionality: flat DST no tactical 0.710, 3-dim 0.715, 8-dim 0.708; multi-entity 3-dim 0.758, 8-dim 0.778. Encoder components: base 0.736; removing global refinement 0.778; removing spatial attention 0.733; removing role embeddings 0.569 (reduction 16.7 percentage points); 1 block 0.749; 1 block no refine 0.753. Per-class: Cross +0.216, Header +0.211, Block +0.173, Drive +0.129, Pass +0.094, Throw-in +0.005, Tackle F1 0.044; overall +0.111; class substitutions 224 to 200; recall ball-visible 0.760 to 0.826, ball-hidden 0.391 to 0.480, replay 0.474 to 0.513, live-play 0.720 to 0.794; ball-hidden +8.9 percentage points. Overall X3D-L+DST P/R/F1 0.678/0.656/0.667, TP 3981, FN 2089; ME-DST P/R/F1 0.792/0.765/0.778, TP 4646, FN 1424.

data.paper_title: ARC-SORT: Adaptive, Robust, Compensated Multi-Object Tracking with Interacting Multiple Models
data.authors: Girish Kumar Adari
data.core_methodology: Tracking-by-detection; ARC-SORT (Adaptive, Robust, Compensated SORT); Interacting Multiple Model (IMM) Kalman filter; uncertainty-adaptive Expansion IoU (EIoU); constant-velocity (CV) model; constant-acceleration (CA) model; coordinated-turn (CT) model with turn rate ω handled by an extended Kalman filter (EKF) with analytic Jacobian; IMM cycle of mixing, per-model prediction, log-space probability update, and combination; reduced-state approximation of textbook IMM; camera motion compensation (CMC) using a 4-DOF similarity transform estimated per frame pair by sparse optical flow (1,000 corners, pyramidal Lucas–Kanade, 2× downscale, RANSAC, identity fallback); CMC-corrected re-update; observation-centric re-update (ORU); observation-centric momentum (OCM); observation-centric recovery (OCR); BYTE second pass; deferred identity commitment using the assignment permutation margin, two-hypothesis corrective swap, and von Mises–Fisher observation model; appearance-only tracklet merge with union-find and greedy descending prototype cosine order; OSNet embeddings; YOLOX-X detector; FastReID SBS-S50 for DanceTrack rows

data.paper_title: Domestic Violence and Football in Glasgow: Are Reference Points Relevant?
data.authors: Alex Dickson, Colin Jennings, Gary Koop
data.core_methodology: Count data regression models using Poisson versions (Stata’s poisson and xtmepoisson commands); fixed effects panel data model; random effects panel data models; mixed effects Poisson model with Pr(y_it = y | α_i) = exp(−λ_it) λ_it^y / y! and λ_it = exp(Z_t β + W_t α_i), where α_i has a multivariate Normal distribution with diagonal error covariance matrix; negative binomial regression methods; robust standard errors; pre-match betting odds used to calculate average (across all available bookmakers) pre-match probability and classify outcomes relative to pre-game expectations (q ≥0.7 vs q <0.7).
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Data: 30 police subdivisions; 3200 days; 1st January 2003 to 5th October 2011; 328 Celtic games; 329 Rangers games; 35 Old Firm matches (Celtic won 17, Rangers won 13, draw 5); other matches Celtic won 222, drew 43, lost 28; Rangers won 213, drew 53, lost 28. Summary: all days mean 64.46, SD 22.0, min 12, max 225; over-dispersed mean 65.4, variance 485.5. Model coefficients: xmas ny consistently around 0.33, signifying a 33% increase; Old Firm effect in model (A2) average domestic violence increases by some 36%; overall Old Firm effect 28-41% depending on outcome; oldfirm draw 0.388***; oldfirm close 0.410***; oldfirm rlose 0.285***; Old Firm effect highest at 41% when Celtic lose and lowest at 29% when Rangers lose. Important games: Celtic predicted to win and draw domestic violence increases by 37% (p-value 0.008) compared to a reduction of 6.5% in non-important games; Celtic predicted to win but lose increases by 21% (p-value=0.104); Rangers predicted to win and draw increases by some 24%; Rangers tight and lose significant 16% (p-value=0.028); Rangers expected draw negative 9% (p-value=0.027); Celtic favourite and draw against traditional rival 15% increase (p-value=0.038). Extended importance: Rangers losing games expected tight 16% based on a single match; average midweek 2008 61.5; following Rangers’ defeat on 22nd May 2008 there were 77 reported domestic violence incidents. Equations: Pr(y_it = y | α_i) = exp(−λ_it) λ_it^y / y!; λ_it = exp(Z_t β + W_t α_i).

data.paper_title: Can Geometry Save Central Views for Sports Field Registration?
data.authors: Floriane Magera1,2, Thomas Hoyoux1, Martin Castin1, Olivier Barnich1, Anthony Cioppa2, Marc Van Droogenbroeck2
data.core_methodology: A fully geometric bottom-up approach that converts a circle correspondence into point and line correspondences for homography estimation via direct linear transform (DLT) or a Perspective-n-Point (PnP) solver. It uses the pole-polar relationship of conics, the ellipse E = H−T C H−1, the projected circle center c = H o, and the vanishing line lvanishing = E c. Three cases are defined: Case 1: Line correspondence (v = l1 × lvanishing; l2 = v × c; l3 = E v), Case 2: Point correspondence (l1 = x × c; v = E l1; l2 = v × c), and Case 3: Unknown center, using concentric circles and the eigenvector of the E2−1E1 matrix. The method is combined with the calibration algorithm of PnLCalib. Experiments use TVCalib semantic segmentation, Fitzgibbon’s method for ellipse fitting, RANSAC, Canny’s edge detector, Theiner’s line segmentation neural network, zero-centered Gaussian noise, and synthetic pinhole cameras converted to homographies mapping the synthetic image to the top-view soccer field template with the playfield located in the plane Z = 0.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: JaC5 (↑) [%], MRE (↓) [px], CR (↑) [%]; TVCalib [38]: 10.2, 28.8, 100; PnLCalib [21]: 22.4, 12.8, 79.5; PnLCalib*: 22.4, 12.9, 79.5. MRE = 1/N Σ_i ||H xi − Hhat xi||_2. OOD test set: 300 central views; SoccerNet test set: 8,565 images; PnLCalib predicts 8 points on the center circle; method gives 8 point correspondences and 8 lines from their tangents; field marking thickness about ten centimeters; synthetic field marking thickness 8 centimeters; 8 points along the inner and outer ellipses; full-HD (1080p); σ between 0 and 25 pixels; 100 randomly generated cameras; dictionary size e.g., 450 samples; JaC5 at 5 pixels.

data.paper_title: Padded Helmet Shell Covers in American Football: A Comprehensive Laboratory Evaluation with Preliminary On-Field Findings
data.authors: Nicholas J. Cecchi1*, Ashlyn A. Callan1*, Landon P. Watson1, Yuzhe Liu1, Xianghao Zhan1, Ramanand V. Vegesna2, Collin Pang1, Enora Le Flao1, Gerald A. Grant3,4,5, Michael M. Zeineh6, David B. Camarillo1,3,7
data.core_methodology: Laboratory helmet impact testing with a pneumatic linear impactor (Biokinetics and Associates Ltd.; Ottawa, Ontario, Canada) impacting a helmeted 50th percentile male Hybrid III headform mounted on a sliding table; three helmet models (Riddell Speedflex Diamond, Xenith X2E+, Schutt Vengeance Pro LTD) with and without the Guardian Cap padded helmet shell cover; six impact locations (Side, Oblique Rear, Side Upper, Oblique Front, Facemask Side, Facemask Central Oblique); three impact velocities (3.5, 5.5, and 7.4 m/s); three repeat impacts per helmet-location-velocity combination; identical padded helmet shell cover on the linear impactor end cap. Repeated impact testing: 100 consecutive impacts to the oblique front location at 3.5 m/s with a Riddell Speedflex Diamond helmet and padded helmet shell cover on both helmet and impactor end cap, approximately 80 seconds between impacts. Sensors: DTS A64C accelerometers, DTS ARS PRO-8k gyroscopes, DTS 6DX Pro sensor, DTS SLICEWare software, SLICE MICRO data acquisition system at 20,000 Hz. Processing: fourth-order Butterworth filter at 300 Hz; five-point stencil derivative for angular acceleration; peak linear acceleration (PLA) and peak angular acceleration (PAA); Diffuse Axonal Multi-Axis General Evaluation (DAMAGE) calculated according to equations described by Gabler et al.18; Head Acceleration Response Metric (HARM) calculated according to equations described by Bailey et al.4. Vertical drop testing: twin-wire drop apparatus; nine identical sample sections cut from the crown of padded helmet shell covers; force plate (430_00_LCEL; Cadex Inc; St-Jean-sur-Richelieu, Canada); impacted at 2.0 m/s by a 2.5kg dropping mass; ambient 21ºC, cold -18ºC, hot 50ºC; 18-hour exposure; testing within 90 seconds; three consecutive impacts at ambient with 80 seconds between impacts; repeated twice after 24 hours; six trials per condition; 2nd-order low-pass Butterworth filter with cut-off frequency 300 Hz; peak force. On-field data collection: MiG2.0 instrumented mouthguards (Stanford University; Stanford, CA); triaxial accelerometer at 1000 Hz and triaxial gyroscope at 8000 Hz; 200 ms time window upon linear acceleration exceeding 10 g threshold (50 ms pre-trigger, 150 ms post-trigger); MiGNet deep learning algorithm; visual verification using 1080p resolution and 60 frames per second video from four camera angles simultaneously with a world clock; only helmet-to-helmet impacts retained; shell vs facemask classification; fourth-order Butterworth filter at 160 Hz; five-point stencil derivative; PLA, PAA, DAMAGE, and HARM calculated. Statistical analyses in Prism 9.0.1 (Graphpad Software, Inc; San Diego, CA): twelve two-way ANOVAs for shell locations and twelve two-way ANOVAs for facemask locations; simple main effects analysis; one-way ANOVA for repeated drop impact count; simple linear regression for HARM across 100 consecutive impacts; one-way ANOVA for temperature; separate Mann-Whitney tests for on-field PLA, PAA, DAMAGE, and HARM; Tukey’s multiple comparisons tests.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Impact velocities: 3.5, 5.5, and 7.4 m/s; all impacts within +/- 2% of target impact velocity. HARM reductions across all impact locations and helmet models: average 25% at 3.5 m/s (range: 9.7 – 39.6%), 18% at 5.5 m/s (range: -5.5% – 40.5), and 10% at 7.4 m/s (range: -6.0 – 31.0%). 33 of 36 helmet shell test conditions had lower average HARM with padded cover; all 18 facemask test conditions had lower average HARM. Repeated drop testing: 3% increase in mean peak force after two impacts compared to one impact (p = 0.047); 5% increase after three impacts compared to one impact (p = 0.002); second vs third impacts p = 0.276; one-way ANOVA F(2, 15) = 9.125, p = 0.003. Full helmet repeated impacts: HARM values ranged from 1.55 to 1.79; simple linear regression slope not significantly different from zero; R2 = 0.04187, p = 0.830. Temperature: 13% difference between means in peak force at cold and hot conditions (p = 0.011); cold vs ambient p = 0.072; ambient vs hot p = 0.597; one-way ANOVA F(2, 15) = 6.080, p = 0.012. data.paper_title: Multiple Object Tracking with Siamese Track-RCNN
data.authors: Bing Shuai, Andrew G. Berneshawi, Davide Modolo, and Joseph Tighe
data.core_methodology: Siamese Track-RCNN, a two stage detect-and-track framework with three functional branches: (1) detection branch localizes object instances; (2) Siamese-based track branch estimates object motion; (3) object re-identiﬁcation branch re-activates previously terminated tracks. Built on Faster-RCNN with Region Proposal Network (RPN), multi-class cross entropy loss, and smooth ℓ1-loss. Track branch uses a fully connected network φ inspired by GOTURN, matching target template feature map ftargett and search region feature map fsearcht+δ. Re-id branch is a fully-connected network trained with triplet loss. Backbone: ResNet-101 with feature pyramid network and deformable convolutions (ResNet-101-DCN). Uses ROI Align layer, stochastic gradient descent, and an online solver. data.paper_title: A PageRank Model for Player Performance Assessment in Basketball, Soccer and Hockey
data.authors: Shael Brown
data.core_methodology: A PageRank model based on Google's PageRank and Markov chain theory. A directed graph (digraph) is built for a game with one node for each of the n players plus one additional goal node. Arcs between player nodes indicate a pass in reverse order; turnovers are dealt with separately. For same-team pass from player i to player j, an arc is drawn from node j to node i; if players are on separate teams and player i loses the ball/puck to player j, an arc is drawn from node i to node j; if player i scores, the sport-specific value of the score is the number of arcs drawn from the goal node to node i. The digraph is initialized with arcs in both directions between each player node and the goal node, plus a loop from the goal node to itself. Sport-specific rules for basketball, soccer, and hockey address fouls, out-of-bounds, play-stoppages, turnovers, missed shots, and defensive plays. Additional arcs ensure the associated matrix is primitive, so there is a unique PageRank vector. The PageRank vector of the associated matrix is used to rate and rank

data.core_methodology: End-to-end natural-language agentic search workflow orchestrated with LangGraph and surfaced through a React front-end, implemented in the AWS ecosystem using Amazon Bedrock converse API, Redis memory, and OpenSearch. A low-latency model such as Claude 3 Haiku assesses user intent; the LLM extracts Entities, Actions, and Conditions; a router LLM selects relevant NGS schema(s); an API-formulation LLM maps actions and conditions to fields and emits OpenSearch API calls; a python runner executes the API call and an LLM summarizes returned results. Semantic caching stores prior queries and responses with player/team names redacted and replaced by placeholders such as “[PLAYER]” and “[TEAM]”, using vector search to find similar queries. Upon syntax failure, the LLM attempts auto-correct using error messages, and if the final API call still fails after three tries, the model prompts the user to rephrase the original query. Play IDs are serialized and sent to NFL’s MAM system to retrieve unique URLs for each asset.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: 240 Question and Answer (QA) pairs; 30% easy questions, 50% medium questions, 20% complex questions; 100 questions set aside for the test set; over 95-percent accuracy; over 95% accuracy on the 100 QA pairs; 250 users onboarded within the first month; average time reduced from 10 minutes to 30 seconds; down from over 10 minutes per query; nearly 6 times faster for simple searches; up to 20 times faster as search complexity increases; NGS captures every play from every NFL game since 2016; 184 million domestic and 100 million international fans; auto-correct after three tries.

data.core_methodology: Machine learning framework integrating team-level historical data with player-specific performance metrics such as goals, assists, passing accuracy, and tackles; processes multi-year data to create year-specific team profiles; binary classification task focusing on whether Team A wins or Team B wins and excluding draws; label encoding, feature engineering, standardization of aggregated features, dimensionality reduction using Principal Component Analysis (PCA), k-fold cross-validation (with k=5), hyperparameter optimization, and majority voting among multiple classifiers. Baseline model uses historical FIFA World Cup match data dating back to 1930; if two teams have played five or more matches historically, the team with the higher total number of wins is predicted to be victorious; if fewer than five matches exist, the baseline employs a Weighted Win Ratio (WWR) formula: WWR = (v/(v + m)) × R + (m/(v + m)) × C, where v is the total number of matches a team has played, R is its win ratio (computed as total wins divided by v), m is a threshold parameter, and C is the overall win ratio computed across all teams.

data.paper_title: MuyBridge: Mobile Human Center-of-Mass Estimation from Monocular Video via Sparse Fusion
data.authors: Aidan Bradshaw, Marco Giordano, David Rode, Andreas Habersack, Elif Basokur, Annika Kruse, Markus Tilp, Michele Magno, Peter Wolf, Luca Benini, Christoph Leitner
data.core_methodology: Segmental anthropometric CoM model of Zatsiorsky and Seluyanov as re-expressed by de Leva, with sex-specific de Leva segment mass fractions and longitudinal CoM positions; cs = pprox_s + ρ_s(pdist_s − pprox_s), C = Σ_s m_s c_s / Σ_s m_s. MuyBridge couples a compact 2D pose network (RTMPose-style; RTMDet person detector; CSPNeXt backbone; gated attention unit; SimCC regression head) predicting 26 Halpe-26 keypoints on 256 × 192 crops with a single-step monocular depth network (Marigold-based latent depth model: VAE encoder, denoising UNet, VAE decoder; latent consistency distillation to one UNet evaluation) through analytic metric fusion. Sparse keypoint-depth measurements: camera ray df,j ∝ K−1[uf,j, vf,j, 1]^T; sampled depth zf,j = Zf(uf,j, vf,j); retained samples summarized as z̃f = median_{j∈Vf} zf,j. Metric range: tsize_f,k = Lk / ||df,i − df,j|| with known de Leva segment length Lk scaled by stature or replaced by a measured length, aggregated using a fixed low quantile; ground-contact ray–ground intersection; ballistic motion relating image-space acceleration to gravity; affine-invariant depth anchored by (α, β) = arg min_{α,β} Σ_{f∈A} wf(α z̃f + β − tanchor_f)^2, giving tdepth_f = α z̃f + β; anthropometric, physical, and depth-derived measurements fused with a constant-velocity range model to obtain t̂f. data.paper_title: The role of actively open-minded thinking in information acquisition, accuracy, and calibration
data.authors: Uriel Haran, Ilana Ritov, Barbara A. Mellers
data.core_methodology: Three online studies using Amazon.com Mechanical Turk. data.paper_title: Hand Held Multi-Object Tracking Dataset in American Football
data.authors: Rintaro Otsubo, Kanta Sawafuji, and Hideo Saito
data.core_methodology: Built the first American football MOT dataset from live university-level matches between K-University’s American football team and five opposing teams, captured by two hand-held cameras: Tight view and Wide view; selected two plays from each of five universities, resulting in 10 plays with both tight and wide views; used CVAT annotation tool to annotate bounding boxes and assign unique IDs to players and referees; maximum of 26 bounding boxes per frame; split into train set, val set, and test set in a 5:3:2 ratio. Used a detection-by-tracking approach; fine-tuned YOLO models from version 8 to version 12, as well as RTDETR-x and RTDETR-l, for player detection; compared pretrained and fine-tuned YOLO and RTDETR (Real-Time Detection Transformer) models; fine-tuned re-identification models OSNet and CLIP; compared MOT models BoostTrack, BoT-SORT (Bag of Tricks for SORT), ByteTrack, DeepOCSORT, Imprassoc, OCSORT, and StrongSORT. Training used PyTorch on two NVIDIA TITAN RTX GPUs each with 24 GB of memory and CUDA 10.1. Detection fine-tuning: 50 epochs, batch size 16, input image resolution 640×640, initial learning rate 0.01 scaled down by a factor of 0.01; evaluation metrics Recall, Precision, and mAP. Re-identification fine-tuning: 50 epochs, batch size 32, initial learning rate 3e-4; tracking evaluation metrics HOTA, MOTA, and IDF1. Used RTDETR-l and YOLOv10m for comparison in ablation; used fine-tuned YOLOv10m as detector and fine-tuned OSNet as re-identification feature extractor in MOT model comparison. Analyzed tracklet length distribution, described as left-skewed; covers three main actions run, pass, and punt and three temporal states Huddle, Playing, and Camera Zoom.
