data.core_methodology: Machine Learning (ML) algorithms; Random Forest classifier; Support Vector Machine (SVM); K-Nearest Neighbor (KNN); Extreme Gradient Boost (XGB); Recursive Feature Elimination (RFE); correlation matrix; grid search or randomized search; web scraping; 1x2 (win-draw-win) odds formula Odds = 1/P; evaluation metrics: Accuracy Score, Confusion Matrix, Classification Report; Python programming language; Jupyter Notebook development environment.

data.paper_title: Order and nFl Behavior in UCu4Pd
data.authors: A. Weber, S. K¨orner, and E.–W. Scheidt, S. Kehrein, G.R. Stewart
data.core_methodology: Experimental methodology: annealing as a control parameter; arc–melting under a highly purified argon atmosphere; splat cooling; X–ray powder diffraction; ac–susceptibility measurements; resistivity measurements; specific heat measurements; χ2–analysis. Models/fits: Landau’s Fermi liquid theory; non–Fermi liquid (nFl) behavior; quantum critical point (QCP) scenario; Griﬃths phase model with power–law behavior C/T ∝T −1+λ with λ < 1; Kondo disorder model presupposing a distribution of microscopic exchange couplings; two–parameter logarithmic fit a1 + a2 ln T; three–parameter power–law fit a′1 + a′2 T −1+λ; Fermi liquid expansion ρ−ρr = A T 2 +B T 4.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: γ = C/T = ∆T −δ (∆= 450 mJ moleK2−δ , δ = 0.32); power law between 1 and 10 K; same δ between 1.8 K and 10 K; linearly below 10 K; TN ≈170 mK (unannealed UCu4Pd); ≈140 mK (7 days annealed); < 0.08 K (best ordered); x ≈0.85; 76 % of Pd atoms on 4c sites and remaining 24 % on 16e sites; weight loss 0.2 %; annealed seven days at 750 ◦C and 14 days at 750 ◦C; splat cooling rate more than 104 K/s; resistivity ratio between T=1.8 K and T=400 K decreases by 11%; χ2 = 9.0 and χ2 = 6.1 for T < 10K and T < 1K, resp.; λ →1.0; with λ = 0.9, χ2 ≈80 for T < 10K and χ2 ≈10 for T < 1K; Kondo–like minimum at about 35 K; ρ−ρr = A T 2 +B T 4 between 2 K and 8 K; ρr = 141.5µΩcm; A = −0.024µΩcm K−2; B = −0.00013µΩcm K−4; upturn by about 0.5% below 1 K with maximum at 70 mK; ac–susceptibility maxima at 65 mK (7 days annealed) and at 55 mK (14 days annealed); frequencies 95Hz, 995Hz; full width at half maximum 0.39◦, 0.31◦, 0.27◦, 0.25◦ with ±0.01◦ accuracy; no impurity phases within 1% accuracy; no weight loss within 0.1% accuracy; x ≤0.8 and x ≥1.1.

data.paper_title: New Theoretical Insights and Algorithmic Solutions for Reconstructing Score Sequences from Tournament Score Sets
data.authors: Bowen Liu
data.core_methodology: Tournament graphs; score sequence as sequence of out-degrees; degree set D = {α_i | α_i ∈ N, α_i ≥ 0, i =∈{1, . . . , n}}; exponent set E = {x_i | x_i ∈ N, x_i ≥ 1, i =∈{1, . . . , n}}; Landau’s theorem; Theorem 2 reformulation; necessary and sufficient condition (Theorem 3); necessary condition (Theorem 4); group-theoretic extension (Theorem 5) using sol = {s_i | s_i = ((2α_n + 1 − 2i)i) mod (α_n − α_{n−1}), i =∈{0, 1, . . . , α_n − α_{n−1} − 1}}, grp = {g_i | g_i = (α_n − α_i) mod (α_n − α_{n−1}), i =∈{1, 2, . . . , n − 1}}, and mingen = {m_i | m_i = gcd(g_i, g_{i+1}, . . . , g_{n−2}, g_{n−1}, α_n − α_{n−1}), i =∈{1, . . . , n − 1}}; dynamic programming; polynomial-time algorithm (Algorithm 1: first part of building net, second part of building net, part for find all correct score sequences, reconstruction of score sequence); scalable algorithm (Algorithm 3: first part of reconstruction score sequence, second part of reconstruction score sequence); Theorem 12; Algorithm 2 Control Algorithm; Hole-Shift algorithm special case.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Landau: S = s1, s2, . . . , sm is a score sequence of an m-tournament if and only if Σ_{i=1}^k s_i ≥ k(k−1)/2, ∀k ∈ N, 1 ≤ k ≤ m, with equality when k = m; Example S = {0, 1, 3, 3, 3, 5} for k = 3: Σ_{i=1}^k s_i = 4, k(k−1)/2 = 3, 4 ≥ 3; Example D = {0, 1, 3, 5}, E = {1, 1, 3, 1}; p_i = Σ_{k=1}^i x_k, p0 = 0; q_i = Σ_{k=1}^i α_k · x_k, q0 = 0; Theorem 2: Σ_{i=1}^k α_i · x_i ≥ (Σ_{i=1}^k x_i)(Σ_{i=1}^k x_i − 1)/2, ∀k ∈ N, 1 ≤ k ≤ n, with equality holding when k = n; Theorem 3: ∀k ∈ N, 1 ≤ k ≤ n, 1 ≤ x_k ≤ ((2(α_k − p_{k−1}) + 1) + √((2(α_k − p_{k−1}) + 1)^2 + 8(q_{k−1} − p_{k−1}(p_{k−1} − 1)/2)))/2, and q_{k−1} − p_{k−1}(p_{k−1} − 1)/2 ≥ 0, with the right side of the inequality becoming equal when k = n; Δ = (2(α_k − p_{k−1}) + 1)^2 + 8(q_{k−1} − p_{k−1}(p_{k−1} − 1)/2); Theorem 4: ∃f ∈ N, f ≤ (2α_n + 1)/2, (2α_n + 1 − 2f)f = Σ_{i=1}^{n−1}(α_n − α_i)x_i; Theorem 6: ∀k ∈ {1, 2, . . . , n}, p_k ≤ 2α_k + 1, q_k ≤ α_k(2α_k + 1); Theorem 7: O(nα4 n) time and space, O(nα3 n) space for reconstructing score sequence; Example D = {2, 4, 7, 14}: 1 ≤ x1 ≤ 5, if x1 = 5 then x2 ≤ 0, no valid score sequence where x1 ≥ 4; Algorithm 2 Control Algorithm loops: i1 from 1 to size_of_score_set, i2 from 1 to 2 × maximum_of_scores + 1, i3 from 1 to 2 × maximum_of_scores + 1, i4 from 1 to (2 × maximum_of_scores + 1) × maximum_of_scores, Const from 1 to 8; Table 3 Time [s]: 0.003, 0.001, 0.003, 0.002, 0.008, 0.005, 0.008, 0.008, 0.006.

data.paper_title: Bye-Bye, Bye Advantage: Estimating the competitive impact of rest differential in the National Football League
data.authors: Michael J. Lopez, Thompson Bliss
data.core_methodology: Bayesian state space models on both game outcomes and betting market data; Bayesian state-space models with time-varying team strength estimates; extensions of paired comparison models; 2011 CBA change treated as a natural experiment; Models 1-4 fit using Stan with Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC), 4 parallel chains of 3000 iterations and a burn in of 1000 draws; weakly informative prior distributions; rest indicators I(MNF), I(Mini), I(Bye); log pointwise predictive density (ELPD) estimated via leave-one-out cross validation. Model 1, Constant Bye Effect, Point Differential: E[Ys,ij] = θs,i −θs,j + µHA,s + αMNF × I(MNF) + αMini × I(Mini) + αBye × I(Bye). Model 2, Pre/Post CBA Bye Effect, Point Differential: E[Ys,ij] = θs,i −θs,j + µHA,s + αMNF × I(MNF) + αMini × I(Mini)+ αBye,pre × I(Bye) × I(S ≤2010) + αBye,post × I(Bye) × I(S ≥2011). Model 3, Constant Bye Effect, Point Spread: E[Zs,ij] = θs,i −θs,j + µHA,s + αMNF × I(MNF) + αMini × I(Mini) + αBye × I(Bye). Model 4, Pre/Post CBA Bye Effect, Point Spread: E[Zs,ij] = θs,i −θs,j + µHA,s + αMNF × I(MNF) + αMini × I(Mini)+ αBye,pre × I(Bye) × I(S ≤2010) + αBye,post × I(Bye) × I(S ≥2011). Home advantage: µHA,s = (αHA Trend × s + αHA Intercept) × I(HA); team strength: θ(s,i) ∼N(γ × θ(s−1,i), σ2 teamstrength). Priors: θ2002,i ∼N(0, σ2 teamstrength) ∀i; σteamstrength ∼HalfNormal(0, 52); σgame ∼HalfNormal(0, 52); γ ∼Uniform(0, 1); αHA Trend ∼N(0, 52); αHA Intercept ∼N(0, 52); αMNF ∼N(0, 52); αMini ∼N(0, 52); αBye ∼N(0, 52); αBye,pre ∼N(0, 52); αBye,post ∼N(0, 52).
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Outcome variables: point differential Ys,ij and pre-game point spread Zs,ij; team strength parameters θs,i and θs,j; home advantage µHA,s = (αHA Trend × s + αHA Intercept) × I(HA); rest coefficients αMNF, αMini, αBye, αBye,pre, αBye,post; rest indicators I(MNF), I(Mini), I(Bye). Model 2: Pr(αBye,post < αBye,pre)=0.966; Model 4: Pr(αBye,post > αBye,pre)=0.988. Bye pre-CBA: 99.6% probability positive, best estimate +2.21 points per game (95% credible interval, 0.61 to 3.80). Bye post-CBA: 67.9% probability positive, median +0.31 points per game (95% credible interval, -1.01 to 1.64). Betting market Bye: +0.39 points per game (95% credible interval, 0.00 to 0.78) pre CBA; +0.97 points per game (95% credible interval, 0.65 to 1.28) post CBA. Model 1 Bye: +1.11 points per game (95% credible interval, 0.07 to 2.15). Mini bye Model 2: +0.48 points per game (95% credible interval, -0.65 to 1.57); Model 4: -0.06 (95% credible interval, -0.33 to 0.21), with 31.8% probability of positive impact on point spread. MNF Model 2: +0.14 points per game (95% credible interval, -0.86 to 1.18); Model 4: 99.9% chance of significant impact on betting lines, best estimate +0.37 points per game (95% credible interval, 0.14 to 0.61); discussion states +0.18 points per game for point differential model. Figure 6: median decline in point differential value of nearly 1.9 points per game; point spread increased by roughly 0.6 points per game. Home advantage: Model 2 2023 +1.65 points per game; Model 4 2023 point spread 1.74 points per game; each of Models 1 to 4 suggest a decline of roughly a point per game. ELPD model comparison: Model 2 vs Model 1 difference -0.26, SE 1.80, # SE 0.14; Model 4 vs Model 3 difference -2.54, SE 2.00, # SE 1.27. Data: 5679 regular season NFL games from 2002 to 2023; 256 games per season from 2002 to 2020, 272 per season in 2021 and 2023, and 271 in 2022; 52 games (0.9% percent) dropped. Rest counts: MNF 410 away teams and 290 home teams; 526 Mini and 593 Bye advantages; roughly 80 percent of Mini bye rest edges came after 2011. Baselines: home teams with equivalent rest average point differential +2.69 from 2002 to 2010 and +1.83 from 2011 to 2023; home teams with Bye advantage +4.45 from 2002 to 2010 and +1.76 from 2011 to 2023; decline in Bye benefit from +1.76 to -0.07 for the home team. Cover percentages: 55.8% home teams with a bye advantage, 56.9% road teams with a bye advantage from 2002 to 2010; post 2011 home teams with a Bye edge covered 44.6%, away teams 52.7%.

data.paper_title: EXPLAINABLE EXPECTED GOAL MODELS FOR PERFORMANCE ANALYSIS IN FOOTBALL ANALYTICS
data.authors: Mustafa Cavus∗, Przemysław Biecek
data.core_methodology: Expected goal (xG) model as a supervised binary classification task: X ⊆ R^d, Y ∈ {0,1}, f: X → Y (1), minimizing L(f) = P[Y≠f(X)]; dataset D = {(xi, yi)}n_i=1 independently sampled from joint distribution with density p(x, y). xG calculation (Algorithm 1): Train an xG model y ∼ f(Xi); for i ← 1 to ni predict f(Xi); xGplayer/team = Σ_{i=1}^{ni} f(Xi). Standardized football pitch L = 105m × W = 68m; shot location coordinates Li ∈ [0,1] and Wi ∈ [0,1]; pre-processing calculates distance XDT G_i = p [105 −(Li × 105)]2 + [34 −(Wi × 68)2] (2) and angle XAT G_i = |a_i / b_i × 180/π| (3), where a_i = arctan[7.32 × [105 −(Li × 105)]] and b_i = [105 −(Li × 105)]2 + [34 −(Wi × 68)]2 −(7.32/2)2. Train tree-based classification models from XGBoost, randomForest, LightGBM, and CatBoost libraries using the forester AutoML tool; train-test split (80-20); performance measures calculated for models trained on train, over-sampled train, and under-sampled train set. Handle imbalanced target (90%-10%) by random over-sampling via ROSE package, a smoothed bootstrap-based technique proposed by Menardi and Torelli. Use DALEX for model explanation. Introduce aggregated profiles (AP) as averaging of ceteris-paribus (CP) profiles: g^j_AP(z) = E_{-j X}[f(X_j|z)] (4); estimator ĝ^j_AP(z) = 1/k Σ_{i=1}^k f(x_ij|z) (5), where k is the number of profiles aggregated; AP differs from partial dependence profile (PDP), which aggregates all profiles on the entire dataset. Compare behavior of original, over-sampled, and under-sampled models using PDP curves for some features. Data collected from Understat by using the R-package worldfootballR.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Dataset: 315,430 shots; 33,656 goals ∼10.66% of total shots; 12,655 matches; 7 seasons between 2014-15 and 2020-21; top-five European football leagues (Serie A, Bundesliga, La Liga, English Premier League, Ligue 1); excluded 1,012 shots resulting in own goals. Conversion percent of all leagues 0.107; Bundesliga 0.112; Serie A 0.103. Distance to goal range 0-25 meters; optimal angle to goal about 30°. Example xG: three shots with probabilities 0.50, 0.20, and 0.05 = 0.75 xG. Proposed random forest (over-sampling): Recall 0.958, Precision 0.922, F1 0.940, Accuracy 0.939, AUC 0.985, Mathews correlation coefficient (MCC) 0.879, Brier Score 0.071, Log-loss 0.270, Balanced Accuracy 0.939; Table 4: Precision 0.922, Recall 0.958, F1 0.940, AUC 0.985, Log-loss 0.270, Brier score 0.071, MAE 2.0. Schalke 04 vs. Bayern Munich Jan 24, 2021: Schalke 04 #Goal 0, xG 2.67, #Shot 13, µAT G 25.23, µDT G 17.99; Bayern Munich #Goal 4, xG 9.59, #Shot 31, µAT G 27.79, µDT G 16.96; final score 0-4; expected final score 3-10 in terms of expected goal; total xG 12.26 (2.67 + 9.59); if average distance reduced from 18 meters to 15 meters, average xG for pre-shot by around 40 percent; if average angle 35° instead of 25°, average xG per-shot increased by 20%. Player 2020-21: BY #Game 24, #Goal 16, xG 24.77, #Shots 66, µAT G 22.33, µDT G 19.43; LM #Game 35, #Goal 30, xG 70.00, #Shots 195, µAT G 21.66, µDT G 19.23; RL #Game 28, #Goal 40, xG 65.71, #Shots 132, µAT G 34.69, µDT G 12.94; conversion: Robert Lewandowski 30%, Burak Yilmaz 25%, Lionel Messi 15%; if players take shots at 15 meters from goal instead of observed mean distances, average expected goal per shot may increase about 20%; if players take shots at 50°, highest average xG of Robert Lewandowski about 0.5.

data.paper_title: On Pairwise Costs for Network Flow Multi-Object Tracking
data.authors: Visesh Chari∗, Simon Lacoste-Julien†, Ivan Laptev∗, Josef Sivic∗
data.core_methodology: min-cost network flow tracking; integer linear program (ILP) in Eq. (1) with FLOWK constraints; integer quadratic program (IQP) min_z c⊤z + z⊤Qz s.t. z ∈ FLOWK, z integer; convex relaxation solution with efficient rounding heuristic; linear relaxation to the quadratic term; quadratic optimization with positive semidefinite Q by Qnew_ii = Σ_{j≠i}|Qold_ij| and linear coefficient c_i − Qnew_ii + Qold_ii; equivalent integer linear program with u_ij = z_i z_j and LOCAL(Q) constraints 0 ≤ u_ij ≤ 1, u_ij ≤ z_i, u_ij ≤ z_j, z_i + z_j ≤ 1 + u_ij; LP relaxation; Frank-Wolfe rounding heuristic using min_z (c + (Q + Q⊤)z*)⊤z s.t. z ∈ FLOWK; Hamming rounding; pairwise overlap cost qov_ij x_i x_j for ov(box(x_i), box(x_j)) ≥ othres; negative co-occurrence cost −qco_ij zh_i zb_j for consistent head/body signals; re-detection measure using Precision-Recall and Average Precision (AP).
data.key_metrics_and_variables: othres = 0.5; body detection box top 25% region when computing overlap or looking at intersection; KLT connections for nearby frames (< 10 frames apart); suboptimality certificates ≈10−3; Hamming rounding suboptimality around 3 to 4 times worse than Frank-Wolfe rounding; Case1 Detection=0.1, Overlap=0.0223, FW=4.7e-03, Ham=1.4e-02; Case2 Detection=0.1, Overlap=0.0007, FW=8.7e-06, Ham=9.3e-03; Case3 Detection=0.1, Overlap=2.23, FW=4.3e-03, Ham=1.0e-01; Case4 Detection=3.0, Overlap=0.0223, FW=9.3e-06, Ham=8.9e-03; Case5 Detection=0.074, Overlap=0.0223, FW=3.1e-02, Ham=1.0e-01; Case6 Detection=-1.0, Overlap=0.0223, FW=1.0e-01, Ham=1.3e-01; Figure 3: NF + Ov. + Co-oc. MOTA=55.9%, Prec=93.1%, Recall=60.6%; Ben[4] Head MOTA=45.4%, Prec=73.8%, Recall=71.0%; PETS/TUD Table 1 metrics: Rcll, Prcn, GT, MT, PT, ML, FP, FN, IDs, FM, MOTA, MOTP; MarchingRally NF+Overlap (MOTA, MOTP, IDswap) = (27.7%, 66.5%, 11) vs. Greedy+NMS = (22.5%, 66.0%, 24); PETS/TownCenter: 10–40 detections per frame, PETS pairwise if less than 6 frames apart, about 10 other detections for pairwise terms, TownCenter connected over 30 frames, about 15 pairwise terms per detection, runtime 5–10 seconds on PETS, 30–45 minutes on TownCenter, LP about 5 million variables TownCenter vs about 50 thousand for PETS.

data.paper_title: Machine Learning and Semantic Analysis of In-game Chat for Cyber Bullying
data.authors: Dr Shane Murnion, Prof William J Buchanan, Adrian Smales, and Dr Gordon Russell1
data.core_methodology: Automatic data collection system using a custom-built web crawler/web spider and web scraping of WotReplays.com replay files; decoding encrypted binary replay files using the Blowfish encryption algorithm and a WOT replay parser tool to JSON; combining replay data with player/vehicle information from the WG public API (WOT API) using Extract, Transform and Load (ETL) techniques; message classification using simple feature detection with SQL database queries (SAC), manual classification using a custom-built classification client (MAN), and AI-based sentiment text analysis using Twinword Sentiment Analysis and Microsoft Text Analytics from the Microsoft Azure Cognitive Services; cyberbullying score (CS) and proxy cyberbullying score (PCS); classification accuracy assessed with diagnostic odds ratio (DOR).
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Data collection: 1000 files on every data collection run; approximately 15,000 replays with approximately 44,000 associated player statistic snapshots and a total of approximately 126,000 messages; Table 3: 14930 processed replays, 443150 player statistic snapshots, 126091 replay messages. CS points: IsPositive -1pt; SpecificTarget -3pt; IsNegative +1pt; NoobRelated +1pt; HasBadLanguage or FilteredText +2pt; IsRacist +2pt; SpecificTarget +3pt; score range -4 to +9; every negative message from the same author adds a further +1 points (first +0, second +1, third +2 etc.). Example CS: 'Tiger tank you are useless'=4; 'Go play with Barbie dolls u noob'=6; 'U useless **** tiger'=8. PCS = (IsNegative * 1) + (NoobRelated * 1) + (HasBadLanguage|FilteredText * 2) + (IsRacist * 2) + RepetiveMessageScore. Manual classification: around 5000 chat messages; over 12% messages cyberbullying; 63% of all cyberbullying messages occurred after the player's death; SAC identified less than 45% of manually identified racist cases. DOR: IsRacist = 2,259; HasBadLanguage = 946; IsNegative = 1,627; NoobRelated = 46,101; CS/PCS comparison = 284; Twinword sentiment analysis = 3; Microsoft Azure sentiment analysis = 6.6. Twinword thresholds: negative if sentiment score < -0.05 and positive if > 0.05. Microsoft sentiment scores range from 0% negative to 100% positive.

data.paper_title: Methods for detrending success metrics to account for inﬂationary and deﬂationary factors
data.authors: Alexander M. Petersen, Orion Penner, H. Eugene Stanley
data.core_methodology: Detrending seasonal statistics by normalizing achievements to seasonal averages; individual prowess Pi(t) ≡ xi(t)/yi(t); league-wide average prowess ⟨P(t)⟩ ≡ Σ_i xi(t)/Σ_i yi(t) = Σ_i wi(t)Pi(t), where wi(t) = yi(t)/Σ_i yi(t); detrended metric xD_i(t) ≡ xi(t) P / ⟨P(t)⟩, with P ≡ (1/110) Σ_{t=1900}^{2009} ⟨P(t)⟩; detrended career metric XD_i ≡ Σ_{s=1}^{L} xD_i(s); probability density function (pdf) analysis; power law P(x) ∼ x−α; truncated power-law P(x) ∼ x−α e−(x/xc); Gamma distribution Gamma(x; α, xc)dx = ((x/xc)−α e−x/xc / Γ(1−α)) dx/xc ∝ x−α e−x/xc; Maximum Likelihood Estimator (MLE) for αMLE and xc; inverse regularized gamma function x∗ = xc Q−1[1−α, f]; Gaussian (Normal) distribution P(x) = 1/√(2πσ²) e−(x−⟨x⟩)²/2σ² for comparison; cutoff y′ ≡ 100 and x′ ≡ 0; threshold f = 0.02 and f = 0.01 for benchmarks.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Periods: 90-year period 1920-2009; 133-year period 1876-2009; 139-year period 1871-2009; 110-year normalization period 1900-2009. data.core_methodology: Random-set multi-object tracking with X={x1,...,xn} distributed according to P(X) and measurements Z={z1,...,zm} generated by likelihood P(Z|X); goal is posterior P(X|Z). Object model: multi-bernoulli distribution MB(X|...,r_i,p_i,...) with independent existence probability r_i and independent state distribution p_i(x). Measurement model: standard measurement model with detection probability P_D(x), single-measurement likelihood p(z|x), Poisson-distributed false positives with generation rate κ and distribution p_F(z); separable likelihood model p(z|X)=∑_k c_k(X)p(z|x_k)+c_F(X)p_f(z), c_k(X)=P_D(x_k)∏_{k'≠k}(1-P_D(x_{k'})), c_F(X)=κ∏_k(1-P_D(x_k)). data.paper_title: Evaluating deep tracking models for player tracking in broadcast ice hockey video
data.authors: Kanav Vats, Mehrnaz Fani, David A. Clausi, and John S. Zelek
data.core_methodology: Five state-of-the-art tracking algorithms: SORT [3] (Kalman filter with simple IOU based re-id), Deep SORT [26] (Kalman filter with deep CNN based re-id), Tracktor [1] (JDT algorithm with separate detection and re-id networks), FairMOT [28] (JDT algorithm with combined object detection and re-id network), and MOT Neural Solver [4] (Tracking using graph message passing with edge classification). Four online tracking algorithms [3,26,28,1] and one offline tracking algorithm [4]. SORT [3], deep SORT [26] and MOT Neural Solver [4] are tracking by detection (TBD) algorithms; Tracktor [1] and FairMOT [28] are joint detection and tracking (JDT) algorithms. TBD consists of detecting objects frame-by-frame, calculating affinity between detected objects, and inference linking player detections using calculated affinities to produce tracks. MOT Neural Solver [4] models the tracking problem as an undirected graph G = (V, E), where V = {1, 2, ..., n} is the set of n nodes for n player detections for all video frames; in edge set E, every pair of detections is connected; tracking is posed as splitting the graph into disconnected components where each component is a trajectory Ti; after computing each node embedding and edge embedding using a CNN (affinity calculation), the model solves a graph message passing problem, and the message passing algorithm classifies whether an edge between two nodes in the graph belongs to the same player trajectory. Player detection is performed using a Faster-RCNN network [17] with a ResNet50 based Feature Pyramid Network (FPN) backbone [11] pre-trained on the COCO dataset and fine tuned on the hockey tracking dataset. Evaluation uses CLEAR MOT metrics [2] and Identification F1 score (IDF1) [18].

data.paper_title: SoDA: Multi-Object Tracking with Soft Data Association
data.authors: Wei-Chih Hung1, Henrik Kretzschmar1, Tsung-Yi Lin2, Yuning Chai1, Ruichi Yu1, Ming-Hsuan Yang2,3, and Dragomir Anguelov1
data.core_methodology: Tracking-by-detection; attention measurement encoding with Transformer Network; measurement embedding z0_t,i from raw measurements xt,i via a feed-forward neural network consisting of two fully-connected layers followed by a normalization layer [1] using ReLU and linear activation functions; stacked attention measurement encoding layers on top of z0 to encode spatiotemporal context from detections in past Lenc frames {zτ,i | ∀i, τ ∈ [t − Lenc, t]}; each attention measurement encoding layer consists of a self-attention layer and a point-wise feed forward network, both following the Add-&-Norm structure and layer normalization: zo = LayerNorm(F(zi) + zi); self-attention sub-layer uses scaled dot-product attention: zo_i = Σ_j softmax(Q_i K_j^⊤ / √dk) V_i, where Qi = Wq zi, Ki = Wk zi and Vi = Wv zi are query, key, value features obtained by applying a linear transformation on an embedding feature zi with size dk; Nenc attention layers; relative time encoding from Transformer-XL: Ai,j = Qi K_j^⊤ + Qi R^⊤_{i−j} + u K_j^⊤ + v R^⊤_{i−j}, where Rk ∈ R^dk, k ∈ [−Lenc, Lenc] is a learned relative attention feature, and u, v ∈ R^dk are bias terms; attention association mechanism formulates data association as a dynamic classification problem, with track embedding zT equal to the embedding of the latest associated detection of a trajectory; explicit occlusion reasoning via a learned occlusion state occ with embedding zocc ∈ R^dk, representing the class a track can choose not to associate with any available detection; probability p(di|T) = exp(z_i^d^⊤ z_T) / (exp(zocc^⊤ z_T) + Σ_j exp(z_j^d^⊤ z_T)); cross-entropy association loss L(T) = −yT,o log(p(o|T)) − Σ_i yT,i log(p(di|T)), where yT,i = 1 if track T and detection di belong to the same identity, otherwise yT,i = 0, and yT,o = 1 only if yT,i = 0 for all i; inference associates detection di, i = arg max_j p(dj|t), and if p(o|T) > p(di|T) the track is marked as “occluded” and does not associate with any detection; track management similar to SORT with unpromoted and promoted tracks, kill if no associated detection in consecutive Tlost frames with thresholds T^UP_lost and T^P_lost, and optimal assignment e.g. Hungarian matching or a greedy algorithm; simulation framework: ground truth labels of Waymo Open Dataset treated as detections, randomly dropping Ndrop ∼ U(1, 5) consecutive bounding boxes for every 10 frames in a given track with probability pdrop; synthetic simulation with Np particles of the same size in a box with random initial positions p = (px, py) ∼ U(0, 1) and velocities vi = (vx, vy) ∼ N(0, 0.1), pt+1 = pt + vt, bounce back with reversed velocity (−vx, vy) or (vx, −vy), detection d = p + nd with nd ∼ N(0, 0.05), random force f = (fx, fy) ∼ N(0, 0.01), mutual occlusions by random depth with IOU > 0.3, environmental occlusion block, and social forces fi = Σ_j F0 e^{−||pi−pj|| / R} · ∇(pi − pj); baseline methods: IOU Tracker (constant velocity motion model and intersection-over-union similarity), Center Tracker (constant velocity motion model and negative L2 distance between box centers), Learned Similarity Tracker (4 fully-connected layers producing a 64-d feature, cosine similarity t^⊤d/(∥t∥∥d∥), contrastive loss with margin 0.3, Hungarian matching); Tracktor setup with Faster R-CNN and ResNet-101 backbone; ROI Align appearance features variant.

data.paper_title: Tracking Objects as Pixel-wise Distributions
data.authors: Zelin Zhao1 ⋆, Ze Wu2 , Yueqing Zhuang2 , Boxun Li2 , and Jiaya Jia1,3
data.core_methodology: P3AFormer: transformer-based architecture for tracking objects as pixel-wise distributions with pixel-wise propagation, prediction, and association. It uses a backbone and pixel decoder (multi-scale deformable attention transformer; deformable DETR decoder; six deformable attention layers; L = 3 layers of feature maps) to generate per-pixel representations. It uses pixel-wise flow-guided feature propagation with flow network Φ and bilinear warping function W, fused by pixel-wise cosine similarity weight w^(t-1)->(t). It uses a transformer-based object decoder with N learnable positional embeddings Q_l, L attention layers, masked attention, self-attention, feed-forward networks (FFN), and MLP heads for class E_l^cls, center E_l^ctr, and size E_l^sz; center heatmaps c_l and size maps s_l are computed via sigmoid dot products; attention mask update uses center heatmaps threshold 0.5. Training uses bipartite Hungarian matching with a pixel-wise cost function, Gaussian ground-true heatmaps, cross-entropy loss, focal loss, and L1 size loss. Pixel-wise association uses Kalman Filter, Hungarian algorithm, L1 distance between heatmaps, thresholds η_m and η_s, and track deletion after n_k frames. Training uses mosaic augmentation, Mixup, AdamW, poly learning rate schedule; backbones ResNet-50 and Swin-B; FlowNet pre-trained on Flying Chairs.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: MOT17 test P3AFormer (+W&B): MOTA 81.2, IDF1 78.1, MT 54.5, ML 13.2, FP 17281, FN 86861, IDSW 1893. MOT20 test P3AFormer (+W&B): MOTA 78.1, IDF1 76.4, MT 70.5, ML 7.4, FP 25413, FN 86510, IDs 1332. KITTI test P3AFormer Car: HOTA 78.4, MOTA 91.2, MT 86.5, PT 10.9, ML 2.3; Person: HOTA 49.0, MOTA 67.7, MT 49.1, PT 33.2, ML 14.5. Hyperparameters: d = 128; L = 3; N = 100; ηm = 0.65; ηs = 0.80; nk = 30 frames; input image shape 1440 × 800 for MOT17/MOT20 and 1280 × 384 for KITTI; initial learning rate 6×10−5; weight decay 1×10−4; 200 epochs; eight Tesla V100 GPUs. Equations: P_l^(t-1)->(t) = W(P_l^(t-1), Φ(I^(t-1), I^(t))); P_bar_l^(t) = P_l^(t) + w^(t-1)->(t) P_l^(t-1)->(t); c_l[i,h,w] = sigmoid(P_bar_l[h,w,:] · E_l^ctr[i,:]); s_l[i,h,w,j] = sigmoid(P_bar_l[h,w,:] · E_l^sz[i,:,j]); M_l-1(i,x,y) = 0 if c_l-1[i,x,y] > 0.5, otherwise −∞; L_pixel-wise = Σ_l Σ_i (−log p_hat_l^i(c_l^i) + 1[c_l^i ≠ ∅] |h_hat_l^i − h_l^i|).

(18)-(20). data.paper_title: The Cost of Sybils, Credible Commitments, and False-Name Proof Mechanisms

data.paper_title: Player Pressure Map - A Novel Representation of Pressure in Soccer for Evaluating Player Performance in Different Game Contexts
data.authors: Chaoyi Gu*, Jiaming Na*, Yisheng Pei*, Varuna De Silva
data.core_methodology: The paper proposes a novel method to quantify pressure on individual player with 3D body motion parameters considered using tracking and event data and game footage; generates a defensive pitch control matrix; at timestep tk, for a given location (m, n) on the pitch, calculates the probability of the defending team controlling the ball, atk mn, used to quantify pressure on this location; locates the player, uses him as the center and 1 meter as the diameter to draw a pressure circle, and from 8 directions around this player calculates corresponding pressure values to create the vanilla pressure matrix; extracts passer body orientation using a top-down approach to estimate player 3D pose using broadcast footage, with a tracking model to track players with the same identification across frames within 0.25 second; computes a pressure amplifier based on observed passing data to fine-tune the pressure matrix of the passer based on body orientation; creates Player Pressure Map (PPM), a graph with 12 nodes representing attacking players and the ball and edges connecting all the nodes, where the pressure vector and position are embedded into the node and edges include distances and angles between each two players; uses PPM sequences as input to train a Possession Outcome Prediction (POP) model using a Graph Neural Network (GNN); the GNN contains three Graph Convolution Layers, a ReLu activation layer and a Global Mean Pooling layer applied to each Graph Convolution Layer, dropout rate of the whole model is 0.5, and a fully connected layer to generate the 2 classes prediction outcome.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: 9 games in the Premier League; six soccer games for passer body orientation; 0.25 second; 1 meter as the diameter; 8 directions; 12 nodes representing attacking players and the ball; 11 nodes representing the attacking players; pop value equals to 0.64 means the attacking team has a 64% chance to remain the possession in the next 4 seconds, while 36% possibility to lose; possessions longer than 5 seconds; every two-second possession is converted into a sequence of 50 PPMs; predict the outcome of this possession after 4 seconds; label 0 if the team loses possession and 1 if the team keeps possession; dropout rate of the whole model is 0.5; three Graph Convolution Layers; 2 classes prediction outcome; Prediction Accuracy: Tracking 55.8%, 2D PPM 75.2%, 3D PPM 78.7%; test dataset is one independent Premier League match; More than 750 possessions; accuracy rises with a significant increase of around 20%; 3D PPM model performs around 3% better; both make more than 300 passes; general passing accuracy around 80 percent; level 1: pressure <= 1/3; level 2: 1/3 < pressure <= 2/3; level 3: pressure >2/3; Player 41328 can decrease the pressure on his team by around 0.4 per dribble; 2019/20 season.

data.paper_title: Identification of pattern mining algorithm for rugby league players positional groups separation based on movement patterns
data.authors: Victor Elijah Adeyemo, Anna Palczewska, Ben Jones, Dan Weaving
data.core_methodology: Observational repeated measures design; 10Hz GPS data (Catapult S5) discretized into movement sequences using velocity, acceleration and turning angle thresholds (Table 2); movement unit every 0.1s (10Hz) assigned to a movement unit character; inactive periods filtered out. Three pattern mining algorithms: l-length Closed Contiguous [LCCspm], Longest Common Subsequence [LCS] within the Sequential Movement Pattern-mining (SMP) framework, and AprioriClose. LCCspm parameters: support and length; support set to 5 percent; length set to 20 (i.e. 2 seconds time-frame); AprioriClose support set to 5 percent; LCS has no parameter; AprioriClose and LCS patterns later filtered to exclude patterns containing more than 20 items. Unique movement patterns computed as the union of all sets of extracted movement patterns per algorithm. Jaccard similarity measure [29] with exact matching: J (X, Y ) = |X ∩ Y |/|X ∪ Y |. Overlap movement patterns identified using exact matching method; most frequent-50 and least frequent-50 checked. Separation via machine learning classification modelling with independent variables as unique movement patterns and dependent variable hooker or winger; five algorithms: Decision Tree, Gaussian Na¨ıve Bayes, Random Forest, Logistic Regression, Multi-Layered Perceptron (MLP); k-fold cross-validation with n splits=10, random state=10, shuffle=“True”; evaluation by aggregated accuracy, precision, recall and f1-score metrics; feature importance scores top-20; scikit-learn version 1.1.3. Classification parameter settings: Decision Tree default; Gaussian Na¨ıve Bayes default; Random Forest random state = 1; Logistic Regression penalty = “l1”, solver = “liblinear”; MLP max iter = 300, random state = 5.

data.paper_title: Concussion and head acceleration exposure in elite rugby union and American football: Interpreting indicative trends
data.authors: Dr Gregory Tierney
data.core_methodology: A comparison of current indicative trends in concussion and head acceleration events (HAEs) in elite-level American football and rugby union based on governing body reports and available scientific literature; limited to the men’s games. Concussion incidence in rugby union tends to be reported as the number of concussion injuries per 1000 player-hours; concussion incidence in American football tends to be reported as Athletic Exposures (AE) or on a per match basis; the AE metric provides an overall risk assessment per session of athlete participation. Methodological approaches included instrumented helmets (e.g., Head Impact Telemetry Systems), instrumented mouthguards (iMG; e.g., X2 Biosystems & Prevent Biometric), multibody modelling and Anthropomorphic Test Dummy reconstructions, including reanalysed impacts from earlier studies. The paper also discusses video review of contact event incidence, iMG signal processing approaches, mean peak linear acceleration (PLA) and peak angular acceleration (PAA), and HAEs above 10 g, above 30 g, and above 2.0 krad/s2.

data.paper_title: Instrumented mouthguards in elite sports: Validity and head acceleration event (HAE) incidence in NCAA American Football
data.authors: Mario Pasquale Rotundo1, Nicholas G Murray2, David Allan1, Gregory Tierney1
data.core_methodology: Prospective observational cohort study using data from an NCAA Division 1 American Football team during the 2022 Mountain West Conference Regular Season; 35 male NCAA football players fitted with Prevent Biometrics iMGs (Minneapolis, MN, USA), custom fit following three-dimensional dental scans with a dental assistant under the supervision of a certified dentist; on-field validity determined through video review with positive predictive value (PPV) and sensitivity values calculated; unguided video analysis with reviewer blinded to all iMG data and guided analysis cross-referencing iMG-triggered events with video footage and designating True Positive (TP), False Positive (FP), False Positive Off-Camera (FPOC), or False Positive Inactive (FPI) based on Table 1 definitions; sensitivity calculated with Eq. 1 and PPV with Eq. 2; HAE incidence calculated as the number of HAEs per player match and stratified by Offense and Defense positions; iMGs equipped with triaxial gyroscopes and accelerometers sampling at 3200Hz with measurement range +/-35rad/s2 and +/- 200g, respectively; HAEs identified when linear acceleration exceeded an 8g trigger threshold on any single axis; linear acceleration transformed to head centre of gravity; time series data captured 10ms prior and 40ms after the trigger event with a recording threshold of 5g resultant peak linear acceleration (PLA) and resultant peak angular acceleration (PAA) of 400rad/s2 at the head centre of gravity; noise/artifact classified by a Prevent Biometrics proprietary algorithm as minimal (class 0), moderate (class 1), or severe (class 2); a 4-pole (2x2), zero-phase, low-pass Butterworth filter applied with 200Hz, 100Hz and 50Hz cut-off frequency (-6dB) for class 0, class 1, and class 2 signals, respectively; proximity sensor readings collected to ensure iMGs were seated to the player’s dentition during HAEs; NCAA footage collected from mainstream television broadcasters; video analysis using QuickTime Player v.10.5 on a 32” monitor; only player matches where the instrumented player wore the iMG for at least 90% of their contact events used (n=64, 90.1%); only true positive iMG-triggered events that met the 5g and 400rad/s2 threshold used in incidence calculations; mean values for Offense and Defense calculated across players and 95% CIs estimated using a bootstrapping procedure randomly resampled 2500 times with 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles as lower and upper bounds; mean incidence along with 95% CIs calculated across a range of PLA and PAA magnitude thresholds for Offense and Defense and significant difference assumed if CIs did not overlap.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Sensitivity = True Positives / (True Positives + False Negatives) [1]; PPV = True Positives / (True Positives + False Positives) [2]; sensitivity 0.89 (95% CI 0.86-0.92); PPV ranging from 0.76-0.98 based on false positive definitions; Table 2: True Positive; TP (n) 403; False Negative; FP (n) 51; Guided Analysis True Positive; TP(n) 828; False Positive; FP (n) 19; False Positive Off Camera; FPOC (n) 46; False Positive Inactive; FPI (n) 208; All assumed false positives (n) 254; PPV: True Positive and False Positive (95% CI) 0.98 (0.97-0.99); PPV: True positive, false positive, false positive off camera (95% CI) 0.93 (0.91-0.94); PPV: True positive and all assumed false positive (95% CI) 0.76 (0.73-0.78); incidence of HAEs above 10 g 11.2 and 11.3 HAEs per player match for Defense and Offense, respectively; PAA incidence above 1.0 krad/s2 5.5 and 6.9 HAEs per player match for Defense and Offense, respectively; incidence of HAEs above 30 g 1.6 and 2.6 per player match and 0.9 and 1.4 for HAEs above 2.0 krad/s2 for Defense and Offense, respectively; 35 male NCAA football players; 71 player matches (games) across 4 games; 64 eligible player matches over 4 games (n=64, 90.1%); 517 head impacts in unguided video analysis; n=31 off the teeth; n=32 below 5g and 400rad/s2 threshold; 454 impacts in unguided analysis; 1101 iMG triggered events meeting 5g and 400rad/s2 recording threshold; 828 HAEs; Offensive Linemen n=6; Running Backs n=2; Tight Ends n=4; Defensive Linemen n=2; Linebackers n=14; Defensive Backs n=7; sampling at 3200Hz; measurement range +/-35rad/s2 and +/- 200g; 8g trigger threshold; 10ms prior and 40ms after trigger event; 5g PLA and 400rad/s2 PAA recording threshold; 200Hz, 100Hz and 50Hz cut-off frequency (-6dB); resampled 2500 times; 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles.

data.paper_title: Omni Survey for Multimodality Analysis in Visual Object Tracking
data.authors: Zhangyong Tang, Tianyang Xu Member, IEEE, Xuefeng Zhu, Hui Li, Shaochuan Zhao, Tao Zhou, Chunyang Cheng, Xiao-Jun Wu*, and Josef Kittler Life Member, IEEE
data.core_methodology: Omni survey from the perspective of multimodality analysis; MMVOT differs from single-modal tracking in four key aspects: data collection, modality alignment and annotation, model designing, and evaluation. Categorises existing MMVOT methods based on visible (RGB) and X modalities (X = T, D, E, NIR, L, S) into Replicated Configuration and Non-Replicated Configuration, with non-replicated configurations specified as customised or non-customised to the X branch input; methods are grouped into Integration, Boosting, and Real-World. Unified multi-modal trackers are categorised by training paradigms Uni-A and Uni-B. Evaluation and benchmarking use precision rate (PR), success rate (SR), normalized precision rate (NPR), precision (Pr), recall (Re), F-score, and the VOT protocol (Accuracy (A), robustness (R), expected average overlap (EAO)). Analyses object-category distributions in MMVOT datasets, revealing long-tail nature and scarcity of animal categories compared with RGB datasets.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: 338 references; six MMVOT tasks; 61 distinct challenging attributes; RGB wavelength 0.38 and 0.75 um; infrared 0.75–1000 µm; NIR 0.75–1.4 µm; SWIR 1.4–3 µm; MWIR 3–8 µm; LWIR 8–15 µm; FIR 15–1000 µm; RGB latency 10–20 ms; event camera latency 1 us; sonar ∆t = tre −tem and d = (∆t ∗V)/2; d∗= project(d); TRGB : DRGB →R4; TMMVOT : DMMVOT →R4; X ∈ [T, D, E, NIR, L, S]; TSUTrack : (DRGB, DMMVOT, θRGB) →R4; TOthers : (DMMVOT, θRGB) →R4; bounding-box formats [xtl, ytl, xbr, ybr] and [xtl, ytl, w, h]; performance comparison 0.732 vs. 0.002 and 0.006 vs. 0.378 on two cases; SUTrack results LasHeR 61.9, DepthTrack 66.4, VisEvent 63.8, TNL2K 67.9; SeqTrackV2 results LasHeR 61.0, DepthTrack 62.3, VisEvent 63.4, TNL2K 62.4.

data.paper_title: FEMOT: Multi-Object Tracking using Frame and Event Cameras
data.authors: Shiao Wang1, Xiao Wang*1, Chao Wang1, Yitao Li1, Menghao Liu1, Bo Jiang1, Yaowei Wang2,5, Yonghong Tian2,3,4 and Jin Tang1
data.core_methodology: FEMOTR, a Frequency-aware RGB Frame-Event Multi-Object Tracking method with TRansformer, built upon the MeMOTR framework and initialized with pretrained weights of DAB-Deformable DETR; shared ResNet-50 backbone; Frequency Aware Feature Fusion (FAF) module with three branches (RGB branch, event branch, cross-modal fusion branch), depthwise separable convolution block (DWConv), 2D fast Fourier transform (FFT), amplitude and phase extraction, amplitude/phase attention Attn(V, W) = V + V ⊙ Softmax(V ⊙ W), inverse FFT (F−1), and element-wise addition; multi-scale deformable Transformer encoder; Detection Decoder; Transformer Joint Decoder; Dynamic Temporal Interaction Module (DTIM) with exponential moving average long-term memory update, MLP + Sigmoid channel-wise weights, two-layer MLP, and dynamic memory-attention layer based on multi-head attention; Hungarian-algorithm-based bipartite matching; sigmoid Focal Loss, L1 loss, and GIoU loss; FEMOT dataset constructed with DVS346 camera and MOT-style TXT annotations; benchmarked trackers include ByteTrack, OC-SORT, MixSort-Oc, MixSort-Byte, Hybrid-SORT, SRTrack, PFTrack, TOPICTrack, FairMOT, TraDes, TLDMOT, Samba, MOTRv2, MeMOTR, and MOTIP.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Event definition: e_i = (x_i, y_i, t_i, p_i), t_i ∈ [0, T]; event accumulation window: E_t^p = {e_i = (x_i, y_i, t_i, p_i) | t_i ∈ [t_s, t_e]}; branch inputs: B_t^X = X^t, B_t^Y = Y^t, B_t^Z = Z^t = Concat(X^t, Y^t); DWConv: U_t^b = DWConv_b(B_t^b); FFT: S_b = F(U_t^b); amplitude/phase: A_b = Conv_b(A(S_b)), P_b = Conv_b(P(S_b)); modulation: Attn(V, W) = V + V ⊙ Softmax(V ⊙ W); recombination: S̃_b = Ã_b ⊙ e^{j P̃_b}; residual inverse FFT: B̂_t^b = F−1(Conv_b(S̃_b)) + B_t^b; fusion: F^t = X̂^t + Ŷ^t + Ẑ^t; memory update: M̃_t+1_tck = (1 − λ)M_t_tck + λ · O_t_tck, λ = 0.01; classification: W_t_tck = Sigmoid(MLP1(O_t_tck)); fused embedding: Ô_t_tck = MLP2([W_t_tck ⊙ O_t_tck, O_{t−1}_tck]); total loss: L_total = λ1 L_Focal + λ2 L_L1 + λ3 L_GIoU, λ1 = 2, λ2 = 5, λ3 = 2; matching cost: C_ij = λ4 C_cls(i, j) + λ5 C_L1(i, j) + λ6 C_giou(i, j), λ4 = 2, λ5 = 5, λ6 = 2; detection queries: 300 by default; Transformer: 6 encoder layers and 6 decoder layers, with 3 detection decoder layers and 3 joint Transformer decoder layers; training: 13 epochs, batch size 1, clip length initially 2 then increased to 3 and 4 at epochs 6 and 10, sampling interval 4, AdamW initial learning rate 2 × 10−4, weight decay 10−4, learning rate decay factor 0.1 at epoch 12; FEMOT: 100 video sequences, 200K video frames, 14.58K trajectories, 0.42M bounding box annotations, 14 challenging attributes; categories: 1 for pedestrians and 3 for vehicles; FEMOTR results: HOTA 48.9, DetA 45.2, AssA 53.8, MOTA 52.0, MOTP 76.7, IDF1 62.0; MeMOTR baseline: HOTA 44.0, MOTA 45.4, IDF1 54.9; DSEC-MOT FEMOTR: HOTA 52.4, DetA 40.6, AssA 67.8, MOTA 37.5, IDF1 59.0; DSEC-MOT Samba: HOTA 55.4, DetA 46.4, AssA 66.5, MOTA 50.3, IDF1 64.9. DetA = TP∗Det / (TP∗Det + FN∗Det + FP∗Det); AssA = TP∗Ass / (TP∗Ass + FN∗Ass + FP∗Ass).

data.paper_title: Generative 4D Scene Gaussian Splatting with Object View-Synthesis Priors
data.authors: Wen-Hsuan Chu, Lei Ke, Jianmeng Liu, Mingxiao Huo, Pavel Tokmakov, Katerina Fragkiadaki
data.core_methodology: GenMOJO: compositional Multi-Object JOint splatting for 4D scene GENeration from monocular videos; combines frame-centric test-time rendering error optimization with object-centric generative priors; decomposes the scene into individual foreground objects and background; represents each object with a differentiable and deformable set of 3D Gaussians; jointly splats all Gaussians to compute rendering errors in input video frames accounting for occlusions; individually renders each object's Gaussians from unobserved viewpoints to optimize a score distillation (SDS) objective; differentiable transformations align object-centric Gaussians with frame-centric Gaussians; uses deformable 3D Gaussians and 3D Gaussian Splatting; Score Distillation Sampling (SDS); Zero-1-to-3 diffusion prior; DreamGaussian4D per-frame deformation modeling with 3D displacement µt=(µxt,µyt,µzt), 3D rotation quaternion Rt=(qwt,qxt,qyt,qzt), and 3D scale st=(sxt,syt,szt); deformation network Dθ(Gobj_0,t) outputs the full 10-D deformation vector; K-plane-based deformation networks; motion bases; MLP head for time-varying SH coefficients; L1 regularization term Lreg on SH adjustments; losses include RGB rendering loss Lrgb, optical flow rendering loss Lflow, depth consistency loss, instance segmentation alignment loss Lclass = −Σ_k yk log ŷk, and regularization losses; affine warp Wt maps object bounding box Bt to a canonical bounding box; depth-aware scaling ki = Di/Dj, pi_t = Cr − (Cr − μi_t) × ki, si_t = si_t × ki; static background initialized by unprojecting RGBD information into a 3D point cloud with fixed 3D positions; MOSE-PTS dataset; baselines and comparisons: Consistent4D, DreamGaussian4D, DreamScene4D, Shape of Motion, GMRW, CoTrackerV2, CoTrackerV3; scene-level SDS with ZeroNVS; DepthCrafter and DepthAnything-V2.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Implementation/setup: 48GB NVIDIA A6000 GPU; object-centric lifting crops/scales objects to approximately 65% of image size; static 3D Gaussian optimization 1,000 iterations, batch size 16; deformation optimization 40× number of frames, batch size 8, gradient accumulation over 2 steps. MOSE-PTS: 20 videos selected from MOSE; up to five objects per video, five key points per object, annotations at 1080p; supplement annotates 30 videos selected from MOSE. SDS equation: ∇ϕLt SDS = Et,τ,ϵ,p[w(τ)(ϵθ(ˆIp_t; τ, I1, p) − ϵ) ∂ˆIp_t/∂ϕ]. Depth scaling: ki = Di/Dj, where Di and Dj are the median depth values for objects i and j; pi_t = Cr − (Cr − μi_t) × ki; si_t = si_t × ki. Class loss: Lclass = −Σ_k yk log ŷk. data.core_methodology: Time-to-arrival (TTA) framed as conditional quantile regression, specifically conditional lower-quantile regression estimating Q0.01(Δt | g(k, x)) for state k = (p, v, a) and target x; pinball regression / pinball loss at τ = 0.01; heading-frame geometry g(k, x) with translation to player origin and rotation by −φ so heading aligns with +x; target represented as (d cos θ, d sin θ); six normalized input features d/120, cos θ, sin θ, v/12, ax/10, ay/10; Savitzky–Golay filter and finite differences for track cleaning; hard kinematic bounds for speed, acceleration and frame-to-frame velocity change; sample extraction with five continuous horizon offsets uniformly from [0.10, 8.0] s; SUVAT noise floor with capped acceleration 8 m/s2 and capped top speed 9 m/s, discarding samples whose observed Δt < ΔtSUVAT and degenerate near-zero-distance samples; reachable-area duality R(Δt) = { x : τ(x) ≤ Δt }; six literature motion models re-expressed as TTA predictors and inverted via τ(x) = min{t : x ∈ R(t)}: Constant speed, Constant acceleration, Constant acceleration with speed limit, Two-segment constant speed, Acceleration with free direction, Friction-damped acceleration; learned reachable-hull baseline using per-speed-bin convex hulls; Multilayer perceptron 6 →64 →64 →1 with ReLU hidden activations and Softplus output; Player-profile MLP augmenting input with each player’s maximum speed estimated as the 99th percentile of that player’s cleaned, state-valid speeds pooled over the 45 training matches only; quantile objective L = Lτ + λ Larea with pinball component Lτ and differentiable area-aware auxiliary term Larea using logistic sigmoid on a fixed heading-frame grid G (25 × 25 nodes at 4 m spacing spanning ±48 m, origin node excluded, |G| = 624), horizons h ∈ {3, 5} s, β = 0.25 s, λ = 0.01; evaluation via MAE, RMSE, pinball loss at τ = 0.01, coverage and reachable area under matched coverage using Eq. (2); data pipelines for PFF FC FIFA World Cup 2022 optical tracking, NBA SportVU, and NFL Big Data Bowl 2019.

data.paper_title: How Football Players Determine where to Run to Tackle other Players: A Mathematical and Psychological Description and Analysis
data.authors: Dennis M. Shaffer, Thomas B. Gregory
data.core_methodology: constant target-heading angle (CTHA) strategy; pursuit strategy (also called ‘aiming,’ ‘homing’ or ‘centering’); classic predictive strategy; constant bearing angle (or CBA); proportional leading or mirroring strategy; Cartesian-coordinate mathematical model with origin (0,0), positive x-axis connecting pursuer to ball carrier, P = angle of pursuer's path with positive x-axis, B = angle of ball carrier's path with positive x-axis, a(t) = distance between pursuer and ball carrier at t seconds, a = a(0), vP = pursuer speed, vB = ball carrier speed, ti = time to intercept, d = tvB; Law of Sines: sin(P) = vBsin(B)/ vP; ball carrier position: (a + tvBcos(B), tvBsin(B)); pursuer position: (tvPcos(P), tvPsin(P)); distance squared: (tvPcos(P) - a - tvBcos(B))2 + (tvPsin(P) - tvBsin(B)) 2; simplified distance squared: t2(vP2 + vB2) + a2 - 2t2vPvB (cos(P-B)) + 2ta(vBcos(B) – vPcos(P)); derivative of squared distance: 2t((vP2 + vB2) - 4tvBvP(cos(P-B)) - 2a (vPcos(P) - vBcos(B)); derivative with respect to P: 4tvPvB(sin(P-B)) + 2a(vPsin(P)); optimal angle: tan(P) = (tvBsin(B))/(tvBcos(B) + (a/2)); simplified optimal angle: tan(P) = (sin(B))/(cos(B) + (a/(2d))); predictions: pursuers move in or onto straight-line paths, target-heading angle greater than zero, change in target-heading angle with respect to time close to zero (dP/dt ~ 0), and after a mid-pursuit change dP/dt ~ 0
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Five senior-high-school varsity-football starters; all players were eighteen; 3 cornerbacks, 1 strong safety and 1 defensive end; pursuit area 22.87m laterally and 22.87m in depth; camcorder 30m behind and above the reference line; recorded in 5/30th of a second frames; foot positions marked every 0.167s; potential error equivalent to 0.3m in-depth and 0.3m laterally, or approximately 0.3m x 0.3m for every 0.95m moved; data.paper_title: EVENT DETECTION BASED ON GENERIC CHARACTERISTICS OF FIELD-SPORTS
data.authors: David Sadlier, Noel E. O’Connor
data.core_methodology: Generic framework for event detection in broadcast video of multiple field-sports; Shot Boundary Detection using a standard histogram based approach; Close-up Image Detection & Shot Filtering; Feature Detector 1: Crowd Image Detection using non-zero frequency (AC) Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT) coefficients; Feature Detector 2: Speech-Band Audio Activity using MPEG bitstream scalefactor weights; Feature Detector 3: On-Screen Graphics Tracking using temporal mode values and a SAD operation in the luminance domain; Feature Detector 4: Motion Activity Measure using motion vectors present in the MPEG video bitstream and counting macroblocks whose motion vector length is greater than a pre-selected ‘zero’-threshold; Feature Detector 5: Field Line Orientation using hue space segmentation, Roberts edge detector, and Hough Transform; feature data aggregation into a shot feature vector (SFV); support vector machine; SVM (with radial basis function kernel)
data.key_metrics_and_variables: 100-hours of content was captured in MPEG-1 format; 98% of all events are followed by an action replay; very few reaction-phase durations are in excess of 25s, adopted as a post-event critical-seek-window (CSW); Table-1: Close-up sequence 97%; Crowd sequence 73%; Audio level in excess of broadcast mean level 84%; Removal of scoreboard graphic during update 61%; NFMA in excess of broadcast mean level 76%; 73% of all training corpus events conformed to the end-zone constraint; 94% of all boundaries are hard cuts; 97% of all training corpus events included a close-up image sequence during the reaction-phase; field-end lines mainly lie within the interval 5º-25º relative to the camera; last 6 I-frames preceding the shot-end boundary (critical I-frames); {Fv1}= [Crowd Image Confidence] I-Frames; {Fv2} = [Audio Speech-Band Energy] 0.5s; {Fv3} = SAD [IframeN, Mode] Critical Pixels; {Fv4} = [Near-Field Visual Activity] P-frame; {Fv5} = [Angle of Most Prominent Line] I-frame; SFV = [Vcc1, Vcc2, Vcc3, Vcc4, Vcc5]; Vcc1 is defined as the maximum I-frame crowd image confidence value; Vcc2 is defined as the maximum speech-band energy value; Vcc4 = Max {Fv4}CSW; Vcc5 = i ÷ 6 {i = # critical I-frame orientations within the key range}; regularization parameter, C; training corpus consisted of 210 events – 70 events from soccer, 70 from rugby, and 70 from Gaelic football; data.paper_title: DIGITAL SPORTS GAMES AND THEIR PLAYERS – Playing motivations and player’s assessment of the effects of playing
data.authors: Kati Ahonen
data.core_methodology: Qualitative research using a structured questionnaire, analyzed with a qualitative method, thematic approach and typology; based on questionnaire responses from eight people, four different digital game player profiles were created.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Questionnaire responses from eight people; subject ages between 26 and 46; mean age of all respondents 36.6 years; 4 male and 4 female; men’s average age 32 years; women’s 41.25 years; questionnaires estimated to take approximately 30 minutes; research time span June 2010 until July 2012; four different profiles: Profile A: Sports Heavy User, Profile B: Late Starter, Profile C: Is Not Interested in Exergames, Profile D: Entertainment Player; limitations noted respondents’ age range between 27–46 years.

data.paper_title: Large-Scale Analysis of Soccer Matches using Spatiotemporal Tracking Data
data.authors: Alina Bialkowski, Patrick Lucey, Peter Carr, Yisong Yue, Sridha Sridharan, Iain Matthews
data.core_methodology: Role-based representation with dynamic role assignment; role-representation r_t = P_t x_t using a permutation matrix P_t; formation F as an arbitrarily ordered set of N roles {R1, R2, . . . , RN}; minimum entropy data partitioning; Kullback-Lieber divergence; role probability density functions P_n(x); heat-map modeled as P(x) = sum_{n=1}^N P(x|n)P(n) = (1/N) sum_{n=1}^N P_n(x); penalty V_n = -KL(P_n(x)||P(x)); optimal formation F* = arg min_F V; total overlap cost in terms of entropy V = -H(x) + sum_{n=1}^N P(n)H(x|n) = -H(x) + (1/N) sum_{n=1}^N H(x|n); optimal formation F* = arg min_F sum_{n=1}^N H(x|n); approximate solution using the expectation maximization (EM) algorithm, similar to k-means clustering with the constraint that at every frame each detection requires a unique role; Hungarian algorithm for optimal assignment; agglomerative clustering; Earth Mover's Distance (EMD); 2D Gaussians
data.key_metrics_and_variables: N = 11 players; x_t = [x1, y1, x2, y2, . . . , x11, y11]^T; r_t = P_t x_t; P(x) = sum_{n=1}^N P(x|n)P(n) = (1/N) sum_{n=1}^N P_n(x); KL(P(x)||Q(x)) = integral P(x) log(P(x)/Q(x)) dx; V_n = -KL(P_n(x)||P(x)); F* = arg min_F V; V = -H(x) + sum_{n=1}^N P(n)H(x|n) = -H(x) + (1/N) sum_{n=1}^N H(x|n); F* = arg min_F sum_{n=1}^N H(x|n); EMD(a, b) = min_{fqt>=0} sum_{q,t=1}^D dqt fqt s.t. sum_{q=1}^D fqt = at, sum_{t=1}^D fqt = bq; approximately 400,000,000 data points; 20 teams; 38 games for each team or 380 games overall; five games omitted; 375 games; 480M data points; 981K ball events; 43 possible events; 10 frames-per-second; over 1 million datapoints per game; 1411 formations; 10 distinct role probability distributions; cluster frequencies 50.37%, 20.76%, 12.52%, 5.40%, 3.15%, 0.90%; overall correct classification rate 75.33%

data.paper_title: GAMEDIRECTOR: DECOUPLING GAMEPLAY LOGIC FROM RENDERING FOR PLAYER-CONFIGURABLE GAME WORLD MODELS
data.authors: Zijun Lin1,2,4,∗,†, Zhiyang Deng1,3,∗,†, Yuzhe Wu1,3,†, Bihan Wen2, Yeying Jin1,3,§
data.core_methodology: GameDirector: agentic framework that decouples rule-based gameplay logic from visual rendering; player-configurable initialization I0 = [F0, hp0, hb0, αp, αb, mb0, C]; agentic control layer (Director) with Visual Understanding, State Tracking, Action Planning, Rule Enforcement; Visual Understanding uses SituationNet Sϕ and AttackNet Aϕ, two lightweight ResNet-18 models with single-layer GRU taking the three most recent gameplay frames: (d̂_t, θ̂_t) = Sϕ(Ft−2:t), t ∈ {80n}_{n≥1}; (â^p_t, â^b_t) = Aϕ(Ft−2:t), t ∈ {4n}_{n≥1}; State Tracking updates hp_{t+1}=max(0, hp_t−α_b â^p_t), hb_{t+1}=max(0, hb_t−α_p â^b_t), mb_{t+1}=min(M, mb_t+â^p_t+â^b_t); Action Planning uses a 2B language model as planner, Gemma-4-E2B-it without task-specific fine-tuning, c^b_t = LLM(d̂_t, θ̂_t, C); Rule Enforcement validates actions/movements, death rules, skill activation threshold τ and cooldown; Controllable Generation maps validated action-movement pairs to prompt P_t=M(u^p_t,u^b_t) and conditions a DiT-based world model F_{t+1:t+Δ}=G_θ(F_{0:t}, P_t, ε_t), Δ=4, with Gaussian noise ε_t; video world model initialized from Wan2.2-TI2V-5B, VAE and text encoder frozen, trained with AdamW and three-stage Causal Forcing++ distillation (autoregressive teacher, consistency distillation, DMD); automated gameplay agent collects synchronized keyboard/mouse inputs, gameplay recordings, and temporally aligned state information across three games (No Rest for the Wicked, Vampire, Hollow Knight denoted Game N, Game V, Game H), followed by filtering, synchronization, and annotation; evaluation uses AttackNet as pseudo ground truth for state transitions, a ResNet-18 SkillClassifier for baseline skill legality, and GPT-5.5 and Gemini-3.1-Pro as VLM judges.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Dataset: 51,786 clips; 51,486 train; 300 eval (100 per game); 13 characters (5 playable characters and 8 bosses); Game V 36.0%, Game N 43.8%, Game H 20.1%; total hours 71.93; Game N total 22,705 clips/31.53 hours; Game V total 18,657/25.91; Game H total 10,424/14.48. Variables: Δ=4; M = maximum skill-meter value; τ = activation threshold; αp and αb = attack strengths; hp_t and hb_t = health points; mb_t = boss skill meter; C={ci}N i=1 = selected skill set; I0 = [F0, hp0, hb0, αp, αb, mb0, C]; k = 3 VLM evaluations in Tab. 1. Main metrics: State Alignment 100.0%; Mechanics Fidelity 98.5±0.2% (GPT-5.5), 99.6±0.2% (Gemini-3.1-Pro); Decision Quality 88.4±0.7% (GPT-5.5), 93.0±0.6% (Gemini-3.1-Pro); boss action quality improvement >39.9%; Table 8 overall action validity 88.4±0.7/93.0±0.6, sequence fit 4.34±0.01/4.66±0.04, Ours Pref. 89.8%–95.8%; strongest baseline action validity improvement 39.9% and 45.8%. Table 2: AttackNet average Macro-F1 0.8906, accuracy 92.94%; SituationNet average Dist. MAE 0.2690, Angle MAE 6.51°, Front-Cone 94.17%, Decision-Zone 93.29%, Tactical-Sector 93.25%; per-game AttackNet/SituationNet: Game N 0.8476/90.53/0.3556/10.91/89.29/87.06/86.95; Game V 0.9135/92.48/0.1876/2.22/96.72/96.31/96.31; Game H 0.8871/96.11/0.2637/6.39/96.49/96.49/96.49. Implementation: 60K steps; 20 cell-level prompts; 80 frames at 832×480; AdamW at 5×10−5; four GPUs; AttackNet and SituationNet use ResNet-18 with single-layer GRU, jointly trained 20 epochs, AdamW learning rate 3×10−4, weight decay 10−4, dropout 0.1, hidden size 384, input 336×192; Gemma-4-E2B-it; 20 FPS; 20 intervals of 0.25 s; 5-second clips with 80 frames at 16 FPS; 20 predicted latent frames; three denoising steps; four frames per control interval; autoregressive teacher 20K steps, consistency distillation 12K steps, DMD training 5K steps; initial player and boss health 500, attack strengths 40 and 20, full initial boss meter; 60-s rollouts evaluated every 0.25 s yielding 240 ticks; AttackNet evaluated on 5,779 held-out intervals; SituationNet on 5,576 valid intervals; Front-Cone |θ| ≤ 20°, behind |θ| ≥ 90°; Decision Quality judges Action Validity (0 or 1) and Sequence Fit (0–5). Inference: DiT world model 225.060 ms/cell (220 calls); AttackNet 15.108 ms/call (221 calls); SituationNet 17.749 ms/call (22 calls); Gemma-4-E2B-it 2230.264 ms/request (11 calls); agentic rollout four GPUs 17.449 FPS, two GPUs 17.277 FPS, one GPU 16.729 FPS; DiT-cell ceiling 17.773, 17.524, 17.026 FPS; ceiling utilization 98.18%, 98.59%, 98.25%.

data.paper_title: Automated Referee Whistle Sound Detection for Extraction of Highlights from Sports Video
data.authors: P. Kathirvel, Dr. M. Sabarimalai Manikandan and Dr. K. P. Soman
data.core_methodology: Referee whistle sound detection (RWSD) based on preprocessor, linear phase bandpass finite impulse response (FIR) filter, short-time energy (STE) estimator and decision logic; preprocessing includes blocking and amplitude normalization with mean removal; non-overlapping blocks; filter-bank structure using least squares linear-phase bandpass finite response (FIR) filter; STE estimator includes amplitude squarer and linear filter with a finite rectangular impulse response h[k]; decision rules based on amplitude-dependent threshold and time-dependent threshold comparisons; calculation of number of non-zero values N_nz; sound instants determination; post-processing analysis of extracted audio segments and audio perception to identify false positive (FP) and false negative (FN); implemented in MATLAB 7.0.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Sampling rate of 16000 samples per second; amplitude resolution of 16 bit per sample; sampling rate (Fs) of 16 kHz; single-channel, 16 bit per sample; duration of the block (T_b) is 6 seconds; frequency range approximately is 3750 Hz- 4100 Hz; duration of the referee whistle sound is normally 0.5 to 3.5 seconds; W=0.3*Fs; amplitude-dependent threshold value of 10; time-dependent threshold value of 0.3*Fs; time-dependent threshold value is 0.2*Fs; total duration of the test audio signal is approximately 12 hours and 11 minutes; total duration of the audio tracks is approximately 2 hours and 11 minutes; 1310 blocks with 6-sec in duration; total referee whistle sounds of 103; detection failure rate of 27.18% (14 FP and 14 FN); sensitivity and positive predictivity are 86.41% and 86.41%; detects 89 referee whistle sounds correctly and produces 14 false positives; Table 2: TS 350, TP 324, FP 42, FN 26, Se 92.5%, +P 82.6%, Re 80.5%; overall detection failure rate of 19.4% (42 FP and 26 FN); detects 324 whistle sounds successfully; sensitivity and reliability are 92.5% and 80.5%; computation time is approximately 0.3-second for processing of 1-second block; Intel (R) Pentium (R) Dual Quad CPU @ 2.40 GHz and 3 GB of RAM; MATLAB 7.0 version environment.

data.paper_title: The value of Twitter for sports fans
data.authors: Jo Williams, Susan J. Chinn, James Suleiman
data.core_methodology: Phase one: preliminary assessment of basic categories of sports tweets from the Boston Celtics twitter feed; classification of 26 tweets by N = 24 graduate business students into Conversations/commentary/opinions (g1), News (g2), Community relations/charity (g3), Promotions/advertising/sales (g4), and Fan-generated content (g5), discarding tweets not consistently classified by at least 50 per cent. Phase two: survey of N = 162 undergraduate students, 133 useable responses, 30-item questionnaire with 25 original items and an established 5-item, 7-point Likert TI scale; descriptive statistics; confirmatory factor analysis; item-to-construct balance parcelling into g1, g2, and g4; structural equation modelling (SEM) using the lavaan package in R; base confirmatory model and exploratory model expanded to examine gender and Twitter activity.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Classification: N = 24; 26 tweets classified; at least 50 per cent; eight tweets dropped; eighteen remaining tweets. data.paper_title: Detecting events and key actors in multi-person videos
data.authors: Vignesh Ramanathan1, Jonathan Huang2, Sami Abu-El-Haija2, Alexander Gorban2, Kevin Murphy2, and Li Fei-Fei1
data.core_methodology: Track people in videos using a KLT tracker combined with bipartite graph matching; use a recurrent neural network (RNN) to represent the track features; learn time-varying attention weights to combine these features at each time-instant; process the attended features using another RNN for event detection/classification. Feature extraction: each video-frame is represented by a 1024 dimensional feature vector ft, the activation of the last fully connected layer of the Inception7 network; spatially localized player features pti are 2805 dimensional, containing appearance (1365 dimensional) and spatial information (1440 dimensional), using the cropped and resized player region through the Inception7 network and a 32×32 spatial histogram combined with a spatial pyramid. Event classification: hf_t = BLSTMframe(hf_{t−1}, hf_{t+1}, ft) (Eq. 1); he_t = LSTM(he_{t−1}, hf_t, at) (Eq. 2); squared-hinge loss L = 1/2 Σ_{t=1}^{T} Σ_{k=1}^{K} max(0, 1 − y_k w_k^⊤ h_t^e)^2 (Eq. 3). Attention with tracking: hp_ti = BLSTMtrack(hp_{t−1,i}, hp_{t+1,i}, pti) (Eq. 4); atrack_t = Σ_{i=1}^{Nt} γtrack_ti hp_ti, γtrack_ti = softmax(φ(hf_t, hp_ti, he_{t−1}); τ) (Eq. 5). Attention without tracking: anotrack_t = Σ_{i=1}^{Nt} γnotrack_ti pti, γnotrack_ti = softmax(φ(hf_t, pti, he_{t−1}); τ) (Eq. 6). φ() is a multi layer perceptron; τ is the softmax temperature parameter. Player detection uses a CNN-based multibox detector; person tracking uses the KLT tracker from [62]. Baselines compared: IDT with Fisher encoding, IDT player, C3D, LRCN, MIL, Only player, Avg. player, Attention no track, Attention with track.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Dataset: 257 basketball games; 14K event annotations; 11 event classes; videos typically 1.5 hours long; 212 training, 12 validation and 33 test videos; each event assumed 4 seconds long; videos split into 4 second clips and subsampled to 6fps; 11436 training, 856 validation and 2256 test clips; 850 video clips annotated with ball location in the test set; player bounding boxes annotated in a subset of 9000 frames from training videos; detector confidence threshold 0.5; 6–8 person detections per clip; average overlap of 0.7 at a recall of 0.8 with ground-truth bounding boxes in validation videos. Features and hyperparameters: frame feature 1024 dimensional; player feature 2805 dimensional (appearance 1365 dimensional, spatial 1440 dimensional); 32×32 bins with spatial pyramid pooling; hidden state dimension 256 for all LSTM and BLSTM RNNs; embedding layer with ReLU non-linearity and 256 dimensions; τ value set to 0.25 for the attention softmax weighting; batch size 128; learning rate 0.005 reduced by a factor of 0.1 every 10000 iterations with RMSProp; trained on a cluster of 20 GPUs for 100k iterations over one day. Detection: sliding 4 second window; stride length 2 seconds; windows not overlapping more than 1 second with any of the 11 annotated events treated as negatives; 90200 negative examples across all videos. Equations: hf_t = BLSTMframe(hf_{t−1}, hf_{t+1}, ft) (Eq. 1); he_t = LSTM(he_{t−1}, hf_t, at) (Eq. 2); L = 1/2 Σ_{t=1}^{T} Σ_{k=1}^{K} max(0, 1 − y_k w_k^⊤ h_t^e)^2 (Eq. 3); hp_ti = BLSTMtrack(hp_{t−1,i}, hp_{t+1,i}, pti) (Eq. 4); atrack_t = Σ_{i=1}^{Nt} γtrack_ti hp_ti, γtrack_ti = softmax(φ(hf_t, hp_ti, he_{t−1}); τ) (Eq. 5); anotrack_t = Σ_{i=1}^{Nt} γnotrack_ti pti, γnotrack_ti = softmax(φ(hf_t, pti, he_{t−1}); τ) (Eq. 6). data.paper_title: In Pursuit of Many: A Review of Modern Multiple Object Tracking Systems
data.authors: Mk Bashar1*, Samia Islam1, Kashifa Kawaakib Hussain2, Md. Bakhtiar Hasan2, A.B.M. Ashikur Rahman2,3 and Md. Hasanul Kabir2
data.core_methodology: Survey/review with challenge-driven synthesis organizing methods around the problems they target and the paradigms they adopt; covers historical progression from tracking-by-detection to hybrid and end-to-end designs; taxonomy groups Detection and Target Association, Transformers, Motion Model, Graph Model, Attention Module, Foundation Models, Siamese Network, Tracklet Association, Generative Tracking, and Mamba-Based Tracking; canonical detection-and-target-association pipeline uses a detector producing boxes or masks and confidence scores, an embedding head, a prediction module such as Kalman filter or learned predictor, and an association module computing affinities such as IoU, appearance cosine, and motion cost and solving matching by greedy, Hungarian, or learned matching; transformer methods use detection queries and track queries with cross-attention; graph models use nodes, edge prediction, message passing, GNN, and global assignment; attention methods use spatial/channel attention and short-term and long-term memory banks queried by cross-attention; foundation models include DINOv2/DINOv3, Grounding DINO, SAM-based systems, SAMURAI, SAM2MOT, and DAM4SAM; Siamese networks use a twin encoder with shared weights; tracklet association links short tracklets; generative tracking uses diffusion models to denoise point-sets or bounding box hypotheses; Mamba-based tracking uses SSM/Mamba layers for temporal encoding and motion prediction.

data.paper_title: Salient Object Detection in RGB-D Videos
data.authors: Ao Mou, Yukang Lu, Jiahao He, Dingyao Min, Keren Fu∗, Qijun Zhao
data.core_methodology: RDVS dataset construction from MPI Sintel, WSVD, Stereo Ego-Motion, SBM-RGBD, and TUM-RGBD; annotation guided by Tobii Eye Tracker 4C gaze data with a small Gaussian filter to obtain continuous saliency maps. DCTNet+: a three-stream encoder-decoder architecture with RGB as primary modality and depth/optical flow (OF) as auxiliary modalities; OF maps rendered by RAFT; each encoder stream based on ResNet-34 with ASPP attached to the last layer; five-level RGB features (X_i^r)_{i=1}^5, depth features (X_i^d)_{i=1}^5, and OF features (X_i^f)_{i=1}^5 aligned to 64 channels via compression module (CP), realized by BConv (convolution, BatchNorm and ReLU). Multi-modal attention module (MAM) based on the non-local (NL) module models multi-modal long-range dependencies via query-key matching Wa = softmax(Wθ ⊗ Wϕ^T) and cross-modal long-range attended features hat X_i^rm ← Wa ⊗ W_g^r, hat X_i^m ← Wa ⊗ W_g^m, with Y_i^m = X_i^m + hat X_i^m. Refinement fusion module (RFM) uses coordinate attention (CoA), spatial attention, cross-modal coordinate attention, residual connections, and progressive fusion; universal interaction module (UIM) combines concatenation, multiplication, maximum, and subtraction: output = BConv([Vcat, Vmul, Vmax, Vsub]) with kernel size 3, padding and stride set to 1. Equations: Att_i^p = CoA(T_i^p); hat T_i^p = Att_i^p ⊙ T_i^p, p∈{r,f,d}, i=1,...,5; Att_i^rm = UIM(Att_i^r, Att_i^m), m∈{f,d}; hat C_i^m = Att_i^rm ⊙ T_i^m + hat T_i^m + T_i^m, m∈{f,d}; C_i^rm = Att_i^rm ⊙ T_i^r + hat T_i^r, m∈{f,d}; hat C_i^r = Bconv([C_i^rf, C_i^rd]) + T_i^r; F_i = UIM(Z_i^r, UIM(Z_i^f, Z_i^d)). Holistic multi-modal attentive paths (HMAPs): LastConv (two BConv modules and a convolutional layer) produces L^r, L^f, L^d; coarse map CM = UIM(L^r, UIM(L^f, L^d)); low-level refinement f_i^p = f_i^p ⊙ CM + f_i^p for f_i^p ∈ {X_1^p, X_2^p, Y_3^p}, p∈{r,f,d}; ×2 bilinear interpolation. Supervision: BCE loss plus IoU loss, ltotal = Σ_{i=1}^5 (1/2^{i-1}) l(S_i,G)+l(CM,G), l(S_i,G)=l_bce(S_i,G)+l_iou(S_i,G). Synthetic depth generated with DPT. Evaluation metrics: S-measure (Sα), maximum F-measure (Fβmax), MAE (M).
data.key_metrics_and_variables: RDVS: 57 sequences, 4,087 frames; frame resolution varies from 640×480 to 1280×720; contributing dataset counts: MPI Sintel 13 sequences/569 frames/1024×436; WSVD 29/2139/1280×720; Stereo Ego-Motion 10/884/960×540; SBM-RGBD 4/418/640×480; TUM-RGBD 1/77/640×480; 16 participants (9 males and 7 females, aging between 22 and 35); 10 human annotators; Tobii Eye Tracker 4C sampling rate 90Hz; screen 23.8” with resolution 1920×1080; approximately 70 cm viewing distance; RDVS covers attention-shift cases (28 sequences out of 57); training set 32 sequences/2,208 frames; test set 27 sequences/1,879 frames; compared against 17 VSOD models and 14 RGB-D SOD models; highest metric margins (∼4.9% on Fβ) on RDVS. Implementation: trimodal inputs resized to 448×448; batch size 8; SGD; initial learning rates of backbones and other parts 1e-4 and 1e-3; 30 epochs; ∼17 hours on NVIDIA 3090 GPU; UIM kernel size 3 with padding and stride 1. Metrics: S-measure (Sα), maximum F-measure (Fβmax), MAE (M). DCTNet+ results: DAVIS Fβmax 0.922, Sα 0.930, M 0.012; DAVSOD 0.754, 0.818, 0.055; FBMS 0.918, 0.916, 0.026; SegV2 0.917, 0.931, 0.010; VOS 0.802, 0.858, 0.056; RDVS full 0.836, 0.871, 0.042; RDVS test after fine-tuning 0.814, 0.869, 0.034. Computational efficiency: Speed (s): Overall 0.0844, MAM 0.0081, RFM 0.0325; Params (M): Overall 94.6528, MAM 0.7415, RFM 5.9144. Loss: ltotal = Σ_{i=1}^5 (1/2^{i-1}) l(S_i,G)+l(CM,G), l(S_i,G)=l_bce(S_i,G)+l_iou(S_i,G). MAM/attention: Wa = softmax(Wθ ⊗ Wϕ^T); hat X_i^rm ← Wa ⊗ W_g^r; hat X_i^m ← Wa ⊗ W_g^m; Y_i^m = X_i^m + hat X_i^m. UIM: output = BConv([Vcat, Vmul, Vmax, Vsub]). RFM: Att_i^p = CoA(T_i^p); hat T_i^p = Att_i^p ⊙ T_i^p; Att_i^rm = UIM(Att_i^r, Att_i^m), m∈{f,d}; hat C_i^m = Att_i^rm ⊙ T_i^m + hat T_i^m + T_i^m; C_i^rm = Att_i^rm ⊙ T_i^r + hat T_i^r; hat C_i^r = Bconv([C_i^rf, C_i^rd]) + T_i^r; F_i = UIM(Z_i^r, UIM(Z_i^f, Z_i^d)). HMAPs: CM = UIM(L^r, UIM(L^f, L^d)); f_i^p = f_i^p ⊙ CM + f_i^p for f_i^p ∈ {X_1^p, X_2^p, Y_3^p}, p∈{r,f,d}. Attribute thresholds: FM average per-frame object motion (centroids Euclidean distance) larger than 20 pixels; SV area ratio among any pair of bounding boxes enclosing the target object smaller than 0.5; BO ratio of object and image areas larger than 0.25; SO ratio of object and image areas less than 0.01.

data.authors: Felipe Arruda Moura, Fabio Giuliano Caetano, Ricardo da Silva Torres
data.core_methodology: Narrative review; reviews the fundamentals of the main tracking systems, including algorithms based on computer vision and artificial intelligence for processing videos and global (global positioning system and global navigation satellite system) and local positioning systems; addresses technological advances for obtaining data from human pose estimation and validation or quality analysis studies of each method. Named systems/methods include time-motion analysis, potentiometers coupled to video cameras, video-based systems and computer vision, automatic player detection (background subtraction, shape-based and texture-based algorithms), particle filters algorithms, convolutional neural networks, deep convolutional neural networks, Vision Transformers, human pose estimation, multiple people tracking, OpenPose, FairMOT, BoT-SORT, ConfTrack, ViTPose, DFSTrack, YOLO algorithms, Scaled-YOLOv4, FasterRCNN, HOG algorithm + SVM, Stacked hourglass networks and higher HRNet, GolfPose, Pose2Trajectory (ViTPose), ECA-HRNet, STARKSKI, MobileNet + pose estimation + Hough transformation, TokenPose with Vision transformers, AlphaPose + Dijkstra’s shortest path, Alphapose skeleton detector + YOLOv5, YOLOv3 + DeepSORT, YOLOv7 + mask-RC-NN + BoT-SORT, JDE (joint detection and embedding), Particle filter + template matching + HSV color space, YOLOv7 + IoU threshold + Kalman filter, Background segmentation + neural network + combinatorial optimization, DeepPlayer + individual probability occupancy map (IPOM) + K-shortest path with ID (KSP-ID), Siamese tracklet affinity networks (STAN) + long short-term memory (LSTM), Vol-Bot-SORT (YOLOv8 + Bot-SORT), Cross-dimensional spatio-temporal association (COSTA), YOLOv3 + SORT, Foreground extraction + adaptive multiscale sampling, YOLOv4 + SORT, ResNet + feature pyramid network, Probabilistic and identified occupancy map (PIOM), FairMOT + additional training, Probability distributions and particle filters, Adaptive background subtraction + blob analysis + predictive particle filters, Higher HRNet, YOLOv2; global positioning system (GPS); global navigation satellite system (GNSS); integrated triaxial accelerometers; local positioning system (LPS); ultra-wideband (UWB); radio frequency identification (RFID).
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Main text: more than 12 hours computational processes and more than 6 hours of manual corrections for each player analyzed in a football match; LPS errors lower than 25 cm for the determination of the player's position in football; football matches use more than three cameras with frame rates higher than 15 Hz and resolution ranging from 720 × 480 to 1920 × 1080 pixels; automatic tracking rate: 20 % for wheelchair rugby, 82.6 % for beach volleyball, 94 to 95.9 % for football, 95.5 % for basketball, 91.3 % for handball, 95.9 % for American Football, 97 % for volleyball, and 99.98 % for tennis; 6 % would represent almost 10,000 frames for each player for manual tracking; GPS includes 31 satellites in orbit around the Earth; GNSS considers over 100 active satellites in orbit; receivers use at least four satellites; GPS/GNSS sampling rate ranged from 1 to 50 Hz in team sports; 10 Hz GPS sampling rate may be supplemented with accelerometer data to increase the sampling rate to 15 Hz; 20 Hz devices compared to 5 Hz; 50 Hz devices; systems showed moderate errors when measuring movement at speeds higher than 20 km/h; DOP values may range from 0 to 50, but ideally less than 1; LPS resulting sampling frequency is the ratio between the true sampling rate and the number of transponders, with 1,000 Hz and 22 players giving ~45 Hz; 45 Hz (1000/22) for the local position measurement (LPM) system, ~4 Hz for the ubisense system, and 20 Hz for the kinexon system; Nyquist Theorem: sampling rate not at least twice the highest frequency present in the signal may lead to distorted or misleading data. data.paper_title: PEOPLE DETECTION, TRACKING AND RE-IDENTIFICATION THROUGH A VIDEO CAMERA NETWORK

data.paper_title: The Magnet Player: a geometric proxy for off-the-ball offensive gravity in football, from optical tracking data
data.authors: José María García de Marina López
data.core_methodology: Optical tracking from Skillcorner at 10 frames per second; production analysis samples 1 out of every 5 raw frames (2 Hz effective); coordinates rescaled to the standard 105×68-metre pitch; team identity resolved against the official match roster served by the Skillcorner API; frames with fewer than 4 detected players from both teams excluded; Euclidean distance on the pitch plane; no trajectory smoothing. Geometric proxy computed frame by frame: own_dist(p, t) = min_{q ∈ opponents(p)} ‖pos(p, t) − pos(q, t)‖; compactness(t) = max(3.5, average_p own_dist(p, t)); pull(p, t) = Σ_{q: d(p,q,t) < compactness(t)} [1 − d(p,q,t) / compactness(t)]; Gravity(p) = Σ_t pull(p, t) × Δt. Uses adaptive compactness baseline recalculated at every instant, a 3.5-metre floor, leave-one-out baseline alternative, Pearson correlation sensitivity across 2.0, 1.0 and 0.67 Hz, 95% bootstrap confidence intervals with 2,000 resamples, and possession-phase comparison; IGO compared as a reception-threat index calibrated by regression against real attacking output.
