data.core_methodology: Concurrent validity study comparing broadcast-derived player and ball tracking data from three commercially available broadcast tracking providers across three feeds (PGM, Camera 1, Tactical) against a high-definition multi-camera optical tracking system (TRACAB Gen 5, ChyronHego, New York, USA) capturing data at 25 Hz and using 12 fixed cameras elevated within the stadium infrastructure; temporal alignment by phase shifting players' speeds in the TRACAB dataset to minimize RMSE, with the median phase shift applied across all files; spatial alignment by rotating the tracking data throughout 360 degrees in 0.1-degree increments and applying X–Y translations to minimize positional error, with the resulting transformation parameters applied uniformly to both player and ball tracking data; mean bias and 95% limits of agreement estimated from linear models built using the stats::lm function with separate intercept-only models for each feed (PGM, Camera 1, Tactical) and position error as outcome; RMSE separately calculated for position; linear models with interaction between provider and camera feed and RMSE for position as outcome, with main effects extracted using stats::anova and post hoc tests using emmeans::emmeans with a Tukey adjustment; statistical analyses in RStudio (version 12.1; Posit, Boston, MA) using R programming language (version 4.3.3, R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria); auto-eventing using the Python implementation (version 3.9.12; Python Software Foundation, Wilmington, DE) of a deterministic, rules-based auto-eventing algorithm developed by Vida-Codina et al. data.paper_title: Leveraging Player Tracking for Event Detection in Ice Hockey

data.core_methodology: Multi-stage pipeline for overhead video sequences: annotate timestamps of faceoff or whistle events; detect players with a pre-trained Detection Transformer (DETR) model with a ResNet-50 backbone; use detections as prompts for Segment Anything Model 2 (SAM2) to segment and track objects via iteratively refined masks/tracklets; post-process with padding, data augmentation and discrete differences to obtain velocity spatio-temporal arrays from position spatio-temporal arrays; classify arrays with K-nearest-neighbours using Euclidean distance and majority vote; optimize KNN with GridSearchCV over k and 5-fold cross-validation using accuracy; use principal component analysis (PCA) embeddings for trajectory and velocity arrays; preprocessing includes BGR-to-grayscale conversion, median filter, binary thresholding, largest-contour rink cropping, and DETR confidence filtering.

data.paper_title: Evaluating Advanced Impact Mitigation Technologies for Concussion Risk Reduction in Youth Cycling Helmets
data.authors: Jessica A. Towns1, Fady F. Abayazid2, Gerald A. Grant1,3, David B. Camarillo1, *Nicholas J. Cecchi1
data.core_methodology: Six youth bicycle helmet technologies were tested: two conventional EPS controls (FOAM-A, FOAM-B) and four advanced technologies (CELL, SLIP, SLIDE, HYDRAULIC). Helmeted small NOCSAE headforms were impacted using a monorail drop tower (CADEX, Quebec, Canada) with a custom halo fixture; impact locations were adapted from the Virginia Tech Bicycle STAR helmet testing protocol: front boss, crown, rear boss. Conditions were a 25° anvil at 2.9 m/s and a 45° anvil at 5.2 m/s, with 80-grit sandpaper on the anvil. A 6DX-PRO sensor measured triaxial linear acceleration and triaxial rotational velocity; linear kinematics were filtered at CFC1000 according to SAE J211, and rotational acceleration was obtained from rotational velocity using a five-point stencil derivative, with both filtered at CFC180. YGAMBIT, a concussion risk function derived from youth football concussions, was used with a lognormal cumulative distribution with parameters μ = 0.967 and σ = 0.331. High-speed stereo video was recorded at 3,600 frames per second using FASTCAM SA3 cameras; intrinsic and extrinsic camera parameters were estimated using the MATLAB Stereo Camera Calibrator application, marker trajectories were tracked using Tracker Video Analysis and Modelling Tool (Tracker 4.91; Open Source Physics), and three-dimensional marker coordinates were triangulated in MATLAB. The helmet and headform were modeled as rigid bodies; best-fit rotation was determined by singular value decomposition, and state-zero reconstruction used a least-squares singular-value-decomposition solution. Displacement and relative-rotation signals were low-pass filtered at 235 Hz, and video and sensor time series were synchronized by cross-correlating video- and sensor-measured headform rotational velocity traces. The reference position was defined at the first rising crossing of 15 g. Statistical analysis used Shapiro-Wilk test, Tukey’s 1.5×IQR criterion, two-way analyses of variance (ANOVAs), Tukey's multiple-comparisons tests, Shapley decomposition, linear regression models (statsmodels 0.14.6), beta regression with a logit link, Wald z-tests, and likelihood-ratio tests.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Equation 1: Vmax= √2gh, where g = 9.81 m/s2; maximum impact velocity was 5.64 m/s, with the 2.9 and 5.2 m/s test conditions representing 50% and 90% of this velocity, respectively. YGAMBIT equation: YGAMBIT = sqrt((PLA/62.4)^2 + (PRA/2609)^2). Concussion risk equation: Concussion risk = 1/2 + 1/2 erf[(ln(YGAMBIT) − 0.967)/(√2 × 0.331)]; lognormal cumulative distribution parameters μ = 0.967 and σ = 0.331. Regression equations: PLA = β0 + β1(Peak Displacement) + β2(Impact Condition) + β3(Impact Location); PRA = β0 + β1(Peak Relative Rotation) + β2(Impact Condition) + β3(Impact Location); logit(E[Concussion Risk]) = β0 + β1(Peak Displacement) + β2(Peak Relative Rotation) + β2(Impact Condition) + β3(Impact Location). Key fitted values: greater headform displacement toward the anvil was associated with lower PLA (β = −4.97 g/mm, 95% CI [−7.21, −2.73], p = 9.77 × 10⁻⁵); greater helmet-headform relative rotation was associated with lower PRA (β = −288.5 rad/s2/°, 95% CI [−422.7, −154.4], p = 1.41 × 10⁻⁴); beta-regression displacement β = −0.192 per mm, 95% CI [−0.277, −0.106], p = 1.02 × 10-5; relative rotation β = −0.110 per degree, 95% CI [−0.193, −0.027], p = 0.0097; combined model χ2 = 33.21, p = 6.16 × 10-8; adding relative rotation χ2 = 6.31, p = 0.012; adding displacement χ2 = 16.79, p = 4.19 × 10-5. ANOVA: at 2.9 m/s and 25°, technology F(5,18) = 127.9, p<0.0001; impact locations F(2,18) = 143.6, p<0.0001; technology-by-location interaction F(10,18) = 33.41, p<0.0001; at 5.2 m/s and 45°, technology F(5,18) = 269.2, p<0.0001; impact locations F(2,18) = 165.6, p<0.0001; interaction F(10,18) = 11.47, p<0.0001. Risk reductions: HYDRAULIC reduced mean risk by 94–95% and 77–78% relative to the foam controls at 2.9 and 5.2 m/s, respectively; at 2.9 m/s reductions were 94.1–95.3% relative to FOAM and 90.9%–93.9% relative to CELL, SLIP, and SLIDE; at 5.2 m/s reductions were 76.9–77.5% relative to FOAM-A and FOAM-B and 57.1%–67.9% relative to CELL, SLIP, and SLIDE. Kinematic reductions: at 25°, CELL and SLIP reduced PRA by 29.5–47.1% despite increasing PLA by 13.5–15.4%; SLIDE reduced PLA by -0.80–0.50% and PRA by 30.1–43.0%; at 45°, CELL and SLIP reduced PLA by -1.4–8.9% and PRA by 30.7–56.2%; SLIDE reduced PLA by 8.1–16.2% and PRA by 31%; HYDRAULIC lowered PLA by 30.7–37.8% and PRA by 48.1–57.7%. Kinematics: at 2.9 m/s mean PLA was 111.1 ± 27.1 g and mean PRA was 2756 ± 1064 rad/s²; at 5.2 m/s mean PLA was 125.7 ± 23.1 g and mean PRA was 5128 ± 1888 rad/s2. Stereo quality: mean reprojection error 0.96 ± 0.53 pixels; mean maximum rigid-body residuals 0.26 ± 0.27 mm for the helmet and 0.30 ± 0.10 mm for the headform; video-derived PRV RMSE 3.18 rad/s and MAE 2.31 rad/s. Helmet-headform motion: at 25° and 2.9 m/s, peak anvil-normal displacement averaged 12.68 ± 3.47 mm and peak relative rotation averaged 5.88 ± 3.01°; at 45° and 5.2 m/s, these averaged 17.14 ± 2.94 mm and 12.52 ± 5.22°, respectively.

data.core_methodology: A ridge-regularized Bradley–Terry model uses early pass rush wins and losses within 2.5 seconds of the snap; a multinomial extension models full-play losses, wins, pressures, and sacks; ridge-penalized maximum likelihood; glmnet package; five-fold game-grouped cross-validation; 1,000 game-bootstrap draws; EPA linear regression fitted by ordinary least squares; proportional-odds model; prediction baselines using league-average and smoothed historical player outcome frequencies with smoothing strengths selected by five-fold game-grouped cross-validation.

Final pass rush: η_k,c = α_c + r_i(k),c − (1/m_k) Σ_{j∈J_k} b_j,c + δ_c D_k; Pr(C_k = c) = exp(η_k,c) / Σ_{d∈C} exp(η_k,d), c ∈ C = {loss, win, pressure, sack} (2). Held-out Weeks 16–18: 47 games; early n = 12,205 matchups; final n = 12,198 matchups. Early log loss: league average model 0.448 vs baseline 0.492, reduction 8.8% [7.0, 9.0]; fixed τ = 2 model 0.448 vs baseline 0.469, reduction 4.5% [3.4, 5.2]; retuned historical 0.448 vs 0.469, reduction 4.5% [3.4, 5.0]. Proportional-odds model: logit Pr(C_k ≤ c) = κ_c − η^ord_k; η^ord_k = r^ord_i(k) − (1/m_k) Σ_{j∈J_k} b^ord_j + δ^ord D_k + ξ^ord U_k (9).

data.paper_title: BST: Badminton Stroke-type Transformer for Skeleton-based Action Recognition in Racket Sports
data.authors: Jing-Yuan Chang
data.core_methodology: Video clipping strategy: rally Ri = {S(i)_j}_{j=1}^{n(i)} = {S(i)_1, S(i)_2, ..., S(i)_n(i)} for i = 1, 2, ..., r; fixed-width clip C(i)_j = {F_{h(i)_j−t}, F_{h(i)_j−t+1}, ..., F_{h(i)_j+t}}; proposed strategy \hat h(i)_{j−1} = (h(i)_{j−1}, if j > 1; h(i)_j − t, if j = 1), \hat h(i)_{j+1} = (h(i)_{j+1} + ε, if j < n(i); h(i)_j + t, if j = n(i)), and new stroke clip \hat C(i)_j = {F_{\hat h(i)_{j−1}}, F_{\hat h(i)_{j−1}+1}, ..., F_{\hat h(i)_{j+1}}}. Practical settings: actual time distance of these two frame numbers from the target frame number does not exceed 1.5 seconds (before adding ε); t is set to the half of the FPS of the video representing 0.5 seconds interval; ε is set to t/2. Model inputs extracted using MMPose with RTMPose for 2D pose estimation and MotionBERT for further 3D pose estimation (choose 2D poses); court lines via MonoTrack or TennisCourtDetector; 2D shuttlecock positions generated by TrackNetV31. BST architecture derived from TemPose; BST-0 backbone processes player poses and shuttlecock positions through dedicated TCN modules, then a Transformer Encoder with two Transformer Layers with prepended learnable class token and learnable positional embedding. Transformer Layer: X̃(l) = X(l−1) + MHSA(split(LN(X(l−1)))); X(l) = X̃(l) + FFN(LN(X̃(l))); Q = [Q1 ... QH] = XWQ ∈ R^{S×(DA×H)}; K = [K1 ... KH] = XWK ∈ R^{S×(DA×H)}; V = [V1 ... VH] = XWV ∈ R^{S×(DA×H)}; MHSA(Q, K, V) = [ ... SA(Qh, Kh, Vh) ... ] WO; SA(Qh, Kh, Vh) = softmax(Qh(Kh)^T/√DA) Vh. Cross Transformer Layer (CrossTrans) with Multi-Head Cross Attention (MHCA): K and V derived from shuttlecock trajectory latent, Q generated from player pose latent or player position latent; outputs are shuttlecock trajectory latents belonging to the two players; then second Transformer Encoder; MLP Head; softmax. Trans1 and Trans2 inspired by TemPose (Temporal and Interactional Transformer). Pose Position Fusion (PPF) Module: MLP outputs coefficients multiplied with original poses. Clean Gate (CG) Module: refines information derived from shuttlecock trajectory by leveraging interaction strength between the two players and the shuttlecock. Aim Player (AP) Module: difference between cosine similarities yields α̃; cosine similarity ranges from -1 to 1, so α̃ ∈ [−2, 2]; normalize α = (α̃ + 2)/4 so α ∈ [0, 1]; α denotes coefficient on blue player's information, 1−α on green player's information. BST-CG-AP combines CG and AP modules with BST.

data.paper_title: Reaching the NFL Playoffs Based on Week One Results: A Probability Model with Simulation
data.authors: Brian Kidd, Peter Boyd, Christopher Vincent
data.core_methodology: Statistical analysis of NFL season results from 1978 to 2014 scraped from the NFL & Pro Football League Encyclopedia at pro-football-reference.com and analyzed using R Studio; simplified probabilistic model ranking 32 teams 1-32 with R uniformly distributed on {1,2,...,32}, random week 1 scheduling, and the higher-ranked team always winning; Bayes' rule; win probability function Pk(j) = (j - k)/64 + 1/2; Pk = (95 - 2k)/124; Binomial distribution with n = 15 and p = Pk; Head Start Theory and updated opinion theory; Monte-Carlo simulation of 1000 seasons with no ties, random pairing each week, random tiebreakers, and the 12 teams with the most wins selected as playoff teams; Monte-Carlo estimate P(Playoff | {N = w}∩W) ≈ Number of Playoff Teams That Won Week 1 with w Wins / Number of Teams That Won Week 1 with w Wins.

data.paper_title: Spontaneous pacing during overground hill running
data.authors: Andrew D. Townshend, Charles J. Worringham, Ian B. Stewart
data.core_methodology: Incremental exercise test to exhaustion on a motorized treadmill; ventilatory threshold determined using the ventilatory equivalent method; portable gas analyser breath-by-breath data averaged for every 15 second period; field time trial over 3 laps of a 3175m circuit divided into level 765m, uphill 820m, level 770m, downhill 820m, each section divided into 8 sub-sections; GPS receiver providing speed, position and displacement once each second; activity monitor containing single lead ECG recorder and tri-axial accelerometer with ECG at 300Hz and accelerometer sampled at 75Hz, peaks in vertical acceleration used to detect steps, custom written program used to calculate stride frequencies, direct interpolation from GPS speed data used to derive average stride lengths; three way repeated measures analysis of variance; Tukey’s post-hoc tests and planned comparisons; multiple regression used to develop prediction equations for self-selected running speed based on gradient and lap at Group level (96 sub-sections averaged across subjects) and individual level (96 sub-sections x 8 runners); modified gradient factor using a geometric decay function: Modified gradient = (0.5 x g n + 0.25 x gn-1 + 0.125 x gn-2 …+ 0.003906 x g n-7 ) where g = gradient and n = current sub-section.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Participants: eight healthy male distance runners, age 28.1 ± 9 years, height 178.9 ± 7.3 cm, weight 70.2 ± 7.6 kg; 10000m race in less than 40 mins; treadmill start speed 12 and 14km/hr, speed increased by 0.3km/hr each minute, grade held constant at 1%; gas-exchange averaged every 15 second period; maximal test criteria: heart rate ± 10 beats per minute of age-predicted maximum, respiratory exchange ratio > 1.10, increase in oxygen consumption less than 150mls.min-1; VO2 max determined by averaging the four highest successive 15 second values; field circuit 3175m divided into level section 765m, uphill 820m, level 770m, downhill 820m, each section divided into 8 sub-sections; uphill gradients 6.3%, 9.3%, 11.2%, 6.8%, 11.7%, 10.7%, 1.5%, and 7.8%; additional level section 380m; average change 0.02m/sec or 0.55%; 30 second period; 96 sub-sections; 6-7 am; GPS once each second; ECG 300Hz; accelerometer sampled at 75Hz and rated to ± 2.4g; lab: VO2 max 69.8 ± 5.4 mls. kg. min -1; vVO2 max 4.87 ± 0.40 m/s (17.5 ± 1.4 km/hr); VT 88.2 ± 6.4 % VO2 max; vVT 4.40 ± 0.21 m/s (15.8 ± 0.8 km/hr); results: 23% slower on uphills and 13.8% faster on downhills compared with level; level speeds significantly different for 78.4 ± 7.0 seconds following an uphill and 23.6 ± 2.2 seconds following a downhill; stride length 20.5% shorter uphill and 16.2% longer downhill; VO2 100.4% of individual ventilatory thresholds on uphills, 78.9% on downhills and 89.3% on level; 89% of group level speed predicted using a modified gradient factor; data.paper_title: The development of a HAMstring InjuRy (HAMIR) index to mitigate injury risk through innovative imaging, biomechanics, and data analytics: protocol for an observational cohort study
data.authors: Bryan C. Heiderscheit, Silvia S. Blemker, David Opar, Mikel R. Stiffler‑Joachim, Asheesh Bedi, Joseph Hart, Brett Mortensen, Stephanie A. Kliethermes, and The HAMIR Study Group
data.core_methodology: Longitudinal, prospective observational cohort study; HAMIR index risk prediction models for index HSI injury and re-injury constructed using generalized estimating equations (GEE) for binary outcomes with a logit link and controlling for athletic-exposures; correlation among individuals in repeated years accounted for using an appropriately identified correlation matrix structure; institution-level clustering considered and modeled as necessary; multiple imputation methods considered for missing data; internal validation using standard internal validation criteria; performance assessed using the Brier score; calibration assessed using the Hosmer Lemeshow Goodness of Fit Chi-square; discrimination assessed with the c-statistic; bootstrapping used to assess potential optimization; sample size estimated using the R package pmsampsize; automatic muscle segmentation performed using Springbok machine learning technology; eccentric hamstring strength measured using the NordBord Hamstring Testing System; sprinting biomechanics assessed with seven IMUs (MTw Awinda, Xsens Technologies B.V.) and calibration via Xsens MVN; MRI using 3 T scanners, axial multi-slice 2D gradient echo fast SPGR sequence or axial 3D T1 DIXON sequence, axial T1-weighted tendon images, and fat-suppressed T2-weighted sequence.

data.authors: Lachlan Astfalck1,2, Michael Bertolacci3 and Edward Cripps1
data.core_methodology: Proper scoring rules (squared error (SE), Dawid–Sebastiani score (DSS), energy score (ES), continuous ranked probability score (CRPS)); prediction spaces; Diebold–Mariano test; Monte Carlo; model output statistics (MOS) model; vector auto-regressive (VAR) model; Bayesian models with posterior predictive distributions; Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC); MOS model: y_{t+h}=β_{0,h}+β_{1,h}f_{t,h}+β_{2,h}f_{t−6,h+6}+ε_{t,h}, ε_{t,h}∼N(0,Σ_h), priors β_{0,h}∼N(0,I), β_{1,h}∼ℳN(I,I,I), β_{2,h}∼ℳN(0,I,I), Σ_h∼ℐW(2,0:05*I); VAR model: y_t=μ+Σ_{i=1}^p (Γ_i⊙Φ_i)(y_{t−i}−μ)+ε_t, ε_t∼N(0,Σ), priors μ∼N(0,I), Φ_1∼ℳN(0:9I,I,I), Φ_i∼ℳN(0,I,I) for i∈{2,...,p}, Σ∼ℐW(2,0:05*I), Bernoulli random variable Γ_i^{[a,b]}∼ℬ(0:5), p=24; stochastic selection representation of the VAR process.

data.paper_title: Proper Scoring Rule-based Diffusion for Probabilistic Weather Forecasting
data.authors: Joonhyeong Park1, Giung Nam1, Hyungi Lee2, Kyunghyun Cho3, Byoungwoo Park1,† and Juho Lee1,†
data.core_methodology: Proper scoring rule-based diffusion framework built on distributional diffusion models (DDMs; De Bortoli et al., 2025); auxiliary conditional denoising tasks predict the same clean future from its corrupted version and the forecast context; a shared stochastic predictor learns conditional distributions {p(X | c, X_t, t)}_{t∈[0,1]} by minimizing L_{λ,β}_DDM(θ)=∫_0^1 w_t E_{c,X,X_t∼q_t(·|X)}[S_{λ,β}(p_θ(· | c, X_t, t), X)] dt with uniform weighting (w_t≡1); linear noise schedule q_t(X_t|X)=N(X_t | (1−t)X, t^2 I), X_t=(1−t)X+tε, ε∼N(0,I), t∈[0,1]; generalized energy score S_{λ,β}(P,X)=E_{X̂∼P}[||X̂−X||^β] − λ/2 E_{(X̂,X̂′)∼P⊗P}[||X̂−X̂′||^β], with λ∈[0,1], β∈(0,2]; setting λ=β=1 and applying the score component-wise gives S_{1,1}=S_CRPS; standard CRPS training is the endpoint-only special case; fair CRPS uses Ŝ_CRPS({X̂^(m)}_{m=1}^M, X)=1/M Σ_{m=1}^M ||X̂^(m)−X||_1 − 1/(2M(M−1)) Σ_{m≠n} ||X̂^(m)−X̂^(n)||_1; Algorithm 1 Training samples t=uniform(0,1), eps=randn_like(x), x_t=(1-t)*x+t*eps, generates M stochastic ensemble members, and updates with fair_crps(x_hat, x); DDIM sampling; one-step and multi-step sampling; experiments use FGN, FCN3, Swin Transformer, U-Net, MOSAIC, and U-Cast; at 1.5° both DDM variants use spherical Gaussian corruption noise (SpG) with the heat-kernel schedule (κ0 = 0.01); spherical heat-kernel (HK) schedule with κ0 ∈ {0.01, 0.05}; area and channel weighting as detailed in Appendix C.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Metrics: nCRPS ↓, nRMSE ↓, fair CRPS, ensemble-mean RMSE, spread–skill ratio (SSR), Track CRPS; NFE = 1 unless stated; M=2 training ensemble members in pilot; M=50 ensemble members in evaluation; SSR = 1 / 1:1; 66% ensemble track distribution; t_min values in Figure 4: t_min=1.00, 0.75, 0.50, 0.25, 0.00 with Δ nCRPS vs. CRPS (%) = -0.47%, -3.21%, -5.53%, -7.03%, -8.10%; FGN-3d-100ep t_min results: t=1 -0.41%, U[0.75,1] -4.67%, U[0.50,1] -7.11%, U[0.25,1] -9.73%, U[0,1] -9.96%; Table 1 FGN CRPS nCRPS 0.0581, 0.0792, 0.1868, 0.2463 at 12h,1d,3d,5d and nRMSE 0.1138, 0.1586, 0.3847, 0.5034; FGN DDM nCRPS 0.0577, 0.0778, 0.1692, 0.2290 and nRMSE 0.1130, 0.1559, 0.3542, 0.4760; FCN3 CRPS nCRPS 0.0736, 0.0967, 0.1915, 0.2452 and nRMSE 0.1461, 0.1937, 0.3920, 0.5029; FCN3 DDM nCRPS 0.0735, 0.0942, 0.1759, 0.2283 and nRMSE 0.1461, 0.1894, 0.3664, 0.4755; Table 4 distribution shift: CRPS +3.10 nCRPS, +2.68 nRMSE, +0.017 SSR dev.; DDM +2.60 nCRPS, +2.24 nRMSE, +0.007 SSR dev.; tropical cyclone Table 17: MOSAIC CRPS track error 73,89,189 km (1d,3d,5d) and track CRPS 51,68,125; MOSAIC DDM 38,44,55 and 26,39,63; U-Cast CRPS 39,59,245 and 30,43,148; U-Cast DDM 35,37,210 and 24,38,123; DDM lower CRPS in 93.7% (787/840) for MOSAIC and 82.0% (1,377/1,680) for U-Cast; NFE=2 total 803/840; at 200 km fraction increases from 62% to 94% for MOSAIC and from 36% to 46% for U-Cast.

data.paper_title: Hierarchy-Aware Global Model for Hierarchical Text Classiﬁcation
data.authors: Jie Zhou1,2∗, Chunping Ma2, Dingkun Long2, Guangwei Xu2, Ning Ding3, Haoyu Zhang4, Pengjun Xie2, Gongshen Liu1†
data.core_methodology: Formulates the hierarchy as a directed graph G = (V, −→E , ←−E ); uses prior probabilities of label dependencies P(Uj|Ui) = P(Uj ∩Ui)/P(Ui) = P(Uj)/P(Ui) = Nj/Ni and P(Ui|Uj) = P(Ui ∩Uj)/P(Uj) = P(Uj)/P(Uj) = 1.0; hierarchy-aware structure encoders: Bidirectional Tree-LSTM and Hierarchy-GCN; proposes HiAGM with HiAGM-LA (multi-label attention) and HiAGM-TP (text feature propagation); classification with recursive regularization Lr = P i∈C P j∈child(i) 1 2||wi − wj||2, binary cross-entropy loss Lc = −PN i=1 PC j=1[yijlog(y′ ij)+(1−yij)log(1−y′ ij)], and final loss Lm = Lc + λ · Lr.

Dataset statistics: RCV1 |L| 103, Depth 4, Avg(|Li|) 3.24, Train 20,833, Val 2,316, Test 781,265; WOS |L| 141, Depth 2, Avg(|Li|) 2.0, Train 30,070, Val 7,518, Test 9,397; NYT |L| 166, Depth 8, Avg(|Li|) 7.6, Train 23,345, Val 5,834, Test 7,292. Implementation: one-layer bi-GRU with 64 hidden units; 3 parallel CNN layers with filter region size {2, 3, 4}; vocabulary maximum size 60,000; 300-dimensional pretrained GloVe; out-of-vocabulary minimum count 2; maximum token input length 256; fixed threshold 0.5; dropout rates 0.5, 0.1, 0.05; Adam mini-batch size 64 with learning rate α = 1 × 10−4, momentum parameters β1 = 0.9, β2 = 0.999, ϵ = 1 × 10−6; recursive regularization penalty coefficient 1 × 10−6. data.paper_title: Hierarchical Bayesian Joint Modeling of Athlete Performance Trajectories and Latent Peak Ages
data.authors: K. Ken Peng, Tianyu Guan, Xiong Zhao
data.core_methodology: Hierarchical Bayesian joint modeling framework linking a longitudinal model for athlete-specific performance trajectories to a regression submodel for latent peak age. Longitudinal component: y_ij = μ(t_ij; θ_i, τ_i) + δ^T z_ij + ε_ij, ε_ij ∼ N(0, σ_y^2); θ_i | x_i ∼ F_θ(· | x_i; ψ_θ). Latent peak-age component: parametric accelerated failure time (AFT) model log(τ_i) = β0 + β^T x_i + e_i, e_i ∼ N(0, σ_τ^2), so τ_i | x_i follows a lognormal distribution. Trajectory specifications: symmetric quadratic model μ(t; α, ρ, τ) = α − ρ(t − τ)^2; asymmetric quadratic model μ(t; α, ρ_L, ρ_R, τ) = α − ρ_L(τ − t)^2 for t ≤ τ and α − ρ_R(t − τ)^2 for t > τ. Normal random-effects specification: θ_i = θ0 + Bx_i + b_i, b_i ∼ MVN(0, Σ_θ). Bayesian inference via Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) implemented in Stan. Simulation study with I = 200 athletes and 200 replications comparing the proposed joint model with a pseudo-peak method (Naive 1) and a two-stage approach (Naive 2); Naive 1 implemented using survival::survreg() with a lognormal AFT specification, and Naive 2 first fitted the mixed-effects quadratic trajectory model in Stan via cmdstanr and then applied survival::survreg() lognormal AFT regression to estimated peak ages. R package supporting both symmetric and asymmetric trajectory specifications.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Application dataset: 105,515 records from 3,229 single-event athletes; athletes with at least ten recorded competitions; 366 appeared in multiple selected events and were excluded; athletes without recorded date of birth were excluded (0.03% of the dataset). data.paper_title: ON CONVERGENCE TO A FOOTBALL
data.authors: HAO FANG, MIJIA LAI
data.core_methodology: Gromov-Hausdorff topology; Luo-Tian’s explicit description of conic spheres as boundaries of convex polytopes in S3 (Alexandrov theorem); conformal geometry via singular solutions to Δu = −e^{2u} with asymptotic behavior u ∼ β_i ln |z − z_i| as z → z_i and u ∼ −2 ln |z| as |z| → ∞; a priori estimates and convergence result after proper reparametrization; level set analysis and the isoperimetric inequality; Bonnesen’s inequality; co-area formula; Hölder’s inequality; Sard’s theorem; Lp estimates of the Poisson equation; Sobolev’s embedding; Schauder’s estimate; stereographic projection.

data.paper_title: Poisson Modeling and Predicting English Premier League Goal Scoring
data.authors: Quang Nguyen
data.core_methodology: Poisson process; Poisson distribution; exponential distribution; continuous uniform distribution; Poisson regression; Generalized Linear Models (GLM) with natural logarithm as the link function; fit two Poisson regression models to get scoring rates for every EPL team at home and away from home; back-transform with the corresponding exponential function to get home and away mean (expected) scoring rates; 10000 simulations per season-data subset by randomly generating match final score for every team matchup using clubs' average scoring rates; three season subsets: data from all seasons prior to 2018-19, data from only the 2010s, and data from all seasons with more weight assigned to more recent competitions (weight number equivalent to the number of times the data for a particular season is duplicated); Chi-square goodness-of-fit test; Kolmogorov-Smirnov goodness-of-fit test.

data.paper_title: RUGBY-BOT: UTILIZING MULTI-TASK LEARNING & FINE-GRAINED FEATURES FOR RUGBY LEAGUE ANALYSIS
data.authors: Matthew Holbrook, Jennifer Hobbs, Patrick Lucey
data.core_methodology: Multi-task learning via a single Mixture Density Network (MDN) using a wide and deep learning approach: categorical features are passed through embedding layers; season one-hot vectors are concatenated with team/opponent one-hot vectors; tackle number (1-6) and back-to-back sets are represented as a binary flag; field position (x, y) is treated as both a sparse and dense feature, with the sparse position passed through layers boosting from the original two-dimensions up to 50 at the first hidden layer; embeddings are concatenated with continuous/dense features and passed through 2 final dense layers; the mixture density layer consists of 5 mixture each with a prediction for µ and σ; the model predicts the state-vector [yp, ym, ytt, yts, yw, ys] simultaneously; training uses Cross entropy as the loss, with a single negative log-likelihood over the state-vector; last-tackle decision-making is modeled separately with a simple logistic regressor. DVOA for Rugby League is created from the Expected Try (set) prediction by taking the difference between expected value and actual value and scaling with a mean of 0.

dataset: 2015-2018 National Rugby League seasons, over 750 games, more than 250,000 distinct tackles, split 80-train/20-test; architecture: 2 final dense layers, 5 mixture each with a prediction for µ and σ, 70m x 100m field, 1/3 m × 1/3 m bins = 63,000 dimensional input, boost from original two-dimensions up to 50 at the first hidden layer; data.paper_title: Identifying Player’s Strategies in No Limit Texas Hold’em Poker through the Analysis of Individual Moves
data.authors: Luís Filipe Teófilo, Luís Paulo Reis
data.core_methodology: Opponent modeling methodology applying clustering algorithms to a Poker game database to identify player types from individual actions. Game logs are converted to a common format; a game entity extracts game states and creates ARFF files for WEKA; partitioning clustering algorithms, specifically Expectation-maximization (EM), are applied separately to Pre-Flop and Post-Flop rounds. Actions are simplified to Call or Raise (Fold discarded). Game-state features: win_prob (based on Equation 2 from [14], using HS, NPot and PPot), position, possible_earnings, action, and betted_money; all numerical values normalized between 0 and 1. Each action is assigned to a cluster using Euclidean distance (Equation 4), assigning the cluster with the lowest distance. Each player’s relative frequency of actions in each cluster is calculated; the Expectation Maximization algorithm is applied again to define player strategy clusters. The paper also defines a player tactic as a function receiving the state of the game and returning an action (Equation 3).

Training features: win_prob Numeric {0-100%}; position Nominal {Early, Late}; possible_earnings Numeric {0-100%}; action Nominal {Call, Raise}; betted_money Numeric {0-100%}; all numerical values normalized (interval between 0 and 1); if all-in, betted_money = 1. data.core_methodology: convolutional neural networks (CNN); skip-layer architecture of an autoencoder, with a unified decoder; multiscale features; encoder is a VGG16 pretrained on ImageNet; decoder is a succession of deconvolution layers with RELUs; three feature maps decoded to 3 corresponding saliency maps, combined and passed through a convolutional layer called a fusion layer; Binary Cross Entropy used as a loss function; L1 loss (|gt−f(x)|), L2 distance or Mean Square Error (MSE), and Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence discussed; data augmentation with a sliding window of 3x3, 4x4 and 5x5 squares, color inversion, and board orientation change; datasets ETDS, ETDSa, GDS, and CAT2000

data.paper_title: Multi-Branch Siamese Networks with Online Selection for Object Tracking
data.authors: Zhenxi Li, Guillaume-Alexandre Bilodeau, and Wassim Bouachir
data.core_methodology: Multi-Branch Siamese Tracker (MBST) ensembling Ne siamese networks including Ns context-dependent branches and one AlexNet branch as Ne = Ns + 1; context-dependent branches have the same structure as SiamFC; AlexNet branch has the same structure as AlexNet; each branch is a siamese network applying identical transformation φi to both inputs and combining their representation by a cross-correlation layer. Response maps: hsi(z, X) = corr(fsi(z), fsi(X)), where si indicates the contextual index including the general branch (i = 0); ha(z, X) = corr(fa(z), fa(X)). Context-dependent branches are trained by contextual clustering on the low level feature map from the ImageNet Video dataset to find Nc (Nc = 10) context-dependent clusters; Nc context-dependent branches initialized by the basic siamese network. Online branch selection mechanism selects the most discriminative branch at every T frames using response weights wi: R(wihBi) = wi(P(hBi) − M(hBi)), B* = argmax_Bi R(wihBi); the corresponding branch is then used for T − 1 frames.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Ne = Ns + 1; Ns = Nc + 1; Nc = 10; target patch z: 127×127×3; search region X: 255×255×3; embedding output for z: 6 × 6 × 256; embedding output for X: 22 × 22 × 256; output response map dimension: 17×17; basic siamese branch trained for 50 epochs with initial learning rate of 0.01; learning rate decays after every epoch with decay factor δ of 0.869; context-dependent branches fine-tuned with learning rate 0.00001 for 10 epochs; wi for context-dependent branches = 1.0; AlexNet branch grid search from 8.0 to 12.0 with step 0.5; best wi = 10.5; branch selection interval T = 1, 3, 5, 7, 10, 13; optimal T = 7 frames; rescale inputs into three different resolutions; average testing speed of MBST = 17 fps; OTB precision score threshold = 20 pixels; OTB success plot uses IoU and area-under-curve (AUC). data.paper_title: Identification in discrete choice models with imperfect information
data.authors: Cristina Gualdani, Shruti Sinha
data.core_methodology: Static single-agent discrete choice models with imperfect information; baseline decision problem G := {Y, V, u, PV}; information structure S := {T , PT|V}; game against nature; one-player Bayes Correlated Equilibrium (1BCE) by Bergemann and Morris (2016); sharp identified set characterized by linear equalities and inequalities and solved as linear programs; model-implied choice probabilities as an Aumann expectation; sieve approximation of the linear program along Han and Yang (2023) using Bernstein polynomials of order K, including D-variate Bernstein basis; counterfactual bounds on choice probabilities for information provision and changes in covariates via 1BCE of augmented/linked baseline decision problems following Theorem 1 of BM16 and Theorem 1 of Bergemann, Brooks, and Morris (2022); simulated annealing to construct the parameter grid; MOSEK solver for Matlab; Monte Carlo integration; conditional moment inequalities and generalized moment selection procedure of Andrews and Shi (2013) with bootstrap for inference; spatial model of voting; British Election Study, 2017: Face-to-Face Post-Election Survey; maximum likelihood under complete information; Multinomial Probit formulas.

data.paper_title: Towards Structured Analysis of Broadcast Badminton Videos
data.authors: Anurag Ghosh, Suriya Singh, C.V.Jawahar
data.core_methodology: End-to-end framework for automatic attributes tagging and analysis of sport videos using broadcast videos without special camera setup or additional sensors. Point segmentation: HOG features from every 10th frame; χ2 kernel SVM to label frames as 'point frame' or 'non-point frame'; sequence smoothened using a Kalman filter. Player tracking and identification: finetune a FasterRCNN network for two classes 'PlayerTop' and 'PlayerBottom'; run detector for every other frame in a point segment; moving average background subtraction method; color histogram features from detected bounding box after applying foreground mask; randomly average 10 player features corresponding to point segments to create 2 player features per point; cluster features using a Gaussian Mixture Model into 2 clusters for each match. Player stroke segmentation: Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN) variants described by Lea et al. [18]: Encoder Decoder TCN (ED-TCN) similar to SegNet architecture; Dilated TCN analogous to WaveNet architecture. Dilated TCN equations: ˆS(j,l)_t = f(W (1)Sj,l−1_t−s + W (2)Sj,l−1_t + b); S(j,l)_t = S(j,l−1)_t + V ˆS(j,l)_t + e; Z0_t = ReLU(PB j=1 S(t)(j,L)); Z(1)_t = ReLU(VrZ(0)_t + er); softmax function; categorical cross-entropy with SGD updates; balanced class weighting. Features: HOG with cell size 64; Spatial CNN from two stream convolution network model [31] trained on UCF101, output of FC7 layer; input scale (454 × 340) centered at player track centroid resized to 224 × 224; independently extract features for both players and concatenate per frame. ED-TCN filter size d = 5, 10, 15, 20 (setting s = 2); acausal convolution from Xt−d/2 to Xt+d/2. Dilated TCN sample rate s = 1, 2, 4 and 8 fps; add term W (2)Sj,l−1_t+s to update equation. Point outcome: exploit badminton scoring rule; binary classification task by classifying who is serving player; kernel SVM with polynomial kernel; input concatenated player tracks for first k frames to construct vector of length 8k. Analysis: homography with camera view; bottom of player bounding boxes as proxy for feet; Kalman Filter computes displacement and speed in overhead view; average reaction time using react class.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Dataset: 27 badminton match videos; 10 matches with 20 players; 751 points; 10 Olympic matches with 20 players; 12 (5 · 2 + 2) classes; Table 1: Matches total 10, train 7, test 3; Players total 20, train 14, test 6; Player bboxes classes 2, total 2988, train 2094, test 894; Point segments classes 2, total 751, train 495, test 256; Strokes classes 12, total 15327, train 9904, test 5423. Overall results: 95.44% point segmentation accuracy; 97.38% player detection score (mAP@0.5); 97.98% player identification accuracy; stroke segmentation edit scores of 80.48%. Point segmentation: F1 score 95.44% for optimal parameters (C and order); precision 97.83%; recall 91.02% for point class. Player detection: mAP@0.5 97.85% for bottom player; 96.90% for top player; averaged player identification accuracy 97.98%. Stroke segmentation Table 2: ED-TCN d=5,10,15,20 HOG Acc 71.02,72.56,71.98,71.61; Edit 76.10,80.52,80.12,79.66; SpatialCNN Acc 69.19,68.92,71.31,71.49; Edit 77.63,80.48,80.45,80.40; Dilated TCN s=1,2,4,8 HOG Acc 70.24,68.08,68.25,67.31; Edit 70.11,70.72,73.68,73.29; SpatialCNN Acc 69.59,69.75,69.37,67.03; Edit 59.98,69.46,74.17,71.86. Point outcome: averaged accuracy 94.14% when player bounding boxes of first 50 frames are taken and degree of kernel is six; vector length 8k. Calibration/parameters: every 10th frame; every other frame; 10 player features; 2 clusters; HOG cell size 64; input scale (454 × 340) resized to 224 × 224; ED-TCN d=5,10,15,20 with s=2; Dilated TCN s=1,2,4,8 fps; first 50 frames; degree six. Analysis metrics: Set Dominance; Number of strokes in a point; Average speed in a point; Average Reaction Time.

data.paper_title: MOPT: Multi-Object Panoptic Tracking
data.authors: Juana Valeria Hurtado, Rohit Mohan, Wolfram Burgard, Abhinav Valada
data.core_methodology: Multi-Object Panoptic Tracking (MOPT) task unifying semantic segmentation, instance segmentation, and multi-object tracking; soft panoptic tracking quality (sPTQ) metric; PanopticTrackNet architecture built upon EfﬁcientPS; shared backbone based on EfﬁcientNet-B5 topology with 2-way Feature Pyramid Network (FPN); synchronized Inplace Activated Batch Normalization (iABN sync) followed by LeakyReLU activation; three-module semantic segmentation head with Large Scale Feature Extractor (LSFE), Dense Prediction Cells (DPC), and mismatch correction; weighted per-pixel log-loss; Mask R-CNN instance segmentation head with Regional Proposal Network (RPN) and RoIAlign; object score, proposal, classification, bounding box, and mask segmentation losses; instance tracking head with mask pooling, 256-dimensional feature vector, and batch hard triplet loss across t frames with margin α; Hungarian algorithm for association within window of time NT; MOPT fusion module using Hadamard product; Panoptic Quality (PQ), PTQ, IDS and sIDS; baselines combining Seamless, EfﬁcientPS, RangeNet++, KPConv, PointPillars, Track R-CNN, and MaskTrack R-CNN.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: MOPT task maps each pixel i of frame Ik ∈ {I0, ..., It−1} to (ci, ψi)k ∈ C×N; C := {0, ..., C −1}; ψi is unique for each segment throughout the sequence; if ci ∈ Cst, ψi is irrelevant. Equations: Lsemantic(Θ) = −1/n Σ Σij wij log pij(p*ij) (1); Linstance = Los + Lop + Lcls + Lbbx + Lmask (2); Ltrack = 1/|S| Σs∈S max(max_e∈S ||a^{c,ψ}_s − a^{c,ψ}_e|| − min_e∈S ||a^{c,ψ}_s − a^{c,\bar{ψ}}_e|| + α, 0) (3); B = (σ(Bd) + σ(Bs)) ⊙ (Bd + Bs) (4); TPc = {pc ∈ P | IoU(pc, gc) > 0.5, ∀gc ∈ G} (5); FPc = {pc ∈ P | IoU(pc, g) <= 0.5, ∀g ∈ G} (6); FNc = {gc ∈ G | IoU(gc, p) <= 0.5, ∀p ∈ P} (7); IDSc = {p ∈ TPc | ψp ≠ ψg} (8); sIDSc = {IoU(p, g) | (p, g) ∈ TPc ∧ ψp ≠ ψg} (9); sPTQc = (Σ_(p,g)∈TPc IoU(p,g) − Σ_s∈IDSc s) / (|TPc| + 1/2|FPc| + 1/2|FNc|) (10); PTQc = (Σ_(p,g)∈TPc IoU(p,g) − |IDSc|) / (|TPc| + 1/2|FPc| + 1/2|FNc|) (11); sPTQ = 1/|C| Σ_c∈C sPTQc (12); PTQ = 1/|C| Σ_c∈C PTQc (13). data.paper_title: Football tracking networks: Beyond event-based connectivity
data.authors: J.M. Buldú1,2, D. Garrido1,2, D.R. Antequera1,2, J. Busquets3, E. Estrada4,5, R. Resta6 and R. López del Campo6
data.core_methodology: Network Science applied to tracking datasets supplied by LaLiga software Mediacoach® and Tracab Optical Tracking System; four tracking networks: (a) Ball Flow Networks (BFN) constructed by partitioning the pitch into an NxM grid, counting how many times the ball traverses the frontier between partitions as link weights, and using node size proportional to ball retention time; (b) Signed Proximity Networks (SPN) constructed per frame by connecting players below a threshold distance R, with +1 links for same-team players and -1 links for different-team players, producing {r}x{t} signed networks; (c) Marking Networks (MN) constructed as bipartite networks using the time accumulated by a defender with an opponent closer than a threshold distance R=1.5 meters, with links filtered at tmin=7 seconds; (d) Functional Coordination Networks (FCN) constructed by computing each player's velocity vector vi(t), the angle θij between velocities of each pair of players, treating velocities as aligned when θij< θthresholf=10º, and computing the percentage (between 0 and 1) of time accumulated by every pair of players during the whole match.

data.paper_title: Pose-Assisted Multi-Camera Collaboration for Active Object Tracking
data.authors: Jing Li*1, 3, Jing Xu*1 , Fangwei Zhong*2, Xiangyu Kong2, Yu Qiao4, Yizhou Wang2, 5, 6
data.core_methodology: Collaborative Multi-Camera Active Object Tracking (CMC-AOT); Partially Observable Multi-Agent Cooperative Game extending the Markov Game to partial observation with tuple < I, S, OI, AI, RI, T, Z > and policy πi(ai,t|oi,t); Pose-Assisted Multi-Camera Collaboration System with each camera equipped with a vision-based controller, a pose-based controller, and a switcher; Behavior Consistency; vision-based controller uses an appearance encoder fa implemented with Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), a sequence encoder fs implemented as an LSTM Network, and a policy network to output action av_i; pose-based controller uses a bidirectional Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) pose encoder fp to encode poses and binary labels gi ∈ {0, 1} into pose features ρ1, . . . , ρI = fp(l1, g1, . . . , lI, gI), where camera pose li = {xi, yi, zi, αi, βi}; pose-based controller learns a policy about behavior consistency based on poses and switcher conditions of all cameras; switcher is a binary classified neural network that receives image features ψi,t and outputs probabilities of choosing controllers, with final action ai = av_i or ai = ap_i; network components include Convolutional neural network (CNN), Fully connected layer (FC), Long short-term memory (LSTM), Gated recurrent unit (GRU); Reinforcement Learning optimized with A3C algorithm; two-phase training strategy: first train pose-based controller in a numerical simulator with randomly set switcher labels and a virtual tracker taking the nearly optimal action to minimize relative-angle errors, randomizing camera distribution and target trajectories; second train vision-based controller and switcher simultaneously, with switcher optimized by binary cross-entropy loss using ground-truth object mask, freezing pose-based controller and backward propagating vision-based controller gradients only when switcher selects vision-based controller; high-fidelity virtual environments including Random Training Room/Random Room with environment augmentation, Garden, and Urban City; reward structure uses direction tracking reward Rd,t = {1 − Δαt/αmax − Δβt/βmax, (a); 0, (b); −1, (c)} and zoom reward Rz,t = 1 − Δξt/ξmax in condition (a), otherwise Rz,t = 0, with Rt = Rd,t + Rz,t and rewards clipped in [−1, 1] while training.

data.paper_title: Group Activity Recognition in Basketball Tracking Data - Neural Embeddings in Team Sports (NETS)
data.authors: Sandro Hauri, Slobodan Vucetic
data.core_methodology: NETS (Neural Embeddings in Team Sports): deep learning approach for group activity recognition (GAR) in team sports combining a Transformer-based architecture with LSTM embedding and a team-wise pooling layer. Tracks objects O = {B, A1, ..., A5, D1, ..., D5}; trajectory τ^{t−L+1:t}_o = [ℓ^{t−L+1}_o, ..., ℓ^t_o]. Base Transformer encoder with multi-head self-attention: inputs z^l_o ∈ R^{d_v}; query Q, key K, value V; trainable matrices W^Q_i ∈ R^{d_g × d_v}, W^K_i ∈ R^{d_g × d_v}, W^V_i ∈ R^{d_g × d_v}, W^O_i ∈ R^{h d_v × d_g}; residual connection and layer normalization; d_g = d_v = d_k = d_h. Uses LSTM [13] to embed trajectories; one-hot positional encoding for object roles (ball, offensive players, defensive players) concatenated to LSTM output z^0_o. Stack of N identical attention layers. FF is a fully connected feedforward network. Trajectory Prediction Head uses separate FeedForward neural networks FF_ball, FF_off, FF_def to generate ν^t_o. Trajectory prediction objective: predict ν^{t+1:t+H} from τ^{t−L+1:t}; dataset D = {(τ^{t−L+1:t}, ν^{t+1:t+H}) | t = L, ..., T-H}. Classification Head uses team-level pooling layer summing embeddings of offense and defense: y = softmax(FF(z^N_B ⊕ Σ_{i=1}^5 z^N_Ai ⊕ Σ_{i=1}^5 z^N_Di)); trained by minimizing Negative Log-Likelihood (NLL) loss with class adjustments α_k. GAR dataset D = {(τ^{t−L+1:t}, y_t) | t = L, ..., T}. Multistage training: self-supervised trajectory prediction pretraining; fine-tuning with weak-labels; further fine-tuning with manual labels. Weak-labeling uses rule-based programmatic rules for pick-and-roll and handoff: ball possession if player is closest to ball for at least 5 consecutive frames, ball within 5 ft, ball lower than 10 ft from ground, ball speed slower than 25 ft/s; defensive assignments by linear sum assignment reducing total sum of Euclidean distances; pick-and-roll thresholds δa and δd1 = 6 ft and δd2 = 3 ft; handoff possession change with two players closer than 6.5 ft apart. Shallow baselines: logistic regression LReg, random forest classifier RForest, gradient boosting classifier GBoost; LSTM baseline with 2-layer LSTM (128 hidden nodes each) followed by 2-layer FF network (128 hidden nodes); SocialGAN; M. VRNN; NETSno LSTM. t-SNE [34] for qualitative analysis of embeddings.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Data: 632 NBA games during 2015-2016 season; 113,760 possessions; 1.1 million seconds of game play; locations captured every 0.04s; downsampled by factor of 3 to Δt = 0.12s; L = 10 input time steps = 1.2s; 869,905 play sequences; H = 10, H = 20, H = 40. Labels: K = 3 classes; 45,802 'pick-and-rolls', 15,251 'handoffs', 808,852 'other' weak-labeled play sequences; manual labels total 1,800; 600 pick-and-rolls, 600 handoffs and 600 other plays; 50% manual labels for testing and 50% for fine-tuning; Table 4 tested on 300 pick-and-rolls, 300 handoffs and 300 other plays; Table 2 tested on 4,581 pick-and-rolls, 1,525 handoffs and 80,884 other plays; other plays downsampled to 45,802; weighting factors αk = 0.77, 2.34, and 0.77 for pick-and-rolls, handoffs, and other; 80 / 10 / 10 train-, validation-, and test-split; trivial classifier predicting that the class would achieve 93.0% test accuracy; 220 features for shallow models. Training: Adam optimizer initial learning rate 5 · 10−5; hidden dimension d_h = 256; Transformer with L = 8 layers and h = 64 prediction heads; ReLU activation between all layers except output; batches of 512 samples; early stopping after 50 epochs; trajectory training typically around 400 epochs, about 30 hours on a single GPU; GAR without pretraining around 500 epochs, with pretrained model roughly 200 epochs. Equations: z^{l+1}_o = LN(FF(LN(Att(Q, K, V)))) + z^l_o (1); Att(Q, K, V) = Concat(head_1, ..., head_h)W^O (2); head_i = softmax((QW^Q_i)(KW^K_i)^T / √d_k) V W^V_i (3); y = softmax(FF(z^N_B ⊕ Σ_{i=1}^5 z^N_Ai ⊕ Σ_{i=1}^5 z^N_Di)) (4); L_NLL = −1/|D| Σ_D Σ_{k=1}^K α_k y_k ln(ŷ_k) (5); L_MSE(ν, ν̂) = 1/(2H) ||ν − ν̂||_2^2 (6); precision_i = M_ii / Σ_j M_ji; recall_i = M_ii / Σ_j M_ij; F1_i = 2 · precision_i · recall_i / (precision_i + recall_i) (7)(8). data.paper_title: Early warning signals for predicting cryptomarket vendor success using dark net forum networks
data.authors: Hanjo D. Boekhout1,*, Arjan A.J. Blokland2,3, and Frank W. Takes1
data.core_methodology: Models the Evolution cryptomarket as an evolving communication network and extracts user-to-user communication networks. Creates nodes for all active users; adds an edge for any posts by a pair of users in the same topic that are ten or fewer posts apart and placed at most one month apart; direction is from the later poster to the earlier poster; also forms edges from every user who posted in a topic to the user who placed the first post; all edges are weighted. Uses parameters δo = 10, δt = 1 month, ωlower = 0.2, tlim = 7 days, and ωfirst = 0.5. Merges parallel edges by summing weights to obtain 15 simplified monthly weighted directed networks G = (V,E). Computes four centrality measures: in-degree; bidirectional harmonic closeness centrality; directed weighted betweenness centrality; directed weighted PageRank, using the igraph package. Compares against three forum activity indicators: post activity, topics started, and topic engagement. Uses min-max normalization, relative and absolute difference scores, vendor recall, overlap, post activity recall, and sales recall; uses third polynomial approximations of monthly trends and ROC curves/AUC in supplementary analyses.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Dataset: Evolution active from January 2014 until March 2015; more than half a million posts; over four thousand vendors; 15 network snapshots (January 2014 up to March 2015); 5 groups of success percentiles (top 0-20%, 20-40%, etc.); non-vendors form a separate sixth group; top 20% of all users; top vendor percentile = top 0-20% vendors in terms of sales. Network extraction parameters: δo = 10, δt = 1 month, ωlower = 0.2, tlim = 7 days, and ωfirst = 0.5. Equations: hcc_G(u) = ∑_{v∈V} 1/d_G(u,v) (1); bc(u) = ∑_{v,w∈V,u≠v≠w} σ_vuw/σ_vw (2); s^nu,t,i = (s_u,t,i − min_{u_x∈V} s_{u_x,t,i})/(max_{u_x∈V} s_{u_x,t,i} − min_{u_x∈V} s_{u_x,t,i}) (3); abs_diff_score(a,b,t,i) = ∑_{u∈V_a} s^nu,t,i/|V_a| − ∑_{u∈V_b} s^nu,t,i/|V_b| (4); rel_diff_score(a,b,t,i) = abs_diff_score(a,b,t,i)/(∑_{u∈V_b} s^nu,t,i/|V_b|) (5); vendor_recall(t,i) = |TV_t ∩ TU_t,i|/|TU_t,i| × 100% (6); overlap_t,i,j = |TV_t ∩ TU_t,i ∩ TU_t,j|/|TV_t ∩ TU_t,i| × 100% (7); post_activity_recall(t,i) = ∑_{u∈TV_t∩TU_t,i} pa_u,t / ∑_{u∈TV_t} pa_u,t × 100% (8); sales_recall(t,i) = ∑_{u∈TV_t∩TU_t,i} sales_u,t / ∑_{u∈TV_t} sales_u,t × 100% (9). Reported figures: betweenness relative difference score for vendors over non-vendors 600-1000%; topic engagement detects up to 2/3rd of the most successful vendors for current success; post activity recall up to 98%; sales recall generally between 10-20% higher than vendor recall; among top 25 users, ten (40%) occur in both betweenness and topic engagement rankings; over half of top 25 users have current and/or future sales (56% and 64%); random probabilities 3.47×10−7 and 3.44×10−9; moderator probabilities 2.07×10−11 (2.27×10−9) and 3.10×10−4 (1.82×10−4). data.paper_title: You Only Need Two Detectors to Achieve Multi-Modal 3D Multi-Object Tracking
data.authors: Xiyang Wang1,2, Chunyun Fu*,1, Jiawei He1, Mingguang Huang1, Ting Meng1, Siyu Zhang2, Hangning Zhou2, Ziyao Xu2, and Chi Zhang2
data.core_methodology: YONTD-MOT: end-to-end multi-modal fusion-based 3D MOT framework integrating object detection and multi-object tracking into a single model; uses two-stage 2D and 3D detectors (Faster R-CNN for 2D and CasA for 3D; ablation also uses PointRCNN, Voxel R-CNN, and Mask R-CNN); Kalman filter prediction/propagation of 3D trajectory states; GPS/IMU-based vehicle motion transformation for pose compensation; predicted trajectories used as proposals and regressed by the two-stage 3D detector; regressed 3D trajectories projected onto a 2D image and fed to the 2D detector; Historical Feature Fusion Mechanism with Historical Feature Memory Bank: f^{3d}_{his} = (1/n) Σ_{k=t-n-1}^{t-1}(˜s^{j,3d}_k × f^{j,3d}_k) and ˜s^{j,3d}_t = detector{(1 − s^{j,3d}_t) × f^{3d}_{his} + s^{j,3d}_t × f^{j,3d}_t}; Trajectory Confidence Fusion Mechanism/regression confidence fusion module: ˜s^{3d} = 1/(n + 1)(Σ_{k=t-n-1}^{t-1} ˜s_k^{3d} + ˜s_t^{3d}), s^{2d} = 1/(n + 1)(Σ_{k=t-n-1}^{t-1} s_k^{2d} + s_t^{2d}), s^f = 1/2(˜s^{3d} + s^{2d}); NMS based on trajectory regression confidence (non-maximum suppression) sorts trajectories by fused confidence; trajectory management strategy same as DeepFusionMOT; post-processing of trajectories sets projected 2D historical trajectories to confirmed if confidence exceeds preset threshold; strong object and weak object states are handled by regression confidence fusion.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Equations: f^{3d}_{his} = (1/n) Σ_{k=t-n-1}^{t-1}(˜s^{j,3d}_k × f^{j,3d}_k); ˜s^{j,3d}_t = detector{(1 − s^{j,3d}_t) × f^{3d}_{his} + s^{j,3d}_t × f^{j,3d}_t}; ˜s^{3d} = 1/(n + 1)(Σ_{k=t-n-1}^{t-1} ˜s_k^{3d} + ˜s_t^{3d}); s^{2d} = 1/(n + 1)(Σ_{k=t-n-1}^{t-1} s_k^{2d} + s_t^{2d}); s^f = 1/2(˜s^{3d} + s^{2d}). KITTI test (Table 1): HOTA 79.26%, AssA 84.58%, MOTA 86.55%, MOTP 86.1%, IDSW 43, FN 1784; text reports HOTA 79.26% improved by 3.8% over DeepFusionMOT, MOTP 86.10%, AssA 84.58%, IDSW only 43. Waymo test (Table 2): MOTA/L1 57.28%, MOTP/L1 24.03%, FP/L1 8.24, MOTA/L2 55.7%, MOTP/L2 24.07%, FP/L2 8.44; compared with PK-baseline improvements 30.15% MOTA (L1), 29.78% MOTA (L2), 6.50% MOTP (L1), 6.54% MOTP (L2). Ablation Table 3: CasA + Faster R-CNN HOTA 76.37, MOTA 80.41, FN 1424; CasA + Mask R-CNN HOTA 75.3, MOTA 77.81, FN 1667; PointRCNN + Faster R-CNN HOTA 53.11, MOTA 43.96, FN 4721; PointRCNN + Mask R-CNN HOTA 55.02, MOTA 46.59, FN 4495; Voxel R-CNN + Faster R-CNN HOTA 77.52, MOTA 82.11, FN 610; Voxel R-CNN + Mask R-CNN HOTA 76.5, MOTA 80.36, FN 786. Ablation Table 4: no historical features HOTA 77.52, MOTA 82.11, FN 610, FP 1135; 1 historical frame HOTA 78.34, MOTA 83.26, FN 575, FP 1056; 5 frames HOTA 77.68, MOTA 82.86, FN 602, FP 1069; 30 frames HOTA 77.55, MOTA 82.32, FN 611, FP 1113; ALL HOTA 77.43, MOTA 82.05, FN 609, FP 1138. Ablation Table 5: 3D only with historical features HOTA 71.16, MOTA 69.63, FN 696, FP 2279; 3D+2D with historical features HOTA 78.34, MOTA 83.26, FN 575, FP 1056. Ablation Table 6: Unordered HOTA 77.6, AssA 81.88, MOTA 82.75, FP 1101; Ascending HOTA 74.38, AssA 79.34, MOTA 75.41, FP 1706; Descending HOTA 78.34, AssA 83.01, MOTA 83.26, FP 1056. Evaluation metrics: CLEAR (MOTA, MOTP, IDS); HOTA (DetA, AssA); Waymo LEVEL_1 (L1) and LEVEL_2 (L2).

data.paper_title: Unified Sequence-to-Sequence Learning for Single- and Multi-Modal Visual Object Tracking
data.authors: Xin Chen, Ben Kang, Jiawen Zhu, Dong Wang, Houwen Peng, and Huchuan Lu
data.core_methodology: SeqTrack: sequence-to-sequence learning framework casting visual tracking as a sequence generation task, forecasting object bounding boxes in an autoregressive manner; basic encoder-decoder transformer architecture; encoder uses a bidirectional transformer for feature extraction (standard vision transformer architecture ViT) and decoder uses a causal transformer; decoder blocks contain masked multi-head attention, multi-head attention, and feed forward network (FFN); plain cross-entropy loss; objective Eq. (1): maximize Σ_{j=1}^{L} logQ(ˆzj|s, t, ˆz<j); bounding box represented as [x,y,w,h] discretized into integers in [1, nbins] with shared vocabulary V, input sequence [start,x,y,w,h], target sequence [x,y,w,h,end]; inference uses maximum likelihood ẑj=arg maxzjQ(zj|s, t, ẑ<j); online template update via average softmax scores over the four generated bounding box values with threshold τ and update interval Tu; window penalty multiplying softmax scores by a Hanning window; SeqTrackv2: unified sequence-to-sequence framework for multi-modal tracking tasks (RGB+Depth, RGB+Thermal, RGB+Event, RGB+Language), unified interface converting auxiliary modalities into a unified sequence format, BERT text encoder with max-pooling, PAD token, channel-wise product between text embedding and image-format modality embeddings, low-rank integration of auxiliary-modal sequence Ml−1 and visual feature sequence Vl−1 via projections D→d and d→D, element-wise add, and encoder block El; task-prompt tokens input into encoder and decoder (replace START token in decoder); SeqTrackv2 loads and freezes SeqTrack parameters and trains unified interface and task-prompt token embeddings; encoders initialized with MAE pre-trained parameters; AdamW optimizer.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: nbins = 4,000 (vocabulary size 4,000); decoder blocks = 2; decoder hidden size = 256; attention heads = 8; FFN hidden size = 1024; word embedding dimension = 256; embedding-to-word 3-layer perceptron hidden dimension = 256; output dimension nbins; low-rank dimension d = 32; patch size = 16×16; template/search expansion factor = 4; SeqTrack training: encoder learning rate 1e−5, decoder and remaining modules 1e−4, weight decay 1e−4, total batch size 64, 500 epochs, 60k image pairs per epoch, learning rate decreases by a factor of 10 after 400 epochs; SeqTrackv2 training: 240 epochs, 60,000 samples per epoch, learning rate decreases by a factor of 10 after 192 epochs, batch sizes 128, 48, 64, and 16 for SeqTrackv2-B256, -B384, -L256, and -L384 respectively; online template update interval Tu = 25; update threshold τ = 0.015; 1D Hanning window size 4,000 for 4,000 words; SeqTrack variants: SeqTrack-B256 ViT-B 256×256 89M 66G 40 fps; SeqTrack-B384 ViT-B 384×384 89M 148G 15 fps; SeqTrack-L256 ViT-L 256×256 309M 232G 15 fps; SeqTrack-L384 ViT-L 384×384 309M 524G 5 fps; main reported scores: SeqTrack-B256 74.7% AO on GOT-10k, surpassing OSTrack-256 by 3.7% under aligned settings; SeqTrack-B256 operates 1.4 times faster (40 v.s. 29 fps) while achieving 0.7% superior AUC score on LaSOT; SeqTrack-L384 72.5% AUC on LaSOT, 50.7% AUC on LaSOText, 85.5% AUC on TrackingNet, 74.8% AO on GOT-10k; SeqTrack-L384 EAO 31.9% and 56.1% on VOT2020 bounding box and mask evaluations; SeqTrackv2-L384 61.0% AUC on LasHeR, 74.8% EAO on VOT-RGBD22, 63.4% AUC on VisEvent, 62.4% AUC on TNL2K; SeqTrackv2-L384 outperforming ViPT by an average of 5.1% points and surpassing JointNLT by 5.5%; SeqTrackv2-L256 68.5% AUC on RGBT234, outperforming Un-Track by 6.0%, and 62.7% AUC on TNL2K, surpassing JointNLT by 5.8%; SeqTrackv2-B384 75.5% EAO on VOT-RGBD22; SeqTrackv2-B256 63.2% F-score on DepthTrack and 61.2% AUC on VisEvent; Eq. (1): maximize Σ_{j=1}^{L} logQ(ˆzj|s, t, ˆz<j); inference: ẑj=arg maxzjQ(zj|s, t, ẑ<j).

data.paper_title: Online Parameter Identification of Generalized Non-cooperative Game
data.authors: Jianguo Chena,b, Jinlong Leic,d, Hongsheng Qia,b, Yiguang Hongc,d
data.core_methodology: Generalized non-cooperative game (GNCG); generalized Nash equilibrium (GNE); variational equilibriums; variational inequality VI(X, F) given by F(x*, u, θ)^T(y − x*) ≥ 0, ∀y ∈ X(u), where F(x, u, θ) := (∇_{x_v} f_v(x_v; x_{−v}, u_v, θ_v))_{v=1}^N; Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions; loss function l(θ; y, u) := min_{λ,ν}{L(θ, λ, ν; y, u) | λ ≥ 0}; regularized loss function G_k(θ) with conservativeness distance term D(θ, θ_k) and correctiveness term µ_k l(θ; y_k, u_k); online parameter identification algorithm (Algorithm 1) with two-step updates: ˜θ_{k+1} = arg min_θ G_k(θ), θ_{k+1} = arg min_{θ∈Θ} D(θ, ˜θ_{k+1}); online convex optimization; regret bound O(√K); numerical simulations on a Nash-Cournot problem / natural gas market; uniform distributions; multivariate standard normal distribution; Trust-Region Constrained Algorithm and Sequential Quadratic Programming.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Regret: R_K := Σ_{k=1}^K l(θ_k; y_k, u_k) − Σ_{k=1}^K l(θ_*^K; y_k, u_k). Learning rate: µ_k ∝ 1/√k; Theorem 1: µ_k = µ_1/√k, µ_1 > 0, regret bound O(√K); derived bound R_K ≤ (2B_1^2/µ_1 + µ_1 C^2)√K. Loss function under Assumption 5: l(θ; y, u) = min_{λ≥0,ν}{||F_θ + ∇hλ + ∇gν||_2^2 + ||Hλ||_2^2 + ||g||_2^2}. Regularized loss under Assumption 5: G_k(θ) = 1/2||θ − θ_k||_2^2 + µ_k l(θ; y_k, u_k). Simulation: θ = [10, 7.5, 6]^T; u_k = (a_k, b_k, q_k) sampled independently from uniform distributions with ranges [15, 15 × 120], [1, 1 × 120], and [5, 5 × 120], respectively; observed equilibrium y_k = x_k + ε_k, where ε_k is drawn from the multivariate standard normal distribution; K = 100; µ_k = µ_1/√k with µ_1 = 0.1 in Algorithm 1; additional learning rates µ_1 = 0.1, 0.3 and 0.5; performance metrics: Time(s), R_k/k, and ||θ_k − θ_*^k||_2.

data.paper_title: MambaMOT: State-Space Model as Motion Predictor for Multi-Object Tracking
data.authors: Hsiang-Wei Huang, Cheng-Yen Yang, Wenhao Chai, Zhongyu Jiang, Jeng-Neng Hwang
data.core_methodology: MambaMOT replaces the Kalman filter with a learning-based motion model using the original Mamba [13] block, with an extra linear projection layer and a local multi-layer perception; the motion model is based on a continuous system with parameters A, B, C: y(t)=C·h(t), h(t)=A·h(t−1)+B·x(t); the Selective SSM (state-space model) is the discrete representation Ā_t, B̄_t of the continuous system A, B by applying ZOH (zero-order hold) discretization formulation with a timescale parameter Δ; prediction head MLP_pred: Y_t = MLP_pred(y_t); losses use Generalized IoU loss (GIoU) [23] and MSE loss with L_pred = L_giou + L_mse; data association uses the data-association method BYTE proposed in ByteTrack [39] and the Hungarian algorithm; MambaMOT+ adds a trajectory embedding head with a trainable multilayer perceptron MLP_emb: f_t = MLP_emb(y_t); trajectory representation uses cosine embedding loss L_cos and end-to-end loss L_total = L_pred + L_cos; MambaMOT+ performs tracklet merging using cosine similarity and hierarchical clustering.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Task variables: past n frames {B_{t−n},...,B_{t−1}} ∈ R^{n×[x,y,w,h]}, predict B_T ∈ R^{1×[x,y,w,h]}; Eq. (1) y(t)=C·h(t); Eq. (2) h(t)=A·h(t−1)+B·x(t); Eq. (3) Ā_t = exp(ΔA) = 1 − σ(Linear(x_t)); Eq. (4) B̄_t = (Ā)^−1(exp(ΔA) − I) · ΔB = σ(Linear(x_t)); Eq. (5) y_t = C·h_t and h_t = Ā_t·h_{t−1} + B̄_t·x_t; Eq. (6) Y_t = MLP_pred(y_t); L_pred = L_giou + L_mse; Eq. (7) f_t = MLP_emb(y_t); Eq. (8) L_cos(i,j) = (1 − cos(f_i,f_j), if i = j; max(0, cos(f_i,f_j)), if i ≠ j); L_total = L_pred + L_cos; optimizer Adam with 0.0001 initial learning rate for 500 epochs with a batch size of 32; 2 mamba blocks, hidden dimension of 64, expansion factor of 2; temporal distance threshold of 50 frames and spatial distance threshold of 50 pixels; trajectories randomly selected with length between (2, n), where n is the max input length; O(N^2) computational cost reduced to O(N), with N denoting the number of tracklets; real-time inference speed of 28.8 FPS on a single GPU; previous learning-based methods such as MOTR typically under 10 FPS; DanceTrack MambaMOT HOTA 55.5, DetA 80.8, AssA 38.3, IDF1 53.9, MOTA 90.1; DanceTrack MambaMOT+ HOTA 56.1, DetA 80.8, AssA 39.0, IDF1 54.9, MOTA 90.3; DanceTrack MambaMOT outperforms ByteTrack by 8.2% in HOTA; MambaMOT+ improves HOTA by 0.6% and IDF1 by 1.0%; SportsMOT MambaMOT∗ HOTA 70.4, DetA 86.7, AssA 57.2, IDF1 69.5, MOTA 94.7; SportsMOT MambaMOT+∗ HOTA 71.3, DetA 86.7, AssA 58.6, IDF1 71.1, MOTA 94.9; SportsMOT MambaMOT outperforms ByteTrack by 8.2% HOTA and 7.3% AssA; evaluation metrics include HOTA, CLEAR metrics, IDF1, and MOTA.

data.paper_title: Referring Multi-Object Tracking
data.authors: Dongming Wu1∗‡, Wencheng Han2∗, Tiancai Wang3, Xingping Dong4, Xiangyu Zhang3,5, Jianbing Shen2†
data.core_methodology: referring multi-object tracking (RMOT) task; Refer-KITTI benchmark based on KITTI; TransRMOT, a transformer-based architecture built upon the DETR framework, following Deformable DETR and similar to MOTR; feature extractors with CNN visual backbone ResNet-50 and pre-trained linguistic model RoBERTa; multi-scale features {I3_t, I4_t, I5_t} from visual backbone plus I6_t via 3×3 convolution with spatial stride 2; cross-modal encoder with early-fusion module using 1×1 convolution to reduce channels to d=256, Q=Wq(I^l_t+P^V), K=Wk(S+P^L), V=WvS, fused features Ihat^l_t=(QK^T/sqrt(d))V+I^l_t, followed by a stack of deformable encoder layers E^l_t=DeformEnc(Ihat^l_t); decoder with D_t=Decoder(E^l_t, concat(Q_det, Q_tra_t)), where track query Q_tra_t is from previous frame decoder embedding D_{t-1} via self-attention and feed-forward network and detect query Q_det is randomly initialized; referent head with class branch linear projection (binary probability true/empty object), box branch 3-layer feed-forward network with ReLU except last layer, and referring branch linear projection (binary referent scores); losses decoupled as track loss and detect loss, using focal loss for L_cls and L_ref, L_box=λL1 L_L1+λgiou L_giou, one-to-one computation for tracking predictions, bipartite graph matching for detection objects with L_match=L_box+λcls L_cls, final loss L_final=sum_{t=1}^{T}(L_tra_t+L_det_t); training uses AdamW optimizer, object erasing and inserting to simulate object exit and entrance; evaluation uses Higher Order Tracking Accuracy (HOTA)=sqrt(DetA·AssA).
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Refer-KITTI: 18 videos, 818 expressions, each expression annotated with an average of 10.7 objects; number of objects described per expression ranges from 0 to 105; temporal status varies in 0∼400 frames, longest sequence >600 frames; Table 1: 6,650 images, instances per-expression 10.7, temporal ratio per-expression 0.49; split: 15 training videos and 3 testing videos; model: d=256, N=300 detect queries, λcls=5, λL1=2, λgiou=2, λref=2; training: AdamW, base learning rate 1e−4, backbone learning rate 1e−5, 100 epochs, learning rate decays by factor of 10 at 50th epoch, batch size 1 on 8 Nvidia 2080Ti GPUs; random crop, shortest side 800 to 1536; testing: class score threshold 0.7, referring threshold βref=0.4; HOTA=√(DetA·AssA), overall HOTA averaged across sentence queries; non-referent yet visible objects predicted are viewed as false positives; TransRMOT results: HOTA 35.54(±0.71), DetA 28.25, AssA 46.25, DetRe 39.22, DetPr 45.94, AssRe 50.69, AssPr 80.67, LocA 79.79; ΔHOTA<0.87; ablation cross-modal fusion: HOTA 34.29→17.01, DetA 28.25→19.05, AssA 46.25→15.26; ratios: expressions 50% 35.19±0.68, 75% 35.48±0.81, 100% 35.54±0.71; videos 50% 32.01±0.82, 75% 35.44±0.73, 100% 35.54±0.71.

data.paper_title: Multi-Object Tracking by Hierarchical Visual Representations
data.authors: Jinkun Cao, Jiangmiao Pang, Kris Kitani
data.core_methodology: Compositional-Semantic-Contextual visual hierarchy; object represented by triplet {P, O, U} where P is 2×2 bounding-box bins, O is semantic bounding box, and U is union area enclosing O and overlapping targets; shared feature extractor; concatenate compositional and semantic features, apply self-attention, then cross-attention with contextual features to produce CSC-tokens; CSC-Attention; CSC-Tracker built on spatio-temporal global association paradigm with transformer; global association scores by cross-attention and softmax; Hungarian matching; ResNet-50 backbone pretrained on Crowdhuman; CenterNet detector; BiFPN; AdamW; Lasso association loss; Lfeat triplet loss; optional Ldet detection loss.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: P(Mt_j,i = 1|Qdet_t,Qtraj_t) = exp(St_j,i) / Σ_{k∈{1,2,...,Nt}} 1[tk=ti] exp(St_j,k) (1); max ∏_{q=t+1}^{t+T} P(Mt_j,τj_q = 1|Qdet_t,Qtraj_t) (2); Lasso = -Σ_{j=1}^{Mt+1} Σ_{q=t+1}^{t+T} logP(Mt_j,τj_q = 1|Qdet_t,Qtraj_t) (3); Lfeat = max(0, min_{u=1}^{NP} ||Att(f(Fpu), f(FO)) - f(FO)||2 - ||Att(f(FO), f(Fbg_U)) - f(FO)||2 + α) (4); L = Lasso + Lfeat + Ldet (5); β = 0.3; NP = 4; 2 × 2 bins; T = 8 for training; T = 24 for inference; image size 1280 × 1280 during training; image size 1560 for the longer edge during the test; base learning rate 5e-5; training iterations 20k on MOT17/MOT20 and 80k on DanceTrack; training takes 4 hours on MOT17 or MOT20 and 11 hours on DanceTrack; inference speed 21.3FPS for CSC-Tracker on V100 GPU; 93FPS for CSC-Tracker given detections on MOT17; CSC-Tracker MOT-17 Test: HOTA 60.8, AssA 60.7, MOTA 75.4, IDF1 75.7, FP 2,45, FN 10,8, IDs 2,879; CSC-Tracker MOT-20 Test: HOTA 53.0, AssA 51.1, MOTA 65.8, IDF1 64.4, FP 3.64, FN 13.7, IDs 3,948; CSC-Tracker DanceTrack test: HOTA 55.5, DetA 77.3, AssA 43.1, MOTA 89.5, IDF1 54.0; CSC-Attention default DanceTrack ablation: HOTA 51.9, DetA 71.4, AssA 34.0, MOTA 81.9, IDF1 52.2.

data.paper_title: Multi-Object Tracking in the Dark
data.authors: Xinzhe Wang, Kang Ma, Qiankun Liu, Yunhao Zou, Ying Fu *
data.core_methodology: LTrack; Low-light Multi-Object Tracking (LMOT) dataset built with a dual-camera system; adaptive low-pass downsample module (ALD); spatial low-pass convolution (SConv) with a softmax-constrained low-pass convolution kernel initialized using a standard Gaussian kernel; degradation suppression learning strategy (DSL) using degradation suppression loss (LDS) and Total Variation (TV) loss; tracking-by-detection with YOLOX detector and ByteTrack/OC-SORT trackers; physical-based noise model for RAW image augment.

data.paper_title: Improving Student Self-Confidence in Quantum Computing with the Qubit Touchdown Board Game
data.authors: Kristina Armbruster, Gintaras Duda, and Thomas G. Wong
data.core_methodology: Evaluation of the Qubit Touchdown two-player, competitive board game with 107 public high school students in seven Precalculus, AP Statistics, and/or AP Physics 1 classes over four periods in one school day; pre/post Likert-scale survey (strongly disagree, disagree, neutral, agree, strongly agree) given before playing the game, after playing the game, and after learning about the game's connections to quantum computing; Likert results treated as ordinal data by combining agree and strongly agree into overall agree (A) and disagree and strongly disagree into overall disagree (D), ignoring neutral responses; calculation of favorable shift values (∆A); Friedman test; pairwise paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with a continuity correction; all p-values two-sided and considered significant if p < 0.05.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: 107 public high school students; seven Precalculus, AP Statistics, and/or AP Physics 1 classes; four periods in one school day; 52 cards; four cards to each player; remaining 44 cards; binary die outcomes 0 or 1 with a 50:50 chance; Q1→Q3 favorable shift 10.4%, Wilcoxon p < 0.05; Q3→Q7 favorable shift -0.1%, p > 0.05; Q1→Q7 favorable shift 10.3%, p < 0.05; Q2→Q4 favorable shift 11.3%, p < 0.001; Q4→Q8 favorable shift 21.5%, p < 0.001; Q2→Q8 favorable shift 32.8%, p < 0.001; Friedman interest χ2 = 8.9589, d f = 2, p < 0.05; Friedman self-confidence χ2 = 49.004, df = 2, p < 0.001; 78.5% reported playing Qubit Touchdown made quantum computing concepts less intimidating (Q11); 84.1% reported enjoying playing the game (Q5); 83.2% recommended Qubit Touchdown as a learning tool for quantum computing (Q13).

data.paper_title: Continuous football player tracking from discrete broadcast data
data.authors: Matthew J. Penn, Christl A. Donnelly, and Samir Bhatt
data.core_methodology: Discrete autoregressive moving average with exogenous inputs (ARMAX) model for player positions, using ball position as an exogenous variable; Gaussian position predictions x(t) ∼ N(µ(t, b, X), σ(t, b, X)²I) and xi(t) ∼ N(µ(t, b, Ti), σ(t, b, Ti)²I), with I the 2x2 identity matrix; simple linear interpolation on a one-second temporal grid; trajectory assignment by maximum likelihood using the Hungarian algorithm on the matrix −Q, where Qij = log(P(player i is at visible position j at time t)); player position initialisation assigning non-visible outfield players to plausible positions along the defensive line; continuous path interpolation using average known velocity vk, linear interpolation of these velocities u(t), weighted average velocity w(s,t)=α∫_s^t u(r)dr, and xi(t)=xi(t1)+w(t1,t)+((t−t1)/(t2−t1))(xi(t2)−xi(t1)−w(t1,t2)); Statsbomb 360 data processing.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Pitch measures 120m by 80m; Metrica coordinates given as percentages with centre spot (0.5,0.5) and goals (0,0.5) and (1,0.5); temporal grid size of one second; x(t) ∼ N(µ(t, b, X), σ(t, b, X)²I) (1); for n = 1, xk+1 = N(xk, s²I) for constant s; xk = x(ti) + ((k − ti)/(ti+1 − ti))(x(ti+1) − x(ti)) (2); Ti = {(xi(ti1), ti1), ..., (xi(timi), timi)} (3); xi(t) ∼ N(µ(t, b, Ti), σ(t, b, Ti)²I) (4); Qij = log(P(player i is at visible position j at time t)) (5); w(s,t) = α∫_s^t u(r)dr (6); xi(t) = xi(t1) + w(t1,t) + ((t − t1)/(t2 − t1))(xi(t2) − xi(t1) − w(t1,t2)) (7); α ≈ 0.5; runtime approximately 0.23s/frame on a single core with a clock speed of 2.6GHz, processing a match in 20-25 minutes; frames sampled every second, recording only players within 30 metres of the ball; average 10.60 of 20 outfield players visible; Statsbomb average 14.35 of 20 outfield players visible, ranging from 10.93 to 18.58; Statsbomb frames approximately every 1.9 seconds; ball in play around 60%; total frames sampled 6390; total position predictions 59821; in-phase mean error for all players 3.45m; in-phase mean off-camera error 7.33m; median off-camera error 5.37m; out-of-phase overall mean error 3.55m; error for players observed in previous frame 0.22m; in-phase event-frame mean off-camera error 6.62m; players off-camera for 20 seconds with maximum 10 seconds to nearest observation have mean error under 10m and a 97.5th percentile of less than 25m; maximum pitch distance 145m; total squared error reduces from 2950m² to 900m² in the frame before a goal-kick; radius of 7.33m fills 1.75% of a football pitch; [12] pitch measured 105m by 68m with distances multiplied by 120/105 and mean error 7.86m; our mean error 3.45m and off-camera means at events 6.62m and at all frames 7.33m.

data.paper_title: Multi-Object Tracking based on Imaging Radar 3D Object Detection
data.authors: Patrick Palmer1, Martin Krüger1, Dr. Richard Altendorfer2 and Univ.-Prof. Dr.-Ing. Prof. h.c. Dr. h.c. Torsten Bertram1
data.core_methodology: Tracking-by-detection (TBD) pipeline with five components: pre-processing, track prediction, similarity determination, track assignment, and life cycle management. Compared TBD approaches: AB3DMOT, AB3DMOT-MH, CasTrack, SimpleTrack, and CenterPoint. Pre-processing: prediction confidence score (PCS) thresholding for AB3DMOT, CASTrack, and CenterPoint; non-maximum suppression (NMS) for SimpleTrack. Track prediction: Kalman filter (KF) with constant velocity (CV) for AB3DMOT, AB3DMOT-MH, SimpleTrack, and CenterPoint; KF with constant acceleration (CA) for CasTrack; learned object motion (LoM) + CV for CenterPoint. Similarity: intersection over union (IoU) for AB3DMOT; Mahalanobis distance for AB3DMOT-MH; aggregated pairwise cost (APC) for CasTrack; generalized IoU (GIoU) for SimpleTrack; L2 distance for CenterPoint. APC consists of geometry, appearance, and motion costs. Track assignment: Hungarian algorithm (HA) for AB3DMOT and SimpleTrack; greedy association for AB3DMOT-MH and CenterPoint; prediction confidence-guided data association (PCGDA) for CasTrack. Life cycle management: count-based (CB) for AB3DMOT, CenterPoint, and CasTrack; Two Stage for SimpleTrack. Probabilistic association: squared Mahalanobis distance and association log-likelihood (A-LL) distance, using innovation covariance S_{t+1}=H Σ̂_{t+1} H^T + R, Σ̂_{t+1}=A Σ_t A^T + Q, μ̂_{t+1}=A μ_t. Object detector: PointPillars in OpenPCDet. Dataset: View-of-Delft (VoD) with lidar, camera, and 3+1D imaging radar; radar detection uses an accumulated point cloud spanning over 5 frames. Ego-motion derivations: labeled ego motion, static ego vehicle assumption, and SLAM motion estimation on the lidar point cloud sequence. Evaluation metrics: MOTA, MOTP, DetA, AssA, and HOTA.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Equations: d_Mahalanobis^2 = (d_{t+1} − H μ̂_{t+1})^T S_{t+1}^{-1} (d_{t+1} − H μ̂_{t+1}). (1); S_{t+1} = H Σ̂_{t+1} H^T + R, (2); Σ̂_{t+1} = A Σ_t A^T + Q, (3); μ̂_{t+1} = A μ_t. (4); d_{A−LL}^2 = d_Mahalanobis^2 + ln|S_{t+1}^{-1}| + n ln(2π) − 2 ln(P_D). (5); n = dim(o_{t+1} − H μ̂_{t+1}); P_D treated as constant; MOTA = 1 − (FPT + FNT + IDS)/numgt, (6); MOTP = (Σ_i d_i)/c. (7); DetA = |TPD|/(|TPD| + |FND| + |FPD|), (8); AssA = Σ_{b∈{TPD}} |TPA(b)|/(|TPA(b)| + |FNA(b)| + |FPA(b)|). (9); HOTA = sqrt(DetA · AssA). (10). Dataset/experiment values: range 52.6m; low velocities of up to 30 km/h; accumulated point cloud spanning over 5 frames; IoU of [0.7, 0.5, 0.5] in [x, y, z] direction for the car class and [0.5, 0.5, 0.5] for the pedestrian and cyclist class. Table 2 mAP-3D [%] and mAP-BEV [%]: Lidar Car 49.95, Pedestrian 50.81, Cyclist 65.86; Lidar BEV Car 53.09, Pedestrian 56.89, Cyclist 68.32; Radar Car 36.28, Pedestrian 12.51, Cyclist 30.76; Radar BEV Car 44.54, Pedestrian 22.03, Cyclist 53.59. data.paper_title: From Solo to Social: Exploring the Dynamics of Player Cooperation in a Co-located Cooperative Exergame
data.authors: Derrick M. Wang∗†, Sebastian Cmentowski, Reza Hadi Mogavi, Kaushall Senthil Nathan∗, Eugene Kukshinov, Joseph Tu∗, Lennart E. Nacke
data.core_methodology: Custom two-player exergame Space Scavenger Squad developed in Unity (V2022.3.14f1) on the Mixed Reality (MR)-based ExerCube platform using HTC VIVE VR trackers; three cooperation designs mapped to the Forms of Cooperation category in Pais et al.'s cooperative game mechanics framework: free cooperation (baseline; green orbs; either player; individual timing; spawn interval 1.5s; despawn 3s), coupled cooperation (blue/orange orbs; only same color; individual timing; spawn interval 1.5s; despawn 3s), and concurrent cooperation (purple orbs; either player; concurrent timing; spawn interval 2.25s; despawn 4.5s; maximum delay 0.5 seconds); within-participants mixed-methods user study with 24 participants in 12 dyads and three counterbalanced conditions; measures included demographic questionnaire, Polar H10 heart rate sensor baseline recorded while seated and relaxed for a minimum of five minutes, Patient Experience of Need Satisfaction (PENS) questionnaire (21 items, 7-point Likert scale: Strongly Disagree/1 to Strongly Agree/7; Competence, Autonomy, Relatedness, Presence/Immersion, Intuitive Controls), Physical Activity Enjoyment Scale short version (PACES-S; four items, 5-point Likert scale: Strongly Disagree/1 to Strongly Agree/5), Competitive and Cooperative Social Presence in Gaming (CCPIG) V1.1 cooperation subscale (25 items, 5-point Likert scale: Strongly Disagree/1 to Strongly Agree/5; Team Identification, Social Action, Motivation, Team Value), in-game telemetry (orb status at despawn, player who tapped it, time between tap and spawn, total arm movement), HR, and Ratings of Perceived Exertion (RPE) scale (rated from 6 to 20); quantitative analysis used Shapiro-Wilk tests, Friedman's ANOVAs instead of one-way repeated measures ANOVAs when normality was violated, Greenhouse-Geisser correction, and pairwise comparisons with Holm-Bonferroni corrections; qualitative analysis used Dovetail transcription and thematic analysis (TA) with reflexive and codebook approaches plus affinity mapping.
