data.authors: Harish Prakash, Jia Cheng Shang, Ken M. Nsiempba, Yuhao Chen, David A. Clausi, John S. Zelek
data.core_methodology: MOT as a bipartite graph matching problem infused with homography; spatio-temporal graph with Graph Initialization, MPN, and Classification; undirected graph Gt = (Vt, Et); NodeFeatures(.) concatenation of appearance features and homographic projections; edge encoded as concatenation of relative appearance ∆rid_ij and positional ∆p_ij; off-the-shelf homography estimator [22] trained on an ice hockey top-view rink template to estimate H ∈ R3×3; OSNet architecture [48] as ReID network; F-RCNN [25]; Message Passing Network (MPN) [23], [24]; binary classifier with sigmoid final layer; sigmoid focal loss [50]; pruning and many-to-one violation resolution; tracklet ID assignment; Adam Optimizer [53]; cosine annealing schedule; tracking-by-detection paradigm.

data.paper_title: Offensive Lineup Analysis in Basketball with Clustering Players Based on Shooting Style and Offensive Role
data.authors: Kazuhiro Yamada1, Keisuke Fujii1,2,3∗
data.core_methodology: Shooting style clustering: 17 hand-crafted shot features; principal component analysis to 9 dimensions retaining 99% cumulative contribution ratio; UMAP visualization; p-Wasserstein distance / Wasserstein distance; Earth Mover’s Distance with d = 9 and p = 1 using Euclidean distance; empirical discrete uniform distribution; Ward’s method; silhouette coefficient. Offensive role clustering: playtype percentages plus AST% and USG%; K-means clustering algorithm; Fuzzy C-means clustering with q = 1.2 under c = 10; membership coefficient. Lineup analysis: Support Vector Machine, LightGBM, NGBoost for 5-player combinations; Bayesian hierarchical linear regression model estimated by MCMC with NUTS (No-U-turn Sampler) for 2-player combinations; adjusted offensive rating (adjustedOFFRTG).
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Tracking data: original sampling rate 25 Hz downsampled to 10 Hz; 630 games within the 2015-16 NBA season; 41,160 shots (28,427 two-pointers and 12,733 three-pointers); attack segments lasted more than 3 seconds and ended with a shot; time interval from 3 seconds before the shot to the moment of the shot. Shooting style: 17 features; PCA compressed to 9 dimensions retaining 99% of cumulative contribution ratio; players for whom data for 30 or more shots existed: 325 players; silhouette coefficients calculated for 2 to 20 clusters; 13 clusters adopted. Offensive role: 3051 players; q = 1.2 under c = 10; approximately 66% of the players had a maximum membership coefficient of 0.9 or higher; approximately 97% had a maximum membership coefficient of 0.5 or higher. data.paper_title: Basketball-SORT: An Association Method for Complex Multi-object Occlusion Problems in Basketball Multi-object Tracking
data.authors: Qingrui Hu1, Atom Scott1, Calvin Yeung1, Keisuke Fujii1,2,3*
data.core_methodology: Basketball-SORT is an online tracking-by-detection method for Complex Multi-object Occlusion (CMOO) problems in basketball videos. It uses a fine-tuned yolov8 model to detect players; the bottom midpoint of the detection bounding box is projected onto the 2D court plane by a homography matrix H using 20 standardized court key points (Eq. 1). Association uses a Kalman filter based on the position and speed of the projected position. Basketball Game Restriction (BGR): at the 100th frame, calculate all trajectory lengths and select the top ten longest trajectories as the only player trajectories. Lost state is occlusion for less than B frames; Long-Lost state is lost for more than B frames. Reacquiring Long-Lost IDs (RLLI): compare the Long-Lost player's court position and ReID features before disappearance with a new detection using Cost a_b = 1 − Cosine Similarity = 1 − (a · b)/(∥a∥∥b∥) (Eq. 2) and conditions Costlost_re > α, Distlost_re > β (Eq. 3). Occlusion is categorized as Same Team Occlusion (STO) and Different Team Occlusion (DTO) by ReID similarity (Eq. 4); DTO ID switches use appearance similarity (Eq. 5), and STO ID switches use moving distance and speed (Eq. 6). FastReID is used for player ReID.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Evaluation metrics: HOTA, DetA, LocA, AssA, FP, FN, IDS. Parameters: high-score detection threshold 0.6; low-score detections between 0.6 and 0.1; detections lower than 0.1 filtered; RLLI threshold α = 0.2; β = 260; γ = 0.2; δ = 0.2; ε = 3; ζ = 3. data.paper_title: Uncovering the Effect of Toxicity on Player Engagement and its Propagation in Competitive Online Video Games
data.authors: Jacob Morrier∗1, Amine Mahmassani2, and R. Michael Alvarez1
data.core_methodology: Instrumental variables estimation strategy; two-stage least squares (2SLS); structural model of players’ behavior: 𝑦𝑖𝑗= 𝛼𝑗+ 𝜷· 𝒙𝑖𝑗+ 𝜀𝑖𝑗, where 𝑦𝑖𝑗 is the outcome of interest in match 𝑖 for player 𝑗, 𝛼𝑗 a player-specific intercept, 𝒙𝑖𝑗 a vector including the number of players other than player 𝑗 who have used toxic language in match 𝑖 and to which player 𝑗 was exposed, and 𝜀𝑖𝑗 an error term; the vector 𝒙𝑖𝑗 also contains interactions between the number of other players using toxic language in a match and whether player 𝑗’s team has won or lost the game. Identification strategy adds the first-stage equation: 𝑥𝑖𝑗= 𝛿𝑗+ 𝛾× ∑_{𝑘∈P𝑖,−𝑗} ∑_{ℓ∈M𝑖,𝑘,−𝑗} 𝑥★_{ℓ𝑘}/#M𝑖,𝑘,−𝑗 + 𝑢𝑖𝑗, where P𝑖,−𝑗 is the set of players in match 𝑖 excluding player 𝑗, M𝑖,𝑘,−𝑗 the set of matches prior to match 𝑖 to which player 𝑘 participated but not player 𝑗, and 𝑥★_{ℓ𝑘} a variable indicating whether player 𝑘 used toxic language in match ℓ; the instrument belongs to the general class of spatial or leave-one-out instruments. Player-specific intercepts are fixed effects; instead of explicitly estimating fixed effects, the values of the dependent, independent, and instrumental variables are demeaned for all players at the individual level, then 𝛽 is estimated through standard 2SLS. Toxic language is identified by ToxMod™, Activision’s incorporated Modulate™ proprietary voice chat moderation technology using artificial intelligence and machine learning algorithms to detect toxic language in real-time; a player is classified as having used toxic language in a match if ToxMod™ identified at least one of their statements during it as toxic.

data.paper_title: SpikeMOT: Event-based Multi-Object Tracking with Sparse Motion Features
data.authors: Song Wang*, Zhu Wang*, Can Li, Xiaojuan Qi, Hayden Kwok-Hay So, Senior Member, IEEE
data.core_methodology: SpikeMOT event-based multi-object tracker comprising (i) an object tracker, (ii) an object detector, and (iii) a tracklet matcher. It uses spiking neural networks (SNNs) with Spike Response Model (SRM) neurons in a Siamese architecture to extract sparse spatiotemporal features from event voxels V^t converted from binary sparse event tensors e_t1^t2. The Siamese position estimator f_T, detector f_D, and matcher f_M are defined by P^{t+τ}=f_T(Q^t,V^t,e_t^{t+τ};θ_T), D^{t+τ}=f_D(e_t^{t+τ};θ_D), Q^{t+τ}=f_M(P^{t+τ},D^{t+τ}). The detector is one-stage YOLOv5. The tracklet matcher uses the Hungarian algorithm with Hausdorff distance, validation/dismissal contingent on the Siamese position estimator, and a solver for tracklet updates, initialization, and removal. Training uses backpropagation with surrogate gradients and AdamW. The SNN block contains synapse networks (CNNs) followed by SRM neurons; the SRM membrane potential uses response kernel ε and refractory kernel υ with Heaviside step function H(t).
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Equations: P^{t+τ}=f_T(Q^t,V^t,e_t^{t+τ};θ_T); D^{t+τ}=f_D(e_t^{t+τ};θ_D); Q^{t+τ}=f_M(P^{t+τ},D^{t+τ}); u^l(t)=∫_0^∞ ε(t−τ)o^l(τ)dτ − ∫_0^∞ υ(t−τ)s^{l+1}(τ)dτ; ε=1/τ_s e^{−t/τ_s}H(t); υ=1/τ_r e^{−t/τ_r}H(t); s^{l+1}(t)=f_s(u^l(t)); f_s(u): s(t_i)=δ(t−t_i) if u(t_i)≥V_th, otherwise 0; y_i=1 if ||u_i−c_y||≤R, else 0; w_i=0.5/P[y_i=1] if ||u_i−c_y||≤R, w_i=0.5/P[y_i=0] if ||u_i−c_y||>R; L_neg=Σ−w_i log(1−σ(v_i)); for ||u_i−c_v||>R: l_i=−y_i log(ϵ); for ||u_i−c_v||≤R: l_i=−[y_i log(σ(v_i))+(1−y_i)log(1−σ(v_i))]; L_pos=Σw_i l_i. Parameters: SRM τ_s=10 ms, τ_r=1 ms, spiking threshold 1.0; template voxel [2,127,127,100], search voxel [2,255,255,100]; tracker updates every 10 ms; detector every 50 ms; 100 slices; each slice 10 ms; voxel duration 100; voxel granularity 10 ms. data.paper_title: COST: Contrastive One-Stage Transformer for Vision-Language Small Object Tracking
data.authors: Chunhui Zhanga,b,c, Li Liub, Jialin Gaoa, Xin Suna, Hao Wenc, Xi Zhouc, Shiming Ged, Yanfeng Wanga,e
data.core_methodology: COST contrastive one-stage transformer fusion framework for vision-language tracking; contrastive visual-linguistic fusion (CVLF) module combining contrastive alignment (CoA) and visual-linguistic transformer; CoA uses contrastive learning (CL) to maximize mutual information (MI) between matched video and language, with InfoNCE losses Lv2l and Ll2v and total LCoA; visual branch uses modified ResNet50 (V1) backbone plus visual transformer with MHSA and MHCA encoders and decoder; linguistic branch uses pre-trained BERTBASE linguistic transformer; visual-linguistic transformer uses two linear projections, learnable [OBJ] token, and stack of transformer encoder layers with MHSA; tracking head performs binary classification and bounding-box regression; losses include binary cross-entropy Lce, ℓ1-norm L1, generalized IoU LGIoU, and L=LCoA+Lreg+αLce; optimizer AdamW; online post-processing uses 21×21 Hanning window; dataset methodology defines small object by average relative size < s (1%) and average absolute size < √(k×k) (√(22×22)) pixels and relative speed ∆t = 1/(√(s_{t−1}s_t)) ||p_t−p_{t−1}||_2/(T_t−T_{t−1}), s_t=√(w_t h_t), p_t=(x_t,y_t); builds VL-SOT500 with subsets VL-SOT230 and VL-SOT270.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Equations: ∆t = 1/(√(s_{t−1}s_t)) ||p_t−p_{t−1}||_2/(T_t−T_{t−1}), s_t=√(w_t h_t), p_t=(x_t,y_t); Attn(Q,K,V)=softmax(QK^⊤/√d_k)·V; MultiHead(Q,K,V)=Concat(H1,...,Hh)W^O; H_i=Attn(QW_i^Q,KW_i^K,VW_i^V); X′_l=LN(X_l+MultiHead(X_l)); X_{l+1}=LN(X′_l+FFN(X′_l)); Lv2l(F_i^v,F_i^l)=−Σ_i log(exp(sim(F_i^v,F_i^l)/τ)/Σ_j 1[j,i] exp(sim(F_i^v,F_j^l)/τ)); Ll2v(Fl_i,Fv_i)=−Σ_i log(exp(sim(Fl_i,Fv_i)/τ)/Σ_j 1[j,i] exp(sim(Fl_i,Fv_j)/τ)); LCoA=1/2 E_{(F_i^v,F_i^l)∼(F^v,F^l)}[Lv2l(·)+Ll2v(·)]; Lce=Σ_i y_i log(p_i)+(1−y_i)log(1−p_i); Lreg=Σ_i 1_{y_i=1}[λ1L1(B_i,B̂_i)+λGLGIoU(B_i,B̂_i)]; L=LCoA+Lreg+αLce. data.paper_title: Multi-Modal Soccer Scene Analysis with Masked Pre-Training
data.authors: Marc Peral, Guillem Capellera, Luis Ferraz, Antonio Rubio, Antonio Agudo
data.core_methodology: Multi-modal architecture for soccer scene analysis from tactical camera footage integrating three input modalities: player trajectories, player types, and image crops of individual players. Uses a cascade of sociotemporal transformer blocks; a two-stage transformer-based encoder with coarse encoder and fine encoder, each composed of two Temporal Set Attention Blocks (SABT) followed by a Social Set Attention Block (SABS); temporal positional encoding; two learned CLS tokens; MLP and fully connected prediction heads; ResNet backbone trained on an auxiliary action recognition task; MixSort for bounding boxes; CropDrop modality-specific masking pre-training strategy applied only to the visual modality; cross-entropy losses for ball state and possessor; Average Displacement Error (ADE) for ball position. Tensor shapes include T × (N + 2) × d for fused tokens, T × 1 × d for ball and state CLS tokens, T × 2 for predicted ball coordinates, T × S logits for ball state, and T × N logits for ball possessor. CropDrop randomly selects a percentage of players in each input sequence and masks their visual features across all frames, replacing masked visual embeddings with fixed placeholder values outside the valid range of visual features.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Equations: L_ball = (1/T) Σ_{t=1}^T ||b̂_t − b_t||_2; L_state = −(1/T) Σ_{t=1}^T Σ_{s=1}^S c_t^s log(ĉ_t^s); L_poss = −(1/T) Σ_{t=1}^T Σ_{n=1}^N c_t^n log(ĉ_t^n); L_total = λ1 L_ball + λ2 L_state + λ3 L_poss; MaxErr = max_{t∈{1,...,T}}(||b̂_t − b_t||_2). Hyperparameters: λ1 = 1, λ2 = 3, λ3 = 3; constant masking ratio for all pre-trainings = 0.5. T is the number of frames, N the number of players, d the embedding dimension, S the number of discrete ball state classes. Dataset and sequences: 283 full professional matches; season 2022-2023; 60 frames sampled at 6.25 Hz, corresponding to 9.6 seconds; training, validation, and test sets containing 43,397, 3,968, and 3,347 sequences; 82,961 pass frames, 97,841 possession frames, and 20,018 uncontrolled frames; four ball state labels: pass, possession, uncontrolled, and out of play. data.paper_title: ViTs for action classification in videos: An approach to risky tackle detection in American football practice videos
data.authors: Syed Ahsan Masud Zaidi, William Hsu, and Scott Dietrich
data.core_methodology: Vision transformer-based model with imbalance-aware training; binary classification of tackles as risky or safe using the SATT rubric, specifically SATT3 (Strike Zone, SZ) at the point of contact, with scores 0–3 mapped scores ≤1 to risky and scores ≥2 to safe; temporal localization to first point of contact (FPOC) and extraction of a fixed 32-frame clip (15 frames before and 16 frames after the FPOC); four augmentation types (Noise, Brightness, Rotate, Flip) with discrete levels: 2 for Noise and 3 each for Brightness, Rotation, and Flip, yielding 2×3×3×3 = 54 configurations; Taguchi L18 orthogonal array design of experiments; augmentation applied after stratified fold splitting and only to the training data; stratified 5-fold cross-validation with post-split augmentation; ViViT-B 16×2 architecture pretrained on Kinetics-400 with full fine-tuning; spatiotemporal tokenization with tubelet patches of size 2×16×16, linear projection to D = 768, L = 12 transformer layers with Multi-Head Self-Attention (MSA, 12 heads) and Feed-Forward Network (FFN), and a classification head to 2 class logits; Focal Loss LFL = −αy(1 −py)γ log(py) with γ = 1.6 and α = 0.6 for risky tackles and 1 − α = 0.4 for safe tackles.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Dataset: 733 single-athlete-dummy tackle clips; Safe 474 (64.7%), Risky 259 (35.3%), Total 733 (100.0); expanded previously published dataset of 178 practice videos by adding 555 new tackle training videos; clip durations 200 to 1500 frames at 30fps; natural imbalance approximately 65% safe and 35% risky; trivial classifier predicting safe for all instances achieves 65% accuracy. Temporal localization: fixed 32-frame clip (15 frames before and 16 frames after the FPOC). Augmentation: Noise levels count 2 (None; Noise), Brightness 3 (Same; Increase; Decrease), Rotate 3 (None; Left; Right), Flip 3 (None; Horizontal; Vertical), yielding 2×3×3×3 = 54 configurations; Taguchi L18 reduced from 54 to 18 configurations; 18 augmentation configurations plus one baseline (no augmentation) = 19 distinct experimental runs; Run0 uses oversampling (duplicate risky videos); Runorig uses the original unbalanced dataset; per fold generate Naug = N train safe − N train risky ≈171–173 augmented risky clips, producing ∼757–760 training clips; training sets contain 586−587 originals plus 171−173 augmented risky clips (758−760 total); validation sets remain unaugmented with 146−147 videos and 34.9−35.6% risky. Cross-validation: StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=42); |Sk| ∈{146, 147}; roughly 51–52 risky and 94–95 safe videos per fold; 5 × 20 = 100 runs. Model: ViViT-B 16×2; Kinetics-400 pretraining; D = 768; 12 transformer layers; 16×16 pixel spatial patches; tubelet size 2 frames; 32-frame × 224×224 inputs yield 32/2 × 224/16 × 224/16 = 3,136 spatiotemporal tokens plus one classification token; 12 heads; dk = D/12 = 64; classification head to 2 class logits; Kinetics-400 comprises ∼400 human action classes with over 300,000 videos. Equations: z0 = [xcls; Ep1; Ep2; . . . ; EpN] + Epos, with E ∈RD×(2·16·16·C) and Epos ∈R(N+1)×D; z′ℓ= MSA(LN(zℓ−1)) + zℓ−1, ℓ= 1, . . . , 12; zℓ= FFN(LN(z′ℓ)) + z′ℓ; Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(QK⊤/√dk) V; LFL = −αy(1 −py)γ log(py). Focal Loss: γ = 1.6; α = 0.6; 1 − α = 0.4; with γ = 1.6, an example classified with 90% confidence receives (1 − 0.9)^1.6 = 0.04 weighting—a 25× reduction; examples at 50% confidence receive (1 − 0.5)^1.6 = 0.33 weighting—a 3× reduction. Results: risky recall 0.67 and Risky F1 0.59; previous baseline in a smaller subset risky recall 0.58 and Risky F1 0.56; Run15 risky recall 0.67 and risky F1 0.59; original imbalanced risky recall 0.58; duplicated/oversampled 0.54; Run15 66.7% risky recall and 67.0% safe recall; C3D baseline 58.3% risky recall and 76.9% safe recall; improvement 8.4 percentage points in risky recall; safe recall decrease 9.9 points; several configurations reach high accuracy (0.70–0.71) but with reduced risky recall; Run15 accuracy 0.67; previous validation set 39 videos (26 safe, 13 risky); expanded validation set 146 videos (95 safe, 51 risky); one risky sample changes risky-class recall by ≈7.7 percentage points (1/13) and accuracy by ≈2.6 points (1/39); expanded one risky sample alters recall by ≈2.0 points (1/51) and accuracy by ≈0.68 points (1/146), roughly 3.8× improvement in stability.

data.paper_title: ELASTIC: Trajectory-Based Synchronization of Event and Tracking Data in Soccer
data.authors: Hyunsung Kim∗, Hoyoung Choi, Kunhee Lee, Sangwoo Seo, Tom Boomstra, Jinsung Yoon, Chanyoung Park
data.core_methodology: ELASTIC (Event-Location-AgnoSTIC synchronizer); SPADL (Soccer Player Action Description Language) event format; event categories Open-play outgoing, Set-piece outgoing, Incoming, Minor; virtual termination events goal, out, control inserted between adjacent events; candidate frame selection using (a) local minima of ball-player distance, (b) local minima of ball-pitch boundary distance, (c) local maxima of ball acceleration, with player-ball distance threshold 3 m and ball height threshold 4 m; clipped linear mapping f(x;x0,x1); per-feature scores BA, PBD, KD (Pre-KD/Post-KD), PBDS (pre-slope/post-slope), OD; weighted event-candidate score with λ_BA=λ_PBD=λ_KD=λ_PBDS=λ_OD=0.25; repeat-augmented Needleman-Wunsch algorithm with diag-match, right-gap, down-gap, down-match, g_c=0, g_e=0, r=−0.1; postprocessing with dispossessed-tackle unification, match rejection threshold 0.5, and folding enriched event sequence back to original events; downstream evaluation uses Graph Attention Network (GAT) layers for next action prediction and pass success prediction.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Tracking data at 10 or 25 FPS; 25 FPS = 0.04 s; about 90,000 in-play frames (about 60 minutes); K≈100 episodes; Eq. 1: 1 ≤ t_start_1 ≤ ... ≤ t_start_i ≤ t_end_i ≤ t_start_{i+1} ≤ ... ≤ t_end_M ≤ T; Eq. 2: f(x;x0,x1)=0 if x≤x0, 1 if x≥x1, (x−x0)/(x1−x0) if x0<x<x1; Eq. 3: s_BA(t_c)=f(a(t_c);0,30 m/s2); Eq. 4: s_PBD(t_c,p)=1−f(d(t_c,p);0,3 m); Eq. 5: s^−_KD(t_c,p)=f(max_{t^−_c≤t≤t_c} d(t,p);0,3 m); Eq. 6: s^+_KD(t_c,p)=f(max_{t_c≤t≤t^+_c} d(t,p);0,3 m); v^−(t,p)=(d(t,p)−d(t−h,p))/h and v^+(t,p)=(d(t+h,p)−d(t,p))/h with h=0.2 s; Eq. 7: s^−_PBDS(t_c,p)=1−f(v^−(t_c,p);0,7 m/s); Eq. 8: s^+_PBDS(t_c,p)=f(v^+(t_c,p);−7 m/s,0); Eq. 9: s_OD(t_c,p)=1−f(min_{q∈O(p)} d(t_c,q);0,3 m); Eq. 10: s(e,c)=λ_BA s_BA(t_c)+λ_PBD s_PBD(t_c,p_e)+λ_KD s^+_KD(t_c,p_e)+λ_PBDS s^−_PBDS(t_c,p_e); Eq. 11: s(e,c)=λ_BA s_BA(t_c)+λ_PBD s_PBD(t_c,p_e)+λ_KD s^−_KD(t_c,p_e)+λ_PBDS s^+_PBDS(t_c,p_e); Eq. 12: s(e,c)=λ_BA s_BA(t_c)+λ_PBD s_PBD(t_c,p_e)+λ_KD s_KD(t_c,p_e)+λ_OD s_OD(t_c,p_e); λ_BA=λ_PBD=λ_KD=λ_PBDS=λ_OD=0.25; Eq. 13: F_i,j=max{F_{i−1,j−1}+s(e_i,c_j), F_{i,j−1}+g_c, F_{i−1,j}+g_e}; Eq. 14 includes down-match F_{i−1,j}+s(e_i,c_j)+r; g_c=0; g_e=0; r=−0.1; match rejection threshold 0.5; primary metric W2 = 2 frames = 0.08 s, with W5, W25, W50, MD, Valid; Table 1 agreement total: 6,470 events, MD 0.521 frames, Exact3 6,148 (95.0%), Exact2 6,388 (98.7%), Close3 6,250 (96.6%), Close2 6,425 (99.3%); default candidate configuration: #Cand. 16,979, Start 98.5%, End 98.2%, Total 98.4%, Acc. 95.2%, Time 37.62 ± 5.25 s; downstream ELASTIC-NW: Acc. 0.6863, CE 0.8773, MRR 0.8087, F1 0.9155, AUC 0.9172, Brier 0.0899; unsynchronized: Acc. 0.5796, CE 1.2148, MRR 0.7354, F1 0.9031, AUC 0.9028, Brier 0.1013; ELASTIC-Greedy: Acc. 0.6759, CE 0.9114, MRR 0.8017, F1 0.9072, AUC 0.9103, Brier 0.0966.

data.authors: Ricardo Duarte, Duarte Araújo, Luís Freire, Hugo Folgado, Orlando Fernandes, Keith Davids
data.core_methodology: Group-motion (kinematic) variables: centroid (i.e., team center; mean position of the three players over time in the x- and y-component of motion) and surface area (i.e., occupied space; area of a triangle calculated with Area(A,B,C) = abs((xB·yA − xA·yB) + (xC·yB − xB·yC) + (xA·yC − xC·yA))/2); running correlation technique applied along the entire data time-series with a 0.4-s sliding window (i.e., a 10 data-point window) shifted frame by frame (i.e., every 0.04 s), identifying symmetric, anti-symmetric, and no correlated patterns; mixed-model ANOVA; Tukey’s HSD test; TACTO 8.0; bi-dimensional Direct Linear Transformation method (2D-DLT); Butterworth low pass filter (6 Hz); MATLAB software R2008a; SPSS 17.0; variation accounted for (VAF).

data.paper_title: The TREC-2002 Video Track Report
data.authors: Alan F. Smeaton, Paul Over
data.core_methodology: TREC-2002 Video Track: open, metrics-based evaluation of content-based retrieval from digital video using three tasks—shot boundary determination, feature extraction, and search (manual or interactive); manually created truth data for shot boundary determination and manual assessment of feature extraction and search results; common shot definitions donated by CLIPS-IMAG and formatted by Dublin City University; feature detections distributed in an MPEG-7 format developed by IBM; shot boundary detection measured by precision and recall with a single-frame overlap detection criterion, abrupt transitions treated as effective length two frames, very short gradual transitions (5 frames or less) treated as cuts, abrupt reference transitions expanded by 5 frames in each direction before matching, and frame-precision and frame-recall for gradual-transition accuracy; data.authors: Ergys Ristani, Carlo Tomasi
data.core_methodology: Adaptive weighted triplet loss; batch-hard triplet loss with built-in hard sample mining; softmax/min weight distributions; PK batches; hard identity mining with a hard identity pool and a random identity pool; ResNet50 model pretrained on ImageNet followed by a dense layer with 1024 units, batch normalization, and ReLU, and another dense layer yielding 128-dimensional appearance features; online data augmentation with crops, horizontal flips, contrast normalization, grayscale and color multiplication effects, Gaussian blur of varying σ, perspective transformations, small distortions, and hiding small rectangular image patches; OpenPose person detector with part affinity fields and greedy parsing; linear motion model with forward-backward prediction error em = ef + eb, threshold tm, scaling factor α, and correlation wm = α(tm − em), with impossible associations receiving wm = −∞; appearance correlation wij = (ta−d(xi,xj))/ta with threshold ta = 1/2(µp + µn); correlation matrix W = (Wa + Wm) ⊙ D with discounts D = e−β∆t ∈[0, 1]; correlation clustering X∗= arg max_{xij} Σ_{(i,j)∈E} wijxij subject to xij + xjk ≤1 + xik ∀i, j, k ∈V; multi-level reasoning over one-second long tracklets, single-camera trajectories, and multi-camera identities with an online sliding temporal window that overlaps 50% with the previous window; post-processing interpolation and pruning; general triplet loss L3 = [ m + Σ_{xp∈P(a)} wp d(xa, xp) − Σ_{xn∈N(a)} wn d(xa, xn) ]_+ with m the given inter-person separation margin, d the distance of appearance, and [·]+ = max(0, ·); adaptive weights wp = e^{d(xa,xp)} / Σ_{x∈P(a)} e^{d(xa,x)}, wn = e^{−d(xa,xn)} / Σ_{x∈N(a)} e^{−d(xa,x)}; batch-hard weights wp = [xp == arg max_{x∈P(a)} d(xa, x)] and wn = [xn == arg min_{x∈N(a)} d(xa, x)] using Iverson brackets.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Training: P = 18, K = 4, m = 1, resolution 256×128; learning rate 3 · 10−4 for the first 15000 iterations, decays to 10−7 at iteration 25000; hard and random pools constructed once with features obtained at iteration 5000; hard identity pool size H = 50; similar scores obtained with 30-100 identities (4%-15% of all training identities). data.core_methodology: Three-week repeated-measured design; 4 Vs 4 small-sided games; bio-banding using percentage of estimated adult stature attainment (EASA) by Khamis and Roche (post-PHV 92.0 to 95.0%, circa-PHV 87.0 – 92.0%, pre-PHV 85.0 to 87.0% estimated adult stature attainment), maturity offset by the Fransen, et al. predictive equation with modified thresholds (pre-PHV (< -1.0 years to PHV), circa-PHV (-1.0 – 0.0 years to PHV), post-PHV (>0.0 years to PHV)), and mixed-maturity method; Game Technical Scoring Chart (GTSC); video analysis; 10 Hz GPS; spatial exploration index (SEI) algorithm; Bayesian hierarchical models fitted with different response distributions and different random and fixed effect structures; Bayesian ordinal cumulative model with a probit link function; Bayesian zero inflated Poisson regression models; Gaussian response distribution; weakly informative priors; prior predictive checks; Delta total (𝛿𝑡) effect size; probability of direction (pd); Bayesian R squared; Leave-One-Out cross-validation (LOO); Hamiltonian Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) with a No-U-Turn Sampler in brms/Stan.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: 92 academy soccer players (under 13: n =31; under 14: n = 32; under 15: n = 26; under 16: n =3); initial group of 72 participating players and 20 reserve players; 24 players from each academy (n = 72); 95% credible interval for the mean difference; Khamis and Roche measurement error 2.1% between actual and estimated adult stature in male athletes aged between 4 and 18 years; adjusted threshold 87.0 to 92.0% of final EASA; post-PHV 92.0 to 95.0%, circa-PHV 87.0 – 92.0%, pre-PHV 85.0 to 87.0% estimated adult stature attainment; Fransen, et al. predictive algorithm based on longitudinal sample aged 8-17 years; pre-PHV (< -1.0 years to PHV), circa-PHV (-1.0 – 0.0 years to PHV), post-PHV (>0.0 years to PHV); 8 players changed bio-banding categories; five 4 Vs 4 SSGs (18.3 x 23 m pitch), lasting 5 min each (25 min total playing time); two (2 m × 1 m) goals; maximum of 10 and minimum of 5 min recovery; 52.6 m2 per player; camera mean (SD) height of 7.3 (2.9) m and distance from pitch of 13 m; 10 Hz GPS; 3 Hz Butterworth low pass filter; convergence r̂ = 1; lower bound threshold of 0.4 for 𝛿𝑡; pd = 93.77% to 100%; pd = 99.50% to 99.58%; successful passes difference of 1.87 when pre-PHV groups played each other (pd=100%); dribbling time pd = 98.24% and pd = 85.62%; communication 0.85 standard deviations when post-PHV groups played each other (pd=99.24%); mixed maturity highest difference 0.33 standard deviations (pd= 96.25%); SEI 0.45 (pd= 96.15%); SEI pd=97.17% and 92.90%; nearest team-mate pd= 99.52% and pd= 99.17%; distance to centroid pd=97.62%; Total Technical Score Fransen R2 0.67 (0.64 to 0.69), LOOIC 4421.50; Khamis and Roche R2 0.58 (0.54 to 0.61), LOOIC 4472.00; Fransen best (lowest) LOOIC for 19 out of 25 variables; 76% (19 out of 25); broad credible intervals of 0.0 to 1.49; variables: successful pass, unsuccessful pass, turning, goals, shots on target, shots off target, aerial challenge, ground ball challenge, interception, dribbling; cover, communication, decision-making, passing, first touch, control, one versus one, shooting, assists, marking; SEI, nearest team-mate, nearest opponent, distance to team centroid, distance to opponent centroid.

data.paper_title: Real-time multi-sport action tracking with convolutional neural networks
data.authors: Axel Baldanza, Jean-François Aujol, Yann Traonmilin, François Alary
data.core_methodology: Predicts global camera motion from segmented optical flow of the foreground using a convolutional neural network (3D-CNN architecture; NetMot), avoiding object detection and piecewise situation classification. Foreground/background segmentation sets to 0 all optical flow elements close enough to the 2D median (u*, v*) of the optical flow: F^t ∈ R^{N×M×2}, f^t_i,j = ((u_i,j + u*, v_i,j + v*), if (i,j) ∈ Ω; 0 else), where Ω = {(i,j); ||(u_i,j, v_i,j) − (u*, v*)||_2 ≥ θ}. The model takes as input n foreground optical flows computed with intervals of k frames and outputs the camera displacement for the following frame, normalized in a percentage of the field; predicts only horizontal motion in the experiments. Network architecture: Conv1–Conv4 and FC1–FC4 as in Table I. Trained using ADAM optimizer. Compared with NetMotV0 (single segmented optical flow at time t) and PEN (piecewise linear supervised learning model with d_t = ⟨f^t η, z_s⟩ + e_t).
data.key_metrics_and_variables: θ threshold; k = 10; n = 3; input frames downsampled to 160 × 90; output calculated at 70,5 fps; training databases: 60494 optical flow matrices for basketball and 42654 for handball; test datasets: 15 short basketball videos, 7 long basketball videos (24 seconds to more than two minutes), and 14 handball videos; metrics: MAE, Tracking Error, MAX TE; Tracking Error over 15% of the field means the algorithm has lost the location of the action; MAX TE is maximum MAE computed on 10-second subsequences; 80,6% of videos have lower MAEs with NetMot than with PEN; 80.6% of videos have a lower Tracking Error with NetMot than PEN; Table II short basketball MEAN: PEN MAE 0.18, Tracking Error 12.04; NetMotV0 MAE 0.11, Tracking Error 7.15; NetMot MAE 0.07, Tracking Error 4.06; NUMBER OF MAE >15: 3, 4, 1; Table III handball MEAN: PEN MAE 0.18, Tracking Error 6.92; NetMotV0 MAE 0.08, Tracking Error 12.05; NetMot MAE 0.12, Tracking Error 5.98; NUMBER OF MAE >15: 0, 4, 0; Table IV long videos MEAN: PEN MAE 2.93, NetMot MAE 0.04, PEN Tracking Error 11.34, NetMot Tracking Error 2.46; MAX TE always ≤15.

data.paper_title: Overview of correlation filter based algorithms in object tracking
data.authors: Shuai Liu, Dongye Liu, Gautam Srivastava, Dawid Połap, Marcin Woźniak
data.core_methodology: Review of correlation filter based object tracking algorithms; datasets VOT, OTB (OTB2013/OTB2015), TColor-128, UAV123, LASOT; algorithms: minimum output sum of squared error (MOSSE), circulant structure tracking with kernels (CSK), Kernels correlation filter (KCF), discriminative scale space tracker (DSST), improved fDSST, C-COT, CSR-DCF, SRDCF, STAPLE, LMCF, BACF, DRT, ASRCF, STRCF, SRDCFDecon; motion models: particle filtering and sliding windows; features: Haar, HOG, LBP, color features, depth features; proposed template update judgment methods: object tracking strategy with visual attention features structure (KCF_VAF) using scale change rate, speed, acceleration, and weighted Gaussian distribution N(μ, σ²); object tracking strategy based on visual memory mechanism using optical flow, alternate template Ra, and context regression model Rc; proposed reliability-based visual tracking method using nine tuple features and reliability-assisted decision-making single-layer network model with nine feature inputs, two predictive outputs, and three neurons; optimization/learning methods: FFT, kernel ridge regression, cyclic matrix, PCA, QR-decomposition, triangular interpolation, Gauss–Seidel, ADMM, ALM, SAMF pyramid, Newton iteration, conjugate gradient descent, quadratic programming.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: MOSSE: 669 fps; 26 times faster than advanced MIL; PSR between 20 and 60 good, lower than 7 failure. OTB: threshold typically set to 20 pixels; success threshold generally set to 0.5; SRE uses four center shifts and four angular shifts and four proportional changes; amount of transfer is 10% of target size; scale factor varies among 0.8, 0.9, 1.1, and 1.2; evaluates each tracker 12 times; OTB2013 contains 51 videos; OTB2015 contains 100 video sequences extended from OTB2013 (50 videos). TColor-128: 16 state-of-the-art visual trackers; 10 color models; 128 color sequences; 160 color-coded tracker; accuracy threshold 20 pixels; fast motion >20 pixels; low resolution <400 pixels. UAV123: 123 high-resolution aerial video sequences; >110K frames; Set1 103 sequences at altitude 5–25 m; 30–96 FPS; resolution between 720p and 4K; annotation at 10 FPS then linearly interpolated at 30 FPS; Set2 12 sequences; Set3 8 synthetic sequences; annotations automatically at 30 fps. LASOT: 1400 sequences; >3.5 million frames; average sequence length >2500 frames. DSST: scale factor a of 1.02; scale number S of 33. fDSST: QR-decomposition reduces 1000×17 to 17×17; triangular interpolation supplement to 33. STRCF: 5× acceleration. STAPLE: 80fps. BACF: complexity of O(K3T3) down to O(K3T), finally O(KT). DRT: nine sub-areas. ASRCF: five scales; five-dimensional HOG feature map. Reliability network: nine feature inputs, two predictive outputs, three neurons. data.paper_title: Scene Classification for Sports Video Using Transfer Learning
data.authors: Prakhar Singh1, Nilava Dutta2, Rajvivek Sundriyal3, Pulkit Suri4, Kanika Malik5
data.core_methodology: ResNet152 model pre-trained on imagenet weights with three transfer learning layers applied at the end; fully connected layers in an encoder fashion; dropout process with a threshold of usually 0.5; Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU) activation function f(x) = max(0, x); Adam Optimizer; TensorFlowTM backend with Keras applications; dataset generators; training for 5 epochs.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: mean accuracy: 99.15; robust accuracy: above 99%; epochs: 5; learning rate: 0.0001; dropout threshold: usually 0.5; ResNet152 layers: 152; transfer learning layers: three; scene classes: 5 (batting, bowling, boundary, crowd, close-up); total relevant frames: six thousand; dataset labelling ranges: 0 to 2k, 2k to 4k, 4k to 6k, 6k to 8k; literature classification accuracy: 85% to 95% on five different sports; 94% for 10 and 92% for 15 sports classes; YLI-MED dataset: 1823 videos; self-collected YouTube dataset: 1369 videos; grayscale videos: 36; cricket event detection accuracy: 89.45%.

data.paper_title: A Survey on Video Action Recognition in Sports: Datasets, Methods and Applications

data.paper_title: Accuracy of a smart bottle in measuring fluid intake by American football players during pre‑season training
data.authors: Lindsay B. Baker, Shelby Alfred, Khalil A. Lee, Justina L. Bonsignore, Kristin L. Osterberg, Brandon Shepherd, Peter John D. De Chavez, Kobi Bentkovski
data.core_methodology: Smart bottle technology with optical sensors, microprocessors, batteries, and wireless connectivity; liquid level measured inside the bottle via a laser optical method based on the Time of Flight (ToF) principle; distance between the cap and the top of the liquid correlated to volume in milliliters based on the bottle’s geometry. Reference measurements of fluid intake from the smart bottle determined by gravimetry (change in bottle mass) using a compact digital bench scale (Ohaus CS2000, with a 1 g accuracy) followed by conversion to volume using the density of the fluid consumed (6% carbohydrate-electrolyte solution). Fluid volume measurements conducted in triplicate at each time point; the first value of the triplicate measurements at each time point was used in the calculation for fluid intake. Body mass measured to the nearest 0.01 kg (Mettler Toledo, Model PBD655-BC300). Post-exercise fluid balance calculated as the difference between pre- and post-practice body mass; whole body sweating rate calculated as the difference between pre- and post-practice body mass adjusted for fluid consumed. Statistical analysis: scatterplots; Pearson correlation coefficients; paired t tests; Bland–Altman plots with 95% limits of agreement (LOA); correlation calculation between the outcomes of the y-axis (difference between smart bottle and reference method) and x-axis (average of smart bottle and reference method) of the Bland–Altman plot; orthogonal (Deming) regression comparing the slope and intercept of the regression line and line of identity; Shapiro–Wilk tests; significance level alpha = 0.05.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: n = 30 male American football athletes (n = 10 per practice); age 18 ± 1 years; body mass 92.4 ± 20.4 kg; practice duration 110 ± 30 min (75–130 min); 29.3 ± 3.0 °C; 75 ± 11% relative humidity; reference fluid intake 1236 ± 389 ml vs. smart bottle 1220 ± 371 ml; p = 0.39 paired t test; mean difference − 0.6 ± 7.5%; 95% CI − 3.4% to 2.2%; Bland–Altman mean bias 16 ml; 95% LOA − 212 to 180 ml; approximately ± 15% of overall fluid intake; smart cap mean CV 18% across all 110 measurement time points; absolute variation among triplicate measurements 38 ± 40 ml (range: 0–234 ml); Ohaus scale mean CV 0.1%, varied by no more than ± 2 g among triplicate measurements; r = − 0.18, p = 0.33; r = 0.96, p < 0.0001; Deming regression slope 95% CI 0.95, 1.15 and intercept 95% CI − 178, 85; fluid balance altered by + 0.31% to − 0.17%; whole body sweat loss 1.95 ± 0.82 L; overall fluid balance at end of practice − 0.64 ± 0.73%; sweating rates 0.47–2.51 L/h; total sweat losses 0.77–3.72 L; fluid balance ranging from 2.35% loss to 0.47% gain; Table 1: Practice 1 exercise duration 130 min, air temperature 30.3 ± 3.5 °C, relative humidity 70.6 ± 12.8%, fluid balance − 1.17 ± 0.60%, reference method fluid intake 1419 ± 422 ml, smart bottle fluid intake 1387 ± 390 ml (p = 0.24); Practice 2 exercise duration 125 min, air temperature 30.0 ± 2.1 °C, relative humidity 72.9 ± 6.6%, fluid balance − 0.55 ± 0.70%, reference method fluid intake 1301 ± 269 ml, smart bottle fluid intake 1273 ± 248 ml (p = 0.55); Practice 3 exercise duration 75 min, air temperature 26.9 ± 1.9 °C, relative humidity 86.8 ± 4.8%, fluid balance − 0.09 ± 0.45%, reference method fluid intake 989 ± 357 ml, smart bottle fluid intake 1001 ± 376 ml (p = 0.55).

data.paper_title: Enhancing Reinforcement Learning in Vision-Based Environments with Optical Flow
data.authors: Amartya Mukherjee, Jun Liu
data.core_methodology: Optical flow (OF) computed by solving a PDE-constrained optimization problem and numerically using the Lucas–Kanade method with least squares; Deep Q Learning training a Deep Q Network (DQN) parameterized by weights w; concatenating OF with raw image frames as input; preprocessing an RGB frame by grayscale and resizing it to 84×84 to obtain I(t); computing v(t) using the Lucas–Kanade method; scaling the OF by v(t) ← np.uint8(np.clip(8v(t) + 127.5,0,255)); concatenating I(t) with v(t) to obtain state s_t ∈ R^{3×84×84}; comparing against concatenating the current frame I(t) with the previous frame I(t−1), with I(−1)=I(0); training DQN on 18 different Atari environments for a million time steps each using the DQN implementation by [18] and 4 P100-12gb GPUs on the Cedar cluster in Compute Canada.

data.core_methodology: Physics-informed machine learning (PIML) impact detector using instrumented mouthguard (MiG2.0) data and a Finite Element (FE) head-neck model; FE model developed by modifying the existing open-source, experimentally validated FE model of the standard linear impactor helmet test apparatus created by Biomechanics Consulting and Research, LLC (Biocore) and removing helmet parts, using LS-Dyna explicit FE software with a Hybrid III 50th percentile male anthropomorphic head-neck model and an impactor on a standard NFL linear pneumatic ram testbed; synthetic impacts generated from 1065 initial impact configurations with head orientation angles α and β, head vertical position z, and initial impact velocity v0; deep 1D convolutional neural network architecture based on Domel et al. training/validation/testing split 70%-15%-15%; maximum 5 augmented samples, offset 1-5ms; largest training set approximately 5100 true impact signals and approximately 55,000 false impact signals; true to false impact class ratio 1:10; first network trained on 1024 true impacts and 10990 false impacts with NPV 0.69 and PPV 0.97; including synthetic data maximum NPV 0.72 and PPV 1.0; with augmentation and 25% synthetic data maximum NPV 0.76 and PPV 0.97; balanced false impacts with augmentation factor 2 peak at 100% additional synthetic data with NPV 0.87 and PPV 0.86; pre-training used all synthetic data augmented by a factor of 5, pre-trained network trained 30 epochs on synthetic true impacts and equal verified false impacts then another 30 epochs on balanced video verified true and false impacts, with NPV 0.89 and PPV 0.86; data.core_methodology: Logistic recalibration fitted by maximum likelihood: Eq. (1) logit(P(y_i=1)) = a + b · logit(p_i), with logit(x)=log{x/(1−x)}; Eq. (2) ℓ(a,b)=Σ_{i=1}^{N} [y_i log π_i + (1−y_i) log(1−π_i)], π_i=σ(a+b·logit(p_i)), σ(x)={1+exp(−x)}^−1; analysis restricted to prices between 5 and 95 cents, excludes markets with fewer than 10 trades, requires at least 200 trades per analysis cell, and applies mild L2 regularization (C = 10). Five-term additive descriptive decomposition Eq. (3): θ(d,τ,s)=µ(τ)+α_d+κ(s)+β_d(τ)+γ_d(s)+ε, with constraints Σ_d α_d=0, Σ_d β_d(τ)=0 ∀τ, Σ_τ β_d(τ)=0 ∀d, Σ_s κ(s)=0, Σ_d γ_d(s)=0 ∀s, Σ_s γ_d(s)=0 ∀d; estimated using sequential projection analogous to Type I sums of squares, verified with Type II and Type III sums of squares; inverse-variance weighted decomposition Eq. (10): ϕ̂_WLS=argmin_ϕ Σ_{d,τ,s} w_{dτs}[θ(d,τ,s)−θ̂(d,τ,s;ϕ)]², w_{dτs}=1/SE²_{dτs}. Bayesian hierarchical measurement-error model: Eq. (12) θ_obs(d,τ,s) ∼ N(µ(τ)+α_d+β_d(τ)+δ_d·s̃, σ²+se²_{dτs}), where s̃=log s − log s; priors Eq. (13)–(17): µ(τ)∼N(1.0, 0.52); α_d∼N(0,σ²_α), Σ_d α_d=0; β_d(τ)∼N(0,σ²_β), Σ_d β_d(τ)=0 ∀τ; δ_d∼N(0,σ²_δ); σ_α,σ_β,σ_δ,σ ind.∼Half-Cauchy(0,1); non-centered parameterization. data.paper_title: Multivariate Forecasting Evaluation: On Sensitive and Strictly Proper Scoring Rules
data.authors: Florian Ziel, Kevin Berk
data.core_methodology: Scoring rules for multivariate probabilistic forecasts: continuous ranked probability score (CRPS), energy score (ESβ), variogram score (VSW,p), Dawid-Sebastiani score (DSS), marginal score MS(a)=a′MS, copula score CS, marginal-copula score MCS(a)=MS(a)·CS, copula energy score (CES), copula variogram score (CVSp), copula Dawid-Sebastiani score (CDSS), relative change in scores RelCh(SC)=(SC−SC*)/SC*, and Diebold-Mariano (DM) test for score differences ΔA,B_i=SCA_i−SCB_i with null H0: µA,B=0. Estimation uses empirical distribution function (ecdf), sample means, unbiased sample covariance matrix, empirical copula with mid-point rule, and ranking-based adjusted estimated copula observations u*Yi,h=(2Ri,h−1)/(2N). Forecasting study design uses ensemble forecasting with M iid paths and rolling window forecasting study. Simulation models include bivariate normal Y∼N2(µ, Σ(ρ)) with µ=(0,0)′ and Σ(ρ)=[[1,ρ],[ρ,1]]; sensitivity study II biases with symmetric mean bias, asymmetric mean bias, smaller variance, larger variance, smaller correlation, larger correlation; random peak model Xi=Yi+QZi with Yi∼NH(0,I), Zi∼U({e1,...,eH}); real data AirPassengers models AR(12), AR(13), AR(p) with p∈{1,...,T/2} minimizing AIC, and comonotone/countermonotone residual variants. All AR models are estimated by solving the Yule-Walker equations; ensemble simulations are generated using residual based bootstrap.

data.paper_title: Investigating the efficiency of the Asian handicap football betting market with ratings and Bayesian networks
data.authors: Anthony C. Constantinou
data.core_methodology: Model combines a modified pi-rating system with a hybrid Bayesian Network (BN). The modified pi-ratings use home (H) and away (A) ratings; at time t: R_XH^t = R_XH^(t−1) + e_H λ; R_XA^t = R_XA^(t−1) + γ(R_XH^t − R_XH^(t−1)); R_YA^t = R_YA^(t−1) + e_A λ; R_YH^t = R_YH^(t−1) + γ(R_YA^t − R_YA^(t−1)); e_H = Δo_H − Δp_H; e_A = Δo_A − Δp_A; Δo_H = G_oH − G_oA; Δo_A = G_oA − G_oH; Δp_H = G_pH − G_pA; Δp_A = G_pA − G_pH. The revised pi-ratings exclude Ψ(e) = 3 × log10(1 + e) and include k: R_XH^t = R_XH^(t−1) + e_H λ k and R_YA^t = R_YA^(t−1) + e_A λ k, where k=3 for match instances in which both teams had previously played less than 38 matches; otherwise k=1. The BN is a Hybrid BN designed in AgenaRisk with graphical structure determined by Possession → Shots → Shots on Target → Goals scored and rating difference; nodes include Rating Difference (RD), Rating Difference Level (RDL), P, p(SM), S, p(ST), ST, p(G), G, 1X2, GD, and AH. Distributions: RD is a mixture of Gaussian probability density functions ~N(μ, σ2); P, p(SM), p(ST), p(G) are mixtures of probability density functions ~Beta(a, β); S, ST, G are Binomial probability mass functions ~B(n, p); this creates a Beta-Binomial Hybrid BN process. Validation uses leave-one-out cross validation (LOOCV). Predictive accuracy is measured with the Brier Score for the binary AH outcome and the RPS metric for the multinomial 1X2 distribution. Betting simulation uses fixed singe-unit bets on 1X2 and AH outcomes with payoff higher than the model’s estimated unbiased payoff by at least θ, across all payoff decision thresholds θ, for average and maximum (best available) market odds, optimising return-on-investment (ROI) and profit, with simple stake adjustments.

data.paper_title: Does home advantage without crowd exist in American football?
data.authors: D´avid Zolt´an Szab´o∗, Diego Andr´es P´erez Ruiz†
data.core_methodology: Sample proportion p-hat = (# Wins by home team)/(# Wins by home team + # Wins by away team); binomial distribution Bin(n, π) for number of home team wins; binomial proportion confidence intervals at 95% and 99% confidence levels using normal approximations, p-hat ± Z* sqrt(p-hat(1-p-hat)/n), with Z* = 1.96 for 95% confidence level and 2.58 for 99% confidence level; classical two sample Z-test with statistic z = (p-hat1 − p-hat2)/sqrt(p-hat1(1−p-hat1)/n1 + p-hat2(1−p-hat2)/n2); normal distribution N(μ, σ²) assumed for D = H − A, where H and A are the score of the home and away team at the end of the match; Poisson and negative binomial distributions were precluded from consideration for D; confidence intervals for μ and σ using the “fitdist” and “confint” R functions in packages “fitdistrplus” and “stats”; classical two sample t-test with unequal sample sizes (Welch’s t-test) with statistic T = (Y-bar1 − Y-bar2)/sqrt(s1²/n1 + s2²/n2) and degrees of freedom ν = ((s1²/n1 + s2²/n2)²)/(((s1²/n1)²)/(n1−1) + ((s2²/n2)²)/(n2−1)); Shapiro–Wilk test; autocorrelation function.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Z* = 1.96 for 95% confidence level and 2.58 for 99% confidence level; time period 1970-2020 covers 51 NFL seasons; considered games per season are between 176 and 266, with exception of Season 1982 (n = 136); Season 2020: 144 games played without audience, 122 games played with limited audience, combined sample size 266; none of the teams allowed spectators at more than 25% capacity with the exception of the Super Bowl; average attendance decline from 66151 to 5721 between 2019 and 2020 NFL season; merged 1970-2019 sample: n = 11765, Won = 6822, Lost = 4943, p-hat = 57.99%, 95% C.I. for π [57.09%,58.88%], 99% C.I. for π [56.81%,59.16%]; 2020 No: n = 144, Won = 67, Lost = 77, p-hat = 46.53%, 95% C.I. for π [41.57%,54.67%], 99% C.I. for π [35.80%,57.26%]; 2020 Limited: n = 122, Won = 67, Lost = 55, p-hat = 54.92%, 95% C.I. for π [46.09%,63.75%], 99% C.I. for π [43.30%,66.54%]; 2020 Combined: n = 266, Won = 134, Lost = 132, p-hat = 50.38%, 95% C.I. for π [44.37%,56.38%], 99% C.I. for π [42.47%,58.29%]; p-hat apart from 2020 Season lowest during 1972 NFL season equalling 51.11%; 2020 combined p-hat 50.38% being lowest among all considered seasons; no-audience p-hat 46.53% being the only p-hat value in Table 4.1 below 50%; limited-audience p-hat 54.92%; z = 2.46 with Scenario 1 of Season 2020, z = 0.68 with Scenario 2 of Season 2020, z = 2.74 with Scenario 3 of Season 2020; z = 1.83 for Season 1972, z = −1.94 for Season 1985, z = 1.81 for Season 2019; 95% confidence interval for μ of merged 1970-2019 sample is [2.51,3.04]; average difference D for limited audience = 1.336; average D for no spectators = -0.714; 95% confidence interval for μ in Season 1985 [2.72,6.55]; 95% confidence interval for μ in Season 2006 [−0.67,2.77]; T = 3.00 with Scenario 1 of Season 2020, T = 1.11 with Scenario 2 of Season 2020 and T = 2.92 with Scenario 2 of Season 2020; for α = 95%: 1.96 < t_{1−α/2,ν} < 1.98; for α = 99%: 2.59 < t_{1−α/2,ν} < 2.61; T = −1.88 for Season 1985, T = 1.94 for Season 2006, T = 2.90 for Season 2019; Shapiro–Wilk test gives greater than 0.05 p-value for 42 fits out of the 51 individual seasons’ fit.

data.paper_title: Throwing a Tight Spiral American Football by a Humanoid Robot
data.authors: Zaid Mahboob1, Bowen Weng1
data.core_methodology: Newton-Euler equations (1) for rigid-body football dynamics; tight spiral Definition 1 with ηspin and αnose; floating-base rigid-body humanoid model (4); coupled architecture with legged controller πleg and manipulation controller πmnp; extended Kalman filter (EKF) pelvis-state estimation; offline trajectory optimization with direct multiple shooting, Crocoddyl, and Pinocchio; Crocoddyl’s box-constrained, feasibility-driven differential dynamic programming solver; proportional–derivative controller with feedforward torque compensation; model predictive control (MPC)-based follow-through; sampling based solver; lookup-table MPC; contact-aware football dynamics fb using a differentiable geometric model representing the football as a rigid superellipsoid, softmax weighting, and a penalty-based spring model; GR00T Whole-Body controller for legged joints.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Tight spiral conditions: ∥v∥>0, ∥ω∥>0, ˆn×v=0, ˆn⊤v>0, ˆn×ω=0; ηspin(ˆn, ω)=|ˆn⊤ω|/∥ω∥; αnose(ˆn, v)=arccos(|ˆn⊤v|/∥v∥); g=[0, 0, −9.81]⊤ m/s2; wrun [103, 0.01, 0.05, 103]; T 0.60 s; wterm [104, 2×104, 2×104]; ta 0.55 s; v∗ [3, 0, 0] m/s; ω∗ [−6, 0, 0] rad/s; walign 106; wmpc [103, 0.5, 0.02, 5.0]; H 15; ∆t 0.004 s; vsafe 0.05 m/s; kn 1800; λmax 12 N; µ 0.6; ε 10−6; Jalign(t)=∥ˆn(t) × ˆv(t)∥2; Jvel(T)=∥v(T) − v∗∥2 + ∥ω(T) − ω∗∥2; Jori(T)=∥log(R⊤targetR(T))∥2; Jpose(T)=∥q(T) − qtarget∥2; Jw,k = ∥ω⊥,k∥2/(ω2ax + 1); Jv,k = 1 − (ˆn⊤k ˆvk)2; Jc,k = P i max(0, vi,k − vsafe)2; δ = max(0, −ϕsoft); λ = clip(knδ, 0, λmax); Fi = −λˆns − µλvt/(∥vt∥ + ε); τ i = ri × Fi; Fext = P i Fi; τ ext = P i τ i; 29-DoF Unitree G1 with 7-DoF Dex3-1 gripper; 0.252 kg football at 12 psi; long-axis length 21.6 cm; maximum diameter 12.7 cm; superellipsoid exponent n = 1.66; OptiTrack with six PrimeX 22 cameras at 360 Hz and ≤0.15 mm; trajectory optimization: 50 steps over 0.6 s horizon, converged in 40 iterations and 0.11 s, reduced 10-DoF model, 35◦ launch elevation; throw phase mean ηspin 67.1% ± 12.1% and αnose 18.9◦ ± 5.6◦ across 17 trials; final 50 ms waist pitch joint saturated 90.9%, shoulder pitch and elbow each 54.5%; MPC solve approximately 500 ms; 250 Hz control frequency; 52-dimensional state key; across 61 trials follow-through lasted 78.5 ms on average, sometimes 30-40 ms; peak linear velocity 5.35 m/s; angular velocity 14.5 rad/s; with follow-through up to 93.6% spin efficiency and αnose of 16.4◦; abstract reports 0.286 radians linear-velocity-to-nose-alignment error; without active follow-through average spin efficiency decreased from 67.1% to 60.9% and average nose-angle error increased from 18.9◦ to 34.7◦; worst-case spin efficiency 18.5% and nose-angle error 48.5◦; ideal tight spiral corresponds to 100% spin efficiency and 0 radians nose-angle error.

data.paper_title: Learning Multi-target Tracking with Quadratic Object Interactions
data.authors: Shaofei Wang, Charless Fowlkes
data.core_methodology: Min-cost flow network formulation for multi-target tracking with candidate detection sites x=(l,σ,t), a first-order Markov Model, MAP inference (Eq. 1), appearance likelihood ratio l(φa(x))=pfg(φa(x))/pbg(φa(x)), integer linear program over flow variables f (Eq. 2) with costs ci=−log l(φa(x)), cij=−log p(xj|xi), cs_i=−log ps(xi), ct_i=−log pt(xi) (Eq. 3); augmented with pairwise cost qij and qji for jointly activating flows fi and fj, EC={ij:ti=tj}, yielding an Integer Quadratic Program (IQP, Eq. 4). Inference uses MOSEK’s built-in network simplex solver for min-cost flow; for IQP, LP relaxation and rounding with auxiliary variables uij enforcing uij≤fi, uij≤fj, fi+fj≤uij+1 (Eq. 5), Euclidean rounding minimizing ∥f−bf∥2 and a linear under-estimator (Eq. 6), and Greedy Sequential Search / DP with pairwise Cost Update (Algorithm 1: repeatedly find shortest start-to-end path p; if track cost<0 update cj=cj+qij+qji for all ij,ji∈EC and ci=+∞; T←T∪p until track cost≥0). Linear parameterization C(f)=−wT Ψ(X,f) with w=[wS,wt,ws,wa,wE] and Ψ(X,f)=[Σ_i φS(xs_i)fs_i; Σ_{ij∈E} ψt(xi,xj)fij; Σ_{ij∈EC} ψs(xi,xj)fifj; Σ_i φa(xi)fi; Σ_i φE(xt_i)ft_i] (Eq. 7). Structured SVM with margin rescaling (Eq. 8), cutting-plane optimization, most-violated constraint, loss-augmented inference bf*=argmin_bf ⟨w,Ψ(X,bf)⟩−L(f,bf) (Eq. 9), weighted hamming loss L(bf,f)=Σ_{fi∈f} lossi|fi−bfi| (Eq. 10), and decomposable transition loss for NN, PN, NP, PP+, PP− links. Features include detector score plus a constant 1; transition overlap ratio defined as intersection over union, connect candidates only if overlap ratio exceeds 0.3, feature 1 if ratio is lower than 0.5, up to 7 frames occlusion, binned by transition length yielding a 16 dimensional feature; birth/death constant 1; pairwise spatial-context D relations including on top of, above, below, next-to, near, far and overlap, plus strictly overlap relation with feature 1 if ratio is greater than 0.9; ws is a DK2 vector. Data-dependent transition model uses frame-wise optical flow to predict candidate locations; trajectory smoothing fits a cubic B-spline.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Datasets and settings: KITTI tracking benchmark; 21 training sequences; 8008 frames; 8 classes; evaluated cars, pedestrians and cyclists; 636 labeled car trajectories, 201 labeled pedestrian trajectories, 37 labeled cyclists trajectories; evaluation script excludes objects too far away and truncated by more than 15 percent; training subsequences are 10-frame-long with 5-frame overlap; learned models use detections with scores greater than -0.5 and transition links with overlap ratios greater than 0.3; baselines use detections with a positive score and remove transition links with overlap ratios lower than 0.5; C = 2−9, 2−8, ..., 23; best C = 2−8 for SSP+Flow+Struct and C = 2−7 for LP/DP+Flow+Struct. Metrics: MOTA, MOTP, Rec, Prec, MT, ML, IDSW, FRAG. All Categories DP+Flow+Struct: MOTA 60.6, MOTP 76.7, Rec 65.1, Prec 93.8, MT 28.4, ML 19.7, IDSW 62, FRAG 514; LP+Flow+Struct: MOTA 60.2, MOTP 76.7, Rec 64.8, Prec 93.5, MT 29.2, ML 19.7, IDSW 46, FRAG 510. Figure 5 costs: Relaxed LP cost = −129967.91; DP cost = −129336.88; LP+rounding cost = −129962.09. Greedy algorithm achieves equivalent performance to LP relaxation while being 2-7x faster than a commercial solver; DP gives a lower bound within 1% of relaxed global optimum. 2-pass DP on a 1059 frame-long video with 3 categories: 2-pass DP uses about 6 minutes to finish, 1-pass DP finishes within 1 minute, LP+rounding finishes within 4 minutes; 2-pass DP leave-one-sequence-out cross-validation MOTA 60.4%. Transition loss definitions: NN loss = number of true virtual detections + number of false virtual detections; PN and NP loss = number of true virtual detections + number of false virtual detections + 1; PP+ loss = number of true virtual detections; PP− loss = number of true virtual detections + number of false virtual detections + 2; loss = 1 becomes the hamming loss.

data.paper_title: A network-based ranking system for US college football
data.authors: Juyong Park and M. E. J. Newman
data.core_methodology: One-parameter ranking method based on a directed network representation of college football schedules: vertices represent colleges, directed edges point from winners to losers; adjacency matrix A is an n×n real asymmetric matrix where n is the number of teams and Aij is the number of times team j has beaten team i. Direct wins for team i = ∑j Aji (1); indirect wins at distance 2 for team i = ∑jk AkjAji (2); indirect wins discounted by constant factor α per level of indirection. Total win score wi = ∑j Aji + α∑kj AkjAji + α^2∑hkj AhkAkjAji + ··· = ∑j (1 + α∑k Akj + α^2∑hk AhkAkj + ···) Aji = ∑j (1 + αwj)Aji = kout_i + α∑j A^T_ij wj (3). Loss score li = ∑j Aij + α∑jk AijAjk + α^2∑jkh AijAjkAkh + ··· = ∑j Aij(1 + α∑k Ajk + α^2∑kh AjkAkh + ···) = ∑j Aij(1 + αlj) = kin_i + α∑j Aijlj (4). Total score si = wi − li; teams ranked by total score. Vector forms: w = kout + αA^T·w, l = kin + αA·l (5); w = (I − αA^T)^−1·kout, l = (I − αA)^−1·kin (6). Related to Katz centrality; method is a generalization of Katz centrality applied to the network representation of the schedule of games. α convergence requires α < λmax^−1, where λmax is the largest eigenvalue of A. Algorithm for choosing α: for random directed network with joint in/out-degree distribution P(kin=i,kout=j), largest eigenvalue = ∑ij ijP(kin=i,kout=j)/∑ij iP(kin=i,kout=j) = ⟨kinkout⟩/⟨kin⟩ (7); P(kin=i,kout=j) = 2^−(i+j) (i+j choose i) p_{i+j} (8); λmax = (⟨k^2⟩−⟨k⟩)/(2⟨k⟩) (9); α = 2⟨k⟩/(⟨k^2⟩−⟨k⟩) (10). Monte Carlo randomizations of edge directions and Monte Carlo simulations used to test λmax calculation. Non-football example: dominance hierarchy among 26 male American bison represented as directed network; ranking with α=0.124 from Eq. (10); correlation with breeding success and Lorenz curve/Gini coefficient discussed.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: n = 117 for Division I-A in the 2004 season; Aij usually 0 or 1, but occasionally 2; α = 0 special case gives total score equal to win-loss differential; convergence α < λmax^−1; historical upper bound values in range 0.2 to 0.3; best retrodictive accuracy around values of α around 0.8 of the maximum allowed value; α = 0.8 λmax^−1; Table I: 1998 λmax=3.39401, λmax^−1=0.294637; 1999 4.15120, 0.240894; 2000 3.89529, 0.256720; 2001 3.68025, 0.271721; 2002 4.00933, 0.249418; 2003 3.97901, 0.251319; 2004 3.69253, 0.270817. Table II: 1998 Monte Carlo 4.957 ± 0.068 vs (⟨k2⟩−⟨k⟩)/2⟨k⟩ 4.935; 1999 4.901 ± 0.066 vs 4.882; 2000 4.927 ± 0.066 vs 4.896; 2001 4.896 ± 0.065 vs 4.875; 2002 5.350 ± 0.069 vs 5.334; 2003 5.277 ± 0.064 vs 5.260; 2004 4.859 ± 0.065 vs 4.838. All Table II λmax values are larger by about 20% than actual λmax in Table I; random-graph value imposes a limit about 0.8 of the limit from the true final schedule network. For 2004, α from Eq. (10) is 0.207, or about 0.763 of the maximum. Retrodictive accuracy: 2004 our method 0.81 (35/43), BCS 0.84 (29/37); 2003 our method 0.62 (23/37), BCS 0.69 (25/36); 2002 our method 0.89 (16/18), BCS 0.79 (15/19); 2001 our method 0.47 (7/15), BCS 0.47 (8/17); 2000 our method 0.65 (15/23), BCS 0.75 (12/16); 1999 our method 0.67 (8/12), BCS 0.69 (11/16); 1998 our method 0.83 (15/18), BCS 0.83 (10/12). For top 25 BCS teams of 2004, correlation coefficient between our rankings and official BCS rankings = 0.90; our method classified Pittsburgh and Florida outside top 25; none of other computer polls does any better at predicting final top 25—each gets at least two wrong. In Table IV, α typically between 0.7 and 0.85 of the maximum allowable value. Bison example: 26 male American bison; α = 0.124 from Eq. (10); correlation coefficient of rankings with breeding success = 0.611.

data.paper_title: IMPARTIAL ACHIEVEMENT AND AVOIDANCE GAMES FOR GENERATING FINITE GROUPS
data.authors: DANA C. ERNST, NÁNDOR SIEBEN
data.core_methodology: Impartial combinatorial games GEN(G) (achievement game) and DNG(G) (avoidance game) on a finite group G; positions are jointly selected elements, with terminal/winning conditions as defined; game digraphs and representative game digraphs; structure classes from intersection subgroups; structure digraph and structure diagram; simplified structure digraph and simplified structure diagram via type equivalence; type(XI) := (pty(I), nim(P), nim(Q)), otype(XI), Otype(XI); nim-number nim(P) := mex(nOpt(P)); Sprague–Grundy theory and nim-sum; algorithms implemented via GAP and C++ to compute simplified structure digraphs of DNG(G) and GEN(G). The main computational and theoretical tool is the structure diagram of a game, which is a type of identification digraph of the game digraph that is compatible with the nim-numbers of the positions.

data.paper_title: Unsupervised Deep Representation Learning for Real-Time Tracking
data.authors: Ning Wang, Wengang Zhou, Yibing Song, Chao Ma, Wei Liu, Houqiang Li
data.core_methodology: Unsupervised visual tracking trained from scratch on unlabeled videos by bidirectional motion analysis. The tracker performs forward tracking and backward verification, measures forward/backward trajectory consistency as a loss, and uses the loss for self-supervised/unsupervised training. The framework is a Siamese correlation filter network built on Discriminative Correlation Filters (DCFs), which regress circularly shifted input features to a Gaussian-shaped soft target response map by solving a ridge regression problem; the template filter is convolved with CNN features of the search patch to generate a response map. Network parameters are updated with stochastic gradient descent (SGD). Enhancements: multi-frame validation scheme to enlarge trajectory inconsistency when the tracker loses the target; cost-sensitive loss with binary sample-drop weight A_drop and motion weight A_motion to reduce easy/outlier/noisy samples; image entropy measurement over 5 × 5 overlapped small patches selects the highest-entropy patch for unsupervised annotation and initializes the KCF tracker; online DCF update follows a moving average. The network structure follows DCFNet to use a shallow Siamese network consisting of two convolutional layers and a local response normalization (LRN) layer. Trackers named LUDT (Learning Unsupervised Deep Tracking) and LUDT+.

data.authors: Pengfei Zhu, Jiayu Zheng, Dawei Du, Longyin Wen, Yiming Sun, Qinghua Hu
data.core_methodology: MDOT dataset; automatic fusion score (AFS); ideal fusion score (IFS); agent sharing network (ASNet) with re-detection, self-supervised template sharing and view-aware fusion modules; Dynamic siamese network (DSiam) as base tracker; target appearance variation transformation M^v_{t−1} = arg min ||M ⊗ F^v_1 − F^v_{t−1}||^2 + λ_m ||M||^2; background suppression transformation W_{t−1} = arg min ||W ⊗ F^v_{G^v_{t−1}} − F^v_{\tilde{G}^v_{t−1}}||^2 + λ_w ||W||^2; response map S^{kv}_t = corr(M^v_{t−1} ⊗ f(O^v_1), W^k_{t−1} ⊗ f(Z^k_t)); fusion weights min_u ||D^k_t u^k_t − M^k_{t−1} ⊗ f(O^k_1)||^2 + λ_u ||u^k_t||^2; fused response map S^k_t = Σ_{v=1}^{n} u^{kv}_t S^{kv}_t; view-aware fusion index b_t = arg max(g(s^1_t), g(s^2_t), ···, g(s^v_t)); target re-detection threshold ω^q_t = μ^q_t − λ · σ^q_t and local-to-global strategy; OPE metrics (Success/Precision).
data.key_metrics_and_variables: MDOT: 92 groups of video clips with 113,918 high resolution frames taken by two drones; 63 groups of video clips with 145,875 high resolution frames taken by three drones; total 155 groups with 259,793 high resolution frames; Two-MDOT: 92 groups/113,918 frames; Three-MDOT: 63 groups/145,875 frames; train set 37 groups in Two-MDOT and 28 groups in Three-MDOT; test set 55 groups in Two-MDOT and 35 groups in Three-MDOT; images size 1280×720; low resolution tiny targets pixels less than 400 and frame number more than 50; 10 attributes: DAY, NIGHT, CM, POC, FOC, OV, SO, VC, IV, LR; AFS = (1/n) Σ_{i=1}^{n} Σ_{v=1}^{V} w_v s(h_i^v, y_i^v), w_v is zero or one and automatically learned and online updated for each frame; IFS = (1/n) Σ_{i=1}^{n} max(s(h_i^1, y_i^1), ···, s(h_i^V, y_i^V)); ASNet Two-MDOT success 48.2, precision 74.3, speed 18.5; ASNet Three-MDOT success 53.3, precision 78.2, speed 18.5; GFSDCF precision 59.5 on Two-MDOT and 65.6 on Three-MDOT; precision improved by 14.8 on Two-MDOT and 12.6 on Three-MDOT; IFS precision 79.5 on Two-MDOT and 83.2 on Three-MDOT; ablation λ=2 in Two-MDOT and 1.25 in Three-MDOT; re-detection precision 2.8/2.1 and success 1.5/1.2; template sharing precision 0.9/1.3 and success 0.6/0.6; final ASNet precision 14.9/14.1 and success 10.6/10.4.

data.authors: Paul Voigtlaender1, Michael Krause1, Aljo˘sa O˘sep1, Jonathon Luiten1, Berin Balachandar Gnana Sekar1, Andreas Geiger2, Bastian Leibe1
data.core_methodology: TrackR-CNN, extending Mask R-CNN with two 3D convolution layers (3D convolutions; depthwise separable 3D convolution layers with 3×3×3 filter kernels, ReLU activation, 1024 feature maps) and an association head (128-D association vectors); ResNet-101 backbone; region proposal network (RPN); convolutional LSTM alternatives; Euclidean distance between association vectors d(v,w) := ∥v − w∥; batch hard triplet loss adapted for video sequences; Hungarian algorithm for matching; mask propagation score maskprop(maskd, maske) = IoU(W(maskd), maske) using optical flow computed with PWC-Net; semi-automatic annotation using a fully-convolutional refinement network based on DeepLabv3+ pre-trained on COCO and Mapillary with per-track fine-tuning and manual polygon correction; CLEAR MOT metrics adapted to mask-based MOTS with non-overlapping masks and mask-based IoU; MOTSA, MOTSP, sMOTSA.

data.paper_title: Seeing Behind Objects for 3D Multi-Object Tracking in RGB-D Sequences
data.authors: Norman M¨uller, Yu-Shiang Wong, Niloy J. Mitra, Angela Dai, Matthias Nießner
data.core_methodology: Input RGB-D sequence represented per frame by a sparse grid Si of surface voxels and a dense truncated signed distance field (TSDF) Di, with TSDF obtained by back-projecting observed depth values following volumetric fusion; sparse 3D convolutions structured in encoder-decoder fashion with features bottlenecked to 1/16 of original spatial resolution; multi-head object detection module predicting objectness O(v), 3D center C(v), 3D extents D(v), and semantic class S(v); mean-shift clustering (20 steps, with 8 voxel radius) on predicted center coordinates of voxels with positive objectness, filtering clusters of less than 50 elements, average pooling on bounding box extents and majority voting on semantic classes; Sparse-to-Dense Fusion by cropping sparse features fk from F and dense TSDF grid D, mapping sparse cropped features densely and adding matching TSDF values over feature channels to obtain f′k; object completion using trilinear interpolation down-scaling by factor of 2 and dense 3D convolutions in encoder-decoder fashion to obtain dense object features f o k, then dense 3D convolutional layers predicting complete object geometry mk as a binary mask trained by binary cross entropy; object correspondences ck to canonical space similar to normalized object coordinate space, predicted by dense 3D convolutions and trained with an l1 loss evaluated only where target object geometry exists; differentiable Procrustes analysis with differentiable SVD for object pose; Frobenius norm loss on estimated rotation, ℓ1 loss on predicted scale, ℓ2 loss on translation; minimum rotation error for symmetric objects; multi-object tracking by frame-by-frame tracklets, pairwise 3D IoU of bounding boxes, Hungarian algorithm, rejection of matches with 3D IoU below 0.3, canonical object reconstruction as a 643 grid, running average with 4:1 weighting, and final matching using 3D volumetric IoU of canonical representations binarized at threshold 0.5 with rejection below 0.3; ADAM optimizer.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: MOTA = 1 − Σ_t(mt + fpt + mmet) / Σ_t gt; match positive if ℓ2 distance to ground truth center is less than 25cm; Lo = BCE(O, Ot); Lc = (1/2(C − Ct)^2 for |C − Ct| ≤ 0.5, |C − Ct| − 1/2 otherwise); Ld = (1/2(D − Dt)^2 for |D − Dt| ≤ 0.5, |D − Dt| − 1/2 otherwise); Ls = CE(S, St); c*, R*, t* := argmin_{c∈R+, R∈SO3, t∈R3} ||Po − (cR·Pn + t)||; S = diag(1, 1, det(UV^T)); c* = 1/σn tr(DS), R* = USV^T, t* = µo − c*R*µn; improvement of 6.5% in mean MOTA; Table 1 seq. avg MOTA: MaskFusion 17.2, MID-Fusion 30.1, F2F-MaskRCNN 35.8, Ours (no corr., no compl.) 29.3, Ours (no corr.) 30.6, Ours (no compl.) 35.6, Ours 42.3; completion with no corr. over no completion/no corr. 1.6% mean MOTA; no compl. with canonical correspondences gain 5% mean MOTA; object completion with canonical correspondences further improves by 6.7% mean MOTA; DynSynth pose: Ours (no compl.) 7.4° median rotation error, 15.4cm median translation error; Ours 5.7°, 12.3cm; ScanNet+Scan2CAD pose: Ours (no compl.) 16.6°, 22.0cm; Ours 13.3°, 18.3cm; mAP@0.5 detection: DYNSYNTH 35.8, ScanNet+Scan2CAD 25.6; mAP@0.25 completion: DYNSYNTH 31.1, ScanNet+Scan2CAD 17.1; training: ADAM learning rate 0.001, weight decay 1e-5, batch size 2, up to 10 proposals per input, object detection backbone 100K iterations, full model another 250K iterations, approximately 72 hours; Lc and Ld weighted by 0.1; after warm-up phase of 100k iterations, completion and correspondence loss weighted by 4, rotation/translation/scale loss by 0.2, 0.1, 0.1; DYNSYNTH 3,300 RGB-D sequences (2900/300/100 train/val/test), 97,626 frames; ScanNet+Scan2CAD 944/149/100 scans, 114,000 frames sampled every 20th frame.

data.paper_title: SMOT: Single-Shot Multi Object Tracking
data.authors: Wei Li, Yuanjun Xiong, Shuo Yang, Siqi Deng, and Wei Xia
data.core_methodology: SMOT (single-shot multi-object tracker) is a two-stage online multiple object tracking framework: a tracklet generator followed by an online tracklet linker. It converts a single-shot detector (SSD) into an online tracker using tracking by re-detection. The tracklet generator uses a tracking anchor assignment module with tracking anchors {a_{jk}}_{k=1}^{K}, a tracking anchor assignment function A, and H for location/shape prediction; it re-detects by aggregating detection outputs of tracking anchors (Eq. (1)), with σ_active deciding valid vs failed redetection. Tracking anchor assignment strategies include single-assignment (K=1) and multi-assignment (K>1, top-K highest IoU anchors weighted by IoU). Motion-assisted redetection uses dense optical flow (FarneBack flow and PWCNet flow) and H_motion (Eq. (2)); H can also be the identity function. The online tracklet linking module uses appearance embeddings and solves a bipartite matching problem to link new tracklets to existing tracks. Implementation uses ResNet34 backbone, Feature Pyramid Network, and a face embedding network with 128-dimensional feature vectors proposed in [5]; no appearance model and tracklet linker is used for person tracking.

data.paper_title: Soccer Player Tracking in Low Quality Video
data.authors: Eloi Martins, José Henrique Brito
data.core_methodology: Adaptation of Tracktor++ (a state-of-art Multiple Object Tracking method; second place in the MOT Challenge 2019) to Multiple Soccer Player Tracking (MSPT) in low-quality video; tracking-by-detection paradigm; Tracktor detector uses Faster R-CNN with a pretrained ResNet50 backbone, Region Proposal Network (RPN), Region of Interest (RoI) pooling, classification and regression heads; motion model uses camera motion compensation (CMC) by aligning frames via image registration using Enhanced Correlation Coefficient (ECC) maximization for moving camera, or constant velocity assumption (CVA) for low frame rates; Re-identification Siamese network (Reid) based on appearance vectors generated by a Siamese neural Network/Siamese CNN, storing killed tracks of a predefined number of frames, comparing embedding space distance and re-identifying via a threshold; original Tracktor++ pretrained with MOT-17 dataset; detection dataset created using Faster_RCNN_(RESNET50_FPN) pretrained model in Detectron2; videos degraded with h.264 codec using Constant Rate Factor (CRF) values 40 and 50; retraining detector and Reid networks with suitable data and varying degradation parameters; evaluation with MOTA, MOTP, MT, PT, ML, Recall, Precision.

data.paper_title: SOCCER: An Information-Sparse Discourse State Tracking Collection in the Sports Commentary Domain
data.authors: Ruochen Zhang, Carsten Eickhoff
data.core_methodology: Dataset construction: time-stamped commentary with key events from goal.com; events classified into five types: goal, assist, yellow card, red card and switch; events as keys and event-related players as values, giving ten event-player pairs at each timestamp t (five event types tracked for two teams); comprehensive game state incorporating all event-player pairs for each team and a cumulative score at each timestamp; templated sentences following the format team 1 score - score team 2 removed to avoid trivial leakage. Task formulation: for each match m in M, timestamps T_m = {t}; input stream of commentaries C_m = {c_t}_{t=1}^{T_m}; output set of general match states S_m = {s_t}_{t=1}^{T_m}; s_t contains events e(t)_{i,j}, where i ∈ {goal, assist, yellow card, red card, switch} and j ∈ {home, guest}. Team Level: e(t)_{i,j} = {yes, no}. Player Level: e(t)_{i,j} mapped to related players' names p ∈ P or a none answer. Baselines: GRU classifier with pre-trained BERT embeddings (pretrained weights of HuggingFace's BERT model), 1-layer GRU network followed by two feed-forward layers, mapping 10 event variables e(t)_{i,j} as binary flags to a 10-bit scalar value, with 0th position corresponding to e(t)_{goal, home}; GPT-2 based variant casting player-level state tracking as a sequence generation problem with causal language models such as GPT-2, inspired by simpleTOD and the OpenPI baseline, training sequence concatenation of commentary, event types and player names, event names preprocessed as tokens like goal_home, commentary and event-player pairs encapsulated in special tokens, next token prediction task, greedy decoding compared to beam search and top-k sampling. Input text tokenized using byte-pair encoding. Information density (ID) = Total # of state changes / Total # of turns/steps/timestamps.

data.paper_title: Track to Detect and Segment: An Online Multi-Object Tracker
data.authors: Jialian Wu1, Jiale Cao2, Liangchen Song1, Yu Wang3, Ming Yang3, Junsong Yuan1
data.core_methodology: TraDeS (TRAck to DEtect and Segment), an online joint detection and tracking model built upon the point-based object detector CenterNet. It uses a Cost Volume based Association (CVA) module with an embedding network σ(·) (three convolution layers) to extract re-ID embedding features, construct a 4-dimensional cost volume C by a single matrix multiplication, and infer tracking offsets O/OC; the cost volume is supervised by a logistic regression in the form of the focal loss LCVA. It uses a Motion-guided Feature Warper (MFW) module that takes tracking offsets OC as motion cues, predicts the deformable convolution (DCN) input offset OD through a 3 × 3 convolution γ(·), optionally incorporates the residual feature f t − f t−τ as input of γ(·), propagates previous center attentive features via a single DCN, and aggregates propagated features with the current feature by weighted summation to enhance detection/segmentation. Head networks produce 2D and 3D boxes and instance masks using the same head networks as in CenterNet for 2D and 3D detection and the head network in CondInst for instance segmentation. Data association is a simple two-round long-term data association: DA-Round (i) closest unmatched detection at time t−1 within an area centered at (i,j)+OCi,j with radius r, where r is the geometrical average of width and height of the detected box; DA-Round (ii) cosine similarities of its embedding eti,j with all unmatched or history tracklet embeddings, assigned if similarity is the highest and larger than a threshold, e.g., 0.3. Overall loss L = LCVA + Ldet + Lmask.
