data.paper_title: MeMOT: Multi-Object Tracking with Memory
data.authors: Jiarui Cai1*, Mingze Xu2†, Wei Li2, Yuanjun Xiong2, Wei Xia2, Zhuowen Tu2, Stefano Soatto2
data.core_methodology: MeMOT is an online Transformer-based tracking algorithm that performs object detection and data association under a common framework, linking objects after a long time span by preserving a large spatio-temporal memory of identity embeddings and adaptively referencing/aggregating useful information. It consists of three main Transformer-based modules: 1) Hypothesis Generation ΘH, a Transformer-based encoder-decoder network producing proposal embeddings Q_pro^t ∈ R^{N_pro^t×d} from input image feature maps; 2) Memory Encoding ΘE, which encodes spatial-temporal memory for each tracked object into track embeddings Q_tck^t ∈ R^{N_tck^t×d} using a short-term block f_short, long-term block f_long, and fusion block f_fusion. f_short and f_long are implemented with multi-head cross-attention modules; f_short uses previous Ts states with the most recent state X_{t-1} as query; f_long uses longer history length Tl with Dynamic Memory Aggregation Tokens (DMAT) Q_dmat^{t-1}; outputs Aggregated Short-term Token (AST) Q_AST^t and Aggregated Long-term Token (ALT) Q_ALT^t are fused by f_fusion to output Q_tck^t and updated Q_dmat^t. The Memory Aggregator consists of short-term f_short, long-term f_long, and fusion blocks. 3) Memory Decoding ΘD uses stacked Transformer decoder units, with concatenated proposal and track embeddings [Q_pro^t, Q_tck^t] as queries and encoded image feature z_1^t as key and value; it predicts bounding boxes in the format of offsets w.r.t. learned reference points, objectness scores o_i^t, and uniqueness scores u_i^t; the unified confidence score is s_k^t = o_k^t · u_k^t. It solves object detection and data association simultaneously by thresholding entries with threshold ε and retaining entries with s_i^t ≥ ε, with no further post-processing. Spatio-temporal memory buffer X ∈ R^{N×T×d} is implemented as a first-in-first-out (FIFO) data structure and stores history states of all tracked objects. Training uses tracking loss L_tck = λ_cls(L′_obj + L′_uni) + λ_L1 L′_bbox + λ_iou L′_iou and auxiliary detection loss L_det = λ_cls L_obj + λ_L1 L_bbox + λ_iou L_iou, with focal loss on objectness and uniqueness scores, L1 loss for bounding box regression, generalized IoU loss, bipartite matching, and Hungarian loss. The overall clip loss is L_clip = λ_tck L_clip−tck + λ_det L_clip−det. Hypothesis Generation uses ResNet50 and Deformable DETR pretrained on COCO.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Eq. (1): s_k^t = o_k^t · u_k^t. o_i^t and u_i^t range from 0 to 1. Eq. (2): L_tck = λ_cls(L′_obj + L′_uni) + λ_L1 L′_bbox + λ_iou L′_iou. Eq. (3): L_det = λ_cls L_obj + λ_L1 L_bbox + λ_iou L_iou. Eq. (4): L_clip = λ_tck L_clip−tck + λ_det L_clip−det = λ_tck/(Σ_{t=0}^{T} N_t) Σ_{t=0}^{T} Σ_{i=0}^{|Q_tc,Q_pro|} L^{(i,t)}_tck + λ_det/T Σ_{t=0}^{T} (1/N_t) Σ_{j=0}^{|Q_pro|} L^{(j,t)}_det. Hyperparameters: N_max is set to be significantly large (e.g., 300 or 600); a choice of T_max is 24; implementation memory buffer maximum temporal length is 22 for MOT16/17 and 20 for MOT20; T_s = 3 default; T_l = 24 due to hardware limitation; ε_pro = 0.7 and ε_tck = 0.6; λ_cls, λ_L1 and λ_iou = 2, 5, 2, respectively; λ_det = λ_tck = 1; learning rate initiated to 2 × 10−4 and decreased by 10 at the 100-th epoch; AdamW optimizer for 200 epochs; clip length started from 2 and increased with stride 4 at every 20 epochs; frames sampled with random interval between 1 to 10; batch size 1 clip per GPU; input frames resized such that shorter side is 800 pixels; Transformer layers reduced to 4 (trimmed ablation models use 2). Ablation setting Ts=3, Tl=24: IDF1 73.15, MOTA 68.08, HOTA 59.75, IDsw 93, DetA 57.92, AssA 63.10. MOT16 MeMOT: IDF1 69.7, MOTA 72.6, HOTA 57.4, AssA 55.7, IDsw 845, MT 44.9, ML 16.6, FP 14595, FN 34595. MOT17 MeMOT: IDF1 69.0, MOTA 72.5, HOTA 56.9, AssA 55.2, IDsw 2724, MT 43.8, ML 18.0, FP 37221, FN 115248. MOT20 MeMOT: IDF1 66.1, MOTA 63.7, HOTA 54.1, AssA 55.0, IDsw 1938, MT 57.5, ML 14.3, FP 47882, FN 137983.

data.authors: Noga Alon†, Benjamin Gunby‡, Xiaoyu He§, Eran Shmaya¶, and Eilon Solan‖
data.core_methodology: Finite set of players I with finite action sets Ai, A=∏i∈I Ai, finite realizations A<N, behavior strategies σi:A<N→Δ(Ai), probability distribution Pσ; goal (σ∗,D) with Borel target set D⊆A^N; blame function Borel f:D^c→I; δ-testability if for every i and σi, Pσi,σ∗−i(D^c and {f≠i})≤δ. Main results: Theorem 2.6 and Theorem 2.9. Proof of Theorem 2.6 via auxiliary zero-sum game Γ(D) between an adversary choosing i and σi and a statistician, with Nature choosing s according to Pσi,σ∗−i, statistician observing z∈Z with s∈[Tz] and choosing j; likelihood ratio ℓi(z)=∏n=1^m σi(zn_i|z1,z2,...,zn−1)/σ∗i(zn_i|z1,z2,...,zn−1); blame a player j with maximal likelihood ratio; Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, von Neumann minimax theorem on truncated games Γ(Dn), and diagonal argument. Explicit blame functions: adjacent ones with probabilities μ/n and consecutive-ones target; random-walk target reaching −1 at least once with blame algorithm using limsup An/√(n log log n), divergence of ∑ an/(√n(log n)^{3/4}), and sums of s² increments; finite-horizon modification. Tools named: Law of the Iterated Logarithm, Kolmogorov’s two-series theorem, Markov’s Inequality, Borel-Cantelli Lemma, martingale differences.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Theorem 2.6: 2√(|I|−1)ε-testable if Pσ∗(D)>1−ε; also Pσ∗(D)=1−∑i∈I Pσ∗(D^c and {f=i})=1−1/(|I|−1)∑i∈I Pσ∗(D^c and {f≠i})≥1−|I|/(|I|−1)δ. Theorem 2.9: Pσ∗(D)=1 implies 0-testable. Tightness example: D={00,01,10}; P(D^c)=μ²; any blame function errs with probability at least μ; if f(11)=A and Player B selects 1 with probability 1, Player A is erroneously blamed with probability μ. Adjacent Ones: σ∗A(1|z)=μ/n for odd n and σ∗B(1|z)=μ/n for even n; bad if there is odd n≥1 with bits n and n+1 both 1; ε=∑k=0∞(∏0≤i<k(1−μ²/((2i+1)(2i+2))))·μ²/((2k+1)(2k+2))<μ²; goal O(μ)-testable and μ-testable by f(s)=A if ∑k≥0,s2k+1=1 μ/(2k+2)>μ, otherwise B; expectation ∑k≥0 μ/(2k+1)·μ/(2k+2)<μ². Random walk: D={w∈{−1,1}^N: ∃n, ∑i≤n wi=−1}; Pσ∗(D)=1; w=(a1,b1,a2,b2,...); An=∑i=1^n ai; Bn=∑i=1^n bi; s0=1; s2n=1+An+Bn; s2n−1=1+An+Bn−1; blame steps: 1) if lim supn→∞(An/√(n log log n))>0 choose A, else if lim supn→∞(Bn/√(n log log n))>0 choose B; 2) if ∑n=2∞ an/(√n(log n)^{3/4}) diverges choose A, else if ∑n=2∞ bn/(√n(log n)^{3/4}) diverges choose B; 3) if ∑n=1∞ (s2n+1²−s2n²)/(2n log(2n))=∞ choose B, else if ∑n=2∞ (s2n²−s2n−1²)/((2n−1)log(2n−1))=∞ choose A; 4) otherwise A. Lemma 3.5: if no player is chosen on Steps 1 and 2, and sn is nonnegative for all n, then ∑n=2∞ sn²/(n² log n) converges. Finite horizon: choose A if An/√(n log log n)>ε for any n with log log N<n≤N; else B if Bn/√(n log log n)>ε; C=∑n=1∞1/(n(log n)^{3/2}); if ∑n=2^N an/(√n(log n)^{3/4})>√(3C/ε) choose A; else if ∑n=2^N bn/(√n(log n)^{3/4})>√(3C/ε) choose B; if ∑n=1⌊(N−1)/2⌋(s2n+1²−s2n²)/(2n log(2n))>(log log N)/3 choose B; else if ∑n=2⌊N/2⌋(s2n²−s2n−1²)/((2n−1)log(2n−1))>(log log N)/3 choose A; otherwise A; Proposition 3.8 failure probability at most ε if N sufficiently large in terms of ε. Concluding: constant √(|I|−1) can be improved to ⌈ln2(I)⌉; one-dimensional probability never return for N steps Θ(1/√N) gives O(1/N^{1/4})-testable; two-dimensional probability no return Θ(1/log N) gives O(1/(log N)^{1/2})-testable.

data.paper_title: CAMO-MOT: Combined Appearance-Motion Optimization for 3D Multi-Object Tracking with Camera-LiDAR Fusion
data.authors: Li Wang, Xinyu Zhang, Wenyuan Qin, Xiaoyu Li, Lei Yang, Zhiwei Li, Lei Zhu, Hong Wang, Jun Li, and Huaping Liu
data.core_methodology: Tracking-by-detection camera-LiDAR fusion 3D MOT framework CAMO-MOT based on Combined Appearance-Motion Optimization, with modules Optimal Occlusion State-based Object Appearance Module (O2S-OAM), Confidence Score-based Motion Module (CS-MM), and Multi-category Multi-modal Fusion Association Module (M2-FAM). O2S-OAM uses a modified DLA-34 image feature extractor, an occlusion head with ResNet18 backbone, and a matching head with a 1 × 1 convolutional neural network; it estimates occlusion states Occs, selects optimal appearance features, reconstructs E_(t,t−n) ∈ R^((C×M)×Nmax×Nmax), and uses Softmax to produce association matrices. CS-MM uses Kalman filters with state transformation matrix A, gIoU3D, and confidence-score-based motion cost matrix C_mo. M2-FAM adds category loss Clst to C_mo and C_app, performs first association based on Mot and second association on remaining detections and trajectories using Appt, with Hungarian algorithm thresholds θmo and θApp. Training uses cross-entropy occlusion loss, matching loss, and joint loss L_join = 1/e^λ1 L_detect + 1/e^λ2(L_match + L_occlusion) + λ1 + λ2.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: KITTI test Car: HOTA 79.95%, MOTA 90.38%, MOTP 85.00, MT 84.61, FN 962, IDS 23, ML 7.38, FP 2322; delta vs EagerMOT: HOTA +5.56, MOTA +2.56, MOTP −0.69, MT +8.46, FN +508, IDS −216, ML +4.92, FP −1175. KITTI test Pedestrian: HOTA 44.90%, MOTA 52.19%, MOTP 64.50, MT 35.40, FN 2560, IDS 137, ML 25.43, FP 1112; delta vs EagerMOT: HOTA +5.52, MOTA +2.37, MOTP +0.08, MT +7.91, FN +399, IDS −359, ML +1.38, FP −7847. KITTI validation 3D MOT: Car sAMOTA 95.29, AMOTA 48.04, AMOTP 81.48; Pedestrian sAMOTA 89.83, AMOTA 44.84, AMOTP 72.55. nuScenes test: AMOTA 75.3%, FP 17269, FN 18192, IDS 324; compared with BEVFusion +1.20% AMOTA. nuScenes val best: AMOTA 76.3%, AMOTP 52.7, IDS 239. Parameters: θnms = 0.1 on KITTI, θmo = 0.01, θApp = 1.4, trajectory discarded if not updated in last 15 frames; nuScenes θnms = 0.08, θCSF = [0.03, 0.12, 0.14], θmo = 0.02, θApp = 1.4, θdel = 0, output up to 2 frames of predicted trajectory state, predicted state tracking score = 0.05 times the most recently updated trajectory state. Training: 100 epochs, Adam optimizer, initial learning rate 1.25e−4, batch size 8, at 60 epochs learning rate decreased by e−5; nuScenes 60 epochs, learning rate 1.25e−4, batch size 8. Image object area bilinearly interpolated to 224×224; 13 feature maps; category constants 0, 1, 2 with gap 105; occlusion weights 1, 0.7, 0.3, and 0 for fully visible, partly occluded, largely occluded, fully occluded. Equations: hat Z_t^j = A Z_(t−1)^j; hat S_t^j = A S_(t−1)^j A^T + Q; M_t^(i,j) = 1 − gIoU3D(D_t^i, hat T_t^j) = 2 − V(D_t^i ∩ hat T_t^j)/V(D_t^i ∪ hat T_t^j) − V(D_t^i ∪ hat T_t^j)/Vhull(D_t^i, hat T_t^j); C_mo entries M_t^(i,j)/γ_t^j; Dis_t^(i,j) = D_t^j(cls) − T_(t−1)^j(cls); Cls_t^(i,j) = 105 if Dis_t^(i,j) ≠ 0 else 0; Mot = Cmo + Clst; Appt = Capp + Clst; min Σ Mot + Σ Appt s.t. Mot ≤ θmo and Appt ≤ θApp; L_occlusion = −1/N Σ_i=1^N Σ_c=1^4 y_ic log(p_ic); L_match = (L_matcht + L_matcht−n)/(2(N_t + N_t−n)); L_join = 1/e^λ1 L_detect + 1/e^λ2(L_match + L_occlusion) + λ1 + λ2; AMOTA = 1/L Σ_{r∈{1/L,2/L,...,1}} MOTA_r; sMOTA_r = max(0, MOTA_r/r); sAMOTA = 1/L Σ sMOTA_r.

data.authors: Chensheng Peng, Zhaoyu Zeng, Jinling Gao, Jundong Zhou, Masayoshi Tomizuka, Xinbing Wang, Chenghu Zhou, Nanyang Ye

data.paper_title: ADA-Track++: End-to-End Multi-Camera 3D Multi-Object Tracking with Alternating Detection and Association
data.authors: Shuxiao Ding, Lukas Schneider, Marius Cordts, Juergen Gall
data.core_methodology: ADA-Track++ is an end-to-end framework for 3D MOT from multi-view cameras using an alternating detection and association paradigm. It uses decoupled track queries and detection queries; query-to-query self-attention; query-to-image cross-attention implemented as DETR3D or PETR; query-to-query edge-augmented cross-attention based on an Edge-Augmented Graph Transformer with a fully-connected graph, appearance features in the nodes and geometric features in the edges; an auxiliary token q∅∈Rdk as an additional association target; track update module; Hungarian Algorithm [39] (HM); Focal Loss [64]; categorical cross-entropy; sigmoid activation; softmax normalization; constant velocity assumption and motion update following MUTR3D [35]; DETR3D [7] and PETR [8] detectors; ResNet-101 [65], VoVNet-99 [66] and ViT-Large [67] backbones.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Box b_i = [c_i, s_i, θ_i, v_i] ∈R9 with 3D box center c_i∈R3, 3D box size s_i∈R3, yaw angle θ_i∈R and BEV velocity v_i∈R2. E_pos^(l)=MLP(B_diff^(l)); B_diff^(l)={b_diff,ij^(l)}∈R^(NT×ND×9); b_diff,ij^(l)=|b_T,i^(l)-b_D,j^(l)|. A(l)=softmax((Q_D^(l) W_Q^(l))(Q_T^(l) W_K^(l))^T / √d_k + E^(l) W_E1^(l)). Q_D^(l+1)=Q_D^(l)+Â^(l)(Q_T^(l) W_V^(l)); E^(l+1)=E^(l)+A^(l) W_E2^(l). S=MLP(E^(Ld))∈R^(ND×NT); sigmoid activation; Hungarian Algorithm; τS=0.3; Td=5 frames; τnew=0.4. L = Σ_{t=1}^T (λcls L_{cls,D}^t + λreg L_{reg,D}^t) + Σ_{t=2}^T (λcls L_{cls,T}^t + λreg L_{reg,T}^t + λasso L_{asso}^t); λcls=2.0, λreg=0.25, λasso=10.0. Association Focal Loss with α=0.5 and γ=1.0; L_CE = -Σ_{i=1}^{ND} Σ_{j=1}^{NT+1} Y_ij log( exp S_ij / Σ_{k=1}^{NT+1} exp S_ik ); L_asso = L_FL + λ_CE L_CE; λ_CE=0.1. 6 transformer decoder layers; T=3 frames; initial learning rate 2e−4; AdamW [68] weight decay 1e−2; 24 epochs pre-training and another 24 epochs; DETR3D input images 1600×900; embedding dimension 256; feed-forward dimension 512; ND=300; PETR input images 1600×640; embedding dimension 256; feed-forward dimension 2048; ND=500. ADA-Track++ nuScenes test split: AMOTA 0.500, AMOTP 1.144, Recall 0.595, MOTA 0.456, IDS 658. ADA-Track++ validation: DETR3D R101 AMOTA 0.398, AMOTP 1.336, Recall 0.544, MOTA 0.357, IDS 774; DETR3D V2-99 AMOTA 0.434, AMOTP 1.304, Recall 0.556, MOTA 0.386, IDS 863; DETR3D ViT-L AMOTA 0.522, AMOTP 1.178, Recall 0.630, MOTA 0.465, IDS 664; PETR V2-99 AMOTA 0.504, AMOTP 1.197, Recall 0.608, MOTA 0.445, IDS 613. ADA-Track++ achieves up to 0.7%P and 1.1%P higher AMOTA based on DETR3D and PETR respectively compared to ADA-Track.

data.paper_title: Friends, Key Players and the Adoption and Use of Experience Goods
data.authors: Rhys Murrian, Paul A. Raschky, Klaus Ackermann
data.core_methodology: Linear-probability model based on the Manski (1993) linear-in-means model, adopting the Bramoullé et al. (2020) generic framework for network panels with individual player fixed effects and week fixed effects; standard errors clustered at the player level. Baseline model: y_{i,t} = α_i + β Σ_{t=0}^{n} g_{ij,t} y_{j,t} + W_t + ϵ_{i,t}. Identification uses an instrumental variable (IV) approach that employs the temporal lag of purchasing decisions from second degree friends; first stage: y_{j,t} = α_i + δ′ Σ_{t=0}^{n} g_{jk,t} y_{k,t-1} + W_t + u_{i,t}. Heterogeneity model: y_{i,t} = α_i + β1 Σ_{t=0}^{n} g_{ij,t} y_{j,t} × KP + β2 Σ_{t=0}^{n} g_{ij,t} y_{j,t} × OF + W_t + ϵ_{i,t}. Cross-sectional playtime model: PT_i = μ + γ1 (Purchase × KP)_i + γ2 (Purchase × OF)_i + X_i + u_i, where PT_i is the log of hours. Key player friend defined by Katz centrality measure within the 99th percentile or above four weeks prior to the release of SMB; old friend defined by at least one year of friendship at four weeks prior to the release of SMB. Second-degree friends calculated using GPU parallel computing via RAPIDS cuGraph on a high-performance computing (HPC) cluster at Monash University. Treatment group: players who have at least one or more friends that purchased SMB; control group: players who have friends, but none of them purchased SMB. IV estimates a Local Average Treatment Effect (LATE).
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Panel: 269 weeks over September 2008 to October 2013. Steam network: 108.8 million Steam users; 101.9 million 'public' accounts (93.6%); 42.2 million nodes; 196.4 bidirectional friendship links; 122.2 million friendship links; 22.1 million nodes with at least one friendship link; 20.1 million assumed to have no friends. Super Meat Boy: 1.06 million Steam users; 166,560 SMB players with a purchase date prior to October 2013; 44,773 treatment and 44,773 control, total 89,546; gifting about 3.5% of SMB ownership; 5,227 players removed from the original randomly selected 50,000 in each group. Summary statistics: SMB 89,546 mean 0.022 std. dev. 0.145 min 0 max 1; NV 89,546 mean 0.019 std. dev. 0.136 min 0 max 1; treatment 89,546 mean 0.500 std. dev. 0.500 min 0 max 1; # of Games 89,546 mean 20.625 std. dev. 36.997 min 1 max 1011; # of Groups 89,546 mean 5.172 std. dev. 17.860 min 0 max 952; Start week 89,546 mean 35.809 std. dev. 57.559 min 0 max 113; Friends 89,546 mean 2.150 std. dev. 3.560 min 0 max 134; KP Friends 89,546 mean 0.772 std. dev. 1.491 min 0 max 109; Old Friends 89,546 mean 1.128 std. dev. 2.290 min 0 max 134; SMB purchase 13,790,084 mean 0.013 std. dev. 0.113 min 0 max 1; NV purchase 13,790,084 mean 0.011 std. dev. 0.106 min 0 max 1. Text summary: mean probability of a Steam ID purchasing SMB within panel approximately 2.17%; within a given week approximately 0.01%; mean number of games approximately 21; average approximately 17 friends, maximum 359; approximately 5 key player friends; approximately 7 old friends; key player treatment approximately 12.08%; old friend treatment approximately 4.06%. Regression estimates (Table 2): OLS Friends j adopt SMB_i,t 0.0733 (0.0008); Reduced Form Friends k adopt SMB_i,t−1 0.0077 (0.0013); IV First Stage Friends k adopt SMB_i,t−1 0.0404 (0.0013); IV Second Stage Friends j adopt SMB_i,t 0.0166 (0.0009); Observations 13,700,538; Player FE and Week FE included; Anderson-Rubin stat. 341.17; all estimates statistically significant at the .01 level. data.authors: Hy Nguyen*, Bao Pham*, Hung Du, Srikanth Thudumu, Rajesh Vasa, Kon Mouzakis
data.core_methodology: Collaborative System for Active Object Tracking (CSAOT); multi-agent deep reinforcement learning (MADRL); Mixture of Experts (MoE) framework; Mixture of Policy (MoP); Mixture of Policies (MoP); Top-K MoE; Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO); Dec-POMDP; Decentralized Training - Decentralized Execution (DTDE); role-based approach; role-based collaboration framework; two-layer hierarchical system; ResNet50 pre-trained model for feature extraction; MLP (Multi-Layer Perceptron); LSTM; MoP gating mechanism; PPO clipping mechanism; task-based component rewards; subtask-based reward functions; AirSim; Unreal Engine; Intersection over Union (IoU); Manhattan distance; ε-greedy

collision reward for a state is -50 and episode ends immediately; tracking reward R_track = min(S_mi/(S_frame∗0.25), 2 − S_mi/(S_frame∗0.25)) · λ_track; center(box) = (1/n · ∑_i x_i, 1/n · ∑_i y_i); navigation reward R_nav = −Manhattan(center(m),center(frame))/Manhattan((0,0),center(frame)) · λ_nav; data.paper_title: A Sequential Game Framework for Target Tracking
data.authors: Daniel Leal, Ngoc Hung Nguyen, Alex Skvortsov, Sanjeev Arulampalam, Mahendra Piraveenan*
data.core_methodology: Two-player, imperfect information, non-cooperative, sequential game framework for target tracking; two-dimensional discrete-time tracking scenario with a tracker and an intelligent evader; bearings-only tracking with noisy bearing measurements; independent zero-mean Gaussian measurement noise with standard derivation σ_E (tracker about evader) and σ_T (evader about tracker); Cubature Kalman Filter (CKF) for state estimation, with prediction and update steps using cubature points; tracker and evader each play separate zero-sum games at each time step with an internal (and imperfect) model of the other player (evader∗ and tracker∗), using min-max optimization for the tracker and max-min for the evader; actions include covariance minimisation, linear escape, and zero-sum-game heading selection; process noise w_E,k−1 ∼ N(0, Q_E) with Q_E,◦= diag(q_E,x, q_E,y).
data.key_metrics_and_variables: kmax = 400; tracker initial position randomly initialized within a square grid of 40 × 40 centred upon (x = 400, y = 550); evader initial position randomly initialized within a square grid of 40 × 40 centred upon (x = 1000, y = 1000); average starting distance between evader and tracker is 600 units on the x-axis and 450 units on the y-axis; tracker velocities vT = 1 unit per time step to vT = 3 units per time step; evader velocities vE = 1 unit per time step to vE = 3 units per time step; range of vE/vT was between 0.333 to 3.0; five distinct speed ratios Rv = vE/vT: 1/3, 2/3, 1/1, 3/2, and 3/1; 200 simulation runs per speed ratio; ∆k = 1; ψe = sqrt(trace(Pk|k)) < η; QE = [∆^3/3 QE,◦, ∆^2/2 QE,◦; ∆^2/2 QE,◦, ∆QE,◦]; QE,◦= diag(qE,x, qE,y); motion equations pT,k+1 = pT,k + ∆vT,k and pE,k+1 = pE,k + ∆vE,k; bearing equations ˜zE,k = arctan((yE,k−yT,k)/(xE,k−xT,k)) + nE,k and ˜zT,k = arctan((yT,k−yE,k)/(xT,k−xE,k)) + nT,k; state transition matrix F = [I2×2, ∆I2×2; 02×2, I2×2]; CKF cubature points for i = 1, . . . , 8; win metrics: trace of the covariance matrix of the tracker's position estimate of the evader, Euclidean distance between the tracker's estimated position of the evader and the actual position of the evader, and Euclidean distance between the actual positions of the tracker and the evader; reported win percentages include less than 50%, as low as 10% (covariance minimisation), not lower than 20% (game theoretic), higher than 90%, 70% or above, 55% or above, below 10%, more than 60%, and close to 40%.

data.paper_title: Asynchronous Multi-Object Tracking with an Event Camera
data.authors: Angus Apps, Ziwei Wang, Vladimir Perejogin, Timothy L. Molloy and Robert Mahony

data.key_metrics_and_variables: Eq. (1): p(ek|ζ(tk)) := 1 2π det(Λ(t)) exp(−1 2 ˜ξ⊤ k Λ(t)−2 ˜ξk), ˜ξk = ξk −p(tk) −σk∆(tk); Λ(t) := R(θ(t)) (λ1(t) 0 0 λ2(t)) R⊤(θ(t)). data.paper_title: Locating Tennis Ball Impact on the Racket in Real Time Using an Event Camera
data.core_methodology: Method for locating tennis ball impact on the racket in real time using an event camera. Event representation e_k = (x_k, y_k, p_k, t_k); event packet ε_t = {e_k | t−t_acc/2 < t_k ≤ t+t_acc/2}. Three identification steps: time range of swing using event rate |ε_t| per second with mean and variance for consecutive n_ε event rates, thresholds τ_mean and τ_var, and τ_t; timing at impact using PATS (the amount of polarity asymmetry in time symmetry): split ε_t into ε_prev = {e_k ∈ ε_t | t_k < t} and ε_next = {e_k ∈ ε_t | t ≤ t_k}; ε←_next = reverse(ε_next); F_prev = image(ε_prev), F_next = image(ε←_next); T_prev = timeSurface(ε_prev), T_next = timeSurface(ε←_next); G_prev = focalTime(T_prev), G_next = focalTime(T_next); ρ_t = Σ(|F⁺_prev ∗ G_prev| ∗ |F⁻_next ∗ G_next|); peak detection with the Laplacian filter, optionally n_c candidates in ascending order of peak size selecting the centroid position in the PATS image closest to the center; contours of ball and racket using event images F^b_timp and F^r_timp with activity noise filter, binary images B^b_timp and B^r_timp, morphological transformation performing a closing operation, and ellipse detection; output relative location of ball on racket as a percentage mapped to the axes of the racket’s ellipse in the uv coordinate system with +u upward along the racket and +v toward the tip.

data.paper_title: Antithetic Sampling for Top-k Shapley Identification
data.authors: Patrick Kolpaczki, Tim Nielen, Eyke H¨ullermeier
data.core_methodology: Cooperative game (N, ν); Shapley value; top-k identification problem (TkIP); unbiased equifrequent player-wise independent sampler; Comparable Marginal Contributions Sampling (CMCS) using extended marginal contributions Δ′_i(S):=ν(S∪{i})−ν(S∖{i}) and sampling distribution P(S^(m)=S)=1/((n+1) binom(n,|S|)); Greedy CMCS; CMCS@K; antithetic sampling; central limit theorem with standard normal cumulative distribution function Φ; multi-armed bandit-inspired selection; ApproShapley, KernelSHAP, Stratified SVARM, BUS, SamplingSHAP@K as baselines.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Shapley value: ϕ_i = Σ_{S⊆N∖{i}} 1/(n binom(n−1,|S|)) · [ν(S∪{i})−ν(S)] (Eq. 1); expected MSE: E[MSE] := (1/n) Σ_{i∈N} E[(ϕ_i−ˆϕ_i)^2] (Eq. 2); eligible coalition: Σ_{i∈K} ϕ_i = max_{S⊆N:|S|=k} Σ_{i∈S} ϕ_i (Eq. 3); binary precision ψ_bin(ˆK) := 1 if ˆK∈E_k else 0 (Eq. 4); ratio precision ψ_rat(ˆK) := (1/k) max_{K∈E_k}|K∩ˆK| (Eq. 5); ϕ_{k*} := min_{K∈E_k} min_{i∈K} ϕ_i; inclusion-exclusion error ρ_inc+exc := inf{ε∈R≥0 | ∀i∈ˆK: ϕ_i ≥ ϕ_{k*}−ε, ∀j∈N∖ˆK: ϕ_j ≤ ϕ_{k*}+ε} (Eq. 7); PAC: P(ρ_inc+exc(ˆK) ≤ ε) ≥ 1−δ (Eq. 8); marginal contribution ∆_i(S):=ν(S∪{i})−ν(S); distribution P(S_i^(m)=S)=1/(n·binom(n−1,|S|)) (Eq. 9); estimate ˆϕ_i = (1/M) Σ_{m=1}^M ∆_i(S_i^(m)) (Eq. 10); E[MSE] = (1/(nM)) Σ_{i∈N} σ_i^2, σ_i^2:=V[∆_i(S_i^(m))] (Eq. 11); Theorem 4.1 bound P(ˆK∈K_ε) ≥ Σ_{K∈K_ε}[1 − Σ_{i∈K, j∈N∖K} Φ(√M (ϕ_j−ϕ_i)/σ_{i,j})], σ_{i,j}^2:=V[∆_i(S_i^(m))−∆_j(S_j^(m))]; variance decomposition σ_{i,j}^2=σ_i^2+σ_j^2−2Cov(∆_i(S_i^(m)),∆_j(S_j^(m))) (Eq. 12); extended marginal contribution ∆′_i(S):=ν(S∪{i})−ν(S∖{i}); ∆′_i(S^(m)) = v_{S^(m)}−ν(S^(m)∖{i}) if i∈S else ν(S^(m)∪{i})−v_{S^(m)} (Eq. 14); Proposition 5.2 ϕ_i = Σ_{S⊆N} 1/((n+1) binom(n,|S|)) · ∆′_i(S); sampling distribution P(S^(m)=S)=1/((n+1) binom(n,|S|)) for all S⊆N (Eq. 15); M=⌊T/(n+1)⌋; budget-efficiency n/(n+1) sampled observations per call vs 1/2; E[MSE] = (n+1)/(nT) Σ_{i∈N} σ_i^2 (Eq. 16); Cov(∆′_i(S^(m)), ∆′_j(S^(m))) = 1/(n+1) Σ_{S⊆N∖{i}} ∆_i(S)( ∆′_j(S)/binom(n,|S|) + ∆′_j(S∪{i})/binom(n,|S|+1) ) − ϕ_iϕ_j (Proposition 5.3); Greedy CMCS pairwise probability ˆp_{i,j} := Φ(√M_{i,j} ˆδ_{i,j}/ˆσ_{i,j}) (Eq. 17); selection probability P((i,j)∈Q^(m)) = (ˆp_{i,j}−ˆp_min)/(ˆp_max−ˆp_min) (Eq. 18); empirical settings: M_min=30, δ=0.001; Table 1 uses δ=0.01 and ε=0.0005 for k=5; experiments average over 1000 runs (Table 1 over 200 runs).

data.paper_title: Partially Regularized Ordinal Regression to Adjust Teams’ Scoring for Strength of Schedule and Complementary Unit Performance in American Football
data.authors: Andrey Skripnikov, Sujit Sivadanam
data.core_methodology: Regularized ordinal regression with an elastic penalty; cumulative probability approach for ordinal outcomes; multinomial distribution with probability vector πijkl = (π1,ijkl, . . . , π5,ijkl)⊺ and πs,ijkl = P(Yijkl = s); baseline ordinal regression model (1): Yijkl iid ∼ Multinomial(1, πijk), log(P(Yijkl ≥ s)/P(Yijkl < s)) = µs + αi + βj + δhijl + φ⊺gijkl + ξI.cmpijkl + γ⊺x∗ji(k−1)l × I.cmpijkl, with constraints ∑_{i=1}^n αi = ∑_{j=1}^n βj = 0; partially regularized ordinal regression with a partial elastic net penalty; multinomial log-likelihood ℓ(); semi-parallel optimization approach introduced in Wurm et al. (2021) and implemented in the ordinalNet package; elastic net penalty (Zou and Hastie, 2005) combining LASSO and ridge penalties; relaxation of the proportional odds assumption via non-proportional coefficients γs; surrogate approach (Liu and Zhang, 2018) for residual diagnostics; binarized surrogate residual diagnostics for non-proportional odds models; mixed-effects cumulative link model with random intercept for game id using clmm from the ordinal package and likelihood ratio test; generalized variance inflation factor (GVIF) diagnostics; 10-fold cross-validation with sparse CV; bootstrap resampling; projection mechanism onto league-average opponent, home/away game balance, and league-average complementary unit; out-of-sample comparison using Mean Absolute Error and calibration of scoring category probability predictions.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Scoring outcomes and point designations: Defensive Touchdown = -7, Safety = -2, No Score = 0, Field Goal = 3, Offensive Touchdown = 7 (footnote: can also be 6 or 8 points, albeit rarely); Drive % NFL: 1%, < 0.5%, 65%, 14%, 20%; Drive % College: 1%, < 0.5%, 65%, 8%, 26%. Eq (1) constraints: ∑_{i=1}^n αi = ∑_{j=1}^n βj = 0. Centered complementary statistics: x∗ji(k−1)l = (x1,ji(k−1)l − ¯x1, . . . , xC,ji(k−1)l − ¯xC). α = 0.99; α grid [0.8, 0.9, 0.95, 0.99, 0.999, 0.9999]; α = 1 corresponds to pure LASSO, α = 0 corresponds to ridge, α ∈ (0, 1) represents a mixture. Approximate parameter counts: rising from approximately 80 to 270 for the NFL and from roughly 275 to over 1,100 for college football; approximately 64 for the NFL and 260 for college football; C = 15 complementary football features in the baseline model for both the NFL and college. 10-fold cross-validation; three replicates of 10-fold cross-validation; 1000 bootstrap resamples; 2.5% and 97.5% quantiles for 95% confidence intervals; MAE = mean(|ŷ − y|); SE = sd(CV.MAE)/√10. GVIF values below 2. Approximately 5-to-10% of drives are either not preceded by any other drive or follow a drive by the same team’s offense. Data retention: 65% of the initial halves were retained; over 15,000 drives per season except the shortened 2020 season, which included 9,000 drives; 55–60 drives per team; 32%–35% problematic data; NFL nearly 98% of all games retained, with at least 95% retained in any given season; each NFL team had at least 12 games of data available per season; some college teams as few as 4–5 games. Selection stability: non-scoring turnover selected at least 80% of the time; yards allowed selected in 70% of the cases; non-scoring turnovers selected 90% of the time as having a non-proportional effect on odds of scoring at least a field goal; turnover.nonscor × start.pos selected in 100% of all cross-validation replicates across all NFL and college seasons. Median starting position of 41 yards after a forced turnover is 21 yards better than in its absence. Additional points per drive from a non-scoring takeaway increases up to 0.6–1.0 points; once offenses average more than 2–2.5 points per drive, additional points begin to decline; NFL offenses rarely projected above 2.5–3 points per drive without a turnover; some college teams exceed 4 points per drive. Largest NFL positive shift: CHI 2016, 176 drives, 1.46 points, ⇑0.08 [0.07, 0.11], rank 27 (⇑4); largest NFL negative shift: KC 2013, 209 drives, 1.45, ⇓0.17 [-0.20, -0.15], rank 21 (⇓3). Largest college positive shift: Vanderbilt 2019, 82 drives, 1.64, ⇑0.13 [0.10, 0.17], rank 92 (⇑8); largest college negative shift: GA South 2015, 66 drives, 2.19, ⇓0.28 [-0.30, -0.24], rank 50 (⇓21). data.paper_title: What Makes a Dribble Successful? Insights From 3D Pose Tracking Data
data.authors: Michiel Schepers, Pieter Robberechts, Jan Van Haaren, Jesse Davis
data.core_methodology: 3D pose tracking via Hawk-Eye SkeleTRACK (29 anatomical landmarks plus ball and player centroid at 25Hz); Stats Perform event data; synchronization of event timestamps to tracking frames; cubic spline interpolation with natural boundary conditions for missing pose data; feature engineering of 8 2D positional features and 6 3D pose features capturing ball control, balance, and attacker-defender interaction; center-of-mass estimation using the anthropometric model of Winter; pressure score following Andrienko et al.; maximum change of direction following Kai et al.; baseline 8 × 5 grid success-rate model; logistic regression with L2 regularization, SAGA solver, maximum 1000 iterations, standardized features by removing the mean and scaling to unit variance, and sample weights set inversely proportional to class frequencies; five-fold cross-validation; SHAP value analysis.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Dataset: 125 games from the 2022/23 UEFA Champions League season; 1,736 dribbles (690 successful and 1,046 unsuccessful); success defined as the attacker retaining possession after beating the defender; primary defender is the nearest opponent at the end of the dribble. Equations and coefficients: dside = min(|y(t) − ymin|, |y(t) − ymax|); dgoal = ||p(t) − g||; vmax = max t∈[0,T] v(t); amax = max t∈[0,T] a(t); θ(t) = arctan 2(vy(t), vx(t)); Δθ = |θ(tend) − θ(tstart)|; θmax = max t |θ(t + δt) − θ(t)|; Δvmax = max t∈[0,T] [vatt(t) − vdef(t)]; Δv = (1/T) ∫_0^T [vatt(t) − vdef(t)] dt; ¯P = (1/T) ∫_0^T P(t) dt; Pmax = max t∈[0,T] P(t); dbf = (1/T) ∫_0^T ||b(t) − fmin(t)|| dt; d*bf = dbf P^α with α = 0.1; ball touch threshold 0.15 m and at least 0.25 seconds since previous detected ball contact; ftouch = Ntouch/T; CoMnaive = jmidHip; CoMi = (1 − ri) j1,i + ri j2,i; CoM = Σ_{i=1}^n mi CoMi; I = ||CoMx,y − FMPx,y||; θlean = arccos((zneck − zmidHip)/||vtorso||), vtorso = jneck − jmidHip; SidePass = 1 if attacker passes opposite the defender’s support leg, 0 otherwise; θdefender-attacker = arccos((vdefender · vattacker)/(||vdefender||·||vattacker||)); defender postures side-on (90°−120°), intermediate (120°−150°), squared-up (150°−180°); acceleration threshold athresh = 3m/s2.

data.paper_title: CourtMotion: Learning Event-Driven Motion Representations from Skeletal Data for Basketball
data.authors: Omer Sela, Michael Chertok, Lior Wolf
data.core_methodology: CourtMotion spatiotemporal modeling framework; two-stage approach: (1) Graph Neural Network (GNN) Skeleton Encoder processing high-frequency skeletal joint data through a directed acyclic graph (DAG), DGN blocks, BiTemporal Causal Convolutions with Striding, and temporal stride downsampling from 30Hz to 5Hz; (2) Transformer architecture with specialized attention mechanisms extending the Baller2Vec++ architecture to model player interactions; event projection heads using linear classification heads to predict basketball events in past, current, and future temporal windows; multi-task optimization with trajectory and event prediction losses; trajectory movements discretized into an 11ft×11ft grid yielding 121 trajectory bins; softmax trajectory prediction; binary cross-entropy event loss; Adam optimizer. Event set ℓ = {no action, free throw, shot attempt, pass, deflection, block, rebound, steal, dribble}. Shoulder-Normal Vector nt,i from left and right shoulder joint coordinates u(L)t,i and u(R)t,i: wt,i = u(R)t,i − u(L)t,i; nt,i = (1/∥wt,i∥)(0 −1; 1 0) wt,i. Player state st,i = (rt,i, nt,i, pt,i); ∆st,i = st+1,i − st,i. Event windows: ϵφt,i,past = maxτ∈[−δpast,−1] ϵφt+τ,i; ϵφt,i,current = ϵφt,i; ϵφt,i,future = maxτ∈[1,δfuture] ϵφt+τ,i. Transformer input vectors: zt,i = gz([ψ(i), pt,i, st,i]); ut,i = gu([ψ(i), pt+1,i, st,i, ∆pt,i, ∆st,i]); r0,i = gr([ψ(i), p1,i, s1,i]). Event projection: ˆϵt,i,r = σ(Wrˆzt,i+br), r ∈ {past, current, future}. Trajectory probability: P(vt,i|ˆZ) = softmax(Wtraj · ˆzt,i + btraj).
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Sampled at 5 Hz; 30 Hz 3D skeletal joints compressed to 5 Hz via GNN; 11ft×11ft grid yielding 121 trajectory bins; δpast and δfuture set to 2 seconds each; α = 0.5; 6 transformer layers with 8 attention heads and hidden dimension of 512; GNN encoder consists of 5 DGNN blocks; Adam optimizer with learning rate 5e-4 and batch size 32 on 8 NVIDIA A100 GPUs for approximately 100 hours; NBA SportVU dataset containing spatiotemporal recordings from 631 games during the 2015-2016 season; 160 games for pretraining, 160 different games for training downstream classifiers, and 40 games for evaluation of both stages. Trajectory NLL: Ours 0.38, Baller2Vec++ 0.58, Baller2Vec 0.71; 35% improvement over implementation of Baller2Vec++ and 47% improvement over original Baller2Vec; models with and without events projection achieve identical trajectory NLL 0.38. Shot Taker Prediction: at 2.8s before shot, Ours 0.38 AP, Baller2Vec++ 0.34 AP, baseline 0.35 AP; at 0.8s before shot, Ours 0.91 AP, Baller2Vec++ 0.66 AP, baseline 0.63 AP. Pick Prediction: at 0.6s before pick, Ours 0.82 AP, Baller2Vec++ 0.79 AP, baseline 0.70 AP; at moment of occurrence Ours 0.85 AP; maximum achieved AP approximately 0.85. Assist Prediction: at 2.8s before assist, Ours 0.58 AP, Baller2Vec++ 0.55 AP, baseline 0.53 AP; at 0.8s before completion, Ours 0.65 AP, Baller2Vec++ 0.58 AP, baseline declining performance 0.52 AP; at moment of shot Ours 0.65 AP. 2-Point vs 3-Point Shot Prediction: at 1.6s before shot, Ours 0.73 AP, baseline 0.55 AP; at 0.4s, Ours 0.97 AP, baseline 0.64 AP. Shot Type Classification: at 1.6s before shot, Ours 0.34 AP, baseline 0.31 AP; at 0.4s, Ours 0.50 AP compared to baseline's matching 0.33 AP. Ablation: Ours w/o Events Projection vs Baller2Vec++ shot-taker at later stages 0.80 vs 0.66 AP; Ours vs Ours w/o Events Projection: shot taker 0.91 vs 0.80 AP at late stage, assist 0.65 vs 0.56 AP at late stage; Ours w/o GNN pick prediction 0.82 AP in early stage, 0.85 AP at late stage; TranSPORTmer: shot taker 0.91 vs 0.30 AP, shot location 0.97 vs 0.68 AP, shot type 0.50 vs 0.33 AP. Equations: ∆pt,i = pt+1,i − pt,i; ϵφt,i,past = maxτ∈[−δpast,−1] ϵφt+τ,i; ϵφt,i,current = ϵφt,i; ϵφt,i,future = maxτ∈[1,δfuture] ϵφt+τ,i; wt,i = u(R)t,i − u(L)t,i; nt,i = (1/∥wt,i∥)(0 −1; 1 0) wt,i; st,i = (rt,i, nt,i, pt,i); ∆st,i = st+1,i − st,i; b(m→j)τ,i = v(m)τ,i − v(j)τ,i; h(j,0)τ,i = v(j)τ,i, e(m→j,0)τ,i = b(m→j)τ,i; e−j = sum over e∈E−j of e(e,ℓ)τ,i, e+j = sum over e∈E+j of e(e,ℓ)τ,i; h(j,ℓ+1)τ,i = hv([h(j,ℓ)τ,i, e−j, e+j]); e(m→j,ℓ+1)τ,i = he([e(m→j,ℓ)τ,i, h(m,ℓ+1)τ,i, h(j,ℓ+1)τ,i]); ez(ℓ)τ,i = σ(sum from k=0 to K−1 of Wk z(ℓ)(τ−k), i + b); zt,i = gz([ψ(i), pt,i, st,i]); ut,i = gu([ψ(i), pt+1,i, st,i, ∆pt,i, ∆st,i]); r0,i = gr([ψ(i), p1,i, s1,i]); ˆϵt,i,r = σ(Wrˆzt,i+br), r ∈ {past, current, future}; P(vt,i|ˆZ) = softmax(Wtraj · ˆzt,i + btraj); Ltraj = (1/TN) sum t=1 to T sum i=1 to N of −ln(P(vt,i|ˆZ)); Levents = (1/TN) sum t=1 to T sum i=1 to N sum r∈{past, current, future} sum φ∈ℓ BCE(ˆϵφt,i,r, ϵφt,i,r); BCE(p, y) = −y log(p) − (1 − y) log(1 − p); Ltotal = α · Ltraj + (1 − α) · Levents.

data.paper_title: Concurrent validity of computer-vision artificial intelligence player tracking software using broadcast footage
data.authors: Zachary L. Cranga, Rich D. Johnstona,c,d, Katie L. Millse,f, Johsan Billinghame, Sam Robertsong, Michael H. Colea, Jonathon Weakleya,c,d, Adam Hewitta and, Grant M. Duthiebc
data.core_methodology: Commercially available computer-vision and AI player tracking software using undisclosed computer-vision and AI techniques to track overall position (x, y coordinates) and speed (m.s-1) of each player at 25 fps; comparison against a high-definition multi-camera optical tracking system (TRACAB Gen 5, ChyronHego, New York, USA) capturing data at 25 Hz with 12 cameras elevated within the stadium infrastructure; speed from each provider and the TRACAB system filtered using a 4th order 1 Hz low-pass Butterworth filter; temporal alignment by phase shifting the players’ speeds within the TRACAB data to establish the smallest RMSE and applying the most common phase shift (mode); spatial alignment by rotating the providers’ tracking data throughout 360 degrees in 0.1-degree increments to establish the smallest mean error in XY position and spatially shifting the X and Y coordinates, applying the most common rotation and shift; total distance calculated by multiplying change in speed by change in time; mean bias and 95% limits of agreement (LOA) estimated from linear mixed effects (position and speed) and linear models (total distance) built using lmerTest::lmer and stats::lm functions with restricted estimated maximum likelihood (REML), error as the outcome variable, corresponding variable from TRACAB as a fixed effect, Player ID as a random intercept term, and separate models for each camera (Programme, Camera 1, Tactical) and video resolution (720p, 1080p) across detected, undetected, and combined datasets; appropriately weighted mean bias ± 95% limits of agreement (LOA) extracted; root mean square error (RMSE) separately calculated for position and speed; linear mixed models fit using REML with the RMSE for position and speed and mean bias for total distance as outcome variables, provider, camera feed, and video resolution as fixed effects in a three-way interaction, Player ID as a random intercept term, stats::anova for main effects, and emmeans::emmeans with a Tukey adjustment for post hoc tests; statistical analyses performed in RStudio (version 12.1; Posit, Boston, MA) using R (version 4.3.3, R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria).
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Position accuracy threshold ~ 1m; speed accuracy threshold RMSE ~ 10% (~ 1 m·s-1) of the maximum speed (0 to 10 m·s-1); statistical significance p < 0.05; one match at the 2022 Qatar Fédération Internationale de Football Association (FIFA) World Cup; data.paper_title: Tracking vs. Deciding: The Dual-Capability Bottleneck in Searchless Chess Transformers
data.authors: Quanhao Li, Wei Jiang
data.core_methodology: Decoder-only Transformer with Pre-RMSNorm, rotary position embeddings (RoPE), and SwiGLU activations; next-token prediction over UCI move sequences with input [BOS] [time_control] [elo] [color] move1 ... movet and no board representation; temperature-controlled sampling with no search; AdamW with β1=0.9, β2=0.999, weight decay 0.1, learning rate 10−4 with cosine decay to 10−5, batch size 2048, warmup of 4000 steps, gradient clipping at 1.0, dropout 0.1, and bf16 mixed precision; maximum sequence length 170 tokens; Flash Attention 2 and torch.compile; Elo-weighted training loss L = Σ_i w(e_i) ℓ(x_i) with weighting intensity r = w(emax)/w(emin) and schemes Uniform w(e)=1, Linear w(e)=clip(α(e−emin), wmin, 1), Exponential w(e)=exp(β(e−eref)); dual-capability bottleneck P ≤ min(T, Q); state tracking T measured by illegal-move rate and linear board probes; decision quality Q measured by CPL, move-prediction accuracy on high-rated subsets, and Stockfish agreement rate; effective diversity Div(D)=|{s : s appears in D at least θ times}| and effective quality Qual(D, w)=Σ_e w(e) n_e q(e) / Σ_e w(e) n_e; theoretical sweet-spot model T(r)=T0−α ln r, Q(r)=Q0+β ln r, r*=exp((T0−Q0)/(α+β)); coverage-decay interpretation S(t)≈b^t, k(t)=N/b^t, k(t*)=kcrit, t*=log(N/kcrit)/log b; full 2 × 2 factorial ablation; conditional blunder alignment; history-control intervention on threefold repetition.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Model configurations: Small 28 M parameters, 12 layers, hidden dim 384, 6 attention heads, FFN dim (SwiGLU) 1536; Large 120 M parameters, 16 layers, hidden dim 768, 12 attention heads, FFN dim (SwiGLU) 3072; vocabulary ∼1,900 tokens; maximum sequence length 170 tokens (P99.5); ∼134,000 tokens/s on H100; 28 M models train in ∼2.5 hours on a single NVIDIA H100; 120 M models train in ∼70 hours; 2 epochs. Training data: Lichess open database spanning ∼600–2800 Elo in Bullet and Blitz; Lichess puzzle data 1–5.8 M puzzles; Scale 1 (V1 series) ∼10 M games, ∼20 M sequences, ∼1.4 B tokens; Scale 2 (V2.2) ∼50 M games, ∼100 M sequences, ∼7 B tokens; Scale 3 (V2.3) ∼100 M games, ∼150 M sequences, ∼14 B tokens; V1.0 baseline 9.6 M Lichess games, ∼20 M sequences, ∼1.4 B tokens, 2 epochs; V1.1 filtered Bullet 2500+ and Blitz 2200+, supplemented with tracking patches and puzzles, ∼25.8 M sequences, 2 epochs. Weighting schemes: Uniform r=1:1 high-Elo gradient ∼5%; Linear r∼20:1 high-Elo gradient ∼45%; Exponential r∼200:1 high-Elo gradient ∼85%; linear r=20 low-Elo gradient contribution ∼5%, uniform ∼70%, filtering 0%; exponential r=200 reduced low-Elo gradients to ∼0.5%. Model variants: V1.0 28 M 10 M all-Elo Uniform illegal 1.06%; V1.0w 28 M 10 M all-Elo Linear illegal 1.13%; V1.1 28 M high-Elo only Uniform illegal 1.82%; V2.0 120 M 50 M all-Elo Uniform illegal 0.22%; V2.2 120 M 50 M all-Elo Linear illegal 0.26%; V2.3 120 M 100 M all-Elo Exponential illegal 0%. Filtering experiment V1.0 vs V1.1: illegal-move rate 1.06% vs 1.82% (+72%); opening Top-1 50.0% vs 53.8% (+3.8 pp); middlegame Top-1 43.5% vs 39.9% (−3.6 pp); endgame Top-1 46.8% vs 40.4% (−6.4 pp); cross-evaluation validation loss 1.75 to 2.01, Top-1 46.5% to 41.3%, illegal rate 1.06% to 2.49%; 58 M pure 2000+ model Top-1 40.3% vs 46.5%, illegal rate 2.68% vs 1.06%, loses 0–9–11. Board probes: 315,606 positions (252,967 train / 31,965 validation / 30,674 test), 278,760 non-standard and 36,846 standard; 13 labels per square over 64 squares; best overall square accuracy 93.40% (V1.0) vs 92.29% (V1.1); standard 97.57% vs 97.51%; non-standard 92.78% vs 91.45%; middlegame 92.36% vs 91.08%; endgame 92.08% vs 90.41%; V2.2 98.0%, V1.0 93.4%, V1.0w 93.1%. 2 × 2 factorial offline metrics: V1.0 28M r=1 illegal 1.06%, Top-1 46.5%; V1.0w 28M r=20 illegal 1.13%, Top-1 47.0%; V2.0 120M r=1 illegal 0.22%, Top-1 50.85%; V2.2 120M r=20 illegal 0.26%, Top-1 51.2%. Head-to-head: V1.0w vs V1.0 40–23–37, 100 games, score 58.5%, p=0.043; V2.0 vs V1.0 80–54–66, 200 games, score 56.5%, p=0.030; V2.0 vs V2.2 24–41–35, 100 games, score 41.5%, p=0.046; V2.2 vs V1.0 66–8–26, 100 games, score 79.0%, p<0.001; V2.2 vs V1.0w 66–12–22, 100 games, score 77.0%, p<0.001. V2.2 performance: illegal-move rate 0.26%; Top-1 51.2%; Lichess bullet Elo 2570 (253 games); vs V1.0 66W–8L–26D. V2.2 vs V2.3: validation loss 1.48 vs ∼1.40 (lower); practical play Lichess 2570 vs weaker; Elo conditioning (2600 vs 1200) works (27:13) vs broken (17:16 ≈random); endgame quality normal vs collapsed. Checkpoint ordering by temperature: 0.0: e1_09 50, e1_05 50, draws 0; 0.1: 28, 49, 23; 0.2: 31, 43, 26; 0.3: 43, 39, 18. Intra-game degeneration: baseline 632/1000 (63.2%) detectable degeneration; final V2.2 195/1000 (19.5%); median tdeg move 26 to 31; normalized median 0.588 to 0.694; CPL > 500; Wilcoxon signed-rank p < 10−25 for both models. Human move prediction: 12,000 decision points, four Elo bands (2100–2300, 2300–2500, 2500–2700, 2700+) and three phases (opening, middlegame, endgame), 1,000 positions per Elo × phase cell; Top-1 overall V2.2 55.2%, Maia-2 rapid 50.0%, Maia-2 blitz 50.4%; opening advantage +9.1 pp vs rapid and +8.8 pp vs blitz. Human-blunder alignment: 314,418 positions, CPL > 100; V2.2 P(model blunder | human blunder) 49.2%, P(model blunder | human ¬blunder) 6.6%, lift 7.4×; Maia-2 rapid 43.3%, 6.6%, 6.5×; Maia-2 blitz 44.8%, 6.8%, 6.6×; overall blunder rate 12.5% vs 11.7–12.0%; at CPL > 500 V2.2 45.7% vs 38.4%, Maia-2 rapid lift 31.5× vs 29.4×. Lichess deployment: 253 rated bullet games, rating 2570, record 149 wins, 74 losses, 30 draws. Other negative results: V1.2 short-history variant illegal rate 1.06% to 2.60%; V4.0 pure FEN Transformer loses 0–8–2; SFT on 120 M with 60,000 chess.com games by Hikaru Nakamura yields ∼50–100 Elo improvement.

data.paper_title: PathCRF: Ball-Free Soccer Event Detection via Possession Path Inference from Player Trajectories
data.authors: Hyunsung Kim, Kunhee Lee, Sangwoo Seo, Sang-Ki Ko, Jinsung Yoon, Chanyoung Park
data.core_methodology: PathCRF detects on-ball soccer events from player tracking data by modeling player trajectories as a fully connected dynamic graph over extended node set Ṽ = V ∪ O, with four outside nodes, and formulating event detection as selecting exactly one edge e_t=(u_t,v_t) at each time step (self-loop for control, directed sender-receiver edge for kick). It uses a Conditional Random Field (CRF) on top of a neural backbone: two socio-temporal encoders (coarse and fine) inspired by ROLAND and TranSPORTmer, with social module combining partially permutation-equivariant (PPE) network and fully permutation-equivariant (FPE) network using Induced Set Attention Block (ISAB), and temporal module using positional encoding (PE) with stacked Set Attention Blocks (SABs) (PE-SABs) or Bi-LSTM. Node embeddings are converted to edge embeddings z_e,t = MLPedge([h(2)_u,t; h(2)_v,t]) ∈ R^d'. The Dynamic Masked Conditional Random Field computes sequence probability p(e|X)=exp(S(e))/Σ_e' exp(S(e')), score S(e)=f_1(e_1)+Σ_{t=2}^T(f_t(e_t)+ψ_t(e_{t-1},e_t)), emission f_t(e)=MLPemit(z_e,t) ∈ R, and dynamic transition ψ_t(e',e)=MLPtrans([z_e',t-1; z_e,t]) ∈ R. It masks all transitions except allowed set A (Aid, Akick, Arec, Aout) with a fixed large negative score (e.g., −104). Training minimizes LCRF = −log p(e*|X) = log Z − S(e*), using the forward algorithm for log Z, with final objective L = LCRF + λ1 Lcoarse + λ2 Lemit; Lcoarse uses sender/receiver logits via MLPcoarse and softmax cross-entropy, and Lemit is cross-entropy between emission logits and true possession state. Inference uses Viterbi decoding; events are detected when selected edge changes (ê_{t−1} ≠ ê_t) and categorized as Control, Kick, or Out-of-play. Preprocessing/synchronization uses ELASTIC, Ramer–Douglas–Peucker (RDP) algorithm, and Needleman–Wunsch algorithm.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: PathCRF identifies correct possession edge among 262 = 676 candidate edges with accuracy 69.64%, and achieves F1-score 75.69% in event detection. Dynamic Masked CRF test results: edge accuracy 69.64%, sender accuracy 80.44%, receiver accuracy 82.28%, violation rate 0.00%, event precision 73.18% (1435/1961), event recall 78.37% (1435/1831), event F1 75.69%. Non-CRF: edge accuracy 69.24%, sender accuracy 79.78%, receiver accuracy 81.62%, violation rate 2.80%, event precision 58.77% (1347/2292), event recall 73.57% (1347/1831), event F1 65.34%. Non-CRF & GCD: edge accuracy 66.34%, sender accuracy 76.89%, receiver accuracy 78.19%, violation rate 0.00%, event precision 68.81% (1339/1946), event recall 73.13% (1339/1831), event F1 70.90%. Non-CRF & VCD: edge accuracy 69.68%, sender accuracy 80.16%, receiver accuracy 81.97%, violation rate 0.00%, event precision 69.50% (1413/2033), event recall 77.17% (1413/1831), event F1 73.14%. Static Dense CRF: edge accuracy 69.41%, sender accuracy 80.59%, receiver accuracy 81.61%, violation rate 2.18%, event precision 62.54% (1399/2237), event recall 76.41% (1399/1831), event F1 68.78%. Static Masked CRF: edge accuracy 69.54%, sender accuracy 80.29%, receiver accuracy 82.02%, violation rate 0.00%, event precision 68.57% (1464/2135), event recall 79.96% (1464/1831), event F1 73.83%. Dynamic Dense CRF: edge accuracy 69.08%, sender accuracy 79.56%, receiver accuracy 81.95%, violation rate 2.28%, event precision 61.75% (1377/2230), event recall 75.20% (1377/1831), event F1 67.82%. Ball TP: edge accuracy 47.01%, sender accuracy 58.58%, receiver accuracy 67.01%, violation rate 0.00%, event precision 44.64% (967/2166), event recall 52.81% (967/1831), event F1 48.39%; ball trajectory localization error 2.74 m. Dataset splits: Train matches 5, episodes 379, events 8,792, frames 364,003, windows 54,683; Valid. matches 1, episodes 71, events 1,902, frames 80,076, windows 12,620; Test matches 1, episodes 91, events 1,831, frames 85,304, windows —. Preprocessing uses 10-second sliding windows with stride 5 frames; tracking downsampled from 25 FPS to 5 FPS, resulting in 50 time steps per window, predictions later upsampled to 25 FPS. Team possession: ground-truth home possession share 62.13%, prediction 62.64%; frame-level team possession classification accuracy 92.40%. Pass networks: Home node degree true mean 45.19, MAE 2.64; edge weight true mean 5.18, MAE 1.08; JSD 0.0228; spectral 0.0270. Away node degree true mean 24.27, MAE 2.73; edge weight true mean 3.26, MAE 1.05; JSD 0.0552; spectral 0.0138. Runtime: Non-CRF (5 FPS) event F1 65.34%, training time 184.20 ± 0.34 s/epoch, episode latency 0.2155 ± 0.0013 s, match latency 34.57 ± 0.06 s; Static MCRF (5 FPS) 73.83%, 241.70 ± 0.47, 0.2104 ± 0.0005, 20.17 ± 0.05; Dynamic MCRF (5 FPS) 75.69%, 565.41 ± 4.19, 0.2399 ± 0.0009, 22.88 ± 0.08; Dynamic MCRF (25 FPS) 77.21%, 6726.95 ± 27.80, 0.5272 ± 0.0028, 49.28 ± 0.27. Recall under relaxed matching: nearly 80% under 1 s and 4 m, 86.1% up to 2 s and 10 m. Cross-dataset/LOMOCV: K League→K League edge acc 68.20 ± 2.64%, event prec 84.34 ± 2.42%, event recall 75.79 ± 2.76%, event F1 79.83 ± 2.60%; Sportec→Sportec 66.75 ± 2.76%, 72.05 ± 2.37%, 75.87 ± 2.33%, 73.88 ± 1.90%; K League→Sportec 52.71 ± 9.31%, 71.93 ± 6.43%, 61.52 ± 8.41%, 66.25 ± 7.65%; Sportec→K League 41.65 ± 2.34%, 54.44 ± 3.68%, 44.84 ± 3.28%, 49.16 ± 3.37%. Loss ablation: Static MCRF [LCRF,Lcoarse,Lemit] 69.54%, 68.57%, 79.96%, 73.83%; [✓,✗,✓] 66.96%, 62.66%, 79.36%, 70.02%; [✓,✓,✗] 66.09%, 69.26%, 75.91%, 72.43%; [✓,✗,✗] 65.41%, 66.19%, 73.13%, 69.49%; Dynamic MCRF [✓,✓,✓] 69.64%, 73.18%, 78.37%, 75.69%; [✓,✗,✓] 67.52%, 70.02%, 75.75%, 72.77%; [✓,✓,✗] 65.77%, 67.48%, 74.33%, 70.74%; [✓,✗,✗] 65.64%, 71.32%, 68.05%, 69.65%.

data.paper_title: Analysis of Video-Based 3D Tracking Accuracy by Using Electromagnetic Tracker as a Reference
data.authors: Matjaž Divjak, Damjan Zazula
data.core_methodology: General framework for assessing 3D accuracy of video-based tracker by comparing it to an electromagnetic tracking device; three transformation models for coordinate systems (Model A, Model B, Model C) using homogeneous coordinates and pM = A pC with transformation matrix A containing translation and rotation; Model A uses three control points T1, T2, T3 away from camera and manual distances d1 and d2; Model B uses two points on camera and one away with focal length d; Model C uses one point on camera and two away, focal length d, pixel displacements mH and mV; sensitivity analysis of transformation model parameters via derivatives, spectral norm ||A||2, individual sensitivity S_l, and upper relative sensitivity limit S_MAX; analytical decomposition of vision-based tracking error using multiplicative error model Ae = A·ΔA, pC_e = ΔP_C·pC, compensation matrix C, four selected points, and f_ORTO criterion; statistical decomposition using additive error model with random, normally distributed errors, zero mean, 1000 Monte-Carlo runs and simulated transformation matrix ASIM; video tracking algorithm uses bimodal colour and range information to detect consistent skin coloured regions and Kalman filter-based prediction algorithm; Polhemus 3Space Fastrak magnetic tracker and Videre Design’s STH-MD1-C stereo head.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Equations: pM = A pC (Eq. 1); A = [[i1,j1,k1,o1],[i2,j2,k2,o2],[i3,j3,k3,o3],[0,0,0,1]] (Eq. 2); Model A: iC = T3T1/|T3T1|, kC = T2T1/|T2T1|, jC = kC × iC, oC = T1 − d1 iC − d2 jC, ΘA = {x1,y1,z1,x2,y2,z2,x3,y3,z3,d1,d2}; Model B: kC = T1T2/|T1T2|, iC = T1T3/|T1T3|, oC = T1 − d kC, ΘB = {x1,y1,z1,x2,y2,z2,x3,y3,z3,d}; Model C: α = arctg(mV/mH), iC = T2T3''/|T2T3''|, ΘC = {x1,y1,z1,x2,y2,z2,x3,y3,z3,d,mH,mV}; r_H = h u_H/v_H = h 2 tg φ_H/v_H, r_V = h u_V/v_V = h 2 tg φ_V/v_V (Eq. 7); sensitivity a_u,v = f_u,v(Θ1,Θ2,...,ΘN), ∂A/∂Θl = ∂f_u,v(Θ1,...,ΘN)/∂Θl, S_l relative sensitivity, S_MAX upper relative sensitivity limit, spectral norm ||A||2; error models Ae = A·ΔA, pC_e = ΔP_C·pC, pM = Ae·C·pC_e, f_ORTO criterion; additive model Ae = A + ΔA, pC_e = pC + ΔpC, e = pM − Ae pC_e = ΔA pC + A ΔpC + ΔA ΔpC; random, normally distributed errors (zero mean, 1000 Monte-Carlo runs) and ASIM. Numerical: d1 = 490 mm; d2 = 14 mm; d = 48 mm; mH = 85 pixels; mV = 9 pixels. Model A T1=(201.4,241.9,91.3) mm, T2=(211.2,522.2,100.2) mm, T3=(-68.1,266.0,124.5) mm; Model B T1=(-83.7,204.8,88.9) mm, T2=(-62.4,-99.4,-41.7) mm, T3=(-97.4,198.8,84.8) mm; Model C T1=(-83.7,204.8,88.9) mm, T2=(-62.4,-99.4,-41.7) mm, T3=(107.4,-17.7,-10.6) mm. S_l values (Table 4): Model A x1 398.5, y1 175.2, z1 174.8, x2 1.4, y2 0.7, z2 19.9, x3 10.6, y3 224.3, z3 224.3, d1 398.6, d2 398.6; Model B x1 410.4, y1 390.7, z1 410.2, x2 20.4, y2 3.4, z2 20.3, x3 0.4, y3 6.9, z3 4.5, d 390.1; Model C x1 408.8, y1 389.1, z1 408.5, x2 20.3, y2 3.4, z2 20.2, x3 0.1, y3 0.1, z3 0.8, d 388.5, mH 0.5, mV 4.6. S_MAX: Model A 2026.9, Model B 1661.1, Model C 1651.2. RMS differences (mm): Model A X 16.1 ± 6,1, Y 5.8 ± 1.2, Z 10.7 ± 1.7, Total 20.5 ± 4.9; Model B X 14.8 ± 2.9, Y 12.7 ± 0.7, Z 72.5 ± 6.4, Total 75.1 ± 6.8; Model C X 34.7 ± 3.2, Y 12.7 ± 0.4, Z 55.1 ± 6.7, Total 66.4 ± 6.9. Transformation/algorithm errors (mm RMS): Model A min transformation 2.5 ± 0.002, max transformation 11.6 ± 0.02, min algorithm 17.1, max algorithm 20.5; Model B 2.3 ± 0.02, 9.5 ± 0.23, 20.9, 22.8; Model C 1.7 ± 0.01, 6.3 ± 0.08, 21.4, 22.2. Fastrak tracker: static resolution 0.8 mm RMS position and 0.15° RMS orientation, only when sensor is less than 75 cm away from magnetic transmitter; four wired sensors. STH-MD1-C: two synchronized CMOS sensors, 9 cm baseline, f = 48 mm lenses, 1288 × 1032 pixels at 7.5 fps, 320 × 240 pixels at 110 fps; camera approximately 1 meter away; three trajectories consisting of 500 3D points all together; three video sequences each consisting of 120 – 200 colour image pairs with 320 × 240 pixels.

data.paper_title: Exploring Game Performance in the National Basketball Association Using Player Tracking Data
data.authors: Jaime Sampaio1☯*, Tim McGarry2☯, Julio Calleja-González3‡, Sergio Jiménez Sáiz4‡, Xavi Schelling i del Alcázar5‡, Mindaugas Balciunas6‡
data.core_methodology: Variables expressed as counts per game were divided by average minutes played; records screened for univariate outliers (cases outside the range Mean ± 3SD); descriptive discriminant analysis; structure coefficients greater than |0.30| interpreted as meaningful contributors; leave-one-out method of cross-validation; k-means cluster analysis; cubic clustering criterion together with Monte Carlo simulations; one-way independent measures ANOVA; Tukey post-hoc homogeneous subsets; Cohen’s κ; JMP statistics software package (release 11.0, SAS Institute, Cary, NC, USA) and SPSS software (release 22.0, SPSS Inc., Chicago, IL).
data.key_metrics_and_variables: n = 1230 games; 30 teams; 82 games; October 29, 2013 to April 16, 2014; 548 players; 339 cases (62%); all-star players n = 15; non all-star players n = 324; points per game all-star 22.20±4.70 vs non all-star 9.20±5.10; minutes played all-star 35.90±2.20 vs non all-star 22.50±8.80; descriptive discriminant function p<0.001; canonical correlation 0.59 (Λ = 0.65); reclassification 97.2%; structure coefficients: elbow touches SC = 0.43, defensive rebounds SC = 0.35, close touches SC = 0.34, close points SC = 0.33, pull-up points SC = 0.33, speed in defense SC = -0.33; six cases misclassified (60.0% accuracy) in the all-star group; seven cases misclassified (97.8% accuracy) in the non all-star group; discriminant scores all-star 3.04±1.45 and non all-star -0.13±0.87; cubic clustering criterion CCC = 252.6 for seven clusters; four statistically significant functions (p<.001); first two functions 94.7% total variance with canonical correlations 0.98 and 0.88; reclassification 96.2%; Function 1 (78.3%) and Function 2 (16.1%); structure coefficients total distance covered in offense SC = 0.83 and defense SC = 0.80; clusters 2, 3 and 4 contained all-star players; NBA first team grouped in clusters 2 and 4; minimum Cohen’s κ value for all variables exceeded 0.91; sampling rate around 25 frames per second; 25 Hz sampling frequency limitation; rebound vicinity 3.5 feet; close shots within 12 feet; pull-up/catch-and-shoot outside 10 feet; drives start at least 20 feet and dribbled within 10 feet of hoop; catch and shoot possession for two seconds or less; all-star voting points five points for first team, three points for second team, one point for third team.

data.paper_title: Unsupervised Learning of Event and Object Classes from Video
data.authors: Muralikrishna Sridhar
data.core_methodology: Generative probabilistic model for events; graphical representation for qualitative spatial relationships; interaction graphs; activity graph; RCC-5-derived spatial relations ℜ= {P (Part Of) , PO (Partially Overlaps) , DR (Discrete)}; Allen's temporal relations ℵ= {Before(<), Meets(m), Overlap(o), Starts(s), During(d), Finishes(f), Equal(=)}; Hidden Markov Model (HMM) based technique for computing stable qualitative spatial relationships; Bayesian model; logistic functions; bag of graphemes (BoG) representation and BoG kernel; RBF kernel Kd; non-parametric kernel density estimate; Maximum a Posteriori (MAP) estimation; Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) procedure; spectral clustering; Viterbi decoder and k-best Viterbi paths.

data.paper_title: Do Open-Source Video Ad Clients Follow VAST 4.3? An Empirical Study of Player Conformance
data.authors: Prashant Chaudhary
data.core_methodology: A specification-derived conformance study using a catalog of 108 requirements extracted from VAST 4.3 and the IAB macro list (commit 99d5d51; 59 macros); a recording server serves 69 crafted test vectors (109 documents) and the IAB's 49 sample tags, rewrites URLs to itself, and logs every request; log-file analysis used as a test oracle, with one oracle per requirement grading each cell as conforms, deviates, delegated, or n/a; open-source clients are analyzed white-box with source tracing, and Google IMA HTML5 SDK 3.794.0 is a black-box comparison; execution uses Node.js 22.22.0 with jsdom 26.1.0 and five browsers on three engines through Playwright 1.56.1; generated inputs include an error grid (15 × 12 + 7 = 187 cases per client), a macro grid (56 macros; 580 cells), mutation fuzzing (139 seeds; 1,442 cases; 5 rounds; root causes C1 to C9; differential pass D1 to D4), and a version sweep over 36 releases grading 93 requirements.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: 108 requirements (58 must, 39 should, 2 may, 9 observation); 23 requirements whose graded strength differs from the literal text; 69 crafted test vectors with 109 documents; 49 IAB sample tags; six open-source clients in eight configurations; 86 findings (78 open-source, 8 IMA); 3 to 21 must-level deviations per configuration; 59 macros total, 50 graded macros (the 4.3 set), 56 macros in the macro grid, 580 macro-grid cells; error grid 15 × 12 + 7 = 187 cases per client and 748 cells; mutation fuzzing with 139 seeds, 5 rounds (289, 291, 290, 283, and 289 cases), 1,442 cases (1,437 unique), 12 failure classes and 9 root causes (8 library defects and 1 environment artifact), bias-corrected Chao1 estimate 15.0 classes (95 percent interval 12.4 to 37.3) against 12 observed; version sweep over 36 releases and 93 requirements; timing constants: 50 ms ordering tolerance, 300 ms Node.js settle window, 600 ms browser settle window, 800 ms icon threshold, 2 s client timeout, 30 s wall limit, slow-load limit three times the client's timeout plus 5 s (11 s); 73 minutes for the packaged harness; vast-client-js timeout reproduction: 49 of 49 fault runs crashed and none of 21 controls; 50 concurrent requests with one hanging Wrapper: none of 49 healthy requests completed; self-referencing Wrapper ran nine stalled hops in 54 s; IMA 3.794.0: 8 of 101 cells in Chromium (8 percent) from 7 findings and 9 of 102 in Firefox from 8 findings across browsers; I01 timings: 36 to 68 ms in Linux Chromium, 54 to 111 ms in Firefox, 165 to 237 ms in WebKit, 11 to 12 ms in macOS Chromium, 10 to 13 ms in Chrome, 13 to 50 ms in Firefox, 51 to 58 ms in WebKit; Node.js 22.22.0, jsdom 26.1.0, Playwright 1.56.1, esbuild 0.25.10, Chromium 141, Firefox 142, WebKit 26, Chrome 156, Safari 27.0.1.

data.paper_title: Person Re-Identiﬁcation Using Group Information
data.authors: Alina Bialkowski, Patrick Lucey, Xinyu Wei, Sridha Sridharan
data.core_methodology: Uses group information as contextual feature; linear mapping function to assign each person to a role or position within the group structure; combines appearance and group context cues using a weighted summation. Appearance features: Symmetry-Driven Accumulation of Local Features (SDALF) and region covariance descriptor; also weighted covariance grid (weightedCG). Role assignment: adopts procedure similar to [20]; given initial ordering pt = [x1, y1, x2, y2, ..., x10, y10]T at time instant t, find the 10 × 10 permutation matrix xt that rearranges players into role order rt = xtpt; permutation matrix is binary and xt(i, j) = 1 indicates player i assigned to role j, with every row and column summing to one; role assignment is an optimisation problem minimising the L2 reconstruction error: xt∗ = arg min_xt ∥ˆr − xtpt∥2 2; this is a linear assignment problem with cost matrix C(i, j) = ∥ˆr(i) − pt(j)∥2; find most similar prototype formation ˆr from 25,000 labeled frames based on mean and covariance of the team's formation in the current frame; solve using the Hungarian algorithm. Role distance uses average confusion matrix of automatic assignment accuracy converted to distance by subtracting average assignment probabilities from a matrix of ones. Evaluation uses Cumulative Matching Characteristic (CMC) curves; person detector [22] interprets background subtraction results in terms of 3D geometry with players coarsely modelled as cylinders; team/group assigned based on colour histogram in LAB colour space.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Image patches scaled to 96 × 50 pixels; player heights of 40-100 pixels; eight fixed high-deﬁnition cameras; two parts annotated: 3893 frames and 8838 frames; person re-identiﬁcation evaluation on 94 images for the 13 players; 10 ﬁeld players; 5:3:2 formation roles R = {left back (LB), right back (RB), left halfback (LH), centre halfback (CH), right halfback (RH), inside left (IL), inside right (IR), left wing (LW), centre forward (CF), right wing (RW)}; 10 × 10 permutation matrix; 25,000 labeled frames; automatic role assignment accuracy 66.0% (Part 1 = 59.0%, Part 2 = 69.0%); identification using manually labelled roles = 84.5%; automatically assigned roles = 67.4%; 100 experiments averaged; player substitutions (23/26, 9/28, 15/27); Eq (1) CR = 1/(n − 1) Σ_{k=1}^{n} (zk − µ)(zk − µ)T; Eq (2) zk = [x, y, Rxy, Gxy, Bxy]; Eq (3) ρ(C1, C2) = √(Σ_{i=1}^{n} ln2 λi(C1, C2)); Eq (4) Distance(SubjectA, SubjectB) = Σ_{m=1}^{M} ρ(CA,m, CB,m)/(σA,m + σB,m); Eq (5) σi,m = 1/(n − 1) Σ_{k=1;k≠i}^{N} ρ2(Ci,m, Ck,m); Eq (6) xt∗ = arg min_xt ∥ˆr − xtpt∥2 2; Eq (7) C(i, j) = ∥ˆr(i) − pt(j)∥2.

data.paper_title: EFFECT OF VISION TRAINING AMONG SKILL ABILITY OF FOOTBALL PLAYERS
data.authors: Binu A
data.core_methodology: The study selected twenty (N=20) University level male football players; participants were randomly categorised into Group I- experimental (n=10), Group II- control (n=10); McDonald soccer skill test was conducted as pre-test for both experimental and control groups; specific vision training (Depth perception, Ocular motility, Quick Exposure, Opaque lifesaver card, Dice pursuits, Near-far chart, Gaze work, Vergennes, Tracking and Focusing) was assigned to the experimental group for a period of eight weeks with training of five days in a week; the control group did not undergo any treatment; statistical tests used were paired and unpaired t-test; data were statistically analysed by using 't' ratio; significance was determined at 0.05 levels.

data.paper_title: Extracting spatial knowledge from track and field broadcasts for monocular 3D human pose estimation
data.authors: Tobias Baumgartner, Benjamin Paassen, Stefanie Klatt
data.core_methodology: The paper proposes a method to infer the global geometry of track and field stadium recordings using lane demarcations and a single vanishing point v0. It extracts straight-line segments with a linear Hough transform (Hough Line Transform, default OpenCV implementation), clusters line segments into main track lanes Lj, and determines the main vanishing point as the intersection of the lanes using a majority vote. It assumes a pinhole camera, no digital zoom, fixed camera location, horizontal two main vanishing points, and perfect 2D human pose estimation. It determines extrinsic camera parameters for rotation R = Rx · Ry · Rz ∈R3×3 and location t ∈R3×1, with square pixels, no skew, principal point at the exact center, field-of-view fov, focal length F, intrinsic camera matrix K ∈R3×3, and overall projection matrix P = K · [R|t] ∈R3×4. Projection uses (x, y) = (u/w, v/w), where (u, v, w) = (X, Y, Z, 1) · P. It computes a dense set of azimuth/elevation pairs from v0 using elevation-isolines, computes roll assuming a horizontal horizon line, adapts fov and KC to shift the simulated vanishing point onto v0, adapts the distance d of the camera and ray-traces translation tC, and computes PC = KC · [RC|tC]. The parameter space is sampled densely but discretely at a sampling rate of 0.5° azimuth. It compares monocular 3D HPE methods Strided Transformers, RIE and MeTRAbs, including MeTRAbs + movement knowledge and MeTRAbs + rotation knowledge; uses a 2D HPE method based on a ResNet-50 backbone trained on MPII; and validates with an Xsens motion capture suit (MVN Link). It also experimented with differentiable rendering, and the simulation pipeline can be completely implemented in TensorFlow.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Equations/parameters: R = Rx · Ry · Rz ∈R3×3; t ∈R3×1; K ∈R3×3; P = K · [R|t] ∈R3×4; (x, y) = (u/w, v/w), where (u, v, w) = (X, Y, Z, 1) · P; PC = KC · [RC|tC]. Camera parameters: camera position (x, y, z), camera orientation (azimuth, elevation, roll), field-of-view fov, focal length F; azimuth changes from 89° to 1°; sampling rate of 0.5° azimuth. Annotations: 158 frames of international elite athlete performances; 355 frames; 16 athletes; 5 different venues and distances; 17 major joint locations (head, neck, chest, navel, pelvis, 2 × shoulder, 2 × elbow, 2 × wrist, 2 × hip, 2 × knee and 2 × ankle); 17 default human3.6m joint definitions; lane demarcations 1.22 ± 0.01 m wide. Table 1: Error analysis for 355 frames for 16 athletes over 5 different venues and distances; Mean (Standard Deviation). Strided Transformer: Reprojection error 10.97 (4.26) pixel, 82.33 (16.26) mm; 2D knee error 40.31 (14.75) degree; Approximate 3D knee error 49.44 (27.69) degree. RIE: 12.03 (4.84) pixel, 84.26 (20.74) mm; 40.31 (20.19) degree; 44.24 (26.92) degree. MeTRAbs: 4.75 (3.19) pixel, 42.97 (49.04) mm; 10.31 (10.66) degree; 13.38 (31.15) degree. + movement knowledge: 3.76 (2.85) pixel, 35.01 (46.62) mm; 6.81 (8.55) degree; 9.94 (28.54) degree. + rotation knowledge: 5.30 (4.20) pixel, 42.55 (49.05) mm; 7.47 (7.41) degree; 8.45 (13.19) degree. Best approximated 3D knee error 8.45° with a standard deviation of 13.19°. Ground truth evaluation: Xsens angle errors < 2.6 ± 1.5°; 50 frames; predicted camera location within 5.5% of the correct camera position; average offset in x/y/z direction 1.75m/2.67m/0.72m (min: 0.09m/0.18m/0.01m, max: 4.48m/9.50m/2.05m); athlete average distance 37.56m (min: 14.57m, max: 71.41m); 2D HPE RMSE 7.56 ± 3.75 pixel, equals 50.42 ± 28.51 mm; left/right knee average error 8.39 ± 4.41° / 7.94 ± 5.84°; left/right elbow average error 15.81 ± 7.80° / 11.85 ± 5.65°; overall expected error in 3D angle prediction 11.00 ± 5.93°; 200 separate optimizations; improvements in reprojection error by 0.36±0.48 pixels (lens distortion) and 0.66±0.48 pixels (camera location); TV-typical camera operations pan, tilt, and zoom (up to 30x). Motivating figures: running kinematics account for up to 94% of variance in running economy for novice athletes; knee angle progression differences of 2–3° between indoor and outdoor running; 2–4° knee flexion difference between warm-up and transition phase in triathletes; high angular accuracy below 3° error required.

data.authors: Wenyuan JIANG, Yuhei YAMAMOTO, Kenji NAKAMURA, Chihiro TANAKA, Shigenori TANAKA, Takeshi NARUO, Zhiwei XIAO
data.core_methodology: Proposed method: identify players before and after occlusion via BRISK (Binary Robust Invariant Scalable Keypoints) features and Hamming-distance matching; dynamic background subtraction (Zivkovic et al., 2006); moving-object regions as external bounding rectangles instead of tracking rectangles; occlusion/separation decided by bounding-rectangle overlap of ６割以上; player state pool / tracking state list storing single/occlusion states and pre-occlusion/latest positions and sizes; background-noise removal by excluding BRISK points outside the moving-object region; feature-noise removal using movement set Eq.1, mean movement Eq.2, distance average Eq.3, and removal of points with |d_i - mean| > threshold; player tracking with search regions (occlusion region, separated region, or previous tracking box expanded to ２倍 width/height) and movement correction by testing patterns from 0 to ２倍 mean movement and selecting the pattern maximizing feature points inside a same-size box; player size estimated by linear interpolation Eq.4 between players with maximum and minimum Y coordinates; trajectory obtained by connecting center-bottom points of tracking boxes, with occlusion intervals connected by straight lines. Four functions: moving-object region classification, player state management, player identification, and player tracking. Compared with existing detection/tracking methods Redmon et al. (2015) and Wojke et al. (2017).

data.authors: Sara Akan, Songül Varlı, Mohammad Alfrad Nobel Bhuiyan
data.core_methodology: RFES-ReID framework with a Swin Transformer backbone; uses Swin-T, a sliding-window variant of ViT, with 2, 2, 6, and 2 blocks on each stage; regional feature extraction Swin Transformer (RFES) backbone; regional feature extraction block (RFEB) positioned prior to the Swin Transformer block, converting a token with dimensions (B, H × W, C) into a feature map with dimensions (B, C, H, W), followed by 3 × 3 layer dilated convolutions (dilation = 2), a GELU activation function, a residual connection, and reshaping to (B, H × W, C); Swin Transformer replaces the Multi-Head Attention mechanism (MSA) with W-MSA and SW-MAS and uses non-overlapping M × M local windows, local self-attention with query, key, and value matrices (Q, K and V), shared projection matrices between several windows, a relevant positional encoding B, multi-head self-attention, a multi-layer perceptron (MLP) with two fully connected layers and GELU non-linearity between them, LayerNorm (LN) prior to both the MSA module and the MLP module, residual connections, and shifted window partitioning; fusion loss combining cross-entropy loss, triplet loss, and focal loss, with Euclidean distance da,p and da,n for triplet loss; features are sent to the fusion loss stage and then to a fully connected (FC) layer for ID prediction; re-ranking with k-reciprocal encoding after the initial ID list, using top-k samples encoded as reciprocal neighbor features, k-reciprocal features, Jaccard distance, and final distance averaging the Jaccard distance with the Manhalanobis distance of feature appearance; random horizontal flipping, random cropping, and random erasing augmentation; AdamW optimizer with cosine decay learning rate scheduler and linear warm-up.

data.paper_title: Changes in Drop and Repeated Jump Ground Reaction Forces After A 10-Week Offseason Strength and Conditioning Program in Division I American Football Players

data.core_methodology: Repeated-measures design; each subject visited the laboratory twice (pre-offseason and post-offseason). Three attempts of the DJ and RJ were performed. DJ was performed off a 30 cm box (actual drop heights calculated by touchdown velocity ranged from 30.00 – 32.43 cm). RJ protocol consisted of four consecutive jumps. Ground reaction forces were collected using one force plate (AMTI, AccuGait, Watertown, MA, USA); the z-axis vertical ground reaction forces were sampled at 1 kHz using The Motion-Monitor (Innovative Sports Training, Inc., Chicago, IL, USA), stored on a personal computer, and processed off-line with custom written software (LabVIEW v. 2021, National Instruments, Austin, TX, USA). End of braking phase equation variables: pdownward is the vertical force at the end of the braking phase, m is body mass (kg), g is acceleration due to gravity (m·s-2), and h is drop height (m). Velocity-time tracings were calculated by taking the integral of the force-time curve divided by mass; power-time tracings were calculated by multiplying the force-time tracing by the velocity-time tracing; position-time tracings were calculated by taking the integral of the velocity-time tracing. Jump height was calculated using the impulse-momentum method, where jump height equals the velocity at take-off (calculated as net propulsive impulse divided by body mass) squared, divided by the constant acceleration of gravity multiplied by 2. RSI was flight time divided by the duration from landing to take-off for DJ and jumps 2-4, and flight time divided by the duration from initiation of unweighting to take-off for jump 1 of the RJ. Statistical analyses: Shapiro-Wilk test; dependent samples t-tests; time (pre vs. post) x jump (2 vs. 3 vs. 4) repeated measures analyses of variance (ANOVAs); time (pre vs. post) x jump (1 vs. 2 vs. 3 vs. 4) repeated measures analyses of variance (ANOVAs) with Bonferroni corrections; partial η2 effect sizes (≥ 0.14 large, ≥ 0.06 and < 0.14 moderate, ≥ 0.01 and < 0.06 small, < 0.01 negligible); Hedge’s g effect sizes (≤0.19 = trivial, 0.20-0.59 = small, 0.60-1.19 = moderate, 1.20-1.99 = large, ≥ 2.0 = very large); intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) model 2,1; coefficients of variation (CVs); IBM SPSS v. 28 (Chicago, IL, USA); alpha level p ≤ 0.05.

data.paper_title: Maximin Action Identiﬁcation: A New Bandit Framework for Games
data.authors: Aur´elien Garivier, Emilie Kaufmann, Wouter M. Koolen
data.core_methodology: Two-player two-round zero-sum random game: Player A chooses i∈{1,...,K} and player B chooses j∈{1,...,Ki}; the chosen pair (i,j) yields a Bernoulli distribution with mean µi,j, and the goal is the maximin action i*∈argmax_{i∈{1,...,K}} min_{j∈{1,...,Ki}} µi,j. The problem is formulated as a stochastic bandit model with K=∑_{i=1}^K Ki Bernoulli arms P=(i,j)∈P; fixed-confidence sequential strategy (Pt,τ,ˆı) with δ-PAC guarantee. Proposed algorithms: Maximin-LUCB (M-LUCB), based on lower- and upper-confidence bounds and a LUCB sampling rule; Maximin-Racing, using successive elimination in rounds with high arms elimination and action elimination; M-KL-LUCB using KL-based confidence bounds; M-Chernoff using the Chernoff stopping rule based on the generalized likelihood ratio statistic Z_{P,Q}(t).
data.key_metrics_and_variables: δ-PAC condition (1): ∀µ, Pµ( min_{j∈{1...Ki*}} µi*,j − min_{j∈{1...Kˆı}} µˆı,j ≤ ǫ ) ≥ 1−δ. Notation: i*=1 and µ*=µ1,1; ˆı is an ǫ-maximin action if µ1,1−µˆı,1≤ǫ. Confidence bounds (3): LP(t)=ˆµP(t)−√(β(t,δ)/(2NP(t))), UP(t)=ˆµP(t)+√(β(t,δ)/(2NP(t))). M-LUCB stopping rule (2): τ=inf{t∈2N: min_i[max_{i′≠i} min_{1≤j′≤Ki′} U_{i′,j′}(t)−min_{1≤j≤Ki} L_{i,j}(t)]<ǫ}. H*(µ)=∑_{(i,j)∈P} 1/max[( (µi,1−(µ1,1+µ2,2)/2)^2 ),(µi,j−µi,1)^2] (Theorem 1; Appendix A writes the virtual-arm term as (µ1,1+µ2,1)/2). T(µ,δ)=inf{t∈N:4H*(µ)β(t,δ)<t}. β(t,δ)=log(Ct^{1+α}/δ) (4). Corollary 3: β(t,δ)=log(1/δ)+b log log(1/δ)+c log log(et). Proposition 6: β(t,δ)=log(2K1(K−1)t/δ). Maximin-Racing elimination function (8): f(x,y)=I(x,y):=[d(x,(x+y)/2)+d(y,(x+y)/2)]1(x≥y), with d(x,y)=x log(x/y)+(1−x) log((1−x)/(1−y)); threshold β(t,δ)=log(4CKt/δ); r0:=2/ǫ^2 log(4K/δ). Theorem 5: limsup_{δ→0} Eµ[τδ]/log(1/δ) ≤ 8[ 2/(µ1,1−µ2,1)^2 + 1/(µ1,2−µ2,1)^2 + 1/max[(µ1,1−µ2,1)^2,(µ2,2−µ2,1)^2] ]. Theorem 8: limsup_{δ→0} Eµ[τδ(1,1)]/log(1/δ) ≤ 1/max(ǫ^2/2,I(µ2,1,µ1,1)); for (i,j)≠(1,1), limsup_{δ→0} Eµ[τδ(i,j)]/log(1/δ) ≤ 1/max(ǫ^2/2,I(µi,1,µ1,1),I(µi,j,µi,1)). Theorem 9 lower bound: Eµ[τδ]≥T*(µ)d(δ,1−δ), T*(µ)^{-1}=sup_{w∈ΣK} min[F1(µ,w),F2(µ,w)]. Experiments: δ=0.1, ǫ=0, N=10000 repetitions; µ1=[0.4 0.5;0.3 0.35], µ2=[0.4 0.5;0.3 0.45], µ3=[0.4 0.5;0.3 0.6]; 3×3 model µ=[[0.45,0.5,0.55],[0.35,0.4,0.6],[0.3,0.47,0.52]]; experimental exploration rate β(t,δ)=log((log(t)+1)/δ).
