data.core_methodology: Distributed Tracking (DT) problem with a coordinator and k players, threshold N, and counters n_i; Multinomial Distribution assumption for counter increments: each counter increment occurs in the i-th player with probability µ_i for all i ∈ {1, 2, ..., k}, where Σ_{i=1}^k µ_i = 1; unified ℓ-Notifications-to-End algorithm framework; algorithms StcSlk-KwnDst, DynSlk-KwnDst, StcSlk-LrnDst, DynSlk-LrnDst, CMY algorithm, and UniSlk; CMY uses s_i = ⌊N/(2k)⌋ and ℓ = k; UniSlk uses s_i = N/k and ℓ = 1; Bernstein inequality and Empirical Bernstein Bound; Bernoulli random variables; static slack assignment with s_i = µ_i t + √(2tµ_i(1−µ_i) ln(k/δ)) + 2/3 ln(k/δ); dynamic slack assignment with b_i = µ_i t and s_i = ⌊(N−t)/(2k)⌋; learning the distribution on the fly by running CMY for the first round and estimating µbar_i = n_i/Σ_{i∈[k]} n_i; backup heuristic that switches to CMY when (N−N')/N drops below a pre-specified threshold (say 0.75).
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Variables: N threshold; k number of players; [k] set of integers from 1 to k; n_i counter of the i-th player; s_i slack of the i-th player; µ_i probability that a new item arrives at player i; µbar_i estimation of µ_i; T(N) communication cost with threshold N; δ failure probability; t items tracked; w items tracked in the first round; β algorithm-specified constant. data.authors: 1Anton Smerdov, 2Bo Zhou, 2Paul Lukowicz, 1Andrey Somov
data.core_methodology: Data were collected using twelve types of sensors and synchronized with an NTP server; for preprocessing, outliers for each sensor were removed by clipping values to an interval between 0.5 and 99.5 percentiles, then the signal was smoothed using an exponential moving average with a half-live value of 1 second, and all signals were resampled to a unified timestep of 1 second by averaging or summation. Skill prediction split data into 3-minute sessions, up to 5 sessions per match, used a 37-dimensional representation obtained by averaging sensor signal over time, normalized each feature per player to zero mean and unit variance, and visualized with 2-dimensional embeddings obtained by the t-SNE method. Models used: Logistic regression; k-nearest neighbors classifier with k=16; Support Vector Machine with radial basis functions (RBF) kernel; Random forest classifier with 100 estimators and maximum tree depth 4; Naive Bayes (Gaussian Naive Bayes); Gaussian process. Player re-identification used player id as a target and predicted one of 10 classes corresponding to players, using the One-vs-Rest strategy to calculate ROC AUC for multiclass classification. Team dynamics was calculated as average pairwise Pearson correlations for different features extracted from sensor data, using numpy.corrcoef, with errors estimated on random subsets containing 80% of matches.

(5); cross-level normalized spatial distance Eq. (3) and template cut probabilities Eq. (4) with threshold σ. data.paper_title: ML-Based Approach for NFL Defensive Pass Interference Prediction Using GPS Tracking Data
data.authors: Arian Skoki1, Jonatan Lerga1,2, and Ivan ˇStajduhar1,2
data.core_methodology: ML models for highly imbalanced time-series binary classification: Long-Short Term Memory (LSTM), Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU), Attention Neural Network (ANN), and multivariate LSTM Fully Convolutional Network (MLSTM-FCN). LSTM and GRU models were implemented using Keras deep learning API and Tensorflow 2.0 library. ANN model was constructed using Keras Attention Mechanism library built on top of an LSTM model. data.paper_title: DanceTrack: Multi-Object Tracking in Uniform Appearance and Diverse Motion
data.authors: Peize Sun1∗, Jinkun Cao2∗, Yi Jiang3, Zehuan Yuan3, Song Bai3, Kris Kitani2, Ping Luo1
data.core_methodology: Large-scale multi-human/multi-object tracking dataset DanceTrack constructed from mostly group dancing videos; annotations are bounding boxes and identifications, with full-body boxes for partly-occluded objects, no annotation for fully-occluded objects, and identity kept after re-appearance; annotation propagation tool used. Dataset split: 100 videos, 40 training, 25 validation, 35 test. Evaluation uses HOTA as main metric plus AssA and IDF1 for association performance and DetA and MOTA for detection quality; FP, FN, IDs also provided. Oracle analysis uses ground-truth bounding boxes with IoU matching, Kalman Filter motion modeling under linear motion assumption, and appearance matching with a pre-trained Re-ID model. Benchmark trackers: CenterTrack, FairMOT, QDTrack, TransTrack, TraDes, MOTR, GTR, ByteTrack, OC-SORT. Association algorithms with YOLOX detector: IoU, SORT, DeepSORT, MOTDT, BYTE, OC-SORT. Motion models: None(IoU), Kalman filter, LSTM. Additional modalities: COCOmask, COCOpose, KITTI depth, with CenterNet and BYTE association. Mathematical variables: appearance similarity V, averaged IoU on adjacent frames U, frequency of relative position switch S.

data.authors: Gal Shitrit*, Ishay Be’ery*, Ido Yerhushalmy
data.core_methodology: Player tracking: two-step Tracking-by-detection approach using an optimized state-of-the-art (SoTA) online multi-object tracker with a contemporary object detector; evaluated with DeepOC-SORT++ and Strong-SORT++ using YOLOv8 detector and OSNet appearance models with cosine similarity. Post-processing three phases: missing track detections interpolated using GSI; fine-tuned AFLink model to merge tracks (GSI + AFLink denoted ++); appearance-based track merging with an iterative merging process assuming new track IDs can only be created or terminated near the image boundaries, merging a new track generated within a short time span with a previously terminated track if appearance similarity remains consistently high throughout most of the track duration. Appearance model: fine-tuned OSNet-ain with crop resolution 256x128. Player detector: YOLOv8l fine-tuned on SoccerNet data with image resolution 576x1024 and NMS IoU threshold of 0.45. Ball detector: fine-tuned YOLOv8l on SoccerNet data with image resolution 1080x1920; COCO2017 pre-trained detector used to select frames with IoU>0.7 between label and ball detection.

data.paper_title: Player Re-Identification Using Body Part Appearences
data.authors: Mahesh Bhosale, Abhishek Kumar, David Doermann
data.core_methodology: Two-stream neural network architecture for soccer player re-identification; one stream for appearance map extraction and the other for body part map extraction; bilinear-pooling layer that generates and spatially pools the body part map; each local feature of the body part map is obtained by a bilinear mapping of the corresponding local appearance and body part descriptors; no part annotation on the SoccerNet-V3 re-identification dataset; sub-network of OpenPose initializes the part substream; appearance stream is pre-trained on the ImageNet dataset; ResNet50 appearance extractor initialized with pre-trained weights learned on the classification task of the Zoo dataset [11]; part stream is trained from scratch for the SoccerNet-V3 dataset; sub-network of OpenPose initialized with pre-trained weights on the pose estimation on the COCO dataset; OpenPose multi-stage CNN; Part Affinity Fields (PAF), a 2D vector field; confidence maps of 17 key points; bipartite graph matching; average pooling; compact bilinear pooling; tensor sketch for projections; Layer Wise Similarity; fully connected layers; metric learning loss; triplet loss; L2 distance; cross-entropy loss; Adam optimizer.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Equations: L1 = ϕ1(F); Lt = ϕt(F, Lt−1), ∀2 ≤ t ≤ TP; STP = ρt(F, LTP), ∀t = TP; St = ρt(F, LTP, St−1), ∀TP < t ≤ TP + TC; f = poolingxy{fxy} = 1/S ∑xy fxy; fxy = vec(axy ⊗ pxy); f̃ = f / ∥f∥2; L = max(d(a, p) − d(a, n) + margin, 0); L = −1/m ∑_{i=1}^m yi · log(ŷi). Variables: a ∈ H × W; p ∈ H × W; x and y are spatial locations in the image; S is spatial size; axy is appearance feature at location (x, y); pxy is part feature at location (x, y); d can be any distance metric, such as L1/L2 distance; here, L2 distance is used; yi is ground truth pid; ŷi is predicted pid. Numerical values: 340,993 players’ thumbnails; 400 soccer games; 6 major leagues; 17 key points; batch size 32; trained on 10% of the dataset; learning rate 0.00001; input image resolution 256x128; surpassed OSnet by 2.1% on mAP when training on a 10% dataset; layer-wise similarity increased mAP by 3.7% and Rank-1 score by 3.6%; layer-wise similarity model trained on 10%; ResNet50 activation maps from layer-1 to layer-6. Table 1 Evaluation results on 10% Soccernet data: Our mAP 63.7 Rank 52.8; OSnet mAP 61.6 Rank 51.2; Inceptionv4 mAP 46.7 Rank 32; ResNet50 mid mAP 46.5 Rank 31.7; ResNet50 baseline mAP 46.7 Rank 32.8. Table 2 Evaluation results on 2% Soccernet data: OSnet mAP 55.5 Rank 45.1; Our mAP 55.0 Rank 42.4; Inceptionv4 mAP 49.9 Rank 35.8; ResNet50 mid mAP 42.9 Rank 27.8; ResNet50 baseline mAP 44.2 Rank 28.9. Table 3 Evaluation results with layerwise similarity: Our (layerwise) mAP 50.4 Rank 36.2; ResNet mAP 46.7 Rank 32.8.

data.paper_title: CRICKET PLAYER PROFILING: UNRAVELING STRENGTHS AND WEAKNESSES USING TEXT COMMENTARY DATA
data.authors: Swarup Ranjan Behera*, Vijaya V. Saradhi
data.core_methodology: Computational models to extract strength rules and weakness rules from cricket text commentary using domain-specific features extracted from unigrams and bigrams; Confrontation Matrix (CM) of size 19 × 12 constructed via Filter Tuple ⟨Player, Opponent Player, Time, Type⟩ and Algorithm 1 Construction of Confrontation Matrix (CM); Correspondence Analysis (CA) with Singular Value Decomposition (SVD), Pearson’s ratio, Pearson’s Chi-square statistic, and biplot visualization; CA minimizes the sum of the squared χ2-distance given as χ2 = Σ (observed−expected)^2/expected; inner product matrix ⟨Fm×2, Gn×2⟩ to identify highest inner product values; Procrustes analysis for biplot comparison; standard data holdout strategy for intrinsic validation; extrinsic validation against a strategy sheet and expert analysis.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Dataset: 550 international cricket Test matches, May 2006 to April 2019, 1,088,570 deliveries, thirteen years, more than one million text commentaries, results for over 250 cricket players; 132 batsmen and 130 bowlers with more than 2000 deliveries; typical commentary up to 50 words; CM size 19 × 12; 19 batting features: 0 run, 1 run, 2 run, 3 run, 4 run, 5 run, 6 run, out, beaten, defended, attacked, front foot, back foot, third man, square off, long off, long on, square leg, fine leg; data.paper_title: Moving from Machine Learning to Statistics: the case of Expected Points in American football
data.authors: Ryan S. Brill∗, Ryan Yee†, Sameer K. Deshpande†, and Abraham J. Wyner‡
data.core_methodology: Expected points defined as EP(x)=Σ_k pts(k)·P(y=k|x), where pts(k) is net points and P(y=k|x) is estimated from data; drive outcome has five outcomes: touchdown (7), field goal (3), no score (0), opposing team safety (-2), and opposing team touchdown (-7); epoch outcome has seven outcomes: touchdown (7), field goal (3), safety (2), no score (0), opponent safety (-2), opponent field goal (-3), and opponent touchdown (-7); multinomial logistic model log(P(yij=k|xij)/P(yij=No Score|xij))=fk(xij); traditional drive outcome probability models minimize logloss weighing each play equally: arg min_p{-Σ_{i=1}^{Ndrives}Σ_{j=1}^{Ni}Σ_{k=1}^{K} I(yi=k)·log p(k|xij)}; averaged subsample model with M=100 uniformly drawn one play per drive per subsample, fitting models and averaging M models, minimizing averaged logloss arg min_p{-(1/M)Σ_{m=1}^{M}Σ_{i=1}^{Ndrives}Σ_{j=1}^{Ni} I^m_ij Σ_{k=1}^{K} I(yi=k)·log p(k|xij)} with I^m_ij=I(play j is sampled from drive i in train set subsample m); approximated by weighted logloss arg min_p{-Σ_{i=1}^{Ndrives}Σ_{j=1}^{Ni} w_ij Σ_{k=1}^{K} I(yi=k)·log p(k|xij)} with w_ij=1/N_i; unweighted XGBoost, averaged subsampled XGBoost, and weighted XGBoost; evaluation by rmse, logloss, and marginal coverage on Mtest=100 test set subsamples formed by uniformly drawing one play per drive; standard (i.i.d.) bootstrap resamples plays uniformly with replacement and cluster bootstrap resamples drives uniformly with replacement; B=100 bootstrapped drive outcome probability models; prediction set from bootstrap empirical distribution of outcomes; weighted XGBoost regression with monotonic constraints (monotonic decreasing in yardline, yards to go, point spread, and defensive team timeouts remaining; monotonic increasing in offensive team timeouts remaining); weighted multinomial logistic regression fit with nnet::multinom(outcome_drive ~ factor(down):(bs(yardline_100, df=5) + bs(half_seconds_remaining, knots=c(30))) + log(ydstogo) + utm:as.numeric(posteam_timeouts_remaining==0) + factor(era) + posteam_spread + posteam_spread:yardline_100 + I((score_differential <= -11)) + I((score_differential >= 11)) + I((score_differential <= -4)*(game_seconds_remaining <= 900)) + I((-3 <= score_differential & score_differential <= 0)*(game_seconds_remaining <= 900)) + I((1 <= score_differential & score_differential <= 3)*(game_seconds_remaining <= 900)) + I((4 <= score_differential & score_differential <= 10)*(game_seconds_remaining <= 900)), weights = drive_weights); catalytic prior using Algorithm 1: target model weighted multinomial XGBoost, catalytic prior model weighted multinomial logistic regression, generate approximately M synthetic game-states by sampling drives with replacement, impute synthetic outcomes from catalytic prior model, total synthetic weight fraction φ of total observed weight, fit target model on combined observed and synthetic data, with M=500,000 and φ=1; EPA computed by subtracting the expected points at the beginning of a play from the expected points at the end of a play.

data.paper_title: PitcherNet: Powering the Moneyball Evolution in Baseball Video Analytics
data.authors: Jerrin Bright, Bavesh Balaji, Yuhao Chen, David A Clausi, John S Zelek
data.core_methodology: PitcherNet is an end-to-end automated system with three components: (1) Pitcher Tracking and Identification using tracklets generated by SORT with YOLOX detections, each tracklet assigned a unique identifier and 3D pseudo-pose from MHFormer, and player actions decoupled by classifying each tracklet into pitcher, batter, or others using a Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN) with five TConv layers containing dilated 1D convolutional layer with progressively increasing dilation rates, batch normalization, ReLU activation, dropout layers, and skip connections. (2) 3D Human Modeling using D2A-HMR 2.0, a Distribution and Depth Aware Human Mesh Recovery model with Depth Anything as depth encoder using DINOv2 encoder and DPT decoder, transformer encoder with cross- and self-attention and learnable gate fusions, silhouette decoder, and regression head for mesh vertices and 3D joint coordinates; final 3D pose uses Eq. (1); losses include focal loss for pitch position and handedness and L_RLE, L_SMPL, L_3D, L_2D, L_silh plus L_3D^r. (3) Pitch Statistics using TCN for pitch position and handedness; release point from wrist kinematics in the x-plane using extreme coordinates and peak pitch velocity in a window around Point B; pitch velocity from Eq. (2); release extension from Eq. (3).

data.paper_title: CAMOT: Camera Angle-aware Multi-Object Tracking
data.authors: Felix Limanta, Kuniaki Uto, Koichi Shinoda
data.core_methodology: CAMOT (Camera Angle-aware Multi-Object Tracking), a simple camera angle estimator for multi-object tracking; estimates camera elevation angle θ and object 3D coordinates P by regressing a common plane for all object detections; assumes multiple objects are located on a flat plane in each video frame, at least three objects detected per frame, object in contact with ground with bottom edges on common ground plane, camera parameters unknown except focal length f, and change of camera angles smooth over time; models a human object as a cylinder in 3D space with centroid Pi=(Xi,Yi,Zi), height H, and aspect ratio A (H constant, A can vary); pinhole camera optics with focal length f; bounding-box selection filters boxes clipping frame edge, divides image into nplane regions width-wise, and adds at most one highest-detection-confidence object per region; iterative elevation angle estimation by setting θ(t,u), estimating 3D object points P_i^(t,u), regressing a plane with normal vector n^(t,u), calculating plane angle θ_n^(t,u), and evaluating error ε(t,u) until ε(t,u) > τε false; depth estimation from 2D coordinates converted to rays r_i = κ_c^{-1}[x_i y_i 1]^T using top-middle and bottom-middle 2D positions (x_i,y_it), (x_i,y_ib); plane estimation with normal unit vector n=(n_x,n_y,n_z) and plane P_plane=(0,0,z_plane); if |P_plane| < 3 keep plane from previous frame; Nelder–Mead optimization algorithm [37] minimizes ε; weighted moving average smoothing with window w=fps/2; tracking in 3D camera coordinates using Kalman filter with inverse depth term 1/z and state vector (xi, yi, 1/zi, ai, ẋi, ẏi, ḣi); Gaussian noise scaled by inverse depth in constant velocity model; camera motion compensation (CMC) by image registration using Enhanced Correlation Coefficient (ECC) maximization [17]; angle-aware association by modifying Distance-IoU (DIoU) with camera angle factor φ = 1 + cos^2 θ; object detection with YOLOX-x pre-trained in COCO; baseline ByteTrack; evaluated on MOT17 and MOT20 with CLEAR MOT Metrics and HOTA.

Condition 2: X_ij is 1-sub-Gaussian with mean a_ij and all results are mutually independent; P_A(ϵ) = {x∈S_n | x^T A ≥ −ϵ1^T}; φ(A) = max_{j∈[n]} max_{i∈[n]} |(1^T A_j^{−1} − π)_i|; π_min = min_{i∈[n]} π_i; S_n^α = {x∈S_n | x ≥ α1} for α∈(0,1/n]; Algorithm 1: T = ⌈2U^2/α^2 log(2n^2/δ)⌉ + 1; thresholds t > 2φ(Â)^2/π̂_min^2 log(2n^2/δ); t > 2φ(Â)^2/α^2 log(2n^2/δ); ϵ = α/φ(Â); ϵ = α/U; v̂_j^T = π̂^T − ϵ(1^T Â_j^{−1} − π̂^T); Proposition 31: if |s|/κ ≤ 1/n then max_{i,j,k}|m^k_{ij}| ≤ 4κ^{n−1}n for k=5,7,9,...,19; Proposition 32: if |s|/κ ≤ 1/n then φ(Q) ≤ (4n^2+1)/(3|s|) for n=5,7,...,19; Proposition 33: if 0<s≤κ/n then Q(n,κ,s) has unique Nash equilibrium π and π_min ≥ s/(5κ); for Q(n,κ,κ/n), π_min ≥ 1/(5n); Hoeffding inequality P[|(Σ_{i=1}^n Z_i)/n − μ| ≥ c] ≤ 2 exp(−c^2 n/2); Lemma 17: if t ≥ 2/ε^2 log(2n^2/δ) then P[|â_ij^(t) − a_ij| < ε for all {i,j}∈binom([n],2)] > 1−δ; data.paper_title: GRAZE: Grounded Refinement and Motion-Aware Zero-Shot Event Localization
data.authors: Syed Ahsan Masud Zaidi1, Lior Shamir1, William Hsu1, Scott Dietrich2, Talha Zaidi1
data.core_methodology: Training-free FPOC localization pipeline using Grounding DINO for hierarchical prompt scheduling and progressive threshold relaxation; three prompt levels P = {Pgear, Pnogear, Pgeneric}; six temporal positions searched with three progressively relaxed box-confidence thresholds; candidate collection across all positions, thresholds, and prompt levels; detection classification with Kd = {dummy, pad, bag, tackle, training, blocking} and Kp = {player, person, athlete, helmet, football, running, sprint}; D* selection by weighted confidence, normalized center distance, and verticality; temporal validation over 14 neighboring frames with composite confidence conf(d0,dv); geometric motion scoring using displacement score mdisp(P) and directional approach score mdir(P,D); candidate ranking by confoverall; two-phase backward refinement using sequential backtracking and binary search to recover tFFBO; SAM2 mask propagation initialized at tFFBO and pixel-wise logical intersection as explicit contact verifier; ranked multi-candidate fallback evaluated until SAM2 mask overlap independently confirms contact. Baselines: SOLE (Single-prompt Open-vocabulary Localization Estimator), TRACE (Temporal vAlidation with refinement and Consistency Estimation), MARS (Motion-Aware Region Selection); GRAZE is the complete pipeline with hierarchical multi-prompt progressive search, temporal validation, directional motion scoring, two-phase backward refinement, and ranked multi-candidate SAM2 retry.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: V = {It}T t=1; tFFBO = earliest frame in which both P and D are simultaneously visible; tFPOC = exact frame at which the player first physically intersects the dummy; tend = min(T, tFPOC + Lpost), Lpost = 20 frames; AR(di) = hi/wi; τarea = 0.01 · HW; edge(di) margins: within 15% of frame width from either horizontal edge or within 10% from the top; kind(di): dummy if (AR(di) > 2.0) ∨ (li ∈ Kd); player if li ∈ Kp ∧ area(di) > τarea ∧ ¬edge(di); Dummies with AR(di) < 0.8 rejected; D* = arg max_{d∈Ddummy} [0.4 sd + 0.3 (1 − distc(d)) + 0.3 min(AR(d)/3.0, 1)]; top three player candidates ranked by proximity to D* forwarded; Fval = {t0 + δ} over 14 neighboring frames; τIoU = 0.20; τdist = 200 px; sr(d0, dv) = min(A0, Av)/max(A0, Av); conf(d0, dv) = 0.55 IoU(d0,dv)/τIoU + 0.30 (1 − dist(d0,dv)/τdist) + 0.15 sr(d0, dv); player candidate must match in at least 3 of 14 frames; dummy candidate requires at least 2; mdisp(P) = min(1/|Q| Σ_{m∈Q} ||c0 − cm||2 / 200, 1); mdir(P, D) = (⟨v̂motion, v̂to-dummy⟩ + 1)/2; discard if mdisp < 0.08 or mdir < 0.30; confoverall = 0.3 ccons + 0.3 mdisp + 0.4 mdir; exponential offsets {5, 10, 20, 50} frames back; SAM2 masks M(i)t = SAM2(V, tFFBO, b(i)), i ∈ {P, D}; overlapt = Σ_{x,y} M(P)t(x,y) ∧ M(D)t(x,y); τoverlap = 1; tFPOC = min{t | overlapt ≥ τoverlap}; accepted unless both confoverall < 0.25 and mdir < 0.20 hold simultaneously; dataset 738 untrimmed monocular videos at 30 fps; 681 verified ground-truth FPOC labels; 57 recorded without simultaneous annotation; annotation uncertainty approximately ±3 frames; 719 valid outputs; 666 evaluable clips; 53 segmented clips lack annotations; 15 GT-labeled clips fell into manual review; 19 clips routed to manual review; coverage 719/738 = 97.4%; end-to-end accuracy: |err| < 5 f = 71.4%, |err| < 10 f = 77.5%, |err| < 15 f = 80.8%, |err| < 20 f = 82.7%; data.paper_title: Strategic Gaze: Attention Allocation and Transition Patterns Across Functional Areas of Interest by Gameplay Outcome
data.authors: YUFEI CAO, PENNY SWEETSER
data.core_methodology: Within-subject eye-tracking experiment using Act 1 of Slay the Spire with fixed character, fixed level map, and constant run seed; gameplay outcome coded as Win (defeated final boss) or Loss; two consecutive sessions (Session 1 up to 25 minutes, Session 2 up to 15 minutes); Tobii Pro Fusion screen-based binocular eye tracker at 250 Hz integrated with a 23.8-inch 1920 × 1080 monitor, approximately 60 cm viewing distance, using Tobii Pro Lab for 9-point calibration and data collection; combat episodes segmented with OpenCV multi-template matching based on normalised cross-correlation (threshold = 0.7); gaze preprocessing with linear interpolation for signal loss, removal of off-screen points, Tobii default I-VT fixation detection, exclusion of fixations shorter than 60 ms, and boundaries for timestamp gaps greater than four times the median sampling interval; hybrid top-down and bottom-up AOI definition from functional categories plus fixation-based gaze density maps, percentile thresholding at levels of at least the 70th percentile, morphological closing with elliptical kernel of size 11, connected-component filtering, centroid merging within 120 pixels, retention of top six regions; AOI boundary extraction using RGB-to-HSV colour thresholding, Canny edge detection, contour extraction, bounding rectangles, normalisation by screen resolution, and separate templates for Boss, Single Enemy, and Multiple Enemies; AOI-based measures computed as AOI Hit, Dwell Time, AOI Transition Probability, Transition Matrix Entropy (H_t), and Stationary Entropy (H_s); transitions modelled with first-order Markov process, transition matrix P row-normalised, stationary distribution π satisfying πP = π obtained via eigenvalue decomposition, rows with no outgoing transitions filled with uniform distribution 1/N; Transition Matrix Entropy using Shannon entropy, entropy normalised by theoretical maximum entropy/log2(N), K = N(N−1); group comparisons using Mann–Whitney U (MWU) tests with Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate correction, rank-biserial correlation effect size r, and permutation tests on mean difference.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Sample: 32 participants (16 male, 16 female), aged 18–34 years, 54.3% in 18–24 range and 45.7% in 25–34 range; Win n=16, Loss n=16. Eye tracking: Tobii Pro Fusion at 250 Hz; 23.8-inch monitor at 1920 × 1080 resolution; approximately 60 cm; calibration repeated if mean accuracy exceeded 1.0° or data loss was greater than 10%. Segmentation: normalised cross-correlation threshold = 0.7; signal loss less than 5%; fixations shorter than 60 ms excluded; abnormal timestamp gaps greater than four times the median sampling interval. AOI density: thresholds at levels of at least the 70th percentile; elliptical kernel size 11; regions with area smaller than 80 pixels or integrated density mass below 0.1% discarded; centroids within 120 pixels merged; top six regions retained. AOI validation: 156 validation frames; overall alignment 95.4% (893/936); R4 Player Status 100% (156/156); R6 Energy 100% (156/156); R5 Potion Panel 99.4% (155/156); R2 Hand Cards 97.4% (152/156); R3 Enemy Status 94.2% (147/156); R1 Enemy Intent 82.1% (128/156); within-template rates Boss 94.9%, Single-enemy 96.4%, Multi-enemy 95.1%. data.paper_title: Polycepta: Object-Centric Appearance Estimation for Multi-Object Tracking
data.authors: Mohamed Nagy, Member, IEEE, Naoufel Werghi, Senior Member, IEEE, Jorge Dias, Senior Member, IEEE, Majid Khonji, Member, IEEE
data.core_methodology: Polycepta object-centric appearance state estimation framework within tracking-by-detection; recursive appearance estimation problem; constructs and continuously updates an independent appearance state for each tracked object. Architecture modules: Visual Relational Reasoning (VRR), Appearance State Update, and Appearance Estimation. Uses MobileNetV3 small to extract X_t ∈ R^{n×576}; linear projector B_t into state space d_s = 24; appearance state matrix H_t; time-dependent step size Δ_t; discretization of continuous-time matrices A_t and B_t to Ā_t and B̄_t. Uses structured HiPPO transition matrix A_hippo with learnable diagonal adaptation θ: A_diag = exp(θ), A_t = A_hippo − diag(A_diag); Ā_t = I + Δ_t A_t, B̄_t = Δ_t B_t. VRR: FFT-based frequency-domain circular cross-correlation between B̄_t and H_{t−1}, learnable complex-valued filter Φ_t, selective signal gate IG, cross appearance fusion gate G, latent relational dimension d_l = 6. Appearance State Update: adaptive gated mechanism U_t; H_t = LayerNorm(U_t ⊙ ψ_t + (1 − U_t) ⊙ H̃_t). Appearance Estimation: selection matrix C_t; Y_t = LayerNorm(C_t ⊙ H_t); X̂_{t+1} = (D_t ⊙ X_t) + (W_proj · Y_t). Learning: state-erasure learning H_0 = 0_{n×d_s}; contrastive feature loss L_f with temperature τ_f; orthogonality regularization loss L_orth with temperature τ_h; dynamic loss balancing using exponential moving average with EMA momentum coefficient α = 0.99. Integration: adaptive gated fusion with trajectory cost C_k, appearance similarity M_p, thresholds β_p and β_k, availability vector γ, fusion weights W_k and W_p; integrated into RobMOT and FastTracker; MobileNetV3-small; YOLOv8; CasA detector; Kalman filter (KF) for motion.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Equations: z_t = LayerNorm(X_t); Δ_t = softplus(W_δ z_t + b_δ); B_t = LayerNorm(W_B z_t + b_B); C_t = W_C z_t + b_C. A_diag = exp(θ); A_t = A_hippo − diag(A_diag); Ā_t = I + Δ_t A_t; B̄_t = Δ_t B_t. Φ_t = θ_re + iθ_im. F(B̄_t) = FFT(B̄_t); F(H_{t−1}) = FFT(H_{t−1}); F(I_t) = F(H_{t−1}) ⊙ F(B̄_t) ⊙ Φ_t; I_t = LayerNorm(FFT^{-1}(F(I_t))). G_fused = FFT^{-1}(F(B̄_t) + F(I_t) + F(H_{t−1})); G = σ(LayerNorm(W_g · G_fused)). S_latent = tanh(LayerNorm(W_in I_t + b_in)); S_t = G ⊙ (W_out S_latent + b_out). H̃_t = Ā_t H_{t−1}; ψ_t = tanh(LayerNorm(W_K(B̄_t + S_t))); U_t = σ(LayerNorm(W_u[H_{t−1}; ψ_t])); H_t = LayerNorm(U_t ⊙ ψ_t + (1 − U_t) ⊙ H̃_t). Y_t = LayerNorm(C_t ⊙ H_t); X̂_{t+1} = (D_t ⊙ X_t) + (W_proj · Y_t). M = 1/τ_f (X̂ X^⊤); L_f = −1/N Σ_{i=1}^{N} log(exp(M_ii)/Σ_{j=1}^{N} exp(M_ij)). M_orth = 1/τ_h (H H^⊤); L_orth = 1/N ||M_orth ⊙ (11^⊤ − I)||_F. L_total = L_sim/(μ_sim + ε) + L_orth/(μ_orth + ε); μ_{k,t} = α μ_{k,t−1} + (1 − α) L̄_{k,t}. M_p = X_t X̂_t^⊤; M'_p = max(M_p, β_p); C'_k = min(C_k, β_k); C'_p = 1_n 1_m^⊤ − M'_p; C̃_k = C'_k/β_k; C̃_p = C'_p/(1 − β_p); C_fuse = W_k ⊙ C̃_k + W_p ⊙ C̃_p. Margin M = D_1 − D_2. Dimensions and parameters: d_f = 576, d_s = 24, d_l = 6; EMA momentum coefficient α = 0.99; trained for 5 epochs; Polycepta operates at 90.57 Hz; Feature Extraction (MobileNetV3-Small) 124.78 Hz; Polycepta (Inference & State Evolution) 377.16 Hz; Object Association 2713.25 Hz; Full System Total 90.57 Hz. data.paper_title: Communication Shapes Collective Inference in Self-Adapting LLM Societies: Evidence from Mafia
data.authors: Haonan Huang, Joey Xiao

data.paper_title: PlayerEmbed: Learning Behavioral Fingerprint Representations from Raw Input Sequences
data.authors: Tobias Schneider1,4, Lorenz Sparrenberg3,4, Priya Tomar1,2,3,4, Shahzeb Qamar1,2,3,4, Tobias Deußer3,4, Rafet Sifa1,3,4
data.core_methodology: PlayerEmbed; deep metric learning; hybrid CNN-LSTM encoder; CNN feature extractor inspired by MobileNetV1 using depthwise separable convolutions; 1D depthwise convolution with a kernel size of five and no padding, using 16 depthwise filters per input feature yielding 128 channels per timestep; batch normalization and ReLU; pointwise convolution with 128 output channels followed by batch normalization and ReLU; channel-wise dropout with probability p = 0.1; unidirectional single-layer LSTM with hidden size 128; final hidden state batch normalized and fed into a two-layer MLP projection head with hidden dimension 256 and a GELU activation; L2 normalization to obtain final 128-dimensional output embeddings; Proxy Anchor Loss with default parameters (margin δ = 0.1, scaling factor α = 32) using cosine similarity; random uniform sampling over sequences; separate Adam optimizers with default parameters for model weights and learnable proxies; gradient clipping with a maximum norm of 10; learning rate reduction by a factor of 0.8 if validation loss on KVal does not improve by at least 1% over 10 consecutive epochs; training halted if validation loss does not improve by at least 1% over 20 consecutive epochs; nearest-centroid, nearest-medoid, and k-nearest neighbors (k-NN); cosine similarity s(a, b) = a⊤b/(∥a∥2∥b∥2); centroids computed as ˜cp = 1/Np ∑i xp,i then re-normalized cp = ˜cp/∥˜cp∥2; prediction ˆy(q) = arg maxp s(cp, q); medoid mp = arg maxx∈Rp 1/Np ∑i s(x, xp,i); k-NN prediction ˆy(q) = arg maxc |{i ∈ Nk(q) : yi = c}|; multi-sample averaging ¯q = (∑j qj)/∥∑j qj∥2; 50/50 reference/query split; sequences of fixed length 1,000 timesteps; DDNet physics engine runs at 50 discrete timesteps per second; 8-dimensional feature vector comprising horizontal movement key state encoded as a balanced ternary value (left/none/right), jump key and two mouse buttons encoded as binary values, cursor position in polar form represented by continuous angle and distance, and player velocity in horizontal and vertical directions; all continuous features standardized individually via Z-score normalization using statistics only from training data; traditional baseline with hand-crafted statistical features: state frequencies, transition rates, state durations, raw value statistics, temporal change dynamics, histogram-based properties, and autocorrelations with different lag intervals, resulting in 151-dimensional feature vectors used with MLP, SVM, XGBoost, and nearest-centroid classification; alternative encoders evaluated: Transformer encoder with hidden dimension 128, mean pooling, dropout 0.1, and variable number of layers L; MLP on flattened input with hidden sizes [512, 256], GELU activations and dropout 0.5; ablations removing the CNN feature extractor and removing the projection head; embedding space analysis with UMAP dimensionality reduction to two dimensions and HDBSCAN clustering.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: all evaluation metrics computed in a macro-averaged fashion; 1,000 players in training; held-out sequences from these players and sequences from 1,000 players entirely unseen during training; balanced accuracies 0.950 for players seen during training and 0.879 for players unseen during training; up to 1,000 players for encoder training and a further 1,000 players unseen during training; n ∈ {100, . . . , 1000}; M ∈ {1, 3, 6}; batch size 96; base learning rate 10−3; five random seeds; sequence length 1,000 timesteps equivalent to 20 seconds; DDNet physics engine at 50 discrete timesteps per second; 950 different playable maps; collection from October 30, 2024, to November 8, 2025; restricted to the 3,000 players with highest recorded playtime; available sequences range from 53 to 2,585 corresponding to 17.7 minutes and 14.4 hours of active gameplay, respectively; maximum sample threshold of 1,000 sequences per player corresponding to up to 5.56 hours and retaining 75% of the total input sequences; top 235 players affected by threshold; known set K of 1,000 players; unknown test set UTest of 1,000 players; unknown validation set UVal of 1,000 players; overall split proportions approximately 56% KTrain, 19% KVal, and 25% KTest; Table I balanced accuracy for n = 1000: K→K centroid M = 1 0.790±.007, M = 6 0.950±.003; KU→U centroid M = 1 0.621±.008, M = 6 0.879±.004; Table II nearest-centroid: K→K n = 100 M = 1 0.8990±.009, M = 6 0.9998±.000; K→K n = 1000 M = 1 0.7899±.007, M = 6 0.9503±.003; KU→U n = 100 M = 1 0.2217±.015, M = 6 0.6359±.016; KU→U n = 1000 M = 1 0.6210±.008, M = 6 0.8786±.004; macro F1 K→K n = 1000 M = 1 0.7532±.007, M = 6 0.9385±.005; macro F1 KU→U n = 1000 M = 1 0.6365±.008, M = 6 0.8685±.005; Table III PlayerEmbed n = 100 M = 1 0.8990±.0090, M = 6 0.9998±.0000; n = 1000 M = 1 0.7899±.0070, M = 6 0.9503±.0030; best traditional baseline at n = 100 M = 6 SVM 0.7951±.0077; best traditional baseline at n = 1000 M = 6 MLP 0.3946±.0082; CNN-LSTM runtime 4.5 hours for n = 1000; Transformer runtime 8.1 hours (L = 1), 22.1 hours (L = 2), and 28.6 hours (L = 3); centroid- and medoid-based classification complete in under two seconds; k-NN ranges from 10.4 to 115.3 seconds; relative balanced accuracy decrease when disabling both CNN and projection head: 30.9% for known and 35.1% for unknown at M = 1, and 10.4% and 12.9% at M = 6; four clearly separated clusters each containing 20 to 30 players.

data.paper_title: THE MUSICAL PARAMETERS OF IMMERSION AND FLOW: INVOLVING THE PLAYER, EMOTIONALLY AND PHYSICALLY, IN A VIDEO-GAME.
data.authors: Jennifer Smith
data.core_methodology: A two tier model by the Author (Tier One: Interactivity, Believability, Transitioning, Feedback, Gamer’s Preference; Tier Two: Engagement, Emotional Involvement), informed by Csikszentmihalyi’s flow chart (Ellis’s revision), Brown & Cairns’ theory of the three stages to total immersion (Engagement, Engrossment and Total Immersion), and Winifred Phillips’ model; applied through case studies of Transistor and The Banner Saga and a supporting composition using Whalen’s description of Mickey mousing, Chion’s synchresis, Collins’ kinesonic synchresis, Tagg’s semiotic-based definition of ‘sign’, and mirror neurons and embodied cognition.

Three stages to total immersion: Engagement, Engrossment and Total Immersion. 16 found between 1977 and 1996. 29 tracks; almost 200 cues. (approx.) 8 minute composition. Word Count: 18,535. six months. five songs.

data.authors: Chen-Yu Chen, Jia-Ching Wang, Jhing-Fa Wang, and Yu-Hen Hu
data.core_methodology: Entropy-based criterion; motion entropy feature; entropy motion value (EMV). Angles from 0 to 2π equally divided into AngNum subangles, with AngNum = 16; pk is the fraction of motion vectors whose direction fall within the kth subangle; motion directivity entropy Ek = −pk·log(pk); Mk = Magnitudek / sum_{k=1}^{AngNum} Magnitudek; EMV = sum_{k=1}^{AngNum} Mk·Ek. Motion vectors obtained from uncompressed domain by full-search motion estimation approach. Homoscedastic error model-based time series change point detection algorithm; maximum-likelihood estimation method based on the homoscedastic error model; piecewise linear model y(t) with m line segments y(t)=w11t+w10+e1(t), 0=t0≤t<t1, ..., wm1t+wm0+em(t), tm−1≤t≤tm=n; errors {ei(t)} are independent, identically distributed random variables with zero mean and variance σi^2; homoscedasticity assumption σ1=σ2=···=σm; maximum-likelihood function L(1,n)=sum_{i=1}^{m} miσi^2; iterative method to find change points; p=25; SlopeChange set from zero crossing of the slope of the EMV curve; CP = arg min_j {L(1,j)+L(j+1,n)} subject to p≤j≤n−p and j⊆SlopeChange. Accumulated impact value IVal = PIVal − NIVal, PIVal = mi1, NIVal = mi2; rule-based classifier: if IVal > 0 then semantically significant, otherwise not. Comparison methods: perceived motion model (PME), Triangle model, original homoscedastic error model.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: AngNum = 16; p = 25; EMV and PME calculated once per second; six hours of sports video; 30 fps frame rate. Table 1 lengths: Soccer 101 minutes (Association World Cup 2006, GER - CRC); Basketball 135 minutes (NBA 1998, IND - CHI); Tennis 137 minutes (Wimbledon 2005 (Finale) R. Federer - A. Roddick). Example EMV/PME: near time index 400 EMV ∼60, PME ∼40; around time index 1400 EMV ∼40, PME ∼80. Table 2 (Proposed method (EMV with modified HE model) vs PME [11]): Tennis Fault Precision 85.3%, Recall 81.5%, FScore 83.4%, PME FScore 73.3%; Ace 87.7%, 83.9%, 85.8%, 67.0%; Volley 83.6%, 81.6%, 82.6%, 69.1%; Basketball Scoring 95.4%, 91.8%, 93.5%, 68.8%; Miss 90.7%, 86.6%, 88.6%, 77.6%; Free throw 88.3%, 86.8%, 87.6%, 75.4%; Soccer Goal 98.8%, 96.9%, 97.8%, 84.5%; Free kick 88.5%, 85.6%, 87.0%, 72.7%; Corner 93.8%, 90.9%, 92.3%, 77.4%. Table 3 (Triangle model (T = 45) [11], original [13], modified homoscedastic error model in a soccer video): Modified no. detected segments 26, no. correct segments 21, no. missing segments 0, FSocre(%) 88.7; Original [13] 28, 20, 1, 81.6; Triangle model [11] 39, 28, 0, 76.3. Equations: Ek = −pk·log(pk); Mk = Magnitudek / sum_{k=1}^{AngNum} Magnitudek; EMV = sum_{k=1}^{AngNum} Mk·Ek; L(1,n)=sum_{i=1}^{m} miσi^2; CP = arg min_j {L(1,j)+L(j+1,n)} subject to p≤j≤n−p, j⊆SlopeChange; IVal = PIVal − NIVal, PIVal = mi1, NIVal = mi2; Precision = number of correctly detected events / number of detected events; Recall = number of correctly detected events / number of correct events; FScore = 2*Precision*Recall / (Precision + Recall).

data.paper_title: Cross-View Referring Multi-Object Tracking
data.authors: Sijia Chen, En Yu, Wenbing Tao*
data.core_methodology: CRMOT task; CRTrack benchmark based on CAMPUS and DIVOTrack; CRTracker end-to-end cross-view referring multi-object tracking method combining CrossMOT and APTM; CenterNet backbone with detection head, single-view Re-ID head, cross-view Re-ID head, full Re-ID head; APTM image encoder using Swin Transformer; APTM text encoder using first 6 layers of BERT; APTM cross encoder using last 6 layers of BERT; MvMHAT for frame-to-frame association and multiple cross-views; Prediction Module (Algorithm 1) using frame-to-frame association results as detection results and fusion scores Sf as confidences; Cross-Entropy Loss; Adam optimizer; evaluation metrics CVIDF1, CVMA, CVRIDF1, CVRMA; Fi = Ff + αFAi; Sf = St + βeSa; Lcrmot = Lcmot + Lr; Lcmot = 1/2 (1/ew1 Ld + 1/ew2 (Ls + Lc) + w1 + w2); Lr = −1/N Σ_{i=1}^{N} Σ_{j=1}^{K} yi,j log(pi,j).
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Equations: CVIDF1 = 2 CVIDP × CVIDR / (CVIDP + CVIDR) (1); CVMA = 1 − ((Σ_t mt + fpt + 2mmet) / Σ_t gtt) (2); CVRIDF1 = (Σ_l CVIDF1) / nl (3); CVRMA = (Σ_l max(CVMA, 0)) / nl (4); Fi = Ff + αFAi (5); Lcmot = 1/2 (1/ew1 Ld + 1/ew2 (Ls + Lc) + w1 + w2) (6); Lr = −1/N Σ_{i=1}^{N} Σ_{j=1}^{K} yi,j log(pi,j) (7); Lcrmot = Lcmot + Lr (8); Sf = St + βeSa (9). Parameters: α = 0.01; β = 0.1; Tas = 0.5; Tss = 0.75; Ths = 30; s1 = 3; s2 = 3; s3 = 1; initial learning rate 1×10−4; batchsize 12; 20 epochs; feature dimensions 512; value range 0 to 1 for CVRIDF1 and CVRMA. Dataset: 13 scenes, 82K frames, 344 objects, 221 language descriptions, 8 attributes and 74 words. Results: in-domain all scenes CVRIDF1 54.88 and CVRMA 35.97; Gate2 91.60 CVRIDF1 and 73.40 CVRMA; cross-domain all scenes CVRIDF1 12.52 and CVRMA 2.32; surpasses best single-view by 31.45% CVRIDF1 and 25.83% CVRMA in-domain and by 8.74% CVRIDF1 and 1.92% CVRMA cross-domain; prediction module ablation without 47.54 CVRIDF1 and 28.68 CVRMA, with 54.88 CVRIDF1 and 35.97 CVRMA, gain 7.34% CVRIDF1 and 7.29% CVMA.

data.authors: Lucas Antônio Monezi, Anderson Calderani Junior, Luciano Allegretti Mercadante, Leonardo Tomazeli Duarte, Milton S. Misuta

data.authors: David Varillas-Delgado, Esther Morencos, Jorge Gutie´rrez-Hellı´n, Milla´n Aguilar-Navarro, Alejandro Muñoz, Nuria Mendoza La´iz, Teresa Perucho, Antonio Maestro, Juan Jose´ Tellerı´a-Orriols
data.core_methodology: Transversal prospective study. Genotypic and allelic frequencies were determined. data.paper_title: Quantifying the Effects of American Football Shoulder Pads on Reach Distance and Player Perception of Comfort and Fit
data.authors: Claudia M. Town1*, Ron Jadischke Xenith2, David M. Andrews1
data.core_methodology: Lab-based experimental study; repeated-study design involving each of the three conditions (no shoulder pad, standard shoulder pad, prototype shoulder pad); order of positions within the movement sequence and order of the pad conditions were randomized for each participant; standardized reach distance protocol of three trials of repeated shoulder flexion, extension, abduction, horizontal flexion, and horizontal extension; five GoPro Hero 9 cameras (2.7K resolution, 4:3 aspect ratio, 60 frames/s, shutter speed 1/480, vertically orientated) with modified lenses at a fixed field of view of 47 degrees; five LED lights; retroreflective markers; stabilizing apparatus limiting head and trunk movement; ProAnalyst®3D motion tracking software (Version 1.6.0.2., Xcitex, Cambridge, MA, USA); maximum X (anterior), Y (medio-lateral), and Z (vertical) reach distances; 'Football Shoulder Pad Comfort and Fit' questionnaire using a 5-point Likert scale and yes/no discomfort questions; paired samples t-test for a sub-sample of three participants; full analysis completed only for the right upper extremity; Three-Way Repeated Measures Analyses of Variance (ANOVA) on maximum reach distance (cm) with independent variables trial, condition, and movement.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: n=10 male current or former players; mean height 183.3 cm (± 5.5 cm); body mass 107.1 kg (± 19.6 kg); standard shoulder pad weight approximately 2 kg; five GoPro Hero 9 cameras at 2.7K resolution, 4:3 aspect ratio, 60 frames/s, shutter speed 1/480, fixed field of view 47 degrees; three trials; five LED lights; 5-point Likert scale; left/right paired samples t-test sub-sample of three participants: no differences for every direction (P > 0.05); mean coefficients of variation across all movements and directions 6.3%, 8.4%, and 8.4% for condition 1, 2, and 3, respectively; no shoulder pad vs standard shoulder pad extension X: 9.0 cm (P = 0.007); prototype vs standard extension: 7.0 cm (P < 0.001); no shoulder pad vs standard horizontal extension: 11.4 cm (P = 0.025); no shoulder pad vs standard horizontal flexion Y: 12.6 cm (P = 0.002); no shoulder pad vs standard flexion Z: 17.3 cm (P = 0.008); prototype vs standard flexion Z: 10.3 cm (P = 0.007); prototype vs standard extension Z: 4.7 cm (P = 0.02); no shoulder pad vs standard abduction Z: 25.2 cm (P = 0.005); prototype vs standard abduction Z: 23.1 cm (P = 0.003); prototype more breathable, less restrictive, and lighter than standard (P<0.05); neck collar no discomfort: nine of 10 participants prototype vs three participants standard (P = 0.031); armpit no discomfort: ten participants prototype vs four participants standard (P = 0.031); discomfort descriptors: 'tight' 66% and 'rigid/stiff' 33%; standard size football diameter approximately 17 cm; flexion and horizontal flexion X mean reach differences less than 2.6 cm for all condition comparisons; mean uncertainty values up to 1 cm; sub-analysis three participants (30% of sample).

data.paper_title: SoccerNet-Caption: Dense Video Captioning for Soccer Broadcasts Commentaries
data.authors: Hassan Mkhallati∗,1, Anthony Cioppa∗,2,3, Silvio Giancola∗,3, Bernard Ghanem3, Marc Van Droogenbroeck2
data.core_methodology: Single-anchored Dense Video Captioning (SDVC); two-stage approach: spotting model and captioning model cascaded, denoted M, both using a frozen feature encoder E, aggregator A, and either spotting head S or captioning head C; {tprop_0,...,tprop_N} = S(A(E(video))); caption_n = C(A(E(video[tprop_n−∆/2, tprop_n+∆/2]))); feature encoders ResNet-152, I3D, C3D, and Baidu; feature dimensionality reduced to 512 using PCA for the first three encoders and a linear transformation for Baidu features; aggregator modules NetVLAD, NetRVLAD, NetVLAD++, and NetRVLAD++; spotting head as a dense layer with sigmoid activation outputting 2 classes (foreground comment, background), binary cross-entropy loss, and Non-Maximum Suppression (NMS); captioning head with two fully connected layers with ReLU activation and dropout, a vanilla LSTM with softmax activation, cross-entropy loss, teacher forcing, and greedy inference; Adam optimizer; evaluation metrics METEOR@δ (resp. BLEU@δ, ROUGE@δ, and CIDEr@δ), mAP@δ for action spotting, and SODA c.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Dataset: 471 SoccerNet untrimmed broadcast games; 36,894 timestamped comments; 715.9 hours; average 78.33 temporally localized comments per game; comments range from 4 to 93 words following a long tail distribution with 21.38 words on average; vocabulary size 1,769 words; videos available at 25fps in 224p and 720p; frame features at 2fps pre-extracted using e.g. ResNET or the Baidu feature encoder at 1fps; features extracted at 1 or 2 fps. Training: Adam optimizer with PyTorch’s default β parameters; initial learning rate 10−3; reduce learning rate by a factor of 10 when validation loss plateaus during 10 consecutive epochs; stopping criterion 10−6; temporal pooling module initialized with 64 clusters; LSTM hidden vector dimension 512; dropout after fully connected layers 0.4; word embedding dimension 256. Spotting ablation: input video chunk and NMS window fixed to 15 seconds; best mAP@5 10.5 (Baidu, NetVLAD); Baidu NetVLAD++ mAP@30 44.5 and mAP@60 41.8; chosen window 15 seconds and NMS 30 seconds. Captioning ablation: Baidu and NetVLAD best; chosen window 45 seconds; best L=4, TF ratio=1, B@4 6.0, M 23.7, R 24.1, C 18.5; metrics B@4, M, R, C. SDVC results for Afine−tuned capt.→spot.: mAP@5 9.25, mAP@30 49.40, mAP@60 46.97, B@4 6.62, M 23.84, R 24.53, C 21.45, B@4@30 21.63, M@30 29.44, R@30 22.09, C@30 27.20, SODA c 7.79.

data.paper_title: SportsCap: Monocular 3D Human Motion Capture and Fine-grained Understanding in Challenging Sports Videos
data.authors: Xin Chen, Anqi Pang, Wei Yang, Yuexin Ma, Lan Xu, Jingyi Yu
data.core_methodology: SportsCap; motion embedding space via principal component analysis (PCA); motion embedding function θ = Mm(α) and θ = Σ_{k=1}^K α_k bm_k + am = α⊺Bm + am, also J = M′m(α); pose coefficient α; Skinned Multi-Person Linear model (SMPL); Motion Embedding Module using a ResNet-152 convolutional encoder followed by two fully connected layers to regress pose coefficients α; sub-motion classifier WS-DAN; multi-stream spatial-temporal Graph Convolutional Network(ST-GCN) with J-stream, B-stream, and P-stream; 2s-AGCN structure; 10-layer ST-GCN; 1D convolution with residual blocks; Semantic Attributes Mapping Block (SAMB); semantic attributes (SAs); sub-motions (SMs); weak-perspective project system with only scale s, translation parameters t, t∈R2, and orthographic projection function Π(·); MoSh; Vicon 12 views marker-based motion capture system; Adam optimizer; cross-entropy losses; stage-wise training strategy with Lmem + Lapm.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Metrics: PCK-0.3, PCK-0.5, Top-1 accuracy, Spearman’s rank correlation (Sp. Cor.). Equations/variables: N denotes the joint number of SMPL; K denotes the dimension of pose coefficients α; Mm(α): R^K ↦ R^3N; θ = Mm(α); θ = Σ_{k=1}^K α_k bm_k + am = α⊺Bm + am; J = M′m(α); α(x) = Fm_conv(x; W); J(x) = α(x)⊺Bm + am; Lprior = ∥W(α − α̂)∥2; Ĵ = ŝΠ(J (Mm(α̂), β̂)) + t̂; Ldata = ∥V(J − Ĵ)∥2; Lsmpl = ∥θ − θ̂∥2 + ∥β − β̂∥2; Lmem = Lprior + λdataLdata + λsmplLsmpl; Lattr = Σ_{c=1}^{Ns} Σ_{i=1}^{Nc} y_i^c log (x_i^c); Ltask = Σ_{j=1}^{Nf} y_j log (x_j); Lapm = Lattr + λALtask. Coefficients/parameters: λdata, λsmpl (10 and 2 in our case); λA (2 in our case); 90 consecutive frames; 90×25 (90 frames and 25 dimensions in feature); 256×256 image patches; random rotations (−45° to +45°), random scaling (0.7 to 1.3), and flipping horizontally; first 100 epochs and AMP in the following 50 epochs; complete SportsCap in the last ten epochs; learning rates of the 0th, 70th, and 150th epoch are 10−3, 10−4, and 10−5; 4 NVidia 2080Ti GPUs; 10 hours for the Motion Embedding Module, 5 hours for Action Parsing Module, and 2.5 hours for the whole SportsCap; 0.5s for Motion Embedding Module, 0.05s for Action Parsing Module, and 1.0s for data fetching; dataset: 640 videos (110K frames), about 450,000 annotated skeletons, 25 joints, more than 500,000 motion frames of 30 performers covering nine activities, about 1,000 frames for each performance, 12 views, 63 marks; somersault has 10 categories, indicating rotation angle for 0 to 3240 (0∗360 to 9∗360) degrees. Reported figures: SM-1 to SM-4 sub-motion classification average around 96%; FineGym: Random 16.7/6.7/0.3, ST-GCN 19.5/13.7/11.0, TRN-2stream 31.4/83.0/42.9, Ours 34.2/85.7/46.9; SMART Ours (J+B+P) SAMB 96.4/99.8/89.5/86.5/92.6/82.2; AQA Ours 97.5/99.8/97.9/96.3/94.0; Sp. Cor. SMART C3D-LSTM 53.7, R2+1D 55.6, Ours 61.7; AQA C3D-LSTM 84.9, R2+1D 89.6, Ours 86.2.

data.paper_title: 3D reconstruction system and multiobject local tracking algorithm designed for billiards
data.authors: Francisco J. Rodriguez-Lozano, Juan C. G´amez-Granados, H´ector Mart´ınez, Jose M. Palomares, Joaqu´ın Olivares
data.core_methodology: multiobject local tracking (MOLT); baize segmentation via Canny method, binary dilation, Hough transform, line-equation intersections, rectangle/vertex selection using baize size, ROI generation; ball detection and identification via Sobel method, Hough circle detection, RGB-to-HSV transformation, color voting with HSV ranges, false-ball discarding; MOLT tracker populations/local trackers with center point, size, histogram weight, distance weight, and total weight = α ∗ histogram weight + (1 −α) ∗distance weight; α = 0.5; Bhattacharyya distance for histogram similarity; Euclidean distance normalized by baize diagonal; QuickSort ordering of trackers; diversity-oriented approach for new populations (50% based on best tracker bt1, 30% on second-best tracker bt2, 20% on third-best tracker bt3); z-coordinate/pocket handling; 3D reconstruction using open X3D standard with Extrusion, Sphere, and PositionInterpolator (Key, keyValue); evaluation metrics Jaccard index, IDF1, MOTA, MOTP, and mean opinion score (MOS).
data.key_metrics_and_variables: total weight = α ∗ histogram weight + (1 −α) ∗distance weight; α = 0.5; number of trackers gradually increased from 10 to 2000 in increments of 10; exploration radius fixed at 100 pixels for the cue ball and 80 pixels for the remaining balls; selected 2,000 trackers for the cue ball and 400 for all other balls; diversity-oriented approach: 50% of new positions randomly within exploration radius based on best tracker (bt1), 30% based on second-best tracker (bt2), 20% based on third-best tracker (bt3); Jaccard index ranges from 0 to 1; IDF1 best result is 1; MOTA ranges from −∞ to 1; MOTP ranges from 0 to +∞; MOS response range 0 to 10; MOLT averages: blackball IDF1 1.0000, Jaccard 0.8771, MOTA 1.0000, MOTP 0.3466; carom billiards IDF1 1.0000, Jaccard 0.8751, MOTA 1.0000, MOTP 3.0680; snooker IDF1 1.0000, Jaccard 0.8578, MOTA 1.0000, MOTP 0.9537; HSV color space H [0, 180], S [0, 255], V [0, 255]; blackball red H[120−179], S[180−255], V[100−200]; yellow H[15−30], V[160−255]; black V[0−50]; cue S[0−50]; snooker pink H[130−179], V[190−255]; brown H[0−50], S[0−150], V[0−180]; blue H[90−140], S[150−255], V[150−200]; green H[80−100], S[150−255]; carom billiards same as blackball with no black; RGB sensor: focal length 525 pixels, FOV 62.7 degrees, resolution 640 × 480, frame rate 20 fps, pixel correspondence 3.47 mm (camera placed at 1853 mm over the table); Nvidia jetson nano with ARM A57 @ 1.43 GHz and 4 GB LPDDR4; dataset 300 recorded billiard shots (100 videos per modality) over 85,000 images; ground truth trajectories 21 blackball, 16 carom billiards, 16 snooker; table size 211.5 × 120.5 × 78 cm; baize and cushion area 185.4 × 93.5 cm; balls 57 mm diameter for blackball and carom billiards, 51 mm diameter for snooker; MOS with ten users according to ITU-T Rec. P.911 (above 6 experts); MOS overall score 7.6 (out of 10); fluency average 8; reconstruction quality average 7.9; learning utility average 6.8; overall marks: blackball 7.6, carom billiards 7.7, snooker 7.4.

data.paper_title: Lateral Ankle Joint Injuries in Indoor and Court Sports - A Systematic Video Analysis of 445 Non-consecutive Case Series
data.authors: Timo Bagehorn, Mark de Zee, Daniel T.P. Fong, Kristian Thorborg, Uwe G. Kersting, Filip Gertz Lysdal
data.core_methodology: Descriptive, observational, non-consecutive case series study using systematic video analysis; Kinovea (Version 0.8.27) for slow-motion frame-by-frame viewing, 600% zoom, and event highlighting; independent analysis by two reviewers; classification of injury mechanism according to the IOC consensus statement; Cohen’s Kappa for inter-rater reliability; Microsoft Excel and Python’s sklearn toolkit for data analysis and descriptive statistics.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: 445 unique video-recorded lateral ankle sprain injuries; 585 injury videos collected, 140 discarded, 445 used; 198 videos (45%) one camera angle, 169 (38%) two angles, 67 (15%) three angles, 11 (2.5%) four or more angles; injuries sustained between 1995 and 2021 by 396 different athletes, of which 125 were female (32%), 309 (69%) injuries suffered by men and 136 (31%) injuries suffered by women; basketball (n=184; 41%), volleyball (n=125; 28%), handball (n=54; 12%), tennis (n=50; 11%), badminton (n=22; 5%); 298 (67%) direct contact, 113 (25%) non-contact, 32 (7%) indirect contact; direct contact injuries especially prevalent in basketball (76%), handball (80%), and volleyball (82%), while non-contact injuries dominated in tennis and badminton (4% vs 96% across both); Inversion (65%) and internal rotation (33%) primary distortion motions, lateral forefoot (53%) and lateral midfoot (40%) main fulcrums; landing on another player’s foot leading cause (n=246, 55%), primarily inversion (79%) around a midfoot fulcrum (54%); non-contact landings on floor (n=144, 33%) primarily distortion around a forefoot fulcrum (69%); basketball (n=140, 76%), handball (n=43; 80%), and volleyball (n=103; 82%) mainly direct contact injuries, while tennis (n=48; 96%) and badminton (n=21; 96%) primarily non-contact injuries; majority contact locations with/on top of opponent’s foot (n=200; 45%) or floor (n=187; 42%); more than half after jump landing (n=226; 51%), followed by running (n=55; 12%) and shuffle movements (n=43; 10%); primary distortion motion predominantly inversion (n=288; 65%) or internal rotation (n=146; 33%); secondary distortion internal rotation (n=213; 48%) or inversion (n=135; 30%); primary plantar flexion (n=8; 2%), secondary plantar flexion (n=19; 4%); contact injuries inversion primary (n=213; 73%), followed by internal rotation (n=74; 25%); non-contact evenly distributed between inversion (n=59; 52%) and internal rotation (n=49; 42%); lateral forefoot (n=235; 53%) and lateral midfoot (n=179; 40%) main fulcrum; 249 (56%) caused by contact with another player's foot; contact injuries occurring after ‘foot contact’ (55% of all cases, n=246), and injuries occurring after ‘floor contact’ with no externally distorting object or body (indirect and non-contact; 33% of all cases, n=144); 65% of basketball, 78% of volleyball, and 61% of handball injuries occurred after foot contact; for tennis and badminton, 100% and 95% were floor contact injuries, respectively; foot contact injuries lateral midfoot fulcrum 54% (132 out of 246), lateral forefoot fulcrum 41% (102 of 246), inversion primary 79% (194 out of 246); non-contact and indirect contact injuries occurring after floor contact forefoot fulcrum 69% (100 out of 144), inversion 49% (71 out of 144), internal rotation 47% (68 out of 144); 3.6x higher chance predominantly inversion compared to ‘on floor’ injuries (3.73 vs 1.04 chance of inversion); Cohen’s Kappa IRR 0.94 for type of landing contact, 0.87 for injury mechanism, 0.80 for preceding movement, 0.74 for shoe-surface fixation point, 0.69 for initial contact location of injured foot, 0.66 for primary distortion motion, and 0.59 for secondary distortion motion.

data.paper_title: Revolutionizing sports: Unleashing the power of next-gen markerless motion analytics
data.authors: Dippu Kumar Singh
data.core_methodology: Mixed-methods analysis technique incorporating quantitative and qualitative research methods; questionnaire distribution; in-depth conversations with experts; pilot programs; high-resolution cameras and specialized software to track skeletal landmarks; case studies of NBA and FIFA; evaluation based on accuracy, reliability, scalability, and usability; model comparison of AI-driven pose estimation models that utilize deep learning technology, computer vision-based models, hybrid models, and cloud-based tracking systems; named algorithms/technologies: CNNs and Recurrent neural networks (RNNs).

data.paper_title: The effect of organizational differentiation in football training on young football players
data.authors: Olav Størdal, Terje Dalen, Pål Lagestad*
data.core_methodology: Intervention study with an experimental randomized crossover design; method described as a counterbalanced crossover design. Randomization was performed at the team level, with three teams randomly assigned to begin with either the differentiated or non-differentiated condition; counterbalancing was applied and conditions were implemented on separate days. The intervention consisted of conducting the same session plan four times over 2 weeks; each team experienced two training sessions with differentiation and two without. Within-subject design; stratified sample. Psychological variables measured by a brief questionnaire with single-item measures using a Likert scale from 1-5. Physical measurements used Polar Team Pro GPS technology with GPS and accelerometers; total distance, number of sprints and number of accelerations registered at 10 Hz, heart rate sampled at 1 Hz. Statistical analysis used IBM SPSS Version 29; Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests; Wilcoxon nonparametric tests / Wilcoxon non-parametric test; effect sizes estimated using r (Z/√N), interpreted according to Cohen’s conventional thresholds (0.1 = small, 0.3 = medium, 0.5 = large Cohen, 1988); significant differences set at p ≤0.05; data presented as mean ± standard deviation. Discussion considered Csikszentmihaly’s (1975) flow theory.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Total participants 71; three teams; 13–14-year-old boys; five clubs with Boys U14 teams with more than 15 players contacted; valid physical data UG 30 and LG 20; valid psychological data UG 28 and LG 30; Team 1 valid physical data UG 7, LG 6; valid psychological data UG 8, LG 8; players at training sessions 16–18; Team 2 valid physical data UG 10, LG 5; valid psychological data UG 9, LG 6; players at training sessions 16–31; Team 3 valid physical data UG 13, LG 9; valid psychological data UG 11, LG 16; players at training sessions 30–50. Psychological variables: wellbeing, mastery, joy, satisfaction, experienced development, preference for future sessions; Likert scale from 1-5: 1 = strongly disagree, 2 = disagree, 3 = neither agree nor disagree, 4 = agree, and 5 = strongly agree. Physical variables: total distance, number of sprints, number of accelerations, average heart rate; total distance measured in meters; heart rate measured as average number of heart beats per minute. Locomotor categories: Acc1 (2.00−2.99 m/s²), Acc2 (>3.00 m/s²); sprint threshold 19 km·h−1; total distance, number of sprints, number of accelerations registered at 10 Hz; heart rate sampled at 1 Hz. Training details: rondo 4vs1-exercise in squares of 5x5 meters; 2 vs 2 small sided games (SSG) with floater; final part 5 vs 5 or 6 vs 6 SSGs for 4∗4 min, with 1.5 min recovery between games. Statistical thresholds: Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests p < 0.05; Wilcoxon effect size r (Z/√N); Cohen’s conventional thresholds 0.1 = small, 0.3 = medium, 0.5 = large; significant differences p ≤0.05. Results: UG wellbeing and mastery no significant difference (p > 0.05); UG pleasure Z = −2.4, p = 0.015, r = 0.454; UG satisfaction Z = 2.2, p = 0.025, r = 0.416; UG perceived development Z = 2.6, p = 0.008, r = 0.491; UG preference for differentiated training Z = 2.7, p = 0.008, r = 0.510; LG no significant difference in wellbeing, mastery, pleasure, satisfaction, and perceived development (p > 0.05); LG no difference in desire for differentiated training sessions even when controlled with a negatively worded question. Total distance during entire training: LG Z = −3.4, p = 0.003, r = 0.760; UG Z = −2.7, p = 0.007, r = 0.493; no significant change in total distance during small-sided games for both groups (p > 0.05); no difference in total distance for UG during SSGs; higher total distance in SSGs (2vs2+1) for LG Z = 2.3, p = 0.023, r = 0.325. Accelerations between 2 and 3m/s2: UG Z = 2.1, p = 0.032, r = 0.383; LG Z = −2.4, p = 0.016, r = 0.587; no change in number of sprints between differentiated and non-differentiated training in the SSGs for both groups (p > 0.05); accelerations above 3m/s2: no significant difference for LG (p > 0.05), UG Z = −2.5, p = 0.011, r = 0.456. Heart rate: UG entire training Z = 2.6, p = 0.010, r = 0.475; UG SSGs Z = 2.2, p = 0.026, d = 0.382; UG 2v2+1 games Z = −3, p = 0.003, r = 0.402; UG Rondo 4vs1 Z = 3.4, p < 0.001, r = 0.621; LG no significant differences in heart rate in differentiated vs non-differentiated training for entire training or parts (p > 0.05).

data.paper_title: Towards Temporal Compositional Reasoning in Long-Form Sports Videos
data.authors: Siyu Cao1,2 , Lu ZhangB1,2 , Ruizhe Zeng1,2 , and Zhi-yong LiuB1,2,3
data.core_methodology: SportsTime: large-scale benchmark for long-form sports video understanding with 14K+ open-ended QA pairs and 50K+ step-wise temporal evidence annotations across five team sports and five task types (perception, temporal, tactical, causal, counterfactual); expert-guided semi-automatic annotation pipeline (expert template design, candidate QA generation, two-stage manual review). Chain-of-Time Reasoning (CoTR): problem formulation with trajectory T=[n1,...,nT,a], step nt=<st,τt>, factorization πθ(T|V,q)=(∏_{t=1}^{T}πθ(nt|V,q,n<t))·πθ(a|V,q,n≤T); three stages: Visual Time Anchoring with mm:ss timestamp overlay; Reinforcement Learning with Temporally Grounded Reasoning using temporal-reward GRPO (tr-GRPO), reward R(T)=λ_fmt r_fmt(T)+λ_acc r_acc(T)+λ_temporal r_temporal(T), r_temporal(T)=α r_cov(T)+(1−α) r_cor(T); Anchor-Triggered Interactive Observation (AT-IO)/anchor-observe-infer loop with anchor-triggered local sampling and evidence-grounded reasoning. Evaluation: LLM-as-Judge (Qwen2.5-VL-7B fixed judge) and Step-wise Grounding Alignment (SGA) using temporal IoU and human assessment of ESA, ICR, FLC.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Dataset: 14K+ open-ended QA pairs; 50K+ step-wise temporal evidence annotations; 1,575 videos; 208 full-match videos; 1,367 highlight videos; SportsTime table: 14,326 QA, 1053.25 s, TS+S stepwise time, Open QA type; highlights ∼10 min and full-game broadcasts ∼50 min. Reward variables: R(T)=λ_fmt r_fmt(T)+λ_acc r_acc(T)+λ_temporal r_temporal(T); r_temporal(T)=α r_cov(T)+(1−α) r_cor(T); r_cor∈[0,1]; α is a tunable weight. Experimental settings: 128 frames for training, up to 768 frames for inference, Qwen3-VL-4B backbone, 2× NVIDIA H100 (80GB). Main results: GPT-5 Avg 40.72; Gemini-2.5-Pro Avg 29.37; Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct Avg 27.45; Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct Avg 25.15; CoTR(full) Avg 29.24, human Avg subset 30.50; improvement overall (+4.09%). SGA table: Base Acc 25.15, Anchor 11.95, mIoU 0.2601, H@0.5 30.03; Zero-shot CoT Acc 24.01, Anchor 19.49, mIoU 0.2042, H@0.5 26.34; Time-prompted CoT Acc 19.53, Anchor 91.80, mIoU 0.1244, H@0.5 12.12; Native-GRPO Acc 26.72, Anchor 13.10, mIoU 0.3128, H@0.5 32.09; tr-GRPO Acc 27.31, Anchor 95.76, mIoU 0.5812, H@0.5 56.89% (text also reports mIoU 0.58, Hit@0.5 56.89%). Human SGA: FLC 4.50/5, ICR 4.02/5, ESA 3.65/5. Judge consistency: Avg. pairwise agreement = 88.34%, Fleiss’ κ = 0.57; Cohen’s κ (Qwen/MiniMax/GLM vs Human) = 0.6467/0.5759/0.5882.

data.paper_title: ExposureEngine: Oriented Logo Detection and Sponsor Visibility Analytics in Sports Broadcasts
data.authors: Mehdi Houshmand Sarkhoosh‡§, Frøy Øye‡, Henrik Nestor Sørlie‡, Nam Hoang Vu‡, Dag Johansen¶, Cise Midoglu§, Tomas Kupka§, and P˚al Halvorsen∗‡§
data.core_methodology: ExposureEngine end-to-end system with Oriented Bounding Box (OBB) detection; OBB YOLO model based on YOLOv11; six fine-tuned YOLO-based OBB detection configurations (YOLOv8 and YOLOv11, nano/small/medium/large); Varifocal Loss (VFL) quality-aware objective replacing the default classifier Binary Cross Entropy (BCE) with soft targets from the task-aligned assigner, with Focal Loss (FL) ablated; oriented-box IoU loss and distribution focal loss (DFL) in the overall OBB objective; AdamW optimizer with random rotation, scaling, and contrast adjustment; LangGraph agent framework with Analysis Agent, Highlight Agent, Sharing Agent, and Coordinator Agent using an LLM with a domain-specific system prompt; Tightness Ratio (TR) using the shoelace formula; Orientation Necessity (ON) as the absolute angle between the OBB and the horizontal axis; OBB-IoU; Label Studio annotations converted to YOLO OBB format with four-corner polygon coordinates; 80-10-10 training/validation/test split; minimum enclosing axis-aligned rectangle for HBB derivation.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Dataset: 1,103 frames; 670 unique sponsor logos / 670 unique logo classes; 97 professional soccer highlight clips; 32 matches; 16 teams; 2024 Swedish men’s elite league season; sampled at 1 FPS; videos per match 3 (typically one per event type); event types Goal, Shot, Yellow card, Offside, Substitution; split 80-10-10; dominant sponsors appearing in over 500 instances. Training: 200 epochs; three NVIDIA A100 GPUs (80 GB VRAM each); SLURM-based distributed processing; input resolution 1280×720; batch size 32; AdamW initial learning rate 0.001; model sizes nano 2.7M parameters, small 9.7M parameters, medium 26.4M parameters, large 44.5M parameters. Loss: BCE(p, q) = −q log p −(1 −q) log(1 −p); LVFL = (αpγ(1 −y) + qy) × BCE(p, q) with (γ, α) = (2.0, 0.75); L(ours)_cls = 1/|A| Σ_{a∈A} Σ_{c=1}^C LVFL(p_{a,c}, y_{a,c}, q_{a,c}); L = λbox Lbox + λcls Lcls + λdfl Ldfl. Metrics: N = Tvr frames; Af = W × H; cℓ,i = min(1, Aℓ,i/Af); zℓ,i = 1 if cℓ,i > 0, 0 otherwise; Eℓ = Δt Σ_{i=1}^N zℓ,i, Δt = 1/r; C¯presentℓ = 100 · (Σ_i zℓ,i cℓ,i)/(Σ_i zℓ,i); C¯overallℓ = 100 · (Σ_i zℓ,i cℓ,i)/N; maximum coverage = max cℓ,i over all frames scaled to percentage; detection count is total number of OBB detections assigned to the brand across the entire video; all coverage values derived from clipped OBB polygons and capped at 100% per frame. Table II: YOLOv8-Medium mAP@0.5 0.846, Precision 0.96, Recall 0.88; YOLOv8-Large 0.853, 0.96, 0.88; YOLOv11-Nano 0.781, 0.95, 0.85; YOLOv11-Small 0.817, 0.96, 0.86; YOLOv11-Medium 0.859, 0.96, 0.87; YOLOv11-Large 0.847, 0.95, 0.88. Table III: YOLOv11-Medium (OBB) 0.859, 0.96, 0.87; YOLOv11-Medium (HBB) 0.865, 0.95, 0.88; HBB mAP@0.5 +0.6%; all differences within ±1%. OBB-IoU: at IoU threshold 0.5 over 96.8% of predictions match ground truth; 63.4% achieve IoU more than 0.9; high proportion above 0.7 IoU is 83.8%. TR = area(OBB)/area(HBB); ON = absolute angle between OBB and horizontal axis; six bins spanning 0° to 90° in 5° increments; minimum near 55°–60° (TR around 0.40); Figure 8 examples TR=0.41, TR=0.63, TR=0.49; 95% confidence intervals. Training dynamics: mAP@0.5 steep rise during first 20–30 epochs; loss drop within first 20 epochs; mAP@50–95 stabilizes in high 0.7 range. Inference: 30-second broadcast video segment, each configuration repeated ten times; MacBook M3 CPU row values 12, 18 GB, –, 148.7 ms, 6.72 FPS; G4dn.xlarge GPU row values 4, 16 GB, 16 GB, 50.0 ms, 19.98 FPS; GPU acceleration yields nearly threefold speedup; pipeline reaches 19.98 FPS.

data.paper_title: Harder, shorter, sharper, forward: A comparison of women’s and men’s elite football gameplay (2020-2025)

data.core_methodology: StatsBomb Events Data; team performance tiers (top, mid, bottom) based on percentile ranks of final league standings within each season and competition, dividing teams into approximately equal thirds; linear regression for temporal evolution within tiers using season year as independent variable and metric of interest as dependent variable on individual team-season observations; one-way ANOVA for tier differences; independent-samples t-tests for gender differences by tier; derived spatial/tactical features: pass center of mass (mean x-coordinate of completed pass origins), vertical play (ratio of forward-directed to lateral passes, with forward if x-component exceeds y-component), offsides; pitch-passing networks constructed on a 10×5 grid (50 nodes) using StatsBomb’s standardized 120×80 coordinate system, with directed, weighted edges for successful passes between regions, edge weights corresponding to number of passes exchanged and normalized by total network strength (sum of all edge weights) to sum to 100; network metrics: Average shortest path length, Maximum eigenvalue of the adjacency matrix, Outreach (sum of pass counts multiplied by Euclidean distance between connected regions, normalized by total network strength); all statistical tests two-tailed with significance threshold p < 0.05; visualization significance only when p < 0.05 and absolute percent change over five-year period exceeded 5%.

data.paper_title: AttTrack: Online Deep Attention Transfer for Multi-object Tracking
data.authors: Keivan Nalaie, Rong Zheng
data.core_methodology: AttTrack (online deep attention transfer network): teacher-student framework with a complex teacher and lightweight student; key components: 1) cross-model feature learning to align intermediate representations from teacher and student, 2) interleaving execution of the two models at inference time, 3) incorporating updated teacher predictions as prior knowledge. Teacher runs every K frames (key frames); student runs in the interim K-1 frames. Teacher heatmap: ht_k = Ht(xk) (Eq. 2); student output: ys_{k+i} = g(f(x_{k+i}), Phi(ht_k, i)) (Eq. 3), where Phi extrapolates the teacher heatmap to frame k+i, f is student backbone features, and g is fusion. Attention update: estimate each identified object's velocity from bounding box locations in previous frames and predict subsequent locations with a simple linear kinematic equation; update heatmaps accordingly. Fusion function: g(f(x_{k+i}), Phi(ht_k, i)) = (f(x_{k+i}), Phi(ht_k, i)) (Eq. 4), appending extrapolated teacher features with student features; fused features fed into heatmap and re-ID branches as defined in [39]. Student loss: L_student = 1/2(1/e^omega1(L_heatmap + L_box) + 1/e^omega2 L_identity + omega1 + omega2) (Eq. 5), with learnable task-based parameters omega1 and omega2, heatmap loss, box-size loss, and re-identification loss defined in [39]. Cross-model feature learning: Explicit Feature Mapping (EFM) uses a single linear layer to map re-ID features to the number of identities (encoded as a one-hot vector) in the training set, applied to both student and teacher models; Implicit Feature Mapping (IFM) performs implicit feature mapping for the student by mincing the re-ID feature layer in the teacher model, using extracted teacher features as additional supervision with L_W = L_student(W) + L_id-att(W) (Eq. 6), where L_id-att is L2 loss of re-ID features. Object association: visual features used to match a trajectory and a detected object, then IoU measure to determine a true match; cosine similarity is used for visual-based feature similarity; a Kalman filter [39] updates each trajectory position state. Uses FairMOT one-stage detector; teacher can use DLA34; student uses DLA34-small or YOLOv5-small. Baselines: Teacher-only, Student-only, Naive-Mix, AttTrack-no-update (Phi(ht_k, i) = ht_k), and Layerwise.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Equations and parameters: MOTA = 1 - (sum_t FP_t + FN_t + IDSW_t)/(sum_t GT_t), Eq. 1, where t is frame index, FP_t, FN_t, and IDSW_t are false positives, false negatives, and ID switched objects, and GT is ground truth bounding boxes. ht_k = Ht(xk) (Eq. 2). ys_{k+i} = g(f(x_{k+i}), Phi(ht_k, i)) (Eq. 3). g(f(x_{k+i}), Phi(ht_k, i)) = (f(x_{k+i}), Phi(ht_k, i)) (Eq. 4). L_student = 1/2(1/e^omega1(L_heatmap + L_box) + 1/e^omega2 L_identity + omega1 + omega2) (Eq. 5). L_W = L_student(W) + L_id-att(W) (Eq. 6). K values: Figure 2 uses K = 4; Table 3 uses K = 6; Table 4 and Table 6 use K = 2, 4, 6; Figure 7 uses 11 Ks in [2, 12]. Implementation: Adam optimizer, 35 epochs, starting learning rate 1e-5 lowering every 25 epochs, batch size 12, input frame size 1088 x 608 pixels; NVIDIA GTX 3080 with 8 GB GDDR6, Ubuntu 20.04, Pytorch v1.8, CUDA v11.3. DLA34-small has 16.55M parameters. Table 1: YOLOv5 IDF1 65.90, MOTA 62.40, FPS 43.93, Parameter size 5.01 M; YOLOv5-mid IDF1 63.20, MOTA 56.90, FPS 46.16, Parameter size 1.38 M; YOLOv5-small IDF1 44.70, MOTA 38.90, FPS 59.32, Parameter size 0.31 M. data.paper_title: DiffusionTrack: Diffusion Model For Multi-Object Tracking
data.authors: Run Luo123, Zikai Song3*, Lintao Ma3, Jinlin Wei34, Wei Yang3, Min Yang12*
data.core_methodology: DiffusionTrack formulates object detection and association jointly as a consistent denoising diffusion process from paired noise boxes to paired ground-truth boxes; data samples are paired bounding boxes z0 = (Bt−1, Bt), z0 ∈ RN×8, and a neural network fθ(zs, s, Xt−1, Xt), s = {0, · · · , T}, is trained to predict z0 from paired noise boxes zs conditioned on the corresponding two adjacent images (Xt−1, Xt); it uses a YOLOX backbone with FPN and a diffusion head with RoI-feature, spatial-temporal fusion module (STF), and association score head; forward diffusion uses Gaussian noise and a variance schedule β1, · · · , βT with q(xt|xt−1) = N(xt; p 1 −βtxt−1, βtI) and xt = √¯αtx0 + (1 −¯αt)ϵ, where ¯αt = Qt s=0(1 −βs); training samples pairs with an interval of 5, pads boxes to Ntrain, adds Gaussian noise with a monotonically decreasing cosine schedule for αt, and uses Hungarian matching algorithm, 3D GIoU and 3D IoU, focal loss, and L1 loss; inference pads repeated prior boxes to Ntest, adds Gaussian noise by B = (1 −αt) · B + αt · Bnoise under the control of αt, performs denoising with DDIM sampling steps s, uses IoU similarity and a simple Kalman filter to reassociate lost objects, and uses NMS post-processing; perturbation schedule is t = 1000 · f(x) with f(x) = log(x+1)/log2.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Metrics: MOTA, IDF1, HOTA, AssA, DetA, IDs, Frag. Hyperparameters: τconf = 0.25, τnms3d = 0.6, τdet = 0.7, τnms2d = 0.7; Ntrain = 500; Ntest = 500/800/1000; sampling steps 1 to 8; interval length of 5 frames; image size 1440×800; 236M trainable diffusion head parameters; mini-batch size 16; 8 NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3090; FP32; PyTorch 1.10; Python 3.8; initial learning rate 1e-4; warm-up learning rate 2.5e-5 with 0.2 warm-up factor on the first 5 epochs; final decrease factor 0.1; 30 epochs + 30 epochs (MOT17), 40 epochs (DanceTrack); total training time about 30 hours; FPS measured with FP16-precision and batch size of 1. Loss weights: λ1, λ2 and λ3 are assigned as 2, 5 and 2. Equations: Ldet = 1/Npos Σ_{(Td,Tgt)∈M} λ1Lcls(Td, Tgt) + λ2Lreg(Td, Tgt) + λ3(1 −GIoU3d(Td, Tgt)); B = (1 −αt) · B + αt · Bnoise; Bdet = (1−αt)·Bdet + αt·Bnoise; t = 1000 · f(x); f(x) = log(x+1)/log2. Results: MOT17 DiffusionTrack MOTA 77.9, IDF1 73.8, HOTA 60.8, AssA 58.8, DetA 63.2, IDs 3819, Frag 4815; MOT20 DiffusionTrack MOTA 72.8, IDF1 66.3, HOTA 55.3, AssA 51.3, DetA 59.9, IDs 4117, Frag 4446; DanceTrack DiffusionTrack HOTA 52.4, MOTA 89.3, DetA 82.2, AssA 33.5, IDF1 47.5. Ablation default: prior information 50% MOTA 74.5, IDF1 71.2, HOTA 61.8, AssA 60.1; Cat Gaussian MOTA 73.6, IDF1 70.0, HOTA 60.7, AssA 58.4; logarithmic perturbation f(x) = log(x+1)/log2 MOTA 74.4, IDF1 72.0, HOTA 62.6, AssA 61.9; box sampling 800/1 MOTA 73.6, IDF1 70.0, HOTA 60.7, FLOPs(G) 367.3, FPS 15.89.
