data.paper_title: A NON-ASYMPTOTIC APPROACH TO STOCHASTIC DIFFERENTIAL GAMES WITH MANY PLAYERS UNDER SEMI-MONOTONICITY
data.authors: MARCO CIRANT(1), JOE JACKSON(2), AND DAVIDE FRANCESCO REDAELLI(3)
data.core_methodology: N-player stochastic differential games; closed-loop equilibria described by the Nash system (NS); open-loop equilibria described by the Pontryagin system (PS) and the decoupling PDE system (PSPDE); distributed equilibria described by the PDE system (1.6) and the FBSDE system (1.7); displacement semi-monotonicity and Lasry–Lions semi-monotonicity; weak interactions conditions (weak1) and (weak2); dimension-free bounds on solutions to systems of PDE/FBSDE; comparison of closed-loop, open-loop, and distributed equilibria; forward-backward propagation of chaos; universality of mean field game (MFG) equilibria; joint vanishing viscosity and large N limit; McKean–Vlasov FBSDE (6.1).

data.paper_title: AR-MOT: Autoregressive Multi-object Tracking
data.authors: Lianjie Jia∗, Yuhan Wu∗, Binghao Ran∗, Yifan Wang, Lijun Wang†, Huchuan Lu, Fellow, IEEE
data.core_methodology: AR-MOT formulates multi-object tracking as an autoregressive sequence generation task within a large language model (LLM) framework; it uses autoregressive modeling P(x1, x2, · · · , xn) = ∏_{t=1}^n P(xt|x1, x2, · · · , xt−1). The architecture consists of an MLLM of hidden dimension dLM with a vision encoder of hidden dimension dS, an Object Tokenizer equipped with an object detector of hidden dimension dD, and a token alignment module. The MLLM backbone is LLaVA-OneVision of the LLaVA-NeXT framework with a SigLIP image encoder at input resolution 384×384 and Qwen2 0.5B. The Object Tokenizer adopts Deformable DETR (D-DETR) with ResNet-50 backbone and an object adapter of MLPs. The Region-Aware Alignment (RAA) module projects bounding boxes from the Object Tokenizer onto the image tokenizer space, retrieves corresponding image tokens, computes their element-wise average along the channel dimension, and fuses them with original object tokens using a linear layer. The Temporal Memory Fusion (TMF) module, inspired by the Temporal Aggregation Network (TAN), uses multi-head attention (MHA) with fused inputs as queries (Q) and keys (K) and current frame embeddings as values (V). The Temporal Context Manager (TCM) stores the latest object token for each object and removes a trajectory when nloss > τloss. Training maximizes ∑_{j=1}^{Ni} logP(sIDj_i | spastj_i) with spastj_i = Concat({sFt}_{t=i−T}^{i−1}, sIi, {sEn_i, sIDn_i}_{n=0}^{j−1}, sEj_i), and total loss L = λclsLcls + λl1Ll1 + λgiouLgiou + λceLce.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Equations/variables: P(x1, x2, · · · , xn) = ∏_{t=1}^n P(xt|x1, x2, · · · , xt−1); maximize ∑_{j=1}^{Ni} logP(sIDj_i | spastj_i); spastj_i = Concat({sFt}_{t=i−T}^{i−1}, sIi, {sEn_i, sIDn_i}_{n=0}^{j−1}, sEj_i); L = λclsLcls + λl1Ll1 + λgiouLgiou + λceLce; H, W, C; P × P; Qj_i ∈ R^{1×dD}; Ej_i ∈ R^{1×dLM}; sIi ∈ R^{(HW/P^2)×dLM}; nloss > τloss. Hyperparameters: SigLIP input resolution 384×384; Qwen2 0.5B; ResNet-50; shorter side resized to 749; maximum size restricted to 1333; temporal gap uniformly selected from [0, L]; sliding window clip T+1 consecutive frames with 2 ≤ T+1 ≤ L; DanceTrack random sampling interval 1 to 10; clip length initialized as 2 frames and incrementally extended to 3, 4, and 5 frames; trained for 15 epochs; cosine annealing learning rate schedule; initial rate 6.0 × 10−5; AdamW optimizer; bfloat16 precision; confidence threshold τdet; α from 0.4 to 1.0. Final metrics: MOT17 AR-MOT(ours) MOTA 66.1, IDF1 60.7, HOTA 50.1. DanceTrack AR-MOT(ours) HOTA 48.1, DetA 77.2, MOTA 86.3, AssA 30.2, IDF1 43.9. Ablation: vanilla HOTA 19.32, DetA 29.89, MOTA 11.82, AssA 12.77, IDF1 22.36; W/ DETR HOTA 31.88, DetA 69.06, MOTA 75.41, AssA 14.94, IDF1 26.56; box HOTA 31.88, DetA 69.06, MOTA 75.41, AssA 14.94, IDF1 26.56; query HOTA 31.19, DetA 65.19, MOTA 69.47, AssA 15.17, IDF1 26.32; α=1.0 HOTA 37.09, DetA 71.64, MOTA 78.01, AssA 19.48, IDF1 31.67; MLLM+RAA+TMF HOTA 37.09, DetA 71.64, MOTA 78.01, AssA 19.48, IDF1 31.67; τloss=10 HOTA 42.18, DetA 70.61, MOTA 77.62, AssA 25.51, IDF1 37.62; τloss=15 HOTA 42.39, DetA 70.39, MOTA 77.57, AssA 25.88, IDF1 38.48; Transformer Decoder HOTA 15.17, DetA 44.28, MOTA 13.08, AssA 5.24, IDF1 12.36; Qwen2-0.5B HOTA 31.88, DetA 69.06, MOTA 75.41, AssA 14.94, IDF1 26.56; Qwen2-7B (lora) HOTA 29.36, DetA 69.70, MOTA 74.52, AssA 12.57, IDF1 24.01.

data.paper_title: CSP4SDG: Constraint and Information-Theory Based Role Identification in Social Deduction Games with LLM-Enhanced Inference
data.authors: Kaijie Xu1, Fandi Meng2, Clark Verbrugge1, Simon Lucas2
data.core_methodology: CSP4SDG, a training-free probabilistic constraint–satisfaction framework; an SDG-CSP model at time t is M_t=(P,R,C_t), with player set P, role set R, and accumulated constraint set C_t consisting of evidence (E), phenomenon (P), assertions (A), and hypotheses (H); four linguistically-agnostic constraint classes evidence, phenomena, assertions, hypotheses extracted by a lightweight LLM pipeline using gpt-4.1-mini and few-shot JSON constraint schemas; hard constraints E∪P prune infeasible assignments via AS_t={a | a|=E, a|=P} and AS_{t+1}={a∈AS_t | a|=c}; soft constraints scored by S(a)=(∏_{c∈A,a|=c} w_A)·(1+∑_{h∈H,a|=h} w_H(h)) with w_A≫1; posterior Pr(a|C_t)=S(a)/∑_{a′∈AS_t}S(a′); hypothesis weights w_H(h)=IG(h) using Information Gain IG(h)=H(prior)−H(posterior|h) and entropy H(X)=−∑_x Pr(x)log Pr(x); marginals and MAP assignment = arg max_{a∈AS_t}Pr(a|C_t); optional MCMC sampler for larger lobbies; CSP-only settings Strict, +Assert, +HypIG, +HypM, +TurnIG; LLM-only global/turn-based prompting; LLM+CSP augmentation with CSP posterior table and MAP assignment; perspective evidence rules for Merlin/Percival/evil views.

data.paper_title: Sea You Later: Metadata-Guided Long-Term Re-Identification for UAV-Based Multi-Object Tracking
data.authors: Cheng-Yen Yang, Hsiang-Wei Huang, Zhongyu Jiang, Heng-Cheng Kuo, Jie Mei, Chung-I Huang, Jenq-Neng Hwang
data.core_methodology: Metadata-Guided MOT (MG-MOT), a motion-based MOT algorithm that merges short-term tracking data into coherent long-term tracks using UAV metadata (GPS position, drone altitude, camera orientations). It constructs an estimated camera model using intrinsic matrix K from field-of-view, rotation matrix R(α, β, 0) from yaw and pitch, a 3D directional ray_i, and projection to world coordinates on the sea-surface plane z = 0. Re-identification uses Metadata-Guided Re-Identification with Short-Term ReID via Hungarian assignment on world coordinate distance with threshold τ_match, and Long-term Re-ID with Bi-directional Movement Extrapolation (BiME), Matching Threshold Expansion (MTE), and Class-wise Re-ID. Initial tracking uses BoT-SORT with sparse optical flow as Generalized Motion Compensation (GMC); detector uses YOLOv8-x with an additional p2 head, multi-class detector, pretrained on COCO, and an ensemble of detections. Post-processing uses linear interpolation and non-maximum suppression prioritizing larger bounding box areas. Evaluation uses HOTA and CLEAR MOT metrics.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Equations: K = [[w/2 tan (fov/2), 0, w/2], [0, w/2 tan (fov/2), h/2], [0, 0, 0]] (1); R(α, β, 0) = [[cos α cos β, −sin α, cos α sin β], [sin α cos β, cos α, sin α sin β], [−sin β, 0, cos β]] (2); α = 90° − gimbal heading; β = gimbal pitch; ray_i = R · K−1 · xi/||xi|| ∈ R3 (3); X3D_i = Loc_object = Loc_drone + (Z_drone / Z_ray_i) · ray_i (4); X3D_t = Hmt(X̂2D_t) (5); arg min Cdis(Ti, Tj) = ||X3D_texit_i − X3D_tentry_j||_2 (6); T^3D_i = X3D_texit_i + Δt · V^exit_Ti, if Δt < τ_memory (7); V^exit_Ti = (X3D_texit_i − X3D_texit_i−w) / w (8); Δt = t′ − t_exit; τ′_match = λ · (Δt_exit + Δt_entry) · τ_match (9); calibration: fov = 70 deg, image size 3840 × 2160; detector: YOLOv8-x, input size 1280, 100 epochs, initial learning rate 0.01, decay 0.05; tracking: high confidence 0.5, low confidence 0.1, new track confidence > 0.2, buffer 100 frames; final Ours (Team 198): HOTA 69.5%, MOTA 77.9%, IDF1 85.9%, MOTP 20.7%, MT 158, ML 22, FP 9700, FN 11425, Rec 88.1%, Pre 89.7%, IDs 18, Frag 784; dataset Table 1: Training 20 seq., 27,259 frames, 160,470 bboxes, longest 6,296; Validation 17 seq., 8,584 frames, 47,678 bboxes, longest 2,069; Testing 19 seq., 18,253 frames, -, longest 4,138; Total 21 seq., 54,096 frames, 207,938 bboxes, - longest.

data.paper_title: RULE-CONSTRAINED ASSIGNMENT FOR CUE-BALL IDENTIFICATION IN BROADCAST SNOOKER
data.authors: Yuxin Cao1, Wei Song2, Yuezhong Wu3, Jin Song Dong1
data.core_methodology: Rule-constrained assignment for cue-ball identification: construct a candidate pool by applying the same matched-filter detector to two complementary maps of the pre-shot frame (cloth-departure map and a second map with nonwhite regions suppressed), merging detections separated by less than one ball diameter; define rule-defined inventory S with one white slot, one red slot, and one slot for each of the six colors, with capacities b_r = 15 for the red slot and b_j = 1 for every other slot; solve the capacity-limited assignment L(C,S) = min over x in X of sum over i in C sum over j in S c_ij x_ij + ρ r(x) + sum over j in S µ_j m_j(x), where r(x) = |C| − sum over i,j x_ij and m_j(x) = b_j − sum over i x_ij, with reject cost ρ and miss costs µ_j (µ_r = 0); assignment costs c_ij contain color, spot, and isolation terms, with color term measuring weighted Lab distance to the corresponding class prototype computed over both the interior and the full extent retaining the larger value, spot term capped at four ball radii, and isolation term penalizing candidates whose surrounding region departs from the cloth as strongly as the candidate center; incremental-cost decision Δw(i) = c_iw + L(C minus {i}, S minus {w}) − L(C, S minus {w}) and select î = arg min over i in C Δw(i), breaking ties using the lower white-slot cost; the conventional appearance test is the one-slot case with only w retained, L(C,∅) = ρ|C|, and Δw(i) = c_iw − ρ, so Δw(i) ≤ 0 exactly when c_iw ≤ ρ; integrate into CueLift metric state-recovery system, which segments broadcast footage into shots, removes players from the playing surface, registers a three-dimensional regulation table model to the camera, initializes cue-ball tracking in image space, maps the tracked center into table coordinates using the geometric constraint that the center of a ball on the cloth lies one radius above the table surface; the one-slot appearance test uses the same white-appearance cost and a threshold selected on the training venues; the classical pipeline thresholds the cloth in HSV, maps the table to a regulation rectangle using a homography, detects connected components, and classifies them using fixed color thresholds.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: b_r = 15; b_j = 1 for every other slot; µ_r = 0; spot distance capped at four ball radii; reject cost ρ; miss cost µ_j; reject and miss costs and two geometric weights fixed according to the scales of their terms; isolation weight selected on the training venues; each optimization in (2) takes approximately 1 ms per frame; table registration localizes resting balls to 11.3 mm; benchmark: 7,501 shots, 248 matches, 21 venues, 343 videos, 541.0 h, 11 training and 10 held-out venues; class prototypes extracted from a rack frame for 121 of the 248 matches; reference detected automatically names the wrong object on 10.5% of hand-annotated shots; chromatic screen accepts 5,323 references, rejecting 25.5% on held-out venues and 4.4% on training venues; identity annotations: 419 shots, 150 shots sampled from 985, reannotation agrees on 29 of 30 shots; identity accuracy: all 419 appearance test 88.1%, our method 95.5%; held out 80.5% to 95.2%; newly covered 150: 38.0% to 76.7%; our method correct on 36 shots that the appearance test gets wrong, while the reverse occurs on five; exact McNemar test over 41 discordant pairs p = 7.8 × 10−7; on the 150 newly covered shots, the appearance test returns an identity on only 65 shots and is correct on 57; 80 discordant outcomes favor our method 69 to 11, p = 2.1 × 10−11; cue ball absent from candidate pool in 12 shots, limiting any method using this pool to 92.0%; end-to-end: 6,241 scorable shots coverage 36.2% to 55.4%; 3,054 held-out scorable shots coverage 38.9% to 59.4%; 5,323 shots with accepted references: 55.0% coverage, median error 22.1 mm, 93.5% conditional success within 200 mm; 2,275 held-out shots retained by the reference screen: 60.0% coverage, median error 24.8 mm, 92.3% conditional success within 200 mm; appearance-test baseline 41.4%, 22.6 mm, 96.7%; classical pipeline 87.9%, 71.2 mm, 76.2%; across 1,196 paired trajectories, our system has 41.7 mm lower error than the classical pipeline and is nearer on 81.4% of shots; admission threshold: 11 admission thresholds on the same 2,275 held-out shots; increasing threshold from training-selected value of 40 to 90 raises coverage from 41.4% to 50.9%, while conditional success remains between 95.8% and 96.9%; disabling admission raises coverage to 54.9% with 95.9% conditional success, compared with 60.0% and 92.3% for CueLift with the proposed assignment; forced answer: 2,529 moving-cue-ball shots defined by cue-ball travel of at least 100 mm; our system median error 23.2 mm with 89.0% of shots within 200 mm; appearance-test baseline 36.3 mm and 70.0%; classical pipeline 59.3 mm and 75.0%; pre-shot location alone gives an error within 200 mm on 7.3% of these shots; Fig. 2(c) Error > 500 mm (%): 7.8, 23.6, 17.3; sensitivity: 130 one-at-a-time configurations and 72 Latin hypercube samples; held-out coverage changes by at most 1.4% relative to its reported value, and pooled median error by at most 1.1%; tracking returns fewer than three observations on 2,429 of the 6,241 scorable shots.

data.paper_title: SMART: SMPLest-X Mesh Adaptation and RAFT Tracking for Soccer Pose Estimation
data.authors: Parthsarthi Rawat
data.core_methodology: Pipeline stages: (1) SMPLest-X recovers each player’s camera-space root-relative skeleton and absolute pelvis depth from their image crop; (2) RAFT-small propagates per-frame camera rotation Rt ∈SO(3) and translation tt ∈R3 from the provided (R0, t0); (3) skeleton and pelvis depth are combined with (Rt, tt) to place each player in the shared world coordinate system and anchor them to the pitch plane; (4) world trajectories and root-relative joints are independently smoothed. FIFA-15 skeleton: 15 joints comprising Nose, right/left Shoulder, Elbow, Wrist, Hip, Knee, Ankle, and Big Toe (indices 0–14); root joint is mid-hip: rt = 1/2(jt,7 + jt,8). 3D body mesh recovery uses SMPLest-X (ViT-H backbone, 687 M parameters) built on the SMPL-X body representation; bounding box expanded by 1.2×, then resized to 512 × 384 pixels via affine transform; SMPLest-X regresses SMPL-X parameters (shape β, pose θ, global orientation) and produces a full body mesh (V =10,475 vertices); FIFA-15 joints are read off this mesh via a fixed per-joint vertex lookup. Domain-adaptive fine-tuning via stratified clip-boundary split and multi-task loss Ltrain = λ1L3D + λ2L2D + λ3Ldepth, where L3D is weighted MPJPE (extremities at 3× weight), L2D is L2 on projected keypoints, and Ldepth is L1 on camera-space pelvis depth; broadcast augmentation: random resized cropping (scale ∈[0.75, 1.0], 80% probability), horizontal flipping (50%, with symmetric joint permutation), and colour jitter (±0.4 brightness/contrast/saturation, ±0.1 hue). Camera pose estimation replaces Lucas-Kanade sparse tracker with RAFT-small; per frame compute dense flow from It−1 to It and sample inside convex hull of the 714 projected pitch landmarks at stride 4, yielding ∼50× more correspondences; flow vectors contaminated by player motion removed via MAD outlier rejection (3σ threshold); fit inter-frame homography via RANSAC and decompose to (Rt, tt); updates with |∆R| > 60◦ rejected; when field line intersections are detected via Hough transform, an EPnP (Efficient Perspective-n-Point) solve further corrects absolute camera position on the first frame. World-space skeleton placement: root-relative skeleton rotated as \hat S_t = R_t S(cam)_t; camera-space pelvis translation p(cam)_t projected as p_t = R_t p(cam)_t + t_t; foot-plane anchoring back-projects lowest foot pixel using Kt and intersects known pitch-plane equation yielding ground contact point ft; joints translated as J_t,j = \hat S_{t,j} − \hat S_{t,ankle} + f_t; reprojection refinement via two-stage L-BFGS optimisation (50 steps translating skeleton centroid onto bounding-box centre, then 50 steps aligning projected joints with 2D keypoints). Temporal smoothing: first pass global root trajectories cleaned via MAD outlier detection, linear interpolation, Gaussian filter; second pass root-relative joint offsets smoothed independently with narrower Gaussian, world centroid frozen. Fine-tuning: only SMPLest-X decoder and prediction heads trainable; ViT-H backbone frozen; training 15 epochs, batch size 16, Adam, LR 2×10−6, AMP mixed precision, 1× 24 GB A10G GPU; loss weights λ1=1.0, λ2=0.1, λ3=0.5; per-joint weights 3.0 for wrists (5,6), ankles (11,12), big toes (13,14), and 1.0 otherwise. Camera tracking: RAFT-small default pretrained weights; stride-4 dense flow inside 714-landmark convex hull; MAD 3σ outlier rejection; RANSAC homography (2000 iter, 1 px threshold); |∆R|>60◦ rejection. Smoothing: Global MAD (5×) + linear interp + Gaussian (σ=3 fr), clamp at 0.35 m/fr; Local joints independent Gaussian (σ=1.5 fr). Ablations/comparisons: SAM-3D-Body as 3D lifter; learned Placement MLP predicting absolute hip position from camera geometry and foot-ray features; ECC homography; Lucas-Kanade sparse tracking; RAFT-large + MAD; sliding-window temporal refinement network (27-frame window, hidden dim 128). Competition score L = Global MPJPE + 5 × Local MPJPE.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Global MPJPE; Local MPJPE; competition score L = Global MPJPE + 5 × Local MPJPE; root joint rt = 1/2(jt,7 + jt,8); FIFA-15 skeleton indices 0–14; T frames and N tracked players; 20 sequences at 50 fps and 1920×1080 resolution (6 validation, 14 test); per-frame camera intrinsics Kt, radial distortion coefficients kt, initial camera pose (R0, t0); baseline uses Lucas-Kanade sparse optical flow on 714 pre-annotated 3D pitch landmarks; WorldPose 89 clips stratified split: 70 training and 19 validation clips; SMPLest-X ViT-H, 687 M parameters; bounding-box expansion 1.2×; crop resized to 512 × 384 pixels; V =10,475 vertices; Ltrain = λ1L3D + λ2L2D + λ3Ldepth; λ1=1.0, λ2=0.1, λ3=0.5; L3D weighted MPJPE extremities at 3× weight; per-joint weights 3.0 for wrists (5,6), ankles (11,12), big toes (13,14), and 1.0 otherwise; random resized cropping scale ∈[0.75, 1.0], 80% probability; horizontal flipping 50%; colour jitter ±0.4 brightness/contrast/saturation, ±0.1 hue; RAFT flow sampled at stride 4 inside 714-landmark convex hull, ∼50× more correspondences; MAD outlier rejection (3σ threshold); |∆R| > 60◦ rejection; L-BFGS 50 steps then 50 steps; training 15 epochs, batch size 16, Adam, LR 2×10−6, AMP mixed precision, 1× 24 GB A10G GPU; Global smoothing MAD (5×) + linear interp + Gaussian (σ=3 fr), clamp at 0.35 m/fr; data.paper_title: Multiple-target tracking in human and machine vision
data.authors: Shiva Kamkar, Fatemeh Ghezloo, Hamid Abrishami Moghaddam, Ali Borji, Reza Lashgari
data.core_methodology: Review and comparative synthesis of multiple-target tracking (MTT) studies in neuroscience and biologically inspired MTT methods in computer vision. Neuroscience methods reviewed include psychophysical experiments with multiple-object tracking (MOT) and multiple-identity tracking (MIT), behavioral data analysis, eye-tracking, and functional MRI [fMRI]. Computer-vision methods reviewed are categorized as attention-based MTT methods, memory-based MTT methods, and MTT methods based on ANNs, including center-surround mechanism, Kullback–Leibler divergence, normalized cross-correlation (NCC), dynamic CNNs, recurrent neural network (RNN), LSTM (Long–Short-Term Memory), deep reinforcement learning (DRL), particle-filter algorithm, convolutional restricted Boltzmann machine, Atkinson–Shiffrin memory model (ASMM), MUlti-Store Tracker, forward-backward tracker, and CLEAR MOT metrics.

data.authors: Yassine Benzakour, Bruno Cabado, Silvio Giancola, Anthony Cioppa, Bernard Ghanem, Marc Van Droogenbroeck
data.core_methodology: OSL-ActionSpotting is a Python library that unifies action spotting algorithms via backbone, neck, and head components: action spotting is defined as F : V → A × T; F = Backbone(i1, i2, ..., iT); F′ = Neck(F); (A, T) = Head(F′). Integrated algorithms: Temporally-Aware Learnable Pooling [33], Context-Aware Loss Function (CALF) [36], and Precise Temporal Spotting (PTS) [42]. Temporally-Aware Learnable Pooling uses pre-extracted CNN features, learnable and temporal pooling based on feature clustering (e.g. NetVLAD), and linear layers; CALF uses pre-extracted deep CNN features, a segmentation module as neck, and a spotting module for regression of action candidates; PTS learns spatio-temporal features end-to-end with RegNetY and GSM or TSM, no neck, and a recurrent spotting head (e.g. GRU) for frame classification. Data handling uses feature-based and video-based data loaders, OpenCV video reader and NVIDIA DALI (Data Loading Library), a unified action spotting dataset format in a single JSON file inspired by the COCO format, and PyTorch Lightning for training, inference, and evaluation. Evaluation uses loose average mean Average Precision (mAP) and tight average mAP.

data.paper_title: Widely Applicable Strong Baseline for Sports Ball Detection and Tracking
data.authors: Shuhei Tarashima, Muhammad Abdul Haq, Yushan Wang, Norio Tagawa
data.core_methodology: Proposed Widely Applicable Strong Baseline (WASB) for Sports Ball Detection and Tracking (SBDT), composed of (1) high-resolution feature extraction, (2) position-aware model training, and (3) inference considering temporal consistency. High-resolution feature extraction uses HRNet and High-Resolution Modules (HRMs) following the small HRNet design: 4 stages, each stage has parallel sequences of residual blocks followed by a multi-resolution fusion; stem strides are removed to feed higher-spatial-resolution tensors. A MIMO design concatenates N consecutive frames along the channel dimension into an H × W × 3N tensor and generates N heatmaps of spatial resolution H × W (H × W × N). Position-aware training uses a binary GT map (Eq. 1), a real-valued GT map (Eq. 2), a quality focal loss (Eq. 3), and Hard-to-Localize Sample Mining (HLSM). Inference uses Ball Position as a Center of Heatmap (CoH), Online Tracking with a local motion model (Eq. 4), and Oversampling. Compared/re-implemented SBDT methods: DeepBall, DeepBall-Large, BallSeg, TrackNetV2, ResTrackNetV2, MonoTrack. Training uses the Adam optimizer.
data.key_metrics_and_variables: Metrics: F1, Accuracy (Acc.), Average Precision (AP), FPS, #param.; distance threshold τ = 4 [pixel] for F1, Acc., and AP (shown as percentages). Eq. 1: ybin_p = 1 if ∥p−pGT∥≤d, 0 otherwise, where ybin_p is the value of the GT map at location p ∈ R2 and d is a distance threshold set differently between methods. Eq. 2: yreal_p = min(C·exp(−∥p−pGT∥2/d2), 1) if ∥p−pGT∥≤d, 0 otherwise, where yreal_p is the value of the real-valued GT map at p, while C is determined so that the non-zero minimum value is set to a pre-defined value cmin. Eq. 3: L = ∑_p [ −|yp −σp|βn (1−yp)log(1−σp)+yp logσp ]; σp is the sigmoid output of the model prediction at p and β is a parameter to control the down-weighting rate; Eq. 3 is equivalent to the focal loss if GT is binary. Eq. 4: ˆpt+1 = pt + vt + at/2, vt = pt − pt−1 + at, at = pt − 2pt−1 + pt−2. Implementation/training parameters: N = 3; image resized to 288×512; Adam optimizer; 30 epochs; batch size = 8 for both training and testing; d = 2.5; cmin = 0.7; HLSM run at the beginning of epoch 20; heatmap binarization threshold 0.5; step size 3 (i.e., no oversampling) and 1; 4 V100 GPUs. WASB benchmark: #param. 1.5M; AP improvement over best existing methods by 7.8 ~16.8 %; processed over 30 FPS on 4 out of 5 datasets; TrackNetV2 implementation on Badminton accuracy 85.6 vs original implementation 85.2. Dataset calibration figures: Volleyball 3.7% (178 / 4,830) of video clips contain no ball; Basketball manually annotated 45% (81/181 games), resulting in 275,328 annotated images composed of 3,824 video clips.

data.paper_title: Spatial Refinement for 3D Human Mesh Recovery in Ice Hockey Broadcast Videos
data.authors: Zhibo Wang, Sirisha Rambhatla, Yuhao Chen, David Clausi
data.core_methodology: Spatial refinement strategies within the HMR pipeline: reduce vertical drift by estimating a temporally consistent ground plane and correcting each reconstructed mesh’s Z-axis trajectory; project players onto a standardized top-down rink template via homography estimation; integrated into the GVHMR framework with a hockey-specific tracking model. Baseline GVHMR is built upon HMR 2.0 and incorporates a gravity-based coordinate refinement module. Replace the original generic object tracker with a hockey-specific off-the-shelf tracking model [18]. ViT-based backbone predicts SMPL parameters, including pose θ, body shape β, and camera translation π. Z-axis refinement: compute minimal vertex height zmin as an approximate foot–ground contact indicator; for each contact frame t, sample foot-surface points and form tuples (x, y, t, z); fit a plane z = ax + by + ct + d using a RANSAC-regularized linear regressor over overlapping temporal windows of sizes {L, 2L} (with L = 15); each window produces a local estimate ˆzt, and the final ground height is obtained via a kernel-weighted average zt = P wtˆzt / P wt, wt = exp(−|t −tc|/τ), where tc is the window midpoint and τ = L/2; refined root height Δzt = zt −zmin. X–Y axis projection: project the reconstructed human mesh back onto the broadcast frame; extract the mesh vertices corresponding to each player’s left and right feet; connect the two foot points, whose midpoint provides a stable approximation of the player’s current position on the image plane; use the homography matrix predicted by the off-the-shelf model [20] to map the player’s image-plane position onto the standardized rink template according to [x, y, 1]⊤= H [x′, y′, 1]⊤, where (x′, y′) denotes the player’s position in the broadcast frame, (x, y) denotes the corresponding position on the rink template, and H is the estimated 3 × 3 homography matrix.

data.paper_title: Dynamic sports environments: automatic feature players tracking and re-identification with similar appearances
data.authors: Adil Abdulhur Abushana, Riyadh Alsaeedi
data.core_methodology: Proposed framework integrates deep player re-identification (DPRI), individual probabilistic overlapping bounding box occupancy mapping (IPOM) for robust spatial localization under severe overlap, and identity-aware k-shortest path optimization algorithm (KSP-ID) for improved trajectory association. DPRI combines pose-based embeddings, jersey appearance cues, and facial features to generate discriminative identity representations. Training uses an image-centric sampling strategy with stochastic gradient descent (SGD), a pre-trained residual network 50 layers (ResNet-50) backbone, random initialization with a Gaussian distribution, and loss L= λ1L_face+ λ2L_jers. Robust segmentation uses a median background model B = median(F), absolute difference Dn=∣Fn−B∣, grayscale conversion Gn = cvtColor(Dn,COLOR_BGR2GRAY), binary thresholding, morphological opening On = morphologyEx(Tn, MORPH_OPEN, K), contour finding, candidate filtering, and color-based region merging. Multi-object tracking uses nearest-neighbor assignment considering blob size, spatial relationships, and reliable feature descriptors. Color texture extraction uses color–texture features from RGB face images, histogram-based features, color vector difference patterns with a circular neighborhood of radius R and P pixels, and HSV. Face and jersey finder uses a hierarchical top-down parsing tree, kernelized correlation filters, and multiple instance learning. KSP-ID uses appearance similarity S_a(d_k,t_j), motion similarity S_m(d_k,t_j) derived from predicted position t̂_j, proximity similarity S_p(d_k,t_j), total similarity S(d_k,t_j)=ω_a·S_a(d_k,t_j)+ω_m·S_m(d_k,t_j)+ω_p·S_p(d_k,t_j), cost matrix C_kj=1−S(d_k,t_j), the Hungarian algorithm, track-state transitions Lost/Occluded with thresholds T_lost and T_occluded, and a re-identification mechanism using appearance models and probabilistic data association. Knowledge distillation distills a ResNet-50 teacher network into a faster ResNet-18 student network, both enhanced with an FPN, trained on unlabeled SoccerNet broadcast videos. Segmentation comparison includes baseline CNN models, Faster R-CNN, HOG algorithm, and SIFT descriptor.

data.core_methodology: The S team implements a modiﬁed version of the simplex optimization algorithm (Algorithm 1, Modiﬁed simplex) for a scalar field f(x): ℜ2 →ℜ; the implementation uses a leader pattern and a competition for leadership pattern. Coordination and control are formulated in the setting of dynamic optimization using controlled invariance, value functions, set-valued operations, set-valued maps h and J, the distance function dA(B), and graph-connectedness constraints (T and K). Intra-team and inter-team invariance problems are Problem 4.1 and Problem 4.2.
